Chapter9/Proposition9.1.1.title: Existence and uniqueness mean different things
explanation: The first statement lifts any idempotent through the quotient by a nilpotent two-sided ideal. It works over an arbitrary ring; finite dimensionality and an algebraically closed field are unnecessary here.
The second compares two lifts with the same quotient image. It produces a unit u with u − 1 ∈ I and u e₁ u⁻¹ = e₂. Thus uniqueness is up to conjugation, not equality of lifts.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Ideal.Quotient.exists_idempotent_lift_of_is_nilpotent
declarations.label: An idempotent lifts through a nilpotent ideal

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Ideal.Quotient.exists_unit_sub_one_mem_ideal_conj_idempotent_eq_of_quotient_eq
declarations.label: Two lifts are conjugate by a unit in 1 + I

Chapter9/Definition9.1.2.title: Orthogonality includes the sum condition
explanation: This predicate is Mathlib’s CompleteOrthogonalIdempotents for a finite indexed family: every element is idempotent, distinct elements multiply to zero, and their sum is 1. It is not merely pairwise orthogonality.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.FiniteIndexedRingFunctionPredicate.isFiniteIndexedRingFunctionAuxiliary
declarations.label: Complete orthogonal idempotents

Chapter9/Corollary9.1.3.title: Lift the whole family together
explanation: The conclusion supplies a family in A that is still complete and orthogonal, together with equality of each quotient image to the prescribed idempotent. Lifting the elements separately would not establish these simultaneous conditions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Ideal.IdempotentLifting.exists_completeOrthogonalIdempotents_lift_of_isNilpotent
declarations.label: A complete orthogonal family lifts through a nilpotent ideal

Chapter9/Theorem9.2.1.title: Choose one projective for each simple module
explanation: The checked existence theorem assumes a finite-dimensional algebra over an algebraically closed field and a finite, exhaustive family of pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules Mᵢ. It supplies indecomposable finitely generated projectives Pᵢ with Hom dimensions δᵢⱼ.
Uniqueness means uniqueness up to an A-linear isomorphism. The indecomposability predicate in the expanded statement says that P is nonzero and has no decomposition into two nonzero summands.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Artinian.ModuleIdempotents.Auxiliary.statement016753
declarations.label: Existence and uniqueness of the projectives Pᵢ

Chapter9/Theorem9.2.1.title: The regular module remembers the dimensions of the simples
explanation: The second statement is an A-linear isomorphism between A and the direct sum with dimₖ Mᵢ copies of Pᵢ. Lean writes the copies as functions Fin(dimₖ Mᵢ) → Pᵢ; this finite product is also a direct sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Artinian.ModuleIdempotents.regularModule_linearEquiv_directSum
declarations.label: A ≅ ⊕ᵢ (dimₖ Mᵢ) Pᵢ

Chapter9/Theorem9.2.1.title: There are no other indecomposable projectives
explanation: For any indecomposable finitely generated projective Q, the classification produces an index i and an A-linear isomorphism Q ≅ Pᵢ. The chosen simple family and its Hom-dimension condition remain hypotheses, rather than being inferred from arbitrary modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Artinian.ModuleIdempotents.exists_linearEquiv_projective_family
declarations.label: Every indecomposable finitely generated projective is a Pᵢ

Chapter9/Definition9.2.2.title: A cover includes its quotient map
explanation: The checked record packages an indecomposable projective module P, a surjection P → M, and a superfluous kernel: if a submodule N together with the kernel spans P, then N already equals P.

This is the cover data used for the simple modules here. The record also requires indecomposability, so it should not be read as the definition of every projective cover of an arbitrary decomposable module.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingModuleAuxiliary.Auxiliary
declarations.label: An indecomposable projective cover with a superfluous kernel

Chapter9/Proposition9.2.3.title: Count factors by applying exact Hom
explanation: The composition-series invariant counts those successive simple quotients isomorphic to Mᵢ. With the projective family and the Hom-dimension condition from Theorem 9.2.1, the theorem equates this count to dimₖ Homₐ(Pᵢ, N).
The series must start at 0 and end at N. The simple family must cover all factors of N; the count is not attached to an arbitrary partial filtration.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.CompositionSeries.CompositionSeries.moduleNatInvariant_eq_finrank_hom
declarations.label: Hom dimension equals the Jordan–Hölder multiplicity

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.CompositionSeries.CompositionSeries.moduleNatInvariant
declarations.label: Multiplicity in a composition series

Chapter9/Definition9.3.1.title: Rows index the simple factors; columns index the projectives
explanation: The matrix definition takes Cᵢⱼ = dimₖ Homₐ(Pᵢ, Pⱼ). By Proposition 9.2.3 this is the multiplicity of Mᵢ in Pⱼ, so exchanging the two indices would transpose the book’s convention.

Entries are natural numbers. A nonzero finite-dimensional Pᵢ has a nonzero identity endomorphism, giving the positive diagonal. The raw matrix construction works for other module families too; it is a Cartan matrix here because these Pᵢ are the projective covers.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleFamilyNatMatrix.ModuleFamilyNatMatrix.matrix
declarations.label: The matrix of Hom dimensions

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleFamilyNatMatrix.ModuleFamilyNatMatrix.matrix_diagonal_pos
declarations.label: Each diagonal entry is positive

Chapter9/Problem9.3.2.title: Two simple modules and two projective covers
explanation: The algebra is the quotient of the free complex algebra on g and x by the three displayed relations. Its two simple modules have g acting by +1 or −1 and x acting by zero.

The source constructs the two corresponding projective covers and classifies every finite-dimensional indecomposable projective as one of them. It then computes all four Hom dimensions: the Cartan matrix is ((1, 1), (1, 1)), not the identity matrix.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InvolutiveSquareZeroAlgebra.simpleModule_equiv_positive_xor_negative
declarations.label: Every simple module is exactly one of the two signed simples

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InvolutiveSquareZeroAlgebra.finiteProjective_equiv_positive_or_negativeProjective
declarations.label: The two indecomposable projective modules

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InvolutiveSquareZeroAlgebra.projectiveFamilyMatrix_eq_ones
declarations.label: The Cartan matrix has all four entries equal to 1

Chapter9/Definition9.4.1.title: Infinity and the zero module
explanation: The book-facing dimension takes values in the extended natural numbers, with ⊤ meaning infinity. It normalizes the zero module’s dimension to 0; the underlying categorical dimension instead has a separate bottom value for a zero object.
The bound theorem identifies pd(M) ≤ d with the categorical projective-dimension bound. In particular, pd(M) = 0 is equivalent to projectivity, including M = 0.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ProjectiveDimension.projectiveDimension
declarations.label: Projective dimension with the book’s zero convention

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ProjectiveDimension.projectiveDimension_le_iff
declarations.label: A numerical bound is the categorical dimension bound

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ProjectiveDimension.projectiveDimension_eq_zero_iff_projective
declarations.label: Dimension zero ⇔ projectivity

Chapter9/Problem9.4.2.title: Vanishing means that every higher Ext group is zero
explanation: For every coefficient module N and every i > d, the checked criterion requires Extⁱ(M, N) to be a subsingleton. Since Ext is an additive group, this says it is the zero group.
The equivalence works for arbitrary modules over a ring, not only finite-dimensional modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveDimension.hasProjectiveDimensionLE_iff_ext_subsingleton
declarations.label: pd(M) ≤ d ⇔ all higher Ext groups vanish

Chapter9/Problem9.4.2.title: A nonsplit sequence shifts dimension by one
explanation: The checked short exact sequence has M at the left, the projective P in the middle and N at the right. IsEmpty S.Splitting expresses the nonsplitting hypothesis.
The conclusion is pd(N) = pd(M) + 1 in extended natural numbers. It allows infinite dimension; it does not silently assume the two endpoint dimensions are finite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveDimension.right_endpoint_value_eq_left_endpoint_value_add_one_of_shortExact_of_projective_middle_of_no_splitting
declarations.label: The dimension shift across a nonsplit sequence

Chapter9/Problem9.4.2.title: Truncate at the projective syzygy
explanation: The stage object is M in degree 0 and the successive kernel in each higher degree. If pd(M) ≤ d, the dth stage is projective in any projective resolution. This is the kernel K_d at which the book truncates.

For a finite-dimensional algebra and module, the second statement supplies a resolution with finite-dimensional terms and a finite-dimensional projective dth stage. The supplied resolution itself may continue indefinitely; its short exact stage sequences justify replacing the tail by that stage to obtain length d.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveDimension.projectiveResolution_structure_of_hasProjectiveDimensionLE
declarations.label: The dth syzygy is projective, with exact stage sequences

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveDimension.exists_finite_projectiveResolution_of_hasProjectiveDimensionLE
declarations.label: Finite-dimensional terms and a projective dth syzygy

Chapter9/Definition9.4.3.title: A bound must hold for every module
explanation: The left global-dimension bound quantifies over all left A-modules. The numerical invariant is the least such natural-number bound, and is ∞ when no finite bound exists.
Right modules are encoded as left modules over Aᵐᵒᵖ. The right invariant therefore applies the same definition to the opposite ring; no equality of left and right global dimensions is assumed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.RingData.auxiliaryRingNatProperty
declarations.label: Every left module has dimension at most d

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.RingData.auxiliaryRingENatInvariant
declarations.label: Left global dimension

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.RingData.auxiliaryRingENatInvariantThird
declarations.label: Right global dimension

Chapter9/Example9.4.4.title: The number of variables is the exact dimension
explanation: The checked equality is for MvPolynomial (Fin n) k, the polynomial algebra on n commuting variables over any field. It includes both the upper bound and the matching lower bound, not merely the existence of resolutions of length at most n.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.RingAndCategoryProperties.Auxiliary.mvPolynomial_value_eq_natCast
declarations.label: The global dimension of k[x₁, …, xₙ] is n

Chapter9/Problem9.4.5.title: Finite resolutions give an integral inverse
explanation: The proof represents each simple module’s class as an alternating integer combination of the projectives in a finite resolution. These vectors form a right inverse for the integer-valued Cartan matrix.
The conclusion is det(C) = 1 or det(C) = −1. It does not claim the stronger sign +1. The theorem takes an exhaustive, nonrepeating simple family and projectives with Hom dimensions δᵢⱼ as hypotheses.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.Module.Projective.Auxiliary.statement013909
declarations.label: Finite global dimension forces det(C) = ±1

Chapter9/Problem9.4.5.title: Both examples have infinite global dimension
explanation: For k[t]/(tⁿ), the theorem assumes n > 1 and works over any field. The second equality concerns the complex algebra from Problem 9.3.2.
Each result is an equality to ⊤, the infinity value of global dimension; it is not just a lower bound or a claim that one chosen resolution is infinite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.Module.Projective.quotientPolynomialXPower_value_eq_top
declarations.label: k[t]/(tⁿ) has infinite global dimension for n > 1

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.Module.Projective.designatedRing_value_eq_top
declarations.label: The involutive square-zero algebra has infinite global dimension

Chapter9/Problem9.4.6.title: Paths give a length-one resolution
explanation: The checked path-algebra theorem assumes finitely many vertices and at least one arrow. Arrows need not form a finite set for this dimension result. The free-algebra specialization proves dimension 1 for n ≥ 1 generators.
The printed question says “any quiver”; the checked theorem does not cover an arbitrary infinite vertex set.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.LoopQuiver.quiverAssociatedAlgebra_associatedValue_eq_one_of_exists_arrow
declarations.label: A finite-vertex quiver with an arrow has global dimension 1

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.LoopQuiver.freeAlgebra_associatedValue_eq_one
declarations.label: A free algebra on n ≥ 1 generators has global dimension 1

Chapter9/Problem9.4.6.title: Count paths, with an explicit comparison hypothesis
explanation: For a finite acyclic quiver, the matrix on the right counts paths from i to j, including the trivial path when i = j.

The checked comparison assumes a module family P together with isomorphisms Hom(Pᵢ, Pⱼ) ≅ k-valued finitely supported functions on those paths. It then identifies its Hom matrix with the path-count matrix. This statement alone does not construct the canonical projective covers or prove those assumed identifications.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.LoopQuiver.associatedMatrix_eq_quiverNatMatrix_of_pathIndexedLinearEquiv
declarations.label: Hom dimensions equal path counts, given the Hom identifications

Chapter9/Definition9.5.1.title: Linking is the equivalence relation generated by extensions
explanation: The relation starts with simple modules joined by a nonzero Ext¹ in either direction, and closes under reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. It also identifies isomorphic simple modules, so the quotient gives classes of simple isomorphism types.
Nontrivial Ext means that the extension group has a nonzero element, not merely that an extension—including the split one—exists.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleCat.Auxiliary.auxiliaryModuleRelation
declarations.label: Simple modules linked by chains of extensions

Chapter9/Definition9.5.1.title: A block is determined by all composition factors
explanation: The block predicate says that every simple subquotient of M is linked to a chosen simple S. On the finite-length modules in this chapter, these are the simple types appearing in a composition series.
The quotient type indexes blocks. Its elements are classes of simple modules, not extra module structures attached to M.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleCat.Auxiliary.auxiliaryModuleRelation''''
declarations.label: Every simple factor of M belongs to the block of S

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleCat.Auxiliary.AuxiliaryModuleType
declarations.label: The set of block indices

Chapter9/Example9.5.2.title: Three ways the linking relation simplifies
explanation: For a semisimple ring, two simple modules are linked exactly when they are isomorphic. For a commutative local Artinian ring, all simple modules are linked. For the complex algebra of Problem 9.3.2, the two signed simples are linked and every simple belongs to that one class.
These statements check the linking claims. The displayed semisimple result does not itself construct the equivalence of each block with finite-dimensional vector spaces.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.SimpleModuleRelations.auxiliary_relation_iff_nonemptyIso_of_simpleModules
declarations.label: Semisimple blocks separate the simple isomorphism types

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.SimpleModuleRelations.auxiliary_relation_of_simpleModules_of_localArtinian
declarations.label: A commutative local Artinian ring has one simple block

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.SimpleModuleRelations.auxiliary_relation_of_simpleModules
declarations.label: The two-signed-simple algebra has one block

Chapter9/Problem9.5.3.title: Central idempotents select the blocks
explanation: The first statement gives a bijection between block indices and nonzero central idempotents that cannot be split into two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

For the corresponding idempotent e, the module-category equivalence uses A/{a : e a = 0}. This quotient represents the central summand eA with unit e. Its finite-length restriction gives the block of finite-dimensional modules in the present finite-dimensional setting.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleTheory.SimpleModule.PropertyElementActions.nonempty_equiv_property_subtype
declarations.label: Blocks correspond to primitive central idempotents

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.Module.ParameterAssociated.finiteLengthParameterEquivalence
declarations.label: The finite-length block is a module category over the central summand

Chapter9/Problem9.5.3.title: Indecomposables cannot straddle distinct blocks
explanation: The existence theorem assumes that M is indecomposable and of finite length, and finds a simple S whose block contains every composition factor of M.

The second theorem makes Hom(M, N) a subsingleton when their simple factors belong to different linking classes. Thus every map is zero. Together with decomposition into indecomposables, these are the ingredients for the book’s direct-sum decomposition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Category.ModuleCat.RingElementActions.exists_simpleModule_with_condition_of_indecomposable
declarations.label: Every finite-length indecomposable lies in one block

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Category.ModuleCat.RingElementActions.hom_subsingleton_of_simpleModule_conditions
declarations.label: There are no nonzero maps between distinct blocks

Chapter9/Problem9.5.3.title: Two blocks for S₃ in characteristic two
explanation: Over any field of characteristic 2, the checked decomposition is k[S₃] ≅ Mat₂(k) × D, where D is the two-dimensional dual-number algebra. The matrix factor gives the two-dimensional simple representation; the dual-number factor gives the trivial simple and is not semisimple.
The separate block-count theorem confirms two linking classes. This is not the characteristic-zero decomposition of the group algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationRepresentation.CharTwo.nonempty_algEquiv_matrix_prod_auxiliaryAlgebra
declarations.label: k[S₃] is a matrix algebra times the dual-number algebra

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationRepresentation.CharTwo.associatedType_card_eq_two
declarations.label: There are exactly two blocks

Chapter9/Definition9.6.1.title: Finite means finite length and finitely many simple types
explanation: The categorical class stores an abelian category with enough projectives, a finite family covering its simple objects up to isomorphism, and a finite-length condition on each subobject lattice.
It does not say that there are finitely many objects or morphisms. The k-linear structure and End(L) ≅ k for simple L are separate hypotheses in the module-equivalence theorem.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.SubobjectFiniteDimensional.SubobjectFiniteDimensional
declarations.label: Finite-length abelian categories with finitely many simples and enough projectives

Chapter9/Definition9.6.2.title: Finite sums here; arbitrary sums in the general module category
explanation: The general predicate is “projective and a separator”: maps out of P detect distinct morphisms. When the required coproducts exist, this gives the usual epimorphism from a coproduct of copies of P.

In the finite-length setting, the second class supplies a finite direct sum of copies of P mapping epimorphically onto every object. This is the form used below. The free module A generates all A-modules using possibly infinite sums; that example should not be confused with finite generation of every module.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveEpiProperties.IsProjectiveEpiSigmaDesc
declarations.label: A projective separator

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveEpiProperties.HasProjectiveEpiWitnesses
declarations.label: Every object is a quotient of a finite sum of P

Chapter9/Exercise9.6.3.title: The criterion assumes P is already projective
explanation: The checked equivalence has an explicit Projective P hypothesis. Under that hypothesis, a nonzero map P → L for every simple L is equivalent to the finite-quotient generator property.

The printed sentence omits this qualification: nonzero maps to all simples alone do not establish projectivity. The existence statement constructs a projective generator by taking a finite sum of projective objects surjecting onto representatives of the simples.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Projective.Auxiliary.nonempty_auxiliary_iff_forall_simple_exists_ne_zero
declarations.label: A projective object generates iff it maps nontrivially to every simple

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Projective.Auxiliary.exists_object_with_nonempty_auxiliary
declarations.label: Every finite abelian category has a projective generator

Chapter9/Theorem9.6.4.title: Hom(P, −) takes values in finite modules
explanation: The functor sends M to Hom(P, M), a left module over End(P)ᵐᵒᵖ by precomposition. The opposite ring accounts for the order of composition; the action is not postcomposition on M.

The checked target is FGModuleCat, the finitely generated modules, not the category of all modules. End(P) is finite-dimensional under the finite-length, k-linear and scalar-endomorphism hypotheses, so these modules are also finite-dimensional over k.

The categorical equivalence is proved with those hypotheses and the finite-sum generator data. The phrase “category of modules” in the theorem’s last sentence is read in the finite-dimensional context immediately above it.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Preadditive.FGModuleEquivalence.fgModuleFunctor_isEquivalence
declarations.label: Hom(P, −) is an equivalence with finitely generated modules

Chapter9/Problem9.6.5.title: Balanced tensor products are cokernels in the category
explanation: An arbitrary abelian category need not have a tensor product of two objects. Here P ⊗ V means the finite copower of P by a finite-dimensional k-vector space V.

The relation map subtracts the two actions: on a generator b ⊗ x it gives the endomorphism b acting on the P-copy indexed by x, minus the P-copy indexed by b x. Its cokernel is the balanced object P ⊗ᴮ X used by G.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.modulePresentationRelation
declarations.label: The balancing relation p b ⊗ x − p ⊗ b x

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.modulePresentationObject
declarations.label: The balanced tensor object is the cokernel

Chapter9/Problem9.6.5.title: A natural isomorphism, not just matching dimensions
explanation: The first comparison is a natural isomorphism F(G(X)) ≅ X. In Lean, G ⋙ F means apply G first, then F; this is the book’s F ∘ G.

The exposed construction uses the full finite-category and projective-generator hypotheses from the section. It is not a separate formal verification of the parenthetical claim that only a nonzero projective object is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.presentationThenModuleIso
declarations.label: F ∘ G is naturally isomorphic to the identity

Chapter9/Problem9.6.5.title: Evaluation gives the map back to X
explanation: The natural map evaluates a homomorphism P → X on its P-input. It descends through the balancing relation, and the generator property makes every component epimorphic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.moduleThenPresentationHom
declarations.label: The natural evaluation G ∘ F → Id

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.moduleThenPresentationHom_app_epi
declarations.label: Evaluation is epimorphic

Chapter9/Problem9.6.5.title: Detect the zero kernel with the generator
explanation: Applying F to evaluation gives an isomorphism by the first comparison. The proof then uses P as a separator to show that the kernel is a zero object. An epimorphism with zero kernel is an isomorphism.
The final equivalence packages both functors and both natural comparisons, rather than asserting only that corresponding objects happen to be isomorphic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.kernel_presentationEvaluation_isZero
declarations.label: The evaluation kernel is zero

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Linear.FiniteModulePresentationEquivalence.finiteModuleEquivalence
declarations.label: The functors F and G form an equivalence

Chapter9/Definition9.7.1.title: Equivalent module categories, not isomorphic algebras
explanation: The first predicate records an equivalence of finitely generated module categories. For the finite-dimensional algebras in this section, these are the categories A-fmod and B-fmod.

The second explicitly requires that the equivalence respect k-linear maps. The source also has predicates for categories of all modules; those are different interfaces and are not substituted for the book’s finite-module definition here.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingAuxiliary.RingAuxiliary'
declarations.label: Morita equivalence of finitely generated module categories

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingAuxiliary.AlgebraAuxiliary'
declarations.label: A k-linear equivalence of finitely generated module categories

Chapter9/Definition9.7.2.title: Basic refers to the radical quotient
explanation: The checked predicate says that multiplication in B/Rad(B) is commutative. It does not require B itself to be commutative.
The finite-dimensional and algebraically closed-field assumptions belong to the surrounding classification. They are not part of the bare commutativity predicate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FieldAlgebraProperties.fieldAlgebraProperty
declarations.label: The quotient by the radical is commutative

Chapter9/Corollary9.7.3.title: Existence, minimum dimension and uniqueness up to algebra isomorphism
explanation: The combined theorem starts with a finite-dimensional algebra A over an algebraically closed field. It produces a basic finite-dimensional B, a k-linear equivalence of the categories of all modules, dimₖ B ≤ dimₖ A, and uniqueness up to a k-algebra isomorphism among basic algebras with such an equivalence.

This is an algebra-level result. The exposed statement is not directly quantified over every finite abelian category in (i), and its uniqueness hypothesis uses k-linear equivalences of all modules rather than arbitrary equivalences of the finite-module categories in Definition 9.7.1. Those distinctions are not erased by calling each interface Morita equivalence.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.FiniteAlgebraCandidates.Auxiliary.exists_type_with_three_conditions_finrank_le_and_unique
declarations.label: A basic Morita representative, its dimension bound and uniqueness

Chapter8/Theorem8.1.1.title: Lifting maps and splitting surjections
explanation: Lean’s Module.Projective is the lifting property in (i). The first equivalence checks that it is enough to lift the identity of P: every surjection onto P then has a section.

The statements work over any ring, not just an algebra over a field. Small is a universe-sizing condition used to compare modules in the same universe; it is not a finite-generation or finite-dimensionality assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Projective.Module.Projective.iff_surjective_splits
declarations.label: Projectivity ⇔ every surjection onto P splits

Chapter8/Theorem8.1.1.title: A free retract and exact Hom
explanation: The free-module statement uses maps P → F → P whose composite is the identity, with F free. Thus P is a direct summand of F. Its bound variable Q denotes the free module F, not the complementary summand called Q in the book.

The second statement checks injectivity, middle exactness and surjectivity after applying Hom(P, −) to every short exact sequence. In particular, surjectivity of the final Hom map is the lifting property.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Projective.Module.Projective.iff_exists_retract
declarations.label: Projectivity ⇔ a retract of a free module

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Projective.Module.Projective.iff_hom_preserves_short_exact
declarations.label: Projectivity ⇔ Hom(P, −) preserves short exact sequences

Chapter8/Definition8.1.2.title: One property, four equivalent tests
explanation: This definition is an alias for Mathlib’s projective-module property. The preceding equivalences connect its lifting formulation with all four tests in the book; no new structure is placed on P.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Property.ModuleProperty
declarations.label: Projective modules

Chapter8/Problem8.1.3.title: Projective implies flat
explanation: A right A-module is represented as a left module over the opposite ring Aᵐᵒᵖ. The flatness predicate says that tensoring this module with a short exact sequence of left A-modules gives a short exact sequence of abelian groups.
The checked implication uses projectivity over Aᵐᵒᵖ; it does not assume that A is commutative.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.Flatness.Module.Projective.oppositeRingModuleProperty
declarations.label: Every projective right module is flat

Chapter8/Problem8.1.3.title: Localization need not be projective
explanation: Localization at a multiplicative submonoid is flat over any commutative ring. For ℂ[x], the counterexample is Localization.Away X, the ring obtained by inverting x; this is the Laurent-polynomial module in the book.

The nonprojectivity proof shows that every ℂ[x]-linear map from this localization to ℂ[x] is zero: its value at 1 would be divisible by every power of x. A projective retract of a free module would instead supply enough coordinate maps to detect 1.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.Flatness.Localization.flat
declarations.label: Localizations are flat

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.Flatness.localizationAwayX_flat_not_projective
declarations.label: ℂ[x, x⁻¹] is flat but not projective

Chapter8/Exercise8.1.4.title: Lift the second map, then combine
explanation: Write the extension as M₁ → M → M₂ with the first map injective, the second surjective and image equal to kernel. Projectivity of P₂ lifts f₂ to M; combine that lift with the inclusion composed with f₁.
Lean uses P₁ × P₂ for this finite direct sum. The conclusion records both restrictions, rather than merely asserting that some map into M exists.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Projective.Lifting.LinearMap.exists_coprod_map_of_exact
declarations.label: A map P₁ ⊕ P₂ → M with the required restrictions

Chapter8/Theorem8.1.5.title: Extending maps reverses the exact sequence
explanation: Module.Injective is the extension property in (i): a map into I extends across any injective module map. The first equivalence checks retractions of embeddings I → M.

Hom(−, I) reverses arrows. The exactness theorem checks the sequence Hom(K, I) → Hom(M, I) → Hom(N, I), including surjectivity of restriction to N. The proof constructs the quotient pushout used below in the book; its order of factors is I × M rather than M ⊕ I.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Injective.Module.injective_iff_every_injective_map_from_splits
declarations.label: Injectivity ⇔ every embedding of I splits

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Injective.Module.injective_iff_hom_exact_on_short_exact
declarations.label: Injectivity ⇔ contravariant Hom is exact

Chapter8/Definition8.1.6.title: Injectivity is an extension property
explanation: This alias is Mathlib’s Module.Injective: extend a map into I across an injective map. It is not a claim that I is itself embedded in, or equipped with, a particular larger module.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Properties.RingModuleProperty
declarations.label: Injective modules

Chapter8/Example8.1.7.title: The checked converse has finite-dimensional hypotheses
explanation: The dual is Homₖ(P, k), with right action (φ · a)(p) = φ(a · p). Dualizing therefore reverses the side of the A-action as well as the direction of maps.

The displayed equivalence assumes that both A and P are finite-dimensional over the field k. Its converse uses the identifications with double duals. This certifies that finite-dimensional case, not the unqualified statement printed in the book. The source also proves the forward implication without these dimension bounds.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Duality.Module.projective_iff_dual_injective
declarations.label: Projective P ⇔ injective P* in the finite-dimensional case

Chapter8/Definition8.1.8.title: Exact Hom without module coordinates
explanation: The Hom functors here take values in abelian groups. Lean expresses exactness by preservation of finite limits and finite colimits in the abelian setting.

For projectivity the functor is Hom(P, −), named preadditiveCoyonedaObj. For injectivity it is Hom(−, I), named preadditiveYonedaObj and defined on the opposite category. That opposite category accounts for reversal of the sequence; neither result requires finite-dimensional objects.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.YonedaFiniteLimitColimitPreservation.coyonedaObjectProperty_iff
declarations.label: Projective P ⇔ exact Hom(P, −)

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.YonedaFiniteLimitColimitPreservation.yonedaObjectProperty_iff
declarations.label: Injective I ⇔ exact Hom(−, I)

Chapter8/Definition8.2.1.title: What a resolution stores
explanation: A ProjectiveResolution stores a natural-number-indexed chain complex, projectivity of every term, and an augmentation to M placed in degree zero.

The augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism: it identifies degree-zero homology with M and forces all positive-degree homology to vanish. In an abelian category this is the exact augmented sequence shown above; M is not an extra projective term.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ObjectData.AbelianCategoryObjectData
declarations.label: A chain complex of projectives resolving M

Chapter8/Exercise8.2.2.title: Resolve successive kernels
explanation: The construction starts with the free module on the underlying elements of M and its surjection onto M. Cover the kernel by another free module, then repeat.

The resulting resolution has free terms in every nonnegative degree. It works for modules over any ring, with no finite-generation hypothesis and no assertion that the resolution eventually terminates.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveResolution.freeProjectiveResolution
declarations.label: The resolution built from free covers

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ProjectiveResolution.exists_free_projectiveResolution
declarations.label: Every module has a resolution with free terms

Chapter8/Definition8.2.3.title: Tor uses a right module and downward differentials
explanation: The tensor product over a possibly noncommutative ring is the balanced quotient of M ⊗ℤ N by (ma) ⊗ n = m ⊗ (an). Aᵐᵒᵖ records the right action on M; it is not an additional commutativity assumption.

The functor is defined as a left-derived tensor functor. The comparison identifies its value with the homology of the chosen resolution after tensoring with N. The book says “cohomology” here, but these differentials lower degree; Lean uses chain-complex homology.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.TensorProductConstruction.degreewiseModuleGroupFunctor
declarations.label: Torᵢ(−, N) as a left-derived tensor functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.TensorProductConstruction.degreewiseModuleGroupIsoResolutionHomology
declarations.label: Compute Torᵢ from any projective resolution

Chapter8/Definition8.2.4.title: Hom turns the resolution into an upward complex
explanation: Precomposition with Pᵢ₊₁ → Pᵢ gives Hom(Pᵢ, N) → Hom(Pᵢ₊₁, N). Thus Ext is contravariant in M and covariant in N.

The general categorical Ext type applies to modules over any ring. Mathlib’s projective-resolution comparison identifies it with cohomology classes in the Hom complex. The more concrete k-vector-space comparison below assumes that A is an algebra over a field k; that extra scalar structure is not required by the book’s definition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ExtensionClasses.CategoryTheory.ExtensionClasses
declarations.label: Ext groups in all nonnegative degrees

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.LinearYoneda.ModuleCat.linearYonedaHomologyIsoOfProjectiveResolution
declarations.label: For a k-algebra, Extᵢ is the Hom-complex cohomology

links.name: CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.extAddEquivCohomologyClass
links.label: General Ext comparison with Hom-complex cohomology

Chapter8/Problem8.2.5.title: A comparison map compatible with the augmentation
explanation: The existence theorem constructs the whole chain map at once, with f followed by Q’s augmentation equal to P’s augmentation. Its component equations give the lifts requested in (i) and (ii).
Any two such lifts are chain-homotopic. Applying an additive functor preserves that homotopy, so the resulting maps on homology agree.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.Comparison.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.existsHom_comp_pi
declarations.label: A chain map between resolutions lifting the identity

Chapter8/Problem8.2.5.title: Canonical comparison for Tor
explanation: The checked equality says that two chain maps compatible with the augmentation induce the same map on Tor. The isomorphism compares their homology objects, independently of either lift.

Comparison from P to itself is the identity, and comparison through a third resolution is the same as direct comparison. Hence these are compatible identifications, not unrelated abstract isomorphisms.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.Comparison.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.modulePairGroupMap_eq_of_comm
declarations.label: The induced Tor map is independent of the lift

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.Comparison.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.modulePairGroupIso
declarations.label: Canonical Tor isomorphism between resolutions

Chapter8/Problem8.2.5.title: For Ext, reverse the comparison map
explanation: A map Q → P of resolutions induces Hom(P, N) → Hom(Q, N), and therefore an Ext comparison in that reversed direction. The argument again uses homotopy independence.
The selected concrete Ext comparisons are k-linear and assume an algebra A over a field k. The Tor comparisons above work over an arbitrary ring.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.Comparison.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.linearYonedaObjMap_eq_of_comm
declarations.label: The induced Ext map is independent of the lift

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.Comparison.CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution.linearYonedaObjIso
declarations.label: Ext isomorphism between the two Hom complexes

Chapter8/Problem8.2.6.title: Degree zero recovers tensor and Hom
explanation: Right exactness of tensor identifies its zeroth left-derived functor with tensor itself. Ext in degree zero is additively equivalent to the group of A-linear maps M → N.
These two comparisons work over an arbitrary ring; degree zero is not merely a vanishing or dimension statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryDegreeZeroIso
declarations.label: Tor₀(M, N) ≅ M ⊗ₐ N

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryDegreeZeroAddEquiv
declarations.label: Ext⁰(M, N) ≅ Homₐ(M, N)

Chapter8/Problem8.2.6.title: Degree one agrees with the earlier extension calculation
explanation: For an algebra over a field k, the checked additive equivalence identifies Ext¹(W, V) with the cocycle quotient used in Chapter 3 to describe extensions 0 → V → E → W → 0.

The order of the arguments matters: the quotient module W is the first Ext argument, and the submodule V is the second. This bridge uses the tensor-bar resolution and the Chapter 3 cocycle construction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryDegreeOneExtAddEquiv
declarations.label: Ext¹(W, V) and the Chapter 3 extension-cocycle quotient

Chapter8/Problem8.2.6.title: The connecting maps account for failure of exactness
explanation: The Ext theorem supplies exact successive pieces in the covariant N argument. The Tor theorem supplies a connecting map Torₙ₊₁(M, N₃) → Torₙ(M, N₁) and exactness of the five adjacent arrows.
Varying n joins these pieces into the sequences in the book; the degree-zero comparisons above identify their endpoints with Hom and tensor. No finite-dimensionality restriction is imposed here.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.covariantSequence_exact
declarations.label: Ext is exact across each adjacent pair of degrees

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryCovariantExactSequence
declarations.label: The five-arrow Tor sequence in the second argument

Chapter8/Problem8.2.6.title: Resolve either tensor factor
explanation: The balancing comparison identifies Tor defined by resolving the right module M with the left-derived functor obtained by resolving N instead.

It works over an arbitrary ring. The selected theorem states existence of an isomorphism in each degree; it does not expose a chosen double complex or a particular chain-level comparison map from the hint.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryLeftDerivedIso
declarations.label: Tor can be computed by resolving the left module

Chapter8/Problem8.2.6.title: The horseshoe construction
explanation: The middle resolution has terms Pᵢ¹ ⊕ Pᵢ³, with a differential chosen to fit the two outer resolutions and the original extension. The constructor includes projectivity and exactness through its augmentation; the sequence of resolution complexes is short exact.

Ext reverses arrows in its first argument. Tor remains covariant, but for a noncommutative ring its first argument must be a right module. Thus the Tor statement below uses a sequence of Aᵐᵒᵖ-modules, rather than the left modules printed in part (v).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.ShortExact.CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.ShortExact.middleProjectiveResolution
declarations.label: Resolve the middle object by the horseshoe construction

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalAlgebra.ProjectiveResolution.ShortExact.CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.ShortExact.resolutionShortComplex_shortExact
declarations.label: A short exact sequence of the three resolution complexes

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.contravariantSequence_exact
declarations.label: The Ext sequence in its first argument

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.DerivedFunctorExactness.AuxiliaryContravariantExactSequence
declarations.label: The Tor sequence in its right-module argument

Chapter8/Problem8.2.7.title: Cyclic integer summands reduce the calculation to gcd
explanation: For a nonzero integer a, the resolution ℤ → ℤ → ℤ/a uses multiplication by a. It gives Ext¹(ℤ/a, N) ≅ N/aN and Tor₁(ℤ/a, N) ≅ {n ∈ N : an = 0}. With N = ℤ/c, both are ℤ/gcd(a, c).

The checked results assemble the cyclic calculations with the free parts of finitely generated groups. Ext⁰ is Hom; a free summand in M contributes a copy of N to Ext⁰ but nothing to Ext¹. Tensor includes free summands from either group. All Tor and Ext groups in degrees at least two vanish.
Module.Finite ℤ M means finitely generated, not a finite underlying group. The finite products in the Lean formulas represent finite direct sums of cyclic contributions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.IntegerModuleStructure.auxiliaryFiniteIntModuleIndexZeroOneEquivsAndAddTwoSubsingleton
declarations.label: Ext for finitely generated abelian groups

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Auxiliary.GcdZModEquivalences.Algebra.Auxiliary.exists_gcdZModComponentEquivalences_and_higher_subsingleton
declarations.label: Tor for finitely generated abelian groups

Chapter8/Problem8.2.7.title: Replace integers by polynomials
explanation: Over k[x], use the analogous cyclic resolution with multiplication by a nonzero polynomial f. For cyclic inputs k[x]/(f) and k[x]/(g), the contributions are k[x]/(f, g), equivalently the quotient by their gcd.

The two checked assemblies include the free parts, compute degrees zero and one, and prove vanishing in every degree at least two. They require finite generation over k[x], not finite dimension over k.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.PolynomialModuleIndexedTypes.Auxiliary.finitePolynomialModules_indexZeroOne_addEquiv_and_indexAddTwo_subsingleton
declarations.label: Ext for finitely generated k[x]-modules

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.PolynomialModuleQuotientEquivalences.auxiliaryDegreeZeroDegreeOneAndHigherSubsingleton
declarations.label: Tor for finitely generated k[x]-modules

Chapter8/Problem8.2.8.title: Tor and the two sides of the action
explanation: For Tor over a noncommutative algebra, M₁ and M₂ must be right modules and N₁ and N₂ left modules, as in Definition 8.2.3. The checked formula encodes the right modules with opposite rings; the book’s opening sentence calls all four modules left modules.

In total degree i, the coproduct is indexed by pairs (j, m) with j + m = i. It is the direct sum in the printed formula. The tensor action hypothesis states that (a₁ ⊗ a₂)(n₁ ⊗ n₂) = (a₁n₁) ⊗ (a₂n₂); it is the usual external action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.TensorProductGradedComparisons.Auxiliary.nonempty_rightModuleTensorProductObjectIsoSigma
declarations.label: Tor over a tensor-product algebra decomposes by total degree

Chapter8/Problem8.2.8.title: The checked Ext formula is more restricted
explanation: The concrete Ext theorem assumes finite-dimensional A₁, A₂, M₁, M₂, N₁ and N₂ over k. The book explicitly bounds only N₁ and N₂. This is a genuine restriction of the supplied checked result, not a proof of the book’s full stated generality.

The proof uses finite projective resolution terms to identify the degreewise Hom tensor product, then applies the cohomology comparison. A separate counterexample shows that tensoring duals does not automatically give the full dual of a tensor product in infinite dimension; it is not itself a counterexample to the book’s Ext statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.TensorProductGradedComparisons.Auxiliary.nonempty_tensorProductGradedPieceLinearEquivDirectSum
declarations.label: Ext decomposition under the additional finite-dimensional hypotheses

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FinsuppDualTensor.dualDistrib_finsuppNat_not_surjective
declarations.label: An infinite-dimensional obstruction to distributing duals

Chapter8/Discussion_after_Problem8.2.8.title: Enough projectives supplies resolutions, not a tensor product
explanation: Lean’s EnoughProjectives says that every object has an epimorphism from a projective object. In an abelian category this supplies projective resolutions, hence Ext and left-derived additive functors.

To call one of those derived functors Tor, one must additionally specify a tensor functor (or analogous right-exact functor). An arbitrary abelian category is not equipped with a tensor product merely by having enough projectives.

links.label: Every object has a projective presentation

links.name: CategoryTheory.ProjectiveResolution
links.label: Projective resolutions in a category

Chapter8/Exercise8.2.9.title: Projectivity is relative to the category
explanation: The first two theorems test lifting only through surjections inside the finite-group or finite-dimensional k[x]-module category. Even that restricted lifting property forces the object to be zero.

Thus these are not just statements about projectivity among all modules. In Lean, Subsingleton expresses the zero module or trivial additive group, rather than a claim that there is no underlying object.

declarations.label: A projective finite abelian group must be zero

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Lifting.subsingleton_of_lifts_along_surjective_polynomialLinearMaps
declarations.label: A projective finite-dimensional k[x]-module must be zero

Chapter8/Exercise8.2.9.title: Finite free covers stay in the category
explanation: Every finitely generated module M is the quotient of Aⁿ for some finite n. This cover is itself finitely generated and projective, so it gives the required projective presentation.
The selected theorem assumes A is a commutative algebra of finite type over ℤ, matching a finitely generated commutative ring. Its underlying finite-cover result needs only finite generation of M.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Lifting.exists_surjective_finFreeLinearMap_of_finite
declarations.label: A finite free module surjecting onto M

Chapter8/Problem8.2.10.title: The free Koszul resolution
explanation: Choosing a finite basis gives the complex with terms S(V) ⊗ ΛⁱV. Its differential is the sum of multiplication by each basis vector followed by contraction with the corresponding coordinate functional.

The projective-resolution record includes the augmentation to the trivial S(V)-module k and its quasi-isomorphism proof. The second statement checks that every term is free. The basis-indexed construction even permits a commutative base ring when V has the specified finite basis.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.ProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary.basisProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary
declarations.label: The Koszul resolution of the trivial module

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.ProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary.basisProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary_free
declarations.label: Every Koszul term is free

Chapter8/Problem8.2.10.title: Resolve S(W) with U acting trivially
explanation: Lean uses U × W for the finite direct sum U ⊕ W. Tensoring the Koszul resolution over S(U) with the regular S(W)-module gives a resolution over S(U × W).
The target has carrier k ⊗ S(W), canonically identified with S(W); U acts through the augmentation and hence by zero. The component isomorphism identifies the terms with S(U × W) ⊗ ΛⁱU.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.ProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary.finiteDimensionalProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary
declarations.label: The complementary symmetric-algebra resolution

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.ProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary.finiteDimensionalProjectiveResolutionAuxiliary_componentIso
declarations.label: Identify its degree-i term

Chapter8/Problem8.2.10.title: The bimodule resolution remembers both actions
explanation: The acting algebra is S(V) ⊗ S(V), and the target is S(V) with action (a ⊗ b) · s = asb. A change of generators transports the complementary resolution to this multiplication action.
The constructor gives a resolution of that target, and the term isomorphism identifies its modules with S(V) ⊗ ΛⁱV ⊗ S(V). This is the bimodule resolution, not another unexplained coefficient module.

declarations.label: The Koszul bimodule resolution of S(V)

declarations.label: Identify the bimodule terms

Chapter8/Problem8.2.10.title: A dimension bound for every S(V)-module
explanation: Tensoring the bimodule resolution with M produces a projective resolution of M. Its terms vanish above dim V because the corresponding exterior powers vanish.

The bound theorem applies to arbitrary modules M and N, not only finitely generated ones. It states projective dimension at most n for a basis indexed by Fin n, vanishing of Ext as a Subsingleton group, and vanishing of Tor as an IsZero object.

declarations.label: A resolution of an arbitrary S(V)-module

declarations.label: Its terms vanish above dim V

declarations.label: Hilbert syzygies: Tor and Ext vanish above dim V

Chapter8/Problem8.2.10.title: Exterior powers and their duals
explanation: For the trivial module k, all generators of V act by zero. After tensoring the Koszul resolution with k, or applying Hom(−, k), the differentials are therefore zero.
The comparisons give Torᵢˢ⁽ⱽ⁾(k, k) ≅ ΛⁱV and Extⁱˢ⁽ⱽ⁾(k, k) ≅ (ΛⁱV)*. They describe the groups in each degree; no assertion about their graded multiplication is included in these two statements.

declarations.label: Extⁱ(k, k) is the dual exterior power

Chapter7/Definition7.8.1.title: Upward differentials, cohomology and exactness
explanation: Lean represents the book’s complex by an integer-indexed cochain complex K. Its terms are K.X i and its differential is K.d i (i+1); the complex structure includes the equation d² = 0. No choice of basis is involved.

Mathlib uses the name homology for the quotient of cycles by boundaries in either indexing convention. Here the differentials raise degree, so K.homology i is the book’s Hⁱ, not the term Cᵢ. ExactAt i means exactness at that term; Acyclic means exactness at every degree.

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.8..title: The commuting square is part of a cochain map
explanation: A cochain map stores one map in each degree and a proof that each square with the differentials commutes. Lean writes f ≫ g for applying f and then g, so its equation fᵢ ≫ dᴰ = dᶜ ≫ fᵢ₊₁ is the same square as the book’s equation.
The induced map on cohomology is then defined from those squares. The general interface works in abelian categories, not just vector spaces or groups.

Chapter7/Definition7.8.2.title: A quotient description of short exactness
explanation: A ShortComplex stores X → Y → Z and the equation that the composite is zero. ShortExact adds exactness in the middle, a monomorphism on the left and an epimorphism on the right; the endpoint zero objects need not be stored separately.

In an abelian category the cokernel of X → Y plays the role of Y/X. The theorem below checks the book’s characterization using the induced cokernel map. The extension record additionally identifies the two endpoints with specified X and Z; it is data for an extension, not a classification of extension classes.

Chapter7/Example7.8.3.title: The inclusion and projection give a split sequence
explanation: The two arrows are the inclusion of X into X ⊕ Z and projection onto Z. A splitting supplies the other projection and inclusion, with their inverse and decomposition identities.
These identities prove short exactness in any abelian category. Unlike the next exercise, this example needs no field hypothesis.

Chapter7/Exercise7.8.4.title: Why vector spaces split, and abelian groups need not
explanation: Over a field, choose a complement to the cocycles in each degree. Exactness identifies that complement with the cocycles in the next degree. This gives a coproduct of two-term complexes whose only nonzero differential is invertible; after identifying the two copies of V, that differential is the identity.

The proof also supplies a splitting of every short exact sequence of vector spaces, with no finite-dimensionality assumption. For abelian groups, multiplication by 2 gives the nonsplit sequence 0 → ℤ → ℤ → ℤ/2 → 0: a retraction would force 2r(1) = 1.

Chapter7/Problem7.8.5.title: The lifted differential defines a map on classes
explanation: Abelian groups are represented here as ℤ-modules. A subcomplex is a family of submodules stable under the differential, and the quotient complex is constructed degree by degree.

The connecting map sends the class of a quotient cocycle to the class of the differential of a lift. One theorem makes it independent of the lift; the stronger theorem makes it independent of the quotient cohomology representative as well. With upward indexing, related degrees i and j satisfy j = i+1.

declarations.label: The connecting map Hⁱ(E) → Hⁱ⁺¹(C)

declarations.label: Independence of the lift

declarations.label: Independence of the cohomology representative

Chapter7/Problem7.8.5.title: Exactness at each of the three kinds of term
explanation: The long sequence repeats three exact pairs: connecting map then inclusion, inclusion then quotient, and quotient then connecting map. The theorem checks all three together, for every adjacent pair of degrees.
The second statement starts from any short exact sequence of these complexes, rather than requiring it to be presented as a chosen subcomplex and quotient.
