declarations.label: Exactness for any short exact sequence of group complexes

Chapter7/Definition7.8.6.title: The connecting map also exists in any abelian category
explanation: The abstract construction does not require elements or chosen representatives. For a short exact sequence of complexes in an abelian category, it provides δ between related degrees and proves the same three exact pairs.
Specializing the shape to upward integer indexing recovers Hⁱ(E) → Hⁱ⁺¹(C). Other complex shapes retain the degree relation explicitly.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplexShortExactHomology.homologyHomThirdToFirstOfRel
declarations.label: The abstract connecting morphism

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplexShortExactHomology.exact_delta_homologyMap_f
declarations.label: Exactness after the connecting map

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplexShortExactHomology.exact_homologyMap_f_g
declarations.label: Exactness between the two induced maps

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplexShortExactHomology.exact_homologyMap_g_delta
declarations.label: Exactness before the connecting map

Chapter7/Problem7.8.7.title: The sign cancels the cross terms
explanation: The two differentials raise the two input degrees separately. Applying the second after the first changes the sign from (−1)ʲ to (−1)ʲ⁺¹, so the mixed terms cancel; the remaining terms vanish by d² = 0 in each input.

The selected checked statement below specializes the tensor complex to modules over a field. The book’s first part allows any commutative ring; this statement alone does not certify that broader specialization. The later parts, including Künneth, explicitly assume a field. The total complex uses direct sums along j+m=i, not products, and does not assume boundedness.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.CochainComplex.HomologyComplex.tensorProduct_d_comp_d
declarations.label: The tensor differential squares to zero over a field

Chapter7/Problem7.8.7.title: An exact factor makes the tensor complex exact
explanation: Over a field, the two-term decomposition gives a contracting homotopy for an acyclic complex. Tensoring that homotopy makes the identity on the total tensor complex null-homotopic, hence its cohomology vanishes.
The theorem accepts acyclicity of either input. This is a field result; exactness of tensoring over an arbitrary ring would need additional hypotheses.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.CochainComplex.HomologyComplex.tensorProduct_acyclic_of_acyclic
declarations.label: A tensor complex is acyclic if either factor is acyclic

Chapter7/Problem7.8.7.title: Splitting off the zero-differential cohomology complex
explanation: The proof chooses sections from cohomology to cycles and projections onto cycles. They split C as an acyclic summand plus the complex with terms Hⁱ(C) and zero differential.

The proof verifies that the inclusion and projection induce inverse maps on cohomology, with their composite on Hⁱ(C) equal to the identity. The choices of complements are not canonical; the next comparison is natural despite those choices.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Homology.CochainComplex.HomologyComplex.exists_biprod_inr_comp_iso_inv_homologyMap_isIso
declarations.label: An acyclic summand and a cohomology-preserving splitting

Chapter7/Problem7.8.7.title: Künneth is a natural comparison, not just an abstract isomorphism
explanation: Tensoring cocycle representatives defines a canonical map from the graded sum of Hʲ(C) ⊗ Hᵐ(D) to Hⁱ(C ⊗ D). Its construction respects boundaries and cochain maps. The proof shows that this map is invertible over a field.

The first isomorphism below has the direction printed in the book. The functor isomorphism packages compatibility with maps in both inputs, which is the naturality asked for in part (iv). No finite-dimensionality or boundedness assumptions are added.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplex.TensorHomology.homologyTensorToSigmaIso
declarations.label: The Künneth isomorphism in degree i

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.HomologicalComplex.TensorHomology.tensorHomologyFunctorIso
declarations.label: Künneth, natural in both complexes

Chapter7/Definition7.9.1.title: Additivity and linearity are properties of the map on Hom
explanation: Functor.Additive requires F to preserve addition of morphisms. Functor.Linear records preservation of scalar multiplication separately. To express the book’s k-linearity as linear maps on Hom spaces, use both properties; the scalar-preservation alias alone does not include additivity.
The aligned definitions are aliases of these Mathlib properties. They do not impose finite-dimensionality, and the linear definition even allows scalars from a semiring.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Preadditive.FunctorProperties.PreadditiveProperty
declarations.label: An additive functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Preadditive.FunctorProperties.LinearProperty
declarations.label: A linear functor on Hom spaces

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.9..title: The biproduct comparison is canonical
explanation: The forward map F(X ⊕ Y) → F(X) ⊕ F(Y) is determined by the images of the two projections; its inverse comes from the two inclusions. Additivity preserves the identity expressing their sum as the identity map.
The result is an isomorphism, not an equality of objects. In Lean, ⊞ denotes this categorical biproduct.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Preadditive.FunctorProperties.PreadditiveProperty.binaryBiproductComparisonIso
declarations.label: The canonical comparison F(X ⊕ Y) ≅ F(X) ⊕ F(Y)

Chapter7/Example7.9.2.title: Induction, restriction and equivariant Hom preserve linear combinations
explanation: The checked instances give additivity and k-linearity for induction and restriction along a group homomorphism. Restriction keeps the underlying linear map; induction gets linearity through its adjunction with restriction.
Hom_G(V,−) is the covariant linear Hom functor, taking values in k-modules. These instances apply to arbitrary groups and representations over a field, without assuming finite-dimensionality.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.indFunctor_additive
declarations.label: Induction preserves addition

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.indFunctor_linear
declarations.label: Induction is k-linear

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.resFunctor_additive
declarations.label: Restriction preserves addition

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.resFunctor_linear
declarations.label: Restriction is k-linear

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.linearCoyoneda_obj_additive
declarations.label: Equivariant Hom preserves addition

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.LinearFunctors.linearCoyoneda_obj_linear
declarations.label: Equivariant Hom is k-linear

Chapter7/Definition7.9.3.title: Left exactness preserves kernels; right exactness preserves cokernels
explanation: For additive functors between abelian categories, the book’s left exactness can be expressed as preservation of finite limits, and right exactness as preservation of finite colimits. Kernels and cokernels are the essential checks; additivity supplies preservation of finite biproducts and the zero object.

The three definitions below use that categorical formulation. Their signatures allow general categories, but the translation to the book’s exact-sequence definition is being used here in the additive, abelian setting.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FunctorPredicateLogic.Left
declarations.label: Preservation of finite limits

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FunctorPredicateLogic.Right
declarations.label: Preservation of finite colimits

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FunctorPredicateLogic.Conjunction
declarations.label: Preservation of both finite limits and finite colimits

Chapter7/Definition7.9.4.title: Semisimplicity asks for a splitting of every short exact sequence
explanation: The definition quantifies over all short exact sequences and asks that a splitting exist. A splitting stores a retraction of the first arrow, a section of the second, and the decomposition identity on the middle object.

Nonempty expresses existence without choosing a preferred splitting. This is the book’s categorical semisimplicity, not merely the assertion that individual objects happen to have a chosen decomposition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.CategoryProperties.AbelianCategoryProperty
declarations.label: Every short exact sequence splits

Chapter7/Example7.9.5.title: Maschke’s hypothesis makes the group-algebra module category semisimple
explanation: The hypothesis is IsUnit (|G| : k): the group order is invertible in the field. For a field this is the characteristic condition in the book.

Maschke’s theorem makes k[G] a semisimple ring, and the proof then splits every short exact sequence of k[G]-modules. Through the usual group-algebra interpretation, these are G-representations. The result does not restrict modules to finite dimension.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Semisimplicity.monoidAlgebra_moduleCat_auxiliaryProperty_of_isUnit_card
declarations.label: Short exact sequences of finite-group representations split

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Example7.9.5.title: An additive functor carries a splitting to a splitting
explanation: Apply F to the section, retraction and decomposition identities. Functoriality preserves the inverse identities; additivity preserves the sum in the middle-object identity.
The resulting splitting proves the image sequence short exact. Only the source category must be semisimple: the target need only be abelian.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.ShortExactPreservation.shortExact_map_of_abelianCategoryProperty
declarations.label: Additive functors out of a semisimple category preserve short exact sequences

Chapter7/Example7.9.6.title: Restriction is exact; the induction witness retains finite index
explanation: Restriction preserves both finite limits and finite colimits because it has induction on one side and coinduction on the other. The checked induction theorem uses both adjunctions for a finite-index subgroup.
The displayed induction witness therefore retains a finite-index hypothesis. That covers the finite-group case; it is not a proof here of induction’s exactness for arbitrary infinite-index subgroups.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorProduct.BalancedRelations.resFunctor_preservesFiniteLimits_and_colimits
declarations.label: Restriction preserves kernels and cokernels

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorProduct.BalancedRelations.indFunctor_preservesFiniteLimits_and_colimits_of_finiteIndex
declarations.label: Induction is exact for a finite-index subgroup

Chapter7/Example7.9.6.title: Hom preserves kernels but can fail to preserve a surjection
explanation: A covariant representable Hom functor preserves limits, giving left exactness. But every homomorphism ℤ/2 → ℤ is zero, whereas Hom(ℤ/2,ℤ/2) contains the identity.
The map obtained by postcomposing with ℤ → ℤ/2 therefore cannot be surjective. The checked obstruction even works for any homomorphism ℤ → ℤ/2, not just the quotient map.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorProduct.BalancedRelations.postcomp_intToZModTwo_not_surjective
declarations.label: The identity of ℤ/2 cannot lift through Hom(ℤ/2,ℤ)

links.name: CategoryTheory.coyoneda
links.label: The covariant representable Hom functor

Chapter7/Example7.9.6.title: Tensor preserves cokernels, not arbitrary injections
explanation: For a possibly noncommutative ring A, the construction starts with X ⊗ℤ M and imposes (xa) ⊗ m = x ⊗ (am). Lean encodes the right A-action as a left action of Aᵐᵒᵖ.

The exactness theorem handles a pair M → N → P with N → P surjective; surjectivity of its tensor map is proved alongside it in the source. With X = ℤ/2, tensoring multiplication by 2 on ℤ kills the nonzero tensor 1 ⊗ 1, so the resulting map is not injective.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorProduct.BalancedRelations.BalancedTensorQuotient.exact_map
declarations.label: Balanced tensor quotients preserve right exact pairs

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorProduct.BalancedRelations.BalancedTensorQuotient.map_mulTwo_not_injective
declarations.label: Tensoring with ℤ/2 destroys injectivity of multiplication by 2

Chapter7/Exercise7.9.7.title: Adjunction gives the required preservation laws
explanation: A left adjoint preserves colimits, hence cokernels; a right adjoint preserves limits, hence kernels. In the additive abelian setting these give right exactness of F and left exactness of G.
The theorem assumes F ⊣ G and records both conclusions together. It does not assert that either functor is exact on both sides.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Abelian.AdditiveAdjunctionAuxiliary.auxiliaryProperties
declarations.label: A left adjoint is right exact and its right adjoint is left exact

Chapter7/Exercise7.9.8.title: Cokernel reflection is left adjoint to kernel reflection
explanation: At the source i, Fᵢ⁻ uses the cokernel of the outgoing-arrow map. In the reversed quiver, Fᵢ⁺ uses the kernel of the incoming-arrow map. The proof constructs the Hom bijection and verifies its naturality in V and W.

The source and target representation categories have different orientations; these are not endofunctors on a single category despite the internal namespace. The checked construction assumes finitely many arrows leaving i, and works over a commutative ring.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.EndofunctorAdjunction.adjunction
declarations.label: The reflection-functor adjunction

Chapter7/Exercise7.9.8.title: The two one-sided exactness statements follow from that adjunction
explanation: The left reflection preserves finite colimits and the right reflection preserves finite limits. This proves the two conclusions in (b), under the same source-vertex and finite outgoing-arrow hypotheses.
No inverse-equivalence claim is made: the simple representation at the reflected vertex remains the familiar exception from Chapter 6.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.EndofunctorAdjunction.auxiliaryEndofunctorConditions
declarations.label: Right exactness of Fᵢ⁻ and left exactness of Fᵢ⁺

Chapter7/Introduction_7.5.title: Two conventions for representability
explanation: The book calls both Hom(X,−) and Hom(−,X) representable. Mathlib calls the covariant version corepresentable and reserves representable for the contravariant version. The distinction is variance, not a different universal property.
A chosen representation includes natural bijections, not just a matching cardinality at each object. The existence classes assert that some representing object and those compatible bijections exist.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsCorepresentable
links.label: Covariant representability: Hom(X,−)

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor.IsRepresentable
links.label: Contravariant representability: Hom(−,X)

Chapter7/Lemma7.5.1.title: Naturality determines the representing isomorphism
explanation: The identity arrows determine the two candidate maps. Naturality then proves their composites are identities and that they induce the original transformation on every Hom set. This fills in the inverse and uniqueness checks omitted by the sketch.

The displayed theorem uses the contravariant form Hom(−,X): a natural isomorphism between these functors comes from a unique X ≅ Y. The book’s covariant form follows by passing to the opposite category and reversing the resulting isomorphism. The uniqueness is relative to the given natural isomorphism φ, not a claim that X and Y have only one possible isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Yoneda.yonedaIsoLiftUnique
declarations.label: Yoneda: a unique isomorphism inducing the given transformation

Chapter7/Remark7.5.2.title: Representability by a hom-object
explanation: In the enriched version, Hom(X,Y) is an object of the enriching category V, not merely a set. The enriched covariant Hom functor eCoyoneda assigns that hom-object to Y.

The definition below asks for an isomorphism with such a functor, with components that are morphisms in V. The second result verifies that eCoyoneda itself has this property, using its identity isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.EnrichedCorepresentability.IsEnrichedCorepresentable
declarations.label: Representability by enriched covariant hom-objects

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.EnrichedCorepresentability.isEnrichedCorepresentable_eCoyoneda
declarations.label: An enriched Hom functor represents itself

Chapter7/Example7.5.3.title: A map from the regular module is determined by its value at 1
explanation: Evaluation at 1 identifies A-linear maps A → M with elements of M. Its inverse sends m to the map a ↦ a·m. Evaluation commutes with every module map, which is the naturality needed for representability.

The witnesses below encode this comparison for the underlying-set forgetful functor over any ring. The book states the vector-space-valued version for a k-algebra; the displayed witnesses do not separately package its k-linear enriched comparison.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.Corepresentability.forgetCorepresentableByFreeModule
declarations.label: The regular module corepresents the underlying-set functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.Corepresentability.freeModuleCoyonedaIsoForget
declarations.label: The natural evaluation-at-1 comparison

Chapter7/Example7.5.3.title: The finite-dimensional counterexample is not packaged here
explanation: The supplied obstruction says that an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space over an infinite field cannot have a one-dimensional dual eigenspace for every scalar. There is a scalar outside its finite set of eigenvalues, whose dual eigenspace is zero.

This is a related linear-algebra obstruction, not a theorem that the restricted forgetful functor in the book’s example is unrepresentable. That categorical counterexample and the vector-space-valued enriched comparison are not separately supplied by the aligned results.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.Corepresentability.not_forall_finrank_dualEigenspace_eq_one
declarations.label: The related dual-eigenspace obstruction

Chapter7/Definition7.6.1.title: A natural Hom bijection, encoded by unit and counit
explanation: Lean writes F ⊣ G for F left adjoint to G. Its adjunction structure stores natural unit and counit maps and their triangle identities. From those it derives the bijection Hom(FX,Y) ≃ Hom(X,GY); the constructor used in the examples below can instead start with these bijections and their naturality laws.

The Hom expressions are contravariant in X and covariant in Y. Thus their bifunctor domain is Cᵒᵖ × D, rather than the C × D printed in the paragraph. Lean’s precomposition and postcomposition laws keep that variance explicit.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FunctorPair.Data
declarations.label: An adjunction, with unit, counit and triangle laws

links.name: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.homEquiv
links.label: The associated Hom bijection

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.6..title: Why a chosen adjunction determines a canonical comparison
explanation: For fixed X, the adjunction makes F(X) corepresent Y ↦ Hom(X,G(Y)). For fixed Y, it makes G(Y) represent X ↦ Hom(F(X),Y). These are the two witnesses below.

Two left adjoints to the same G, equipped with their adjunctions, have a canonical natural isomorphism; likewise for two right adjoints to the same F. Its compatibility comes from the chosen Hom bijections. It is not a statement that unrelated adjoint functors are literally equal.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Adjunction.Representability.corepresentableBy
declarations.label: F(X) represents the covariant Hom composite

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.Adjunction.Representability.representableBy
declarations.label: G(Y) represents the contravariant Hom composite

links.name: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.leftAdjointUniq
links.label: The natural comparison of two left adjoints

links.name: CategoryTheory.Adjunction.rightAdjointUniq
links.label: The natural comparison of two right adjoints

Chapter7/Example7.6.3.title: Tensor duality gives both adjunctions
explanation: Currying an equivariant map V ⊗ W → U produces an equivariant map W → V* ⊗ U. Evaluation and the finite-dimensional double-dual identification supply the inverse correspondence and the adjunction in the other direction.

The group witnesses use the finite-dimensional representation category FDRep; the Lie witnesses use a category whose objects are also finite-dimensional. These displayed results do not package the adjunctions on the category of all representations. The group need not be finite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.tensorLeftRightDualAdjunction
declarations.label: Tensoring by a group representation is left adjoint to its dual tensor functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.rightDualTensorLeftAdjunction
declarations.label: The dual group tensor functor is also a left adjoint

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.tensorDualAdjunction
declarations.label: The tensor-dual adjunction for Lie representations

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.dualTensorAdjunction
declarations.label: The reverse Lie tensor-dual adjunction

Chapter7/Example7.6.3.title: The two directions of Frobenius reciprocity
explanation: Induction is left adjoint to restriction along any group homomorphism, over a commutative ring. The reverse adjunction in the book requires the finite-index situation: restriction to a finite-index subgroup is left adjoint to induction.

For an arbitrary subgroup of infinite index, induction and coinduction need not agree. The second witness retains the finite-index hypothesis instead of presenting the two adjunctions as interchangeable in general.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.inductionRestrictionAdjunction
declarations.label: Induction is left adjoint to restriction

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.restrictionInductionAdjunction
declarations.label: Restriction is left adjoint to induction at finite index

Chapter7/Example7.6.3.title: The enveloping-algebra universal property is natural
explanation: A Lie homomorphism L → A, where A has its commutator bracket, extends uniquely to an algebra map U(L) → A. The construction gives this bijection for every L and A and proves compatibility with maps in both variables.

The categorical witness works over a commutative ring, with no characteristic-zero or finite-dimensional hypothesis. It includes the enveloping functor’s arrow maps, not just an objectwise universal property.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.universalEnvelopingAlgebraAdjunction
declarations.label: Universal enveloping algebra is left adjoint to the commutator-Lie functor

Chapter7/Example7.6.3.title: Group maps to units extend to group-algebra maps
explanation: An algebra map k[G] → A restricts to a group homomorphism G → A× on the basis elements. Conversely, such a group homomorphism extends linearly and multiplicatively to k[G].
The adjunction records these inverse maps and their naturality. It applies to any group over a commutative base ring; no finiteness assumption on G is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.monoidAlgebraAdjunction
declarations.label: The group-algebra functor is left adjoint to the units functor

Chapter7/Example7.6.3.title: Free algebra constructions turn linear maps into algebra maps
explanation: A linear map V → A extends uniquely to an algebra map from the tensor algebra T(V). If A is commutative, it extends uniquely from the symmetric algebra S(V). Restricting to the generators gives the inverse correspondences.
Both witnesses include functor maps and naturality in the generators and the target algebra. They work over a commutative ring, without assuming V is finite-dimensional.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.tensorAlgebraAdjunction
declarations.label: Tensor algebra is left adjoint to forgetting algebra multiplication

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.RepresentationAdjunctions.symmetricAlgebraAdjunction
declarations.label: Symmetric algebra is left adjoint to forgetting commutative multiplication

Chapter7/Introduction_7.7.title: The book’s concrete definition and Lean’s intrinsic one
explanation: Mathlib uses the intrinsic definition: additive Hom groups, finite products, kernels and cokernels, with every monomorphism a kernel and every epimorphism a cokernel. It does not define an abelian category by choosing a ring.
The next two statements bridge this definition and the book’s module-category description. The embedding theorem chooses a ring in a universe large enough for the category’s objects and arrows.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Abelian
links.label: The intrinsic abelian-category axioms

Chapter7/Definition7.7.1.title: The bridge works in both directions
explanation: Starting from the intrinsic abelian-category structure, the embedding theorem gives an equivalence with a full subcategory of modules. The selected property contains zero and is closed under isomorphisms, finite products and coproducts, kernels, cokernels and images.

Conversely, a full subcategory of modules containing zero and closed under finite products, kernels and cokernels inherits an abelian structure. In an additive category finite products are also finite direct sums; images can be recovered as kernels of cokernels.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AbelianCategoryRepresentation.exists_moduleCatFullSubcategoryEquivalence
declarations.label: An abelian category has the book’s module-subcategory realization

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AbelianCategoryRepresentation.categoryDataOfObjectProperty
declarations.label: A suitably closed module subcategory is abelian

Chapter7/Example7.7.2.title: All modules versus finite-dimensional modules
explanation: ModuleCat A is abelian for every ring A. The finite-dimensional result supplied here goes through finitely generated A-modules and assumes A is a finite-dimensional algebra over the base field. Under that hypothesis, finite generation over A and finite dimension over k are equivalent, and A is Noetherian.

The book’s category of finite-dimensional A-modules is abelian even when A is infinite-dimensional. That general case is not supplied by these aligned FGModuleCat results, so the two categories should not be identified without the hypothesis.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.FiniteDimensional.FGModuleCategory.moduleFinite_iff_finiteDimensional
declarations.label: Finite generation agrees with finite dimension when A is finite-dimensional

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.FiniteDimensional.FGModuleCategory.FGModuleCat.instAbelian_of_finiteDimensional
declarations.label: The abelian category of finitely generated modules in that case

links.name: ModuleCat.abelian
links.label: The abelian category of all modules over any ring

Chapter7/Problem7.7.3.title: Noetherianity is what keeps kernels finitely generated
explanation: The proof treats a finitely generated commutative ring as an algebra of finite type over ℤ. Hilbert’s basis theorem makes it Noetherian. Submodules of finitely generated modules are then finitely generated, so kernels stay in the subcategory.

Quotients and finite direct sums preserve finite generation without needing that Noetherian step. These closure properties give the abelian structure on the full subcategory. The conclusion is the existence of that structure, not merely a list of closure assertions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModuleObjectProperties.ModuleCat.moduleObjectPropertyFullSubcategoryHasAbelianStructure
declarations.label: Finitely generated modules over a finite-type commutative ring form an abelian category

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Problem7.7.3.title: Categorical kernels and images do not need underlying elements
explanation: Lean expresses kernels, cokernels and images by their universal properties. Mono and Epi are cancellation conditions; only in a concrete module category do they become injectivity and surjectivity of underlying maps.

The additive Hom groups and bilinear composition come from Preadditive. The abelian-category axioms provide the remaining constructions and the compatibility that makes kernel and cokernel arguments work.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Abelian
links.label: The abelian structure

links.name: CategoryTheory.Preadditive
links.label: Additive Hom groups and bilinear composition

Chapter7/Remark7.7.4.title: An explicit Morita-equivalent pair of different rings
explanation: The witness uses ℚ and the ring of 2 × 2 rational matrices. Their module categories are equivalent, but the rings are not isomorphic.

The equivalence is the standard matrix-module equivalence. Nonisomorphism follows because ℚ is commutative and the matrix ring has noncommuting elements. Thus the category of modules cannot recover its presenting ring up to ring isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Rat.MatrixTwo.rat_moduleCat_equivalence_matrix_fin_two_and_ringEquiv_isEmpty
declarations.label: Equivalent module categories without a ring isomorphism

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Remark7.7.4.title: Linearity is extra structure on the Hom groups
explanation: A k-linear category equips every Hom group with a k-module structure and requires composition to be linear in each argument. For ModuleCat A this comes from the k-algebra structure of A, while abelianness only needs A to be a ring.

The displayed finitely generated category uses the finite-dimensional-algebra hypothesis from Example 7.7.2. It is the concrete interface supplied here, not an identification with finite-dimensional modules over an arbitrary algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ModuleCategories.moduleCatLinear
declarations.label: The k-linear category of all A-modules

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ModuleCategories.moduleCatAbelian
declarations.label: The abelian category of all A-modules

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ModuleCategories.fgModuleCatLinear
declarations.label: The k-linear finitely generated category for finite-dimensional A

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ModuleCategories.fgModuleCatAbelian
declarations.label: Its abelian structure

Chapter7/Definition7.1.1.title: Objects, arrows and composition
explanation: Lean represents the objects by a type C. A category structure supplies the arrow types X ⟶ Y, identity arrows and composition, together with proofs of associativity and the two identity laws. The checked declaration below is an alias for Mathlib’s category structure, not a new notion of category.
Lean writes f ≫ g for first f, then g. This is the book’s g ∘ f; the reversed written order matters when reading the later naturality equations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.UniverseTypeOperator.TypeOperator
declarations.label: A category structure

links.name: CategoryTheory.Category
links.label: Read the category fields and axioms

Chapter7/Example7.1.3.title: Passing from maps to homotopy classes
explanation: The ordinary examples use types and functions, bundled groups and rings, module categories and topological spaces. In the homotopy example the objects stay the same, while arrows are continuous maps modulo homotopy.

The checked relation is homotopy of continuous maps. Its congruence proof shows that homotopic maps remain homotopic after composition on either side, so identities and composition descend to the quotient category.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.TopCatCongruence.topCatHomRel
declarations.label: When two continuous maps define the same arrow

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.TopCatCongruence.AuxiliaryType
declarations.label: The homotopy category

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Example7.1.3.title: Universes instead of a type of all types
explanation: Lean handles this size distinction with universe levels. The types in Type u themselves form a type in the next universe; there is no single type containing every type at every level.

A category’s object universe and arrow universe are separate parameters. Each Hom(X,Y) is a type in the specified arrow universe. Thus the checked interface makes the size choices explicit rather than introducing unrestricted classes.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Category
links.label: Inspect the object and morphism universe parameters

Chapter7/Definition7.1.4.title: Restrict the objects, keep every arrow
explanation: The full subcategory is specified by a property P of objects. An object consists of an object of C together with a proof that it satisfies P. Between two such objects, the arrows are the original arrows of C; no extra restriction is imposed on them.
Mathlib’s inclusion functor forgets the property proof and is fully faithful. The checked declaration below names this standard full-subcategory construction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.ObjectProperty.AssociatedType
declarations.label: The full subcategory defined by an object property

links.name: CategoryTheory.ObjectProperty.ι
links.label: The inclusion into the original category

links.name: CategoryTheory.ObjectProperty.fullyFaithfulι
links.label: Why the inclusion is fully faithful

Chapter7/Example7.1.5.title: No additional condition on group homomorphisms
explanation: A homomorphism between abelian groups is already a group homomorphism; forgetting commutativity does not add or remove any arrows between them. Mathlib proves that the forgetful functor from commutative groups to groups is fully faithful. It uses multiplicative notation for this version of the example.

links.name: CommGrpCat.fullyFaithfulForget₂ToGrp
links.label: The fully faithful forgetful functor for abelian groups

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Example7.1.5.title: Composition is a morphism of hom-objects
explanation: An enriched category assigns a hom-object in the chosen monoidal category V to each pair of objects. Its identity comes from V’s unit object, and composition is a morphism from the tensor product of two hom-objects. The tensor, not a Cartesian product, is the general enriched operation.

Lean orders the factors as Hom(X,Y) ⊗ Hom(Y,Z): first the arrow X → Y, then Y → Z. The book writes the opposite order. For vector spaces this encodes bilinear composition; associators and unitors express the enriched associativity and identity laws.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.EnrichedCorepresentability.AuxiliaryMonoidalTypeOperator
declarations.label: An enriched category structure

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.EnrichedCorepresentability.enrichedComposition
declarations.label: The enriched composition morphism

links.name: CategoryTheory.EnrichedCategory
links.label: Read the hom-objects, identities and enriched laws

Chapter7/Example7.1.6.title: Linear hom-spaces and bilinear composition
explanation: For A-modules, the A-linear maps form k-vector spaces, and composing maps is k-linear in either argument. Mathlib records these facts through its linear-category structure on ModuleCat A.

The linked instance works more generally for an algebra over a commutative semiring, with A a ring. This supplies the linear-category formulation of the example; it is not a separate construction here of every field of an enriched-category record.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Linear
links.label: The linear-category interface

links.name: ModuleCat.Algebra.instLinear
links.label: The linear structure on the category of algebra modules

Chapter7/Definition7.2.1.title: A functor acts on arrows as well as objects
explanation: A functor has an object map obj and an arrow map map. Its map_id and map_comp proofs say that identities and compositions are preserved. Specifying only an assignment of objects does not give a functor.
The checked declaration is an alias for Mathlib’s functor structure. Its arrow map takes an arrow X ⟶ Y to an arrow F.obj X ⟶ F.obj Y.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryPair.AssociatedType
declarations.label: The data and laws of a functor

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor
links.label: Read the object map, arrow map and functor laws

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.2..title: The order of functor composition
explanation: Lean writes F ⋙ G for applying F and then G, the book’s G ∘ F. The composite applies both object maps and both arrow maps in that order. The identity functor leaves objects and arrows unchanged.

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor.comp
links.label: Composition of functors

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor.id
links.label: The identity functor

Chapter7/Example7.2.2.title: Postcomposition and precomposition
explanation: For Y ↦ Hom(X,Y), an arrow Y → Z acts by postcomposition. For Y ↦ Hom(Y,X), it acts by precomposition, which reverses direction and explains the opposite category.
In Mathlib these are coyoneda.obj (op X) and yoneda.obj X, respectively. Their definitions include the arrow maps, not just the assignments of sets.

links.name: CategoryTheory.coyoneda
links.label: Hom(X,−), covariant in the second argument

links.name: CategoryTheory.yoneda
links.label: Hom(−,X), contravariant in the first argument

Chapter7/Example7.2.2.title: Tensor maps descend to symmetric and Schur functors
explanation: A linear map f : V → W acts on tensor powers by applying f to each factor. This commutes with permutations, so it descends to the symmetric-power quotient and gives the arrow map of Sⁿ.

For a fixed representation π of Sₙ, the Schur construction sends an equivariant map π → V⊗ⁿ to its composite with f⊗ⁿ. The checked functor allows any π over a commutative ring; it does not require π to be irreducible or V to be finite-dimensional. The Young-diagram classification is not proved by this functor definition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.SymmetricPower.Functor.SymmetricPower.moduleEndofunctorOfNat
declarations.label: The symmetric-power functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Mathlib.RepresentationTheory.PiTensorProduct.Equivariant.equivariantLinearMapsFunctor
declarations.label: The equivariant Hom functor defining a Schur construction

Chapter7/Example7.2.2.title: Reflection also transports morphisms
explanation: The kernel reflection at a sink restricts the componentwise direct-sum map to the kernel. The cokernel reflection at a source descends it to the quotient. Compatibility with the representation’s arrow maps makes both operations well-defined.

The checked constructions include identity and composition laws. Kernel reflection works over a commutative semiring; cokernel reflection uses a commutative ring and assumes finitely many outgoing arrows at the chosen source. At other vertices they keep the original components. The sink/source hypotheses are the ones used when interpreting these constructions as the book’s Fᵢ⁺ and Fᵢ⁻.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverRepresentationAuxiliaryFunctor.auxiliaryRepresentationFunctor
declarations.label: Kernel reflection as a functor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverRepresentationQuotientFunctor.quotientRepresentationFunctor
declarations.label: Cokernel reflection as a functor

Chapter7/Definition7.3.1.title: Naturality is the compatibility condition
explanation: A natural transformation has a component α.app X at each object. For f : X → Y, its naturality law is F.map f ≫ α.app Y = α.app X ≫ G.map f. Remember that ≫ is written in the order of application.

An isomorphism of functors requires natural components, not merely an isomorphism between each pair of values. Mathlib’s component constructor requires that compatibility equation and builds the inverse natural transformation. Natural transformations are the arrows of the functor category.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FunctorPairConstructions.associatedType
declarations.label: A natural transformation and its naturality law

links.name: CategoryTheory.NatIso.ofComponents
links.label: Constructing a natural isomorphism from compatible components

links.name: CategoryTheory.Functor.category
links.label: The category whose arrows are natural transformations

Chapter7/Example7.3.2.title: The canonical double-dual map is natural
explanation: Evaluation sends v to the functional φ ↦ φ(v). The checked natural isomorphism uses this map, rather than choosing unrelated bases for each space. Its naturality proof says evaluation commutes with applying a linear map and then taking its double dual.

The functor is packaged on finitely generated modules over a field, hence on finite-dimensional vector spaces. A separate theorem says V is linearly equivalent to V** exactly when V is finite-dimensional. It rules out even a noncanonical isomorphism for an infinite-dimensional V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.FunctorEndomorphisms.finitelyGeneratedModuleDoubleDualIso
declarations.label: Evaluation gives a natural double-dual isomorphism

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.FunctorEndomorphisms.nonempty_doubleDualLinearEquiv_iff_finiteDimensional
declarations.label: When a vector space is isomorphic to its double dual

Chapter7/Example7.3.2.title: Isomorphic values need not give isomorphic functors
explanation: Here the category has only invertible arrows. Dualization sends an isomorphism a to the inverse of its dual map, so that the direction is covariant.

The checked obstruction works over every field. Naturality would make the component at a three-dimensional space commute with every linear automorphism. The proof uses transvections to show that such a map to the dual cannot be invertible. This is a statement about the whole category, not a claim that every individual dimension has the same obstruction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.FunctorEndomorphisms.isEmpty_iso_id_finitelyGeneratedModuleDualFunctor
declarations.label: There is no natural isomorphism with dualization

Chapter7/Example7.3.2.title: A natural operation on every module comes from an algebra element
explanation: For a natural endomorphism η of the forgetful functor, evaluate its component on the regular module A at 1. Calling that element a, naturality with the map A → M, x ↦ x·m, forces η_M(m) = a·m on every module.

The checked result is a ring equivalence End(F) ≃ A, including compatibility with addition and composition. It assumes an algebra over a commutative ring, not just a field, and ranges over all modules in the chosen universe; no finite-generation condition is imposed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.FunctorEndomorphisms.restrictionEndRingEquivAlgebra
declarations.label: Natural endomorphisms of the forgetful functor form the acting algebra

Chapter7/Example7.3.2.title: Why the identity functor leaves only the center
explanation: The same evaluation-at-1 argument determines a natural endomorphism of the identity functor by an element a of A. Now every component must itself be A-linear. On the regular module this forces a to commute with each element of A.
Conversely, a central element acts A-linearly on every module and commutes with every module map. The checked ring equivalence holds for any ring A, without a field or algebra hypothesis.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.FunctorEndomorphisms.moduleIdentityEndRingEquivCenter
declarations.label: Natural endomorphisms of the identity functor form the center

Chapter7/Definition7.4.1.title: A quasi-inverse up to natural isomorphism
explanation: Lean’s equivalence structure records a functor F, a quasi-inverse G, and natural isomorphisms id ≅ F ⋙ G and G ⋙ F ≅ id. It does not identify the two object types or require the composite functors to be literally equal to the identities.
The structure also includes a triangle compatibility law for the chosen unit and counit. Thus the witness carries coherent choices of the isomorphisms, beyond the existence formulation in the book.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Categories.ParameterizedType
declarations.label: An equivalence with quasi-inverse, unit and counit

links.name: CategoryTheory.Equivalence
links.label: Read the equivalence structure and triangle law

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.4..title: One object and two isomorphic objects
explanation: The checked example uses a one-element object type on one side and a two-element object type on the other, with exactly one arrow between each pair of objects. The functors send the single object to one of the two objects and send both back.
The unit and counit are natural isomorphisms, with their inverse and triangle laws checked. This is an equivalence of categories, not a bijection between their object types.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AbstractTypeEquivalence.equivalence
declarations.label: The one-object and two-object categories are equivalent

Chapter7/Discussion_after_Definition7.4..title: Finite sets and their cardinality skeleton
explanation: Mathlib’s skeleton uses natural numbers as objects and functions between the corresponding standard finite types as arrows. Its equivalence with finite types is fully faithful and essentially surjective: every finite type is isomorphic to a standard one.

The standard type Fin n is numbered from 0 to n − 1 rather than 1 to n. Choosing an identification with it is noncanonical; the equivalence does not assert that all finite sets of size n are literally the same set.

links.name: FintypeCat.Skeleton.equivalence
links.label: The equivalence between the skeleton and finite types

Chapter6/Definition6.7.1.title: The rightmost reflection acts first
explanation: The checked Coxeter action is the composition s₁ ∘ s₂ ∘ ⋯ ∘ sₙ on integer coordinate vectors. Thus it applies sₙ first, matching the sink order used in the next section. Lean numbers the vertices from 0 to n − 1 rather than 1 to n.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegerMatrixVectorCoordinateFunction.matrixVectorCoordinateValue
declarations.label: The Coxeter action on integer vectors

Chapter6/Lemma6.7.2.after: for all i, and since B is nondegenerate
Chapter6/Lemma6.7.2.title: The integer-vector result needed for dimension vectors
explanation: The checked theorem assumes a connected finite Dynkin adjacency matrix and a nonzero integer vector with nonnegative coordinates. Some Coxeter iterate has a negative coordinate. These are the hypotheses needed when applying the lemma to a representation’s dimension vector.

Its proof sums one period of the integer orbit. If all iterates stayed nonnegative, that sum would be nonzero and fixed by the Coxeter action; the fixed-vector theorem says it must be zero. The aligned result does not separately state the book’s operator-sum identity on all of ℝⁿ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegerMatrix.ReflectionDynamics.exists_iterate_apply_lt_zero
declarations.label: A nonnegative integer vector eventually leaves the positive cone

Chapter6/Section6.8_heading.title: Why the sink sequence can be repeated
explanation: Lean records an ordering containing each vertex once and checks that each is a sink after the preceding arrow reversals. A full round restores the original quiver, so the same ordering can be repeated.
The construction assumes a simple orientation of a connected finite Dynkin graph. It records the vertex list and successive quivers instead of introducing the book’s infinite sequence as one object.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverConstructions.auxiliary_exists_list_property
declarations.label: An ordering of successive sinks exists

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverConstructions.auxiliary_property_get_replicate_append_take
declarations.label: Every step in repeated rounds is a sink

Chapter6/Theorem6.8.1.title: Reaching a vertex-simple representation
explanation: For a nonzero indecomposable with finite-dimensional vertex spaces over any field, the checked reduction supplies a finite reflection list taking its dimension vector to a coordinate simple root, together with a terminal indecomposable having those dimensions. This is the stopping point of the book’s argument.

A separate arithmetic result reduces an already-known positive root to a simple root. It assumes Cartan norm two; it is not used as a substitute for proving that an arbitrary indecomposable has a root dimension vector.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverConstructions.auxiliary_exists_data_of_representation
declarations.label: Reduction of an indecomposable to a simple-root dimension

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.IntegerMatrixReflections.exists_iteratedCoordinateReflection_eq_single_of_quadraticForm_eq_two
declarations.label: Reduction of a positive root by coordinate reflections

Chapter6/Corollary6.8.2.title: What “positive root” checks
explanation: The vertex dimensions are cast to integers. The result proves that this vector is nonzero, coordinatewise nonnegative and has Cartan norm two. Reflection invariance of the pairing gives the norm equation after reduction to a simple root.
The connected Dynkin and simple-orientation assumptions from the section remain in force; this is not a claim about arbitrary quivers. No algebraic-closure hypothesis is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverConstructions.auxiliary_property_finrank
declarations.label: An indecomposable’s dimension vector is a positive root

Chapter6/Corollary6.8.3.title: Isomorphism, not equality of chosen models
explanation: The checked conclusion supplies linear equivalences at every vertex that commute with all arrow maps. It does not assert literal equality of the two representations or merely equality of their vector-space dimensions.

Both representations are nonzero indecomposables with finite-dimensional vertex spaces over the same field and the same simple Dynkin orientation. The proof reduces them in parallel and recovers an arrow-compatible isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverRepresentationRelations.auxiliary_nonempty_of_finrank_eq
declarations.label: Equal dimensions determine an indecomposable up to isomorphism

Chapter6/Corollary6.8.4.title: Constructing an indecomposable for each positive root
explanation: The checked result realizes every positive integer root as the dimension vector of an actual finite-dimensional indecomposable, for any field and any simple orientation of the connected Dynkin graph.

Its proof combines descent on root height with reflection constructions. At a source or sink it realizes a smaller root in the reversed orientation and reflects back; when the selected vertex is neither, it falls back to a successive-sink sequence. The existence result is not tied to one preselected Coxeter order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuiverRepresentationDimensions.auxiliary_exists_representation_finrank_eq
declarations.label: Every positive root is realized by an indecomposable

Chapter6/Example6.8.5.title: The first three reflections add the leaf dimensions
explanation: Here the central vertex is last: the initial vector is (0, 0, 0, 1). Reflecting at the three leaves gives (1, 1, 1, 1). The checked calculation uses indices 0, 1, 2 for those leaves; their reflections commute.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegerMatrices.integerMatrixB_operationAtZeroOneTwo_eq_ones
declarations.label: Leaf reflections send the central simple root to (1, 1, 1, 1)

Chapter6/Example6.8.5.title: The central reflection produces the three-line dimension vector
explanation: The final reflection gives (1, 1, 1, 2), with a two-dimensional central space and one-dimensional leaves. The earlier D₄ classification puts the centre first, so its tuple for the same dimensions is (2, 1, 1, 1).

These cards check the dimension calculations and the tuple’s occurrence in that classification. The arrow maps and preservation of indecomposability come from the reflection-functor results above, not from integer-vector arithmetic alone.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegerMatrices.integerMatrixB_operationAtThreeZeroOneTwo_eq_oneOneOneTwo
declarations.label: Central reflection gives (1, 1, 1, 2)

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegerMatrices.tuple2111_mem
declarations.label: The same dimensions with the centre listed first

Chapter6/Problem6.9.1.title: The four families are genuinely different
explanation: The formal model is a pair of finite-dimensional complex spaces with opposing linear maps. Its equivalences are pairs of linear equivalences intertwining both maps. The four constructors represent Eₙ,λ, Eₙ,∞, Hₙ and Kₙ, with positive n.

One result proves each representative nonzero and indecomposable; another says equivalent representatives have identical family parameters. The Jordan matrix uses the transpose convention for the off-diagonal ones, which changes the chosen basis, not its isomorphism class.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteDimensionalLinearMapPair.AuxiliaryClass.rep_auxiliaryCondition
declarations.label: Each of the four families is indecomposable

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteDimensionalLinearMapPair.AuxiliaryClass.eq_of_rep_equiv
declarations.label: Equivalent representatives have the same parameters

Chapter6/Problem6.9.1.title: A nonzero-eigenvalue Jordan block splits off
explanation: If AB is not nilpotent, the checked result supplies a subsystem equivalent to Eₙ,λ with λ ≠ 0, together with compatible embedding and retraction maps to the original pair. Their composite on the subsystem is the identity. This gives a direct summand; the remaining summand is the kernel of the retraction.
The witness type is named “Iso” in this source, but only requires a split embedding, not a two-sided inverse. It must not be read as saying the whole representation is one Jordan block.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TwoSpaceSystem.Nilpotent.TwoSpaceSystem.exists_related_nonzero_scalar_of_not_isNilpotent
declarations.label: A nonzero-eigenvalue Jordan block is a retract

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteDimensionalLinearMapPair.FiniteDimensionalLinearMapPair.Iso
links.label: The embedding, retraction and arrow-compatibility laws

Chapter6/Problem6.9.1.title: Alternating Jordan chains give the classification
explanation: The coupled operator is X(v, w) = (Bw, Av). Nilpotency of AB implies nilpotency of X. The block-basis witness records a starting vector wholly in V or W, its successive iterates and its annihilating length; the iterates from all blocks form a basis. Since X swaps the two summands, each chain alternates between them.

The final classification proves that every nonzero indecomposable pair over ℂ is equivalent to one of the four models. Its parameter is unique. These are statements about the two-vertex cycle with opposing arrows.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteDimensionalLinearMapPair.combinedEndomorphism_isNilpotent_of_comp_isNilpotent
declarations.label: Nilpotency of AB implies nilpotency of X

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TwoSpaceSystem.Nilpotent.TwoSpaceSystem.nonempty_nilpotentBlockDecomposition
declarations.label: A basis of alternating nilpotent chains exists

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TwoSpaceSystem.Nilpotent.TwoSpaceSystem.Auxiliary.property_of_compatibility
declarations.label: Every indecomposable belongs to one of the four families

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TwoSpaceSystem.Nilpotent.TwoSpaceSystem.Auxiliary.eq_of_nonempty_rep_relations
declarations.label: The classifying parameter is unique

Chapter6/Problem6.9.1.title: The harder generalizations remain outside these results
explanation: The aligned sources cover parts (a)–(c). They do not supply the classification for the Kronecker quiver in part (d), or for longer cycles and their orientations in part (e). Those questions remain in the original text without a claim of checked coverage.

Chapter6/Problem6.9.2.title: An integer lattice inside rational coordinates
explanation: Lean uses exact rational coordinates for L: either all coordinates are integers or all are integers plus ½, and their sum is an even integer. The eight listed vectors generate exactly this set by integer linear combinations.

The linked independence result says a zero integer linear combination has all coefficients zero. Together with the spanning characterization, this gives the requested ℤ-basis, not just a rational spanning family.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.rationalVectorSetC_integerSpan_characterization
declarations.label: L is the integer span of the eight displayed vectors

links.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.integralBasisVector_integer_independent
links.label: The integer coefficients are unique

links.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.integralBasisVector
links.label: The eight basis vectors, with zero-based indices

Chapter6/Problem6.9.2.title: Checking the E₈ roots and their inner products
explanation: Roots are the vectors of squared norm two in L. The checked rational-coordinate root-set structure proves finiteness, closure under negation and reflections, integral pairings and the reduced-root condition. The eight basis vectors have the E₈ Cartan pairings, up to a recorded relabeling of the Dynkin graph.
This is an explicit rational-coordinate model. The root-set predicate itself does not assert spanning; the preceding basis results supply that part separately.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RationalVectorRootSystems.eightVectorAuxiliarySet_isCrystallographicRootSet
declarations.label: The norm-two vectors satisfy the root-set axioms

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RationalVectorRootSystems.eightRationalVectors_configuration
declarations.label: The explicit vectors have the E₈ Dynkin configuration

Chapter6/Problem6.9.2.title: E₇ and E₆ are coordinate slices
explanation: The E₇ set imposes x₀ = x₁; the E₆ set imposes x₀ = x₁ = x₂. These are the first two and three coordinates in the book’s one-based convention. The paired results check the E₇ and E₆ Cartan matrices of explicit seven- and six-vector families in these slices.

These matrix computations identify the Dynkin configurations; they are not, by themselves, proofs that the smaller families are integer bases of the complete slice lattices. The aligned results do not separately provide those two integer-span characterizations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.Auxiliary.rationalVectorSetB
declarations.label: The E₇ slice: the first two coordinates agree

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.Auxiliary.rationalVectorSetA
declarations.label: The E₆ slice: the first three coordinates agree

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RationalVectorRootSystems.sevenRationalVectors_integerPairingMatrix_eq_adjacency
declarations.label: The seven-vector Gram matrix is the E₇ Cartan matrix

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RationalVectorRootSystems.sixRationalVectors_integerPairingMatrix_eq_adjacency
declarations.label: The six-vector Gram matrix is the E₆ Cartan matrix

Chapter6/Problem6.9.2.title: Counting all roots, not only the positive ones
explanation: For E₈ the integer roots are ±eᵢ ±eⱼ with i < j: 28 choices of positions and four sign choices give 112. The half-integer roots have all coordinates ±½ with an even number of plus signs, giving 128 more. Thus there are 240 roots.
Filtering these same two families by the equal-coordinate conditions gives 126 roots for E₇ and 72 for E₆. These totals include both signs; the earlier counts of positive roots were 120, 63 and 36.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.ncard_setTransform_rationalVectorSetA
declarations.label: E₆ has 72 roots

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.ncard_setTransform_rationalVectorSetB
declarations.label: E₇ has 126 roots

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.EightDimensionalRationalVectors.ncard_setTransform_rationalVectorSetC
declarations.label: E₈ has 240 roots

Chapter6/Problem6.9.3.title: The checked obstruction criterion is not a packaged Ext¹ theorem
explanation: The aligned result proves surjectivity of the map sending vertex maps f to the arrow maps W(a) ∘ f_source − f_target ∘ V(a). For W equal to the simple at a source, or V equal to the simple at a sink, the target arrow-map space is zero, so surjectivity is immediate.

This is the concrete obstruction criterion used for splitting extensions of quiver representations. The supplied results do not identify its cokernel with a categorical Ext¹ object or separately prove the two displayed Ext¹-vanishing statements.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Auxiliary.any_relates_to_auxiliaryObjectAtVertex
declarations.label: The obstruction map is surjective into a source simple

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Auxiliary.auxiliaryObjectAtVertex_relates_to_any
declarations.label: The obstruction map is surjective out of a sink simple

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Auxiliary.auxiliaryRelation
links.label: The relation means surjectivity of the arrow-map obstruction

Chapter6/Problem6.9.3.title: A series of actual subrepresentations
explanation: Choose a vertex order in which every arrow points toward an earlier vertex, and choose a basis at each vertex. Adding basis vectors in that order gives an arrow-stable chain from zero to the whole representation. Each successive quotient is the one-dimensional simple at the vertex whose basis vector was added.

The checked witness contains the subrepresentations and surjective maps onto these simples, with the preceding subrepresentation as kernel—not just a list of dimensions. Its length is the sum of the vertex dimensions, and the simple at i occurs αᵢ times. The general construction works for any finite acyclic quiver with the stated order and finite bases; the final card specializes it to a positive-root Dynkin indecomposable.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverRepresentation.VertexCompositionSeries.IsElementaryExtensionAt
declarations.label: One step has vertex-simple quotient

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverRepresentation.VertexCompositionSeries.VertexCompositionSeries
declarations.label: The chain and its vertex-simple successive quotients

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverRepresentation.VertexCompositionSeries.exists_vertexCompositionSeries_with_multiplicity
declarations.label: Construct the chain and count each simple factor

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Auxiliary.existsAuxiliaryDataWithVertexValues
declarations.label: The length is the total dimension

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.VertexOrder.Quiver.exists_witness_with_prescribed_values
declarations.label: A Dynkin positive root has a realizing representation and series

Chapter6/Definition6.6.1.title: Sinks and sources are conditions on arrow types
explanation: Lean expresses a sink by requiring every outgoing arrow type i → j to be empty, and a source by requiring every incoming arrow type j → i to be empty. This includes j = i, so either condition excludes loops at i.
An isolated vertex satisfies both conditions. No field, representation or dimension hypothesis is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverVertexPredicates.vertexProperty
declarations.label: A sink has no outgoing arrows

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverVertexPredicates.vertexCondition
declarations.label: A source has no incoming arrows

Chapter6/Definition6.6.2.title: Keep the vertices, reverse the incident arrows
explanation: The construction changes the quiver’s arrow types, not its vertex set. Away from i, an arrow a → b stays the same; an original arrow j → i becomes an arrow i → j, and conversely.
The arrow-type definition works at any selected vertex. The sink or source hypothesis is needed when defining the corresponding reflection functor.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverVertexReversal.reversedAtHom
declarations.label: Arrow types after reversal at i

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuiverVertexReversal.reverseAtVertex
links.label: The reversed quiver on the same vertices

Chapter6/Definition6.6.3.title: The new sink space is a kernel
explanation: The incoming direct sum is indexed by arrows, each paired with its source vertex. Thus parallel arrows contribute separate summands. The map φ adds their images in Vᵢ; kernel reflection replaces Vᵢ by ker φ and leaves every other space unchanged.

The checked functor also acts on representation morphisms and proves the identity and composition laws. Its construction works over a commutative semiring, without finite-dimensionality or finiteness of the incoming-arrow set.

Chapter6/Definition6.6.3_maps.title: Arrow maps and representation morphisms are different maps
explanation: For a reversed arrow i → j, the new arrow map includes ker φ into the incoming direct sum and then projects onto Vⱼ. The final Vᵢ in the printed projection paragraph is an indexing typo: the target must be the summand belonging to j. The linked construction uses that target.

A morphism between two original representations gives a componentwise map between their direct sums. Compatibility with the arrows makes it carry one kernel into the other; restricting this map gives the reflected morphism at i.

Chapter6/Definition6.6.4.title: The source construction is the cokernel counterpart
explanation: The outgoing map ψ records all images of a vector in Vᵢ. Reflection replaces Vᵢ by the outgoing direct sum modulo im ψ. A reversed arrow j → i uses the inclusion of Vⱼ into its summand followed by the quotient map.

The checked functor works over a commutative ring and assumes finitely many outgoing arrows at i, so these components define a map into the direct sum. It does not require finite-dimensional vertex spaces merely to construct the functor.

Chapter6/Proposition6.6.5.title: The only exception is the simple supported at i
explanation: The exceptional predicate says that Vᵢ has dimension one and all other vertex spaces have dimension zero. Otherwise, an indecomposable has a surjective incoming map at a sink or an injective outgoing map at a source.

The proofs split off a complement to the incoming image or the outgoing kernel, just as in the book. They assume a field and finite-dimensional vertex spaces; the source statement also assumes finitely many outgoing arrows.

Chapter6/Proposition6.6.6.title: Recovery means an isomorphism compatible with every arrow
explanation: At a surjective sink, taking the cokernel of the kernel inclusion recovers Vᵢ. At an injective source, taking the kernel of the quotient map recovers Vᵢ. Elsewhere the spaces are unchanged.

The checked conclusions supply vertexwise linear equivalences commuting with every arrow map, after identifying the twice-reversed quiver with the original one. This gives isomorphic representations, not literal equality of their underlying types. Both results assume finite-dimensional spaces and the finite arrow set needed for the cokernel construction.

Chapter6/Proposition6.6.7.title: Zero is a separate outcome, not an indecomposable
explanation: The two checked results cover kernel reflection at a sink and cokernel reflection at a source. Their zero alternative means that every reflected vertex space is a subsingleton; the indecomposable alternative includes a nonzero requirement.

The proof separates off the vertex-simple case, which reflection sends to zero. In the other case, compatible splittings of the reflected representation are pulled back to splittings of the original. The hypotheses are finite-dimensional spaces over a field, with finitely many outgoing arrows for the source construction.

Chapter6/Proposition6.6.8.title: Rank–nullity gives the reflection formula
explanation: At i, the new dimension is the sum of incident-arrow source or target dimensions minus dᵢ; every other coordinate is unchanged. The theorems cast finrank from ℕ to ℤ so this subtraction is ordinary integer subtraction, not truncated natural subtraction.

Surjectivity gives the kernel dimension formula; injectivity gives the quotient dimension formula. Both require finite-dimensional spaces and finitely many relevant arrows. In the simple Dynkin setting, this coordinate rule is the simple-root reflection sᵢ from the preceding root section.

Chapter6/Definition6.4.1.title: Adjacency R, Cartan matrix A and pairing B
explanation: The definition takes the graph’s integer adjacency matrix R and returns A = 2I − R. For a simple loopless graph, A has diagonal entries 2 and off-diagonal entries −1 at edges and 0 otherwise.
The pairing B(x, y) is the dot product of x with Ay. The checked definition and the linked pairing use integer-valued vectors; the book also considers the same matrix on real space.

Chapter6/Lemma6.4.2.title: Positive even norms are at least two
explanation: The Dynkin matrix hypothesis includes strict positivity of xᵀAx for every nonzero integer vector. The first checked statement extracts that lattice positivity; its displayed type does not separately quantify over real vectors.

Evenness needs only symmetry and zero diagonal of R, not the whole Dynkin classification. Pairing the off-diagonal terms (i, j) and (j, i) makes their sum twice an integer, while each diagonal term is 2xᵢ². Thus a nonzero lattice vector has norm at least 2.

Chapter6/Definition6.4.3.title: The root predicate uses the norm-two characterization
explanation: Lean defines a root as a nonzero integer vector whose Cartan norm is 2. It does not define an optimization problem over all lattice vectors.

For a Dynkin graph, positivity and evenness give a minimum nonzero norm of at least 2, and each coordinate simple root has norm 2. This explains why the norm-two predicate describes the shortest nonzero lattice vectors here. The predicate alone does not assume the graph is Dynkin.

Chapter6/Remark6.4.4.title: A finite box instead of a real ball
explanation: The source proves finiteness arithmetically. For a positive root d, every coordinate of Ad lies between −2 and 2; the proof compares the norm of d with those of d ± αᵢ. Strict positivity also makes d ↦ Ad injective.

Thus positive roots inject into the finite integer box [−2, 2]ⁿ. The sign lemma below puts every root in the positive set or its negative, so the full root set is finite. This is a different route from the book’s bounded-ball argument.

Chapter6/Definition6.4.5.title: Simple roots are the coordinate basis
explanation: The checked function Pi.single i 1 is 1 at vertex i and 0 elsewhere. Lean indexes the n vertices by Fin n, whose values run from 0 to n − 1; this is a relabeling of the book’s 1 through n.
These coordinate vectors form the integer lattice’s usual basis. With zero diagonal of R, their Cartan norm is 2, so they are roots as well as basis vectors.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryFiniteIndexIntegerFunction.auxiliaryValue

links.label: Coordinate simple roots satisfy the root predicate

Chapter6/Lemma6.4.6.title: Lean splits by signs instead of cutting an edge
explanation: The source sets βᵢ = max(xᵢ, 0) and γᵢ = min(xᵢ, 0). If x has both signs, β and γ are nonzero, x = β + γ and βᵢγᵢ = 0 at every vertex.

Positivity and evenness give B(β, β) ≥ 2 and B(γ, γ) ≥ 2. Off-diagonal Cartan entries are nonpositive, so the cross terms between β ≥ 0 and γ ≤ 0 are nonnegative. The total norm is therefore at least 4, contradicting the root norm 2.
This proves the same conclusion without choosing an edge or constructing the two component graphs in the printed proof.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IntegralVectorSign.all_nonnegative_or_all_nonpositive
declarations.label: Every root has all coordinates nonnegative or all nonpositive

Chapter6/Definition6.4.7.title: Positive does not mean every coordinate is strictly positive
explanation: A positive root has norm two and all coordinates at least zero; some coordinates may vanish. A negative root has the same norm condition and all coordinates at most zero. Both predicates retain the root’s nonzero requirement.
The sign lemma shows that every root belongs to one of these sets. No root belongs to both, because that would force every coordinate to be zero.

Chapter6/Example6.4.9.title: Adjacent differences identify the A-type lattice
explanation: Lean maps a coefficient vector in ℤⁿ to the corresponding sum of adjacent differences eᵢ − eᵢ₊₁ in ℤⁿ⁺¹. A prefix-sum map supplies the inverse on the zero-sum sublattice.
The source proves this is an integer-linear equivalence and verifies that the ordinary dot product of two images is their Aₙ Cartan pairing. Here the source’s n is the book’s N − 1.

Chapter6/Example6.4.9.title: A positive root is a consecutive interval of simple roots
explanation: In the zero-sum model, norm two forces exactly two nonzero coordinates, one 1 and one −1. The checked characterization identifies all roots as eᵢ − eⱼ with i ≠ j.

When i < j, the coefficients in the adjacent-difference basis are 1 from i through j − 1 and zero elsewhere. Choosing these ordered positions gives n(n + 1)/2 positive roots of Aₙ. The cardinality statement counts this explicit strict-pair image.

Chapter6/Example6.4.9.title: The D and E numbers count positive roots
explanation: The source sets contain nonzero norm-two vectors with nonnegative coordinates. Thus these are the positive-root counts, not the size of the full root system; including their negatives doubles each number.

For Dₙ the theorem assumes n ≥ 4 and gives n(n − 1). The exceptional types give 36, 63 and 120. Coordinate bounds reduce these infinite integer sets to bounded finite collections; the source verifies the D-type counting argument and the exceptional finite calculations.

Chapter6/Definition6.4.10.title: Why the reflection formula has no denominator
explanation: The general reflection formula subtracts 2B(v, α)/B(α, α) times α. Since a root has norm two, this becomes v − B(v, α)α. Integer pairings make it an integral lattice map.

The checked general formula accepts a matrix A and a vector α without automatically assuming they are Cartan data and a root. The simple-reflection definition substitutes the coordinate vector αᵢ. In both definitions A means the Cartan matrix, not the adjacency R.

Chapter6/Remark6.4.11.title: The checked reflections act on the integer lattice
explanation: With a symmetric matrix A and B(α, α) = 2, the source proves that reflection fixes vectors paired to zero with α, sends α to −α and preserves the pairing of any two vectors. It also proves that applying the reflection twice is the identity.

The Weyl group in the source is the subgroup of integer-linear automorphisms generated by the simple reflections. This is the lattice action behind the book’s real orthogonal action; the displayed theorems do not package a separate subgroup of O(ℝⁿ).

Chapter6/Remark6.4.11.title: Finiteness needs a faithful action on the roots
explanation: Preserving a finite root set gives a homomorphism to its permutation group. To conclude that the Weyl group is finite, the source also proves this homomorphism is injective.

If two lattice automorphisms agree on every root, they agree on the coordinate simple roots. Those form a basis, so the automorphisms are equal. The Weyl group therefore embeds in the finite permutation group of all roots.

Chapter6/Definition6.5.1.title: Dimensions are recorded vertex by vertex
explanation: The checked function assigns Module.finrank k (spaces v) to each vertex v. Its values are natural numbers; the root statements later cast them to integers so they lie in the Cartan lattice.

This function records only the family of vertex spaces, not the arrow maps. Different representations can have the same dimension vector. Gabriel’s uniqueness below applies to indecomposables of Dynkin type, not to arbitrary representations.

Chapter6/Theorem6.5.2.title: Every positive root gives one isomorphism class
explanation: The first checked statement realizes each positive root as a finite-dimensional indecomposable representation and shows that any two indecomposables with that vector are isomorphic. ‘Exactly one’ is uniqueness up to isomorphism, not a unique choice of spaces, bases or arrow matrices.
The combined statement adds that every indecomposable dimension vector is a positive root and that the root set is finite. Together these give the claimed finite classification.

The hypotheses are a connected simple Dynkin adjacency matrix and an orientation with at most one arrow between any two vertices. The theorem works over any field; no algebraic-closure hypothesis is present.

Chapter6/Theorem6.5.2.title: The norm-two condition connects the two sides
explanation: A nonzero, nonnegative dimension vector of Cartan norm two satisfies the positive-root predicate. The source proves the norm-two property for indecomposables, then applies this small predicate lemma.

The separate finiteness statement uses the finite-box argument from the root discussion. Existence and uniqueness come from the underlying Dynkin representation constructions, not from finiteness of the root set alone.

Chapter6/Problem6.1.6.title: Tensor multiplicities from intertwiner spaces
explanation: Lean lists the irreducible complex representations as a complete family W: each entry is simple, no two entries are isomorphic, and every simple representation occurs. The multiplicity rᵢⱼ is the dimension of the intertwiner space Hom(Wᵢ, V ⊗ Wⱼ), where V is the two-dimensional representation from the subgroup’s inclusion into SU(2).
The symmetry proof expresses this dimension as a character sum and changes g to g⁻¹. The character of V has the same value at g and g⁻¹, so the two indices can be interchanged.

Chapter6/Problem6.1.6.title: Connectivity means a path of nonzero multiplicities
explanation: The checked statement produces a finite list joining any two irreducible indices; each consecutive multiplicity is at least one. Thus it proves connectivity of the graph, not a direct edge between every pair.
The source uses the faithful two-dimensional representation and occurrence in its tensor powers. Character identities propagate occurrence along tensor-product edges.
