Chapter5/Proposition5.21.1.title: Why decreasing exponent tuples suffice
explanation: In characteristic zero an alternating polynomial has zero coefficient whenever two exponents agree: swapping those positions negates the coefficient but leaves the monomial unchanged. Every tuple with distinct exponents can be permuted into decreasing order, with the corresponding sign.

Homogeneity then forces a decreasing tuple to be λ+ρ for a unique padded partition of n. In Dλ, only the identity permutation contributes to that decreasing monomial, with coefficient one. The source compares these coefficients after multiplying by D₀, then cancels the nonzero polynomial D₀. It follows the book's coefficient argument, rather than dividing at particular values of the variables.

Chapter5/Proposition5.21.2.title: When the geometric-progression fraction is defined
explanation: The complex-valued checked formula assumes z ≠ 0 and that every denominator z^(−i) − z^(−j) is nonzero for i < j. These are genuine restrictions on the fraction, not on the Schur polynomial itself. For N ≥ 2, z = 1 violates the denominator condition; other roots of unity can do so too.
The Lean indices are zero-based, so its negative powers use −i−1 rather than the book's −i. Evaluation sends xᵢ to zⁱ, producing (1,z,…,z^(N−1)).

Chapter5/Proposition5.21.2.title: At one, use a separate polynomial identity
explanation: For decreasing λ, the checked all-ones value is the product of λᵢ − λⱼ + j − i divided by the product of j − i. This result is stated over ℚ. Each denominator is a positive integer, so none vanishes there; no restriction on z or analytic limiting hypothesis is involved.
Empty products also cover N = 0 and N = 1. The decreasing-tuple hypothesis is explicit, unlike the geometric-progression identities, which accept any natural exponent tuple.

Chapter5/Proposition5.21.2.title: Cancel geometric sums instead of using L'Hôpital
explanation: Specializing the determinant makes its transpose a Vandermonde matrix. Its factors are yⱼ − yᵢ, where yᵢ = z^(λᵢ+N−i); the book's proof writes the opposite order. Reversing every factor contributes the same sign to numerator and denominator, so the quotient formula is unchanged. Using nonnegative exponents gives the ratio of products of z^(λᵢ+N−i) − z^(λⱼ+N−j) and z^(N−i) − z^(N−j). The checked version below works in any characteristic-zero field when the denominator factors are nonzero. A denominator-cleared identity holds even when they vanish.

For the all-ones value, the proof factors each difference as (1−z) times a power of z times a finite geometric sum. It cancels the common powers of 1−z for rational z ≠ 1, then promotes the result to a polynomial identity because it holds at infinitely many rational values. Evaluating that identity at 1 turns the geometric sums into the exponent differences. Thus Lean proves the book's limiting value algebraically, without formalizing the L'Hôpital argument.

Chapter5/Proposition5.19.1.title: Invertible maps already span the tensor-action algebra
explanation: GL(V) is represented by the invertible k-linear maps V ≃ₗ[k] V. Its action here sends g to g⊗⋯⊗g on E = V⊗⋯⊗V. The proposition is about their linear span, not just the subalgebra they generate.

The first statement works over any infinite field: invertible factorwise maps span the algebra generated by all endomorphism powers b⊗⋯⊗b. The second statement identifies that span with Endₐ(E) in characteristic zero, using Section 5.18. Neither requires k to be algebraically closed.

Chapter5/Proposition5.19.1.title: Interpolation gives an explicit linear combination
explanation: Only finitely many shifts b+t·1 are singular: their parameters are roots of the nonzero characteristic polynomial of −b. Over an infinite field, choose n+1 distinct good parameters tᵢ.

The tensor map (b+t·1)⊗⋯⊗(b+t·1) has degree at most n in t. Evaluating its Lagrange interpolation formula at zero gives b⊗⋯⊗b = ∑ᵢ Lᵢ(0)(b+tᵢ·1)⊗⋯⊗(b+tᵢ·1). Every term is an invertible tensor action, so the sum belongs to B′.

This is the proof used in Lean. It replaces the book's argument with an annihilating linear functional by a concrete interpolation identity. The formula includes n=0, when the tensor action is the identity on k.

Chapter5/Corollary5.19.2.title: GL(V) acts on the multiplicity spaces by postcomposition
explanation: A permutation of the tensor factors commutes with every g⊗⋯⊗g. Thus g acts on a multiplicity map f by f ↦ (g⊗⋯⊗g)∘f, preserving its Sₙ-equivariance. The Specht factor carries the permutation action, while the multiplicity factor carries the GL(V) action.

By Proposition 5.19.1, invariance under all invertible tensor actions is equivalent to invariance under their span B. This is why simple, pairwise inequivalent B-modules give simple, pairwise inequivalent GL(V) representations in the book's decomposition.

The result below supplies partition-labelled simple A-submodules, equivariant Specht identifications, their Hom multiplicity spaces, and a decomposition compatible with A and B. It assumes k is algebraically closed as well as characteristic zero. It is not a separately bundled Sₙ×GL(V) representation isomorphism, nor a proof of the corollary over every characteristic-zero field.

Chapter5/Example5.19.3.title: The one-row factor consists of symmetric tensors
explanation: For the one-row partition, the Specht representation is trivial. Evaluating a map from the one-dimensional trivial representation identifies its multiplicity space with the tensors fixed by every permutation.

Lean defines this invariant subspace by the equations σ·x=x. The symmetric-power quotient map restricts to an isomorphism from it to Symⁿ(V); averaging tensor permutations and dividing by n! gives the inverse. This makes the invariant and quotient realizations used in the preceding section compatible.
The second statement checks that the identification commutes with every induced endomorphism of V, hence with the GL(V) action. These results work over any characteristic-zero field.

Chapter5/Example5.19.3.title: Irreducibility requires the power to be nonzero
explanation: The invariant-subspace conclusion is W=0 or W=the whole power, for every subspace stable under GL(V). Together with nonzeroness, this says that the representation is irreducible. The symmetric-power result is linked below; both proofs were discussed in Problem 4.12.3.

For exterior powers, the dimension is binomial(dim V,n), so Λⁿ(V)=0 when n>dim V. Lean expresses the zero vector space by Subsingleton. There is also a symmetric-power edge case: Symⁿ(0)=0 for n>0, so it is not a nonzero irreducible representation. At n=0, both powers are k.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.1.title: The first two conclusions do not require a splitting field
explanation: The centralizer is the subalgebra of k-linear endomorphisms commuting with every element of A. Lean checks that its centralizer is A, and that it is semisimple, for any field k and finite-dimensional E with a faithful semisimple A-action.

The double-centralizer proof uses Jacobson density on a finite spanning set. Semisimplicity is transferred from the ring of A-linear endomorphisms. These arguments do not require the scalar form of Schur's lemma used in the book's tensor-product proof.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.1.title: The tensor factors are simple modules and their multiplicity spaces
explanation: For a simple A-submodule Vᵢ, the second factor is Wᵢ = Homₐ(Vᵢ,E). The inverse of the decomposition sends v⊗f in the i-th summand to f(v). A acts on v; an element b of B acts on f by postcomposition, f ↦ b∘f. The checked decomposition records compatibility with both actions, not only an equality of dimensions.

The tensor-evaluation result below assumes k is algebraically closed. That assumption is not needed for conclusions (i) and (ii); it supplies the scalar endomorphism form of Schur's lemma for this decomposition. Over a nonsplitting field, the general simple-module decomposition involves its endomorphism division algebra, rather than automatically this tensor product over k.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.1.title: The correspondence classifies simple types, not individual copies
explanation: An isotypic component is the sum of all simple submodules of one isomorphism type. The checked correspondence pairs the A-isotypic components with the B-isotypic components using their multiplicity spaces.

A further theorem shows that every simple B-module is isomorphic to Homₐ(V,E) for some simple A-submodule V of E. These correspondence results also assume an algebraically closed field. Choosing an isomorphic representative for V changes its Hom space by precomposition, giving an isomorphic B-module.

Chapter5/Discussion_before_Theorem5.18.2.title: Two commuting actions on the same tensor power
explanation: The tensor power E is represented as a tensor product indexed by Fin n, whose labels are 0,…,n−1. Permutations act by reindexing tensor factors. The algebra A is the image of k[Sₙ] under this action; it need not be a faithful image of the entire group algebra.

An endomorphism b of V acts infinitesimally on E by the sum Δₙ(b), acting on one factor at a time and leaving the others unchanged. This is a Lie algebra homomorphism for the bracket ab−ba, and it extends to an algebra homomorphism from U(gl(V)). It is not the factorwise map b⊗⋯⊗b.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.2.title: The enveloping-algebra image is the full commuting algebra
explanation: For finite-dimensional V over a characteristic-zero field, the checked equality says that the endomorphisms commuting with A are exactly the image of U(gl(V)) acting through Δₙ. No algebraic-closure assumption is used here.

The word image matters: the theorem identifies a subalgebra of Endₖ(E), not U(gl(V)) itself with B. In the Lean statement, the subalgebra on the left is generated by permutation reindexings, and the range on the right is the enveloping-algebra action.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.2.title: Commuting endomorphisms are permutation-invariant tensors
explanation: The book's SⁿEnd(V) here means the permutation-invariant tensors inside End(V)⊗⋯⊗End(V), acting on V⊗⋯⊗V. A commuting endomorphism is fixed by conjugation with each permutation operator.

Lean expresses an endomorphism as a linear combination of factorwise maps, sums its permutation conjugates, and divides by n!. Since the original endomorphism is invariant, this recovers it inside the algebra generated by f⊗⋯⊗f. The linked generator equality then puts this algebra inside the enveloping-algebra image. Characteristic zero makes n! invertible.

Chapter5/Lemma5.18.3.title: Polarization spans the symmetric power by pure powers
explanation: The checked spanning theorem uses Lean's symmetric-power quotient: tensors are identified when their factors are permuted. Its designated subset consists of the classes of u⊗⋯⊗u.

Instead of using irreducibility of GL(U), the proof expands an alternating sum over subsets of {0,…,n−1}. That sum equals n! times any symmetric pure tensor. Dividing by n! expresses it as a linear combination of repeated-vector powers. The theorem does not require U to be finite-dimensional and also includes n=0.

The book uses the invariant-tensor realization of SⁿU. In characteristic zero, averaging over permutations identifies that realization with the symmetric quotient. The spanning statement below is about the quotient; the centralizer proof handles invariant tensor endomorphisms by averaging directly.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PiTensorProduct.Constructions.span_symmetricPowerSubset_eq_top
declarations.label: Pure powers span Symⁿ(U)
declarations.documentation: The subset is the range of u ↦ the symmetric class of u⊗⋯⊗u; its linear span is the whole symmetric-power quotient.

links.label: Definition of the repeated-vector subset

Chapter5/Lemma5.18.3.title: Newton identities recover tensor powers from Δₙ
explanation: The checked algebra equality compares two subalgebras of A⊗⋯⊗A: one generated by all Δₙ(a), the other by all a⊗⋯⊗a. It works for any unital k-algebra A, not necessarily commutative or finite-dimensional.

For a fixed a, the n elements obtained by putting a in one tensor factor commute with each other. Newton identities can therefore be evaluated in the commutative subalgebra they generate. Recursively dividing by the positive integers recovers their product a⊗⋯⊗a from the power sums Δₙ(aʲ).

For the reverse containment, the proof extracts the coefficients of (t·1+a)⊗⋯⊗(t·1+a) using a Vandermonde matrix evaluated at 0,…,n. The coefficient of tⁿ⁻¹ is Δₙ(a). The equality includes n=0, where the sum is zero and the empty tensor product supplies the scalar unit. This compares generated algebras; it does not give the symmetric-power quotient a multiplication when A is noncommutative.
This is also the generator step used in Theorem 5.18.2; the book's closing sentence returns to that theorem.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PiTensorProduct.Constructions.piTensorSubalgebra_eq_alternate
declarations.label: Δₙ(a) and a⊗⋯⊗a generate the same tensor subalgebra
declarations.documentation: The equality is between subalgebras of the ordinary n-fold tensor product of A over a characteristic-zero field.

Chapter5/Discussion_before_Theorem5.18.4.title: Maschke applies to the image even when the action has a kernel
explanation: In characteristic zero, |Sₙ| = n! is nonzero and hence invertible in k. Maschke's theorem makes k[Sₙ] semisimple, and semisimplicity passes to its surjective image A in Endₖ(E).

A acts faithfully on E because it is the actual image subalgebra of endomorphisms. This does not assert that the map k[Sₙ] → Endₖ(E) is injective. These are the hypotheses needed for the double-centralizer theorem.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.4.title: Mutual centralizers over any characteristic-zero field
explanation: The checked theorem gives both centralizer equalities. In its statement, B is defined as the algebra generated by the factorwise powers f⊗⋯⊗f, with f any endomorphism of V. Theorem 5.18.2 and the generator equality identify it with the image of U(gl(V)); it is not defined as gl(V) itself.
The reverse centralizer equality then follows from semisimplicity of the permutation-action image and the double-centralizer theorem. Neither equality requires k to be algebraically closed.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.4.title: Both image algebras are semisimple
explanation: Lean checks the semisimplicity of A and B as rings over any characteristic-zero field. For B, it uses the centralizer theorem rather than claiming that the enveloping algebra itself is semisimple.

Because the action of gl(V) generates B through U(gl(V)), invariant subspaces for this Lie action are exactly B-submodules. Thus semisimplicity of B supplies the semisimple tensor representation discussed in the book.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Auxiliary.MutualCentralizers.associatedSubalgebras_semisimple
declarations.label: The permutation and enveloping-action images are semisimple
declarations.documentation: This statement concerns their finite-dimensional images in Endₖ(E), not the full group or enveloping algebras.

Chapter5/Theorem5.18.4.title: The partition-labelled decomposition has a stronger field assumption
explanation: For this part, the checked decomposition assumes k is algebraically closed as well as characteristic zero. The surrounding book discussion starts with an arbitrary characteristic-zero field; the declarations below do not establish the decomposition in that full generality.

The first result chooses simple A-submodules Sᵢ, assigns distinct partition labels, and identifies each Sᵢ equivariantly with the corresponding Specht module. Its multiplicity space is Homₐ(Sᵢ,E), a simple B-module; inequivalent Sᵢ give inequivalent multiplicity spaces. The decomposition records compatibility with the A- and B-actions.

The second result packages the factors into a direct sum over all partitions. An unused label has zero factors, represented by Subsingleton types; a used label has simple factors. Its statement alone only asserts a k-linear equivalence and does not explicitly name the canonical Specht modules or record intertwining. Those identifications and action laws are supplied by the first result, not by reading extra claims into the bare linear equivalence.

declarations.label: Simple tensor factors have distinct Specht labels and compatible actions
declarations.documentation: This is the checked indexed decomposition, including equivariant Specht identifications and simple, pairwise distinct multiplicity spaces.

declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, the nonzero Lλ are pairwise inequivalent as B-modules. This declaration packages a linear equivalence.

Chapter5/Discussion_hook_length_derivati.title: The falling-factorial determinant computes the dimension coefficient
explanation: At the identity permutation, the cycle partition is n copies of 1, so the power-sum polynomial is (x₁+⋯+xN)ⁿ. The linked trace calculation identifies its shifted Vandermonde coefficient with dim Vλ. The source computes this coefficient over ℚ and evaluates the falling-factorial polynomials over ℤ.

The checked formula below is the factorial prefactor times the determinant just obtained in the book. In the determinant expansion, a falling factorial is zero when its degree exceeds its argument. This accounts for the inequality in the book's first sum without taking a factorial of a negative integer.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.YoungDiagram.PartitionFormulas.auxiliary_partition_value_eq_descPochhammer_determinant_formula

Chapter5/Discussion_hook_length_derivati.title: Monic polynomials give the same determinant as powers
explanation: Each degree-d falling-factorial polynomial is monic with lower-degree terms. Replacing the power columns by these polynomials is a triangular change of columns with diagonal entries one, so it preserves the determinant. The first theorem checks that equality without needing the lj to be distinct.

For the partition formula, lj = λj+N−j is strictly decreasing. The second theorem gives the book's product of positive differences li−lj. Lean's row labels start at zero, so its shift is N−1−i; the exponent list is N−1,…,0. Reversing both row and column order in the Vandermonde calculation leaves the determinant unchanged.
The source packages the padded row lengths as a decreasing N-tuple of natural numbers summing to n. Thus N is independent of n, and any N at least the number of rows can represent λ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.YoungDiagram.PartitionFormulas.det_descPochhammer_eval_eq_det_pow

declarations.documentation: This identity is proved over ℤ for any natural-number evaluation vector.

declarations.documentation: The natural dimension is cast into ℚ for the quotient formula; the differences are positive.

Chapter5/Discussion_hook_length_derivati.title: Hook lengths count the starting cell once
explanation: The book writes (column, row), with both labels starting at 1. Lean writes (row, column), with both starting at 0. At a cell (r,c), its hook length is rowLen(r)+colLen(c)−r−c−1: the cells to the right, the cells below, and the starting cell counted once.
The hook-product definition multiplies those lengths over all cells of the diagram. Each factor is positive; for an empty diagram the product is one.
One supporting finite set in the source omits the starting cell and contains only the strict arm and leg. It is not the book's full hook: the linked result checks that its cardinality is h−1.

Chapter5/Theorem5.17.1.title: The checked dimension formula uses an exact integer quotient
explanation: The theorem computes the complex dimension of the source Specht ideal for every partition of n. The linked equivariant ideal equivalence identifies this representation with the book's Vλ.

Its right-hand side uses natural-number division, not rational division. This is not an approximation: the linked divisibility theorem proves Hλ divides n!, and Hλ is positive. The empty partition is included, with 0! = 1 and empty hook product 1.

Chapter5/Theorem5.17.1.title: The cancellation is checked; the final dimension proof passes through tableaux
explanation: The source checks the book's cancellation row by row. For row i, its hook lengths together with the differences li−lk for k>i partition the factors 1,…,li. Multiplying these row identities gives Hλ∏i<j(li−lj) = ∏i li!, the cancellation required by (5.17.1). The first link below opens that checked identity.

The final dimension theorem proceeds through the equality below: dim Vλ is the number of standard tableaux of shape λ. Here a standard tableau is a bijective filling by 0,…,n−1 increasing across rows and down columns, not an arbitrary filling. A separate counting proof removes the largest entry at a removable corner and uses a hook-product identity to obtain the factorial quotient.
The coefficient/dimension bridge, row cancellation and tableau count are all checked, but this dependency route differs from treating the book's first-row induction as the entire proof.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.1.title: Restriction removes one corner
explanation: The checked restriction rule uses μ of size n+1 and the subgroup Sₙ that fixes the last label. Its finite index set consists of diagrams of size n contained in μ: because their sizes differ by one, these are exactly R(μ). Each resulting Specht representation occurs once.

The type asserts the existence of an isomorphism, not literal equality of representations. Its right-hand side is a coordinatewise finite product; the linked isomorphism identifies that product with the book's finite direct sum. The proof compares characters and then uses character rigidity.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.1.title: Induction adds one corner
explanation: For induction, μ now partitions n, and the result is a representation of Sₙ₊₁. The summands are indexed by diagrams of size n+1 containing μ, hence by A(μ), again with multiplicity one.

The proof uses Frobenius reciprocity to compute the multiplicity of each simple representation from the restriction rule. It then identifies the induced representation with the finite sum by matching these multiplicities. Nonempty in the statement means that an equivariant linear isomorphism exists.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.2.title: The content is the scalar for the central transposition sum
explanation: Lean sums column minus row over the cells of λ, with both coordinates starting at zero. Shifting both coordinates by one leaves their difference unchanged, so this integer is the book's c(λ). The group-algebra element sums each transposition once, using i < j.

The action theorem is written as Cx = c(λ) • x for every x in the source Specht ideal. Thus it describes scalar action on the whole module, not just on its Young-symmetrizer generator. The previously established equivalence transfers it to the book's Vλ.

The proof first checks that C is central, so Schur's lemma makes its action scalar. It finds that scalar from the coefficient of the identity in C times the Young symmetrizer: transpositions within a row contribute +1, those within a column contribute −1, and the others contribute zero.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.3.title: An eigenvector basis and integer eigenvalues in the stated interval
explanation: The source labels permutations by Fin n, so the book's first label is 0 and E is the sum of swaps (0 j) for j > 0. The theorem assumes n ≠ 0 and an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex representation; no irreducibility hypothesis is imposed.

The first part of the checked conclusion supplies a basis of eigenvectors, which is diagonalizability. Its second part says that every eigenvalue is an integer z with 1−n ≤ z ≤ n−1, including the case n = 1, where E = 0.

For the basis and bounds, the proof chooses an invariant Hermitian inner product. Each transposition acts by a self-adjoint isometry, so their sum has an eigenvector basis. There are n−1 summands, and estimating their action on a unit eigenvector gives |z| ≤ n−1.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.3.title: The difference of two central transposition sums gives integrality
explanation: The smaller sum Cₙ₋₁ must be taken in the subgroup fixing the first label: it sums swaps between the other n−1 labels. The checked identity is E = Cₙ − Cₙ₋₁ for that embedded subgroup.

The proof of integrality uses the integer content eigenvalues of both central sums and their commutation. Inside an E-eigenspace it chooses an eigenvector for Cₙ; that vector is also an eigenvector for Cₙ₋₁. Its E-eigenvalue is therefore a difference of two integers. The subgroup fixing the first label is conjugate to the last-label-fixing subgroup used for branching above.

Chapter5/Problem5.16.3.title: Scalar action detects a rectangle; its scalar is width minus height
explanation: On the restricted Specht module, Cₙ₋₁ acts by the contents of the diagrams obtained by removing a corner. Its action is scalar exactly when all those contents agree. Removing a corner subtracts that corner's column-minus-row value from c(λ); distinct removable corners have distinct such values. They can all agree only when λ has one removable corner, which means λ is rectangular.

The source expresses a rectangle by saying that the multiset of parts is r copies of c: r rows of width c. For n > 0 both are positive. Its only removable corner has content (c−1)−(r−1) = c−r, and the second theorem checks that E acts by this scalar on every vector in the Specht ideal.

Chapter5/Introduction_5.15.title: The exponent shift and the Vandermonde sign
explanation: Lean represents λ by its decreasing row lengths, padded with zeros, and ρ by the natural-number vector whose ith entry is N − 1 − i. Its indices start at zero, so this is the book's (N−1, N−2, …, 0). The first two definitions below supply the two exponent vectors.

The source Vandermonde is ∏i<j(xj − xi), with each factor reversed from the book's Δ. It equals (−1) raised to N(N−1)/2 times Δ. This explains the reversal-permutation sign in the coefficient theorem; it is not an extra sign in the book's character formula.

Chapter5/Theorem5.15.1.title: Frobenius's formula with an independent number of variables
explanation: The checked result allows any N at least the number of parts of λ, independently of n. The character value in its type is the trace of σ on the source Specht ideal; the linked identification makes this an ordinary representation character. The earlier ideal equivalence transfers it to the book's Vλ.

The type uses the source Vandermonde and multiplies the character by the sign of the variable-reversal permutation. Replacing that Vandermonde by the book's Δ cancels the sign, giving the stated coefficient of x^(λ+ρ). The proof first checks N = n, then proves that adding a zero row and one more variable preserves this coefficient.

Chapter5/Remark5.15.2.title: Laurent monomials remove the exponent shift
explanation: The Laurent polynomial algebra is implemented as finite sums of monomials with integer exponent vectors. Multiplication adds those vectors, and each variable has a monomial inverse. These are Laurent polynomials, not infinite series.

The checked identity xρ∏i<j(1 − xj/xi) = Δ shifts the coefficient at λ to the coefficient at λ+ρ. The final result identifies the resulting Laurent coefficient with the Specht character. This Laurent statement uses n variables; the independent-N theorem above is stated in the ordinary polynomial algebra.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.15.title: Expanding the alternating determinant
explanation: Expanding the Vandermonde gives a signed sum of power-sum coefficients. A term whose shifted exponent has a negative entry is zero; in Lean this is a coordinatewise inequality checked before natural-number subtraction. A valid exponent vector is sorted into a partition of n.

The source then substitutes the Specht decomposition of each permutation character. The two statements below check the character expansion and the Kostka-weighted decomposition it uses. The reversal sign reflects the Vandermonde convention just explained.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Frobenius_c.title: Sorting the shifted exponent gives a triangular expansion
explanation: The source proves more than lexicographic comparison: each valid nonidentity shift, after sorting, strictly dominates λ. Sorting can only increase the sums of the largest k entries, while permuting ρ cannot increase its original initial sums. The equality case is checked by the equality criterion for rearrangement.

Combined with Kostka vanishing, this leaves diagonal coefficient one and terms only above λ. The checked alternating-multiplicity identity below is the final cancellation: after accounting for the Vandermonde sign, its coefficient is one for μ = λ and zero for every other μ.

declarations.documentation: The source's diagonal carries the reversal sign; all off-diagonal coefficients vanish.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Frobenius_c.title: Norm one eliminates the remaining integer coefficients
explanation: The source computes the squared norm of the alternating character through formal power-series coefficients and obtains one. Orthogonality of the Specht characters then says that the sum of squares of its integer coefficients is one. Since its diagonal coefficient already has square one, all the other coefficients vanish.

This proves the desired character identity directly from orthogonality and integer coefficients, rather than applying Lemma 5.7.2 to a separately bundled virtual representation. The statement below supplies the orthogonality equation used in that calculation.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Frobenius_c.title: Formal power series make the coefficient calculation algebraic
explanation: The product ∏j,k(1 − xjyk)⁻¹ is a formal multivariate power series: each factor has constant term one and therefore a formal inverse. No analytic convergence assumption is needed.

The source relates the average of products of permutation-polynomial coefficients to a coefficient of this series by finite counting. It proves the Cauchy identity by clearing denominators in a matrix and factoring through Vandermonde matrices. explanation: The theorem assumes zi ≠ yj for every pair of indices, so each reciprocal difference is defined with nonzero denominator. It does not require the z-values to be mutually distinct, or the y-values to be mutually distinct; repeated values make both sides vanish.

The checked type multiplies the determinant by ∏i,j(zi − yj). Dividing by this nonzero product gives the book's quotient identity. Its two Vandermonde factors have exactly the displayed orders (zj − zi) and (yi − yj).

Chapter5/Discussion_footnote_5.15.title: Why only the identity preserves ρ
explanation: At the first index moved by a permutation, the image index is larger. Since ρ is strictly decreasing, the permuted vector is lexicographically smaller there. Thus σρ ≤ ρ, with equality only for σ = 1.

Subtracting from the common vector λ+ρ reverses this comparison. The statements below check the equality criterion and the resulting lower bound before sorting; the sorted dominance argument belongs to the main proof above.

explanation: The book uses divisibility and homogeneity to reduce the determinant formula to a constant. The source instead clears the first column by determinant-preserving row operations, expands along that column, and factors row and column scalars from the smaller matrix.

Induction on N evaluates that smaller Cauchy determinant, with the same nonzero cross-difference hypotheses. This checks the identity without a separate implementation of the book's polynomial-divisibility or specialization argument.

explanation: The determinant is formed in the formal power-series ring, where (1 − xiyj)⁻¹ exists because its constant term is one. The checked expansion below is the signed sum of the products of these inverses.

In a permutation term, the coefficient of xαyβ is one exactly when αj = βσ(j) for every j. With α = β = λ+ρ, strict decrease makes the entries distinct, so only the identity permutation contributes. The linked coefficient theorem checks this for any equal injective exponent vectors.

Chapter5/Remark5.15.5.title: Positive-root order is dominance order
explanation: The source defines λ ≼ μ by a finite list of positive roots ei − ej with i < j whose sum is μ − λ, after padding row lengths with zeros. It proves this is equivalent to μ dominating λ: every initial row sum for μ is at least the corresponding sum for λ.

Conversely, the nonnegative differences of these initial sums give an explicit list of adjacent roots ei − e(i+1). This equivalence supplies antisymmetry, while concatenating root lists gives transitivity. It is a partial order, not the total lexicographic order.

explanation: The matrix has entry Kμλ in row μ, column λ. Its diagonal is one, and an entry is zero unless λ ≼ μ. The source constructs its inverse as a finite geometric series in I−K: strict dominance increases a bounded integer rank, making K−I nilpotent.

The checked character formula expresses χVλ as a sum of permutation characters weighted by the inverse-matrix column λ. The inverse entries also vanish outside λ ≼ μ, so the sum can be restricted to that partial order. The source writes these matrix entries over ℂ; it proves both inverse equations and the support statements.

explanation: Uλ has a basis indexed by the cosets Sₙ/Pλ, with Sₙ acting by permutation of that basis. The checked equivalence identifies induction of the trivial complex representation with the left ideal generated by the row sum rλ = ∑p∈Pλ p, and verifies that the map intertwines the group actions.

The book uses the row average aλ = rλ/|Pλ|. Since |Pλ| is nonzero in ℂ, the two elements generate the same ideal. The inverse map in the source includes this normalization. Sₙ/Pλ is a coset set, not a quotient group; Pλ need not be normal.

explanation: The checked decomposition is an isomorphism of ℂ[Sₙ]-modules. For each partition μ it supplies Kμλ copies of the Specht module Vμ, represented as functions from a finite set of size Kμλ. The multiplicities are natural numbers.

The displayed source type sums over all partitions. Terms with μ < λ are zero: there are no equivariant maps from Uλ to Vμ. On the diagonal the Hom-space has dimension one, so Vλ occurs once. explanation: The book defines Kμλ as the multiplicity of Vμ in Uλ. The source additionally identifies this number with the count of semistandard tableaux of shape μ and content λ: rows are weakly increasing, columns are strictly increasing, and the jth label occurs λj times.

Labels in Lean start at zero, and the decreasing row-length list is padded with zeros. The counting definition takes shape first and content second. Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Proposition.title: From row-fixed vectors to the direct sum
explanation: The source evaluates equivariant maps on the identity coset. Their values are exactly the vectors in Vμ fixed by the row subgroup Pλ, the image of the row average aλ. The sandwich vanishing theorem makes this space zero when μ does not dominate λ, hence in particular when μ < λ. For μ = λ the source proves it is one-dimensional.

Semisimplicity then gives the isotypic decomposition of Uλ. A basis of each row-fixed space identifies its multiplicity with the semistandard-tableau count, producing the group-algebra-linear direct-sum equivalence. This implements the same argument through fixed spaces and isotypic components rather than constructing every displayed Hom-space identification.

explanation: A permutation matrix has trace equal to the number of basis vectors it fixes. For Uλ this means counting cosets of Pλ fixed by the permutation σ. The first definition below is this natural-number count; the trace identity linked here identifies its complex value with the character.

The polynomial is the product of one power sum for each cycle. Lean's cycle-type multiset omits fixed points, so the definition adds H₁ to the power n − |support σ|. Those fixed points must not disappear from the formula. This source uses n variables indexed by Fin n; the exponents are the row lengths of λ, padded with zeros.

explanation: For each length m, an element commuting with σ may rotate each m-cycle and permute the iₘ cycles of that length. The checked group isomorphism organizes these operations as a product of semidirect-product factors; its order is ∏m mⁱᵐ iₘ!.

The source defines iₘ by counting orbits of length m. It proves that i₁ counts fixed points and, for m ≥ 2, that iₘ agrees with the cycle-type multiplicity. The finite product runs through lengths up to n; there are no longer cycles.

Chapter5/Theorem5.14.3.title: The same cycle assignments count both sides
explanation: A fixed coset corresponds to a coloring of the n labels by rows of λ, with λj labels of color j. Being fixed by σ means that every cycle has a single color. The checked proof constructs these correspondences and verifies their inverses.

Expanding the product of power sums also chooses a row color for each cycle. A cycle of length m contributes m to the exponent of its chosen row variable. Requiring the total exponents to be λ is the book's condition ∑m m rjm = λj. Both the fixed-coset count and the coefficient therefore count the same finite set of cycle assignments.

Chapter5/Lemma5.13.1.title: One linear functional controls every sandwich
explanation: The checked statement produces a single ℂ-linear map ℓ on the whole group algebra, with aλxbλ = ℓ(x)cλ for every x. This is stronger than choosing an unrelated scalar for each x. It uses the normalized row and signed-column averages from the preceding section.

The proof first treats permutation basis elements. For g = pq with p in the row subgroup and q in the column subgroup, the scalar is sign(q). Outside that product, the transposition argument makes the sandwich equal its own negative; over ℂ this forces it to vanish. The basis coefficients then extend linearly.

Chapter5/Discussion_end_of_Lemma5.13.1_p.title: The tableau factorization behind the transposition
explanation: The checked proof reaches the same factorization through cell coordinates and finite counting, rather than repeating the book's row-by-row rearrangement. If there is no pair in one row of T and one column of gT, it constructs a permutation q sending each label k to the cell with row(gk) and column(k).

It proves that these cells exist and that q is bijective. Then q preserves columns and gq⁻¹ preserves rows, so g = (gq⁻¹)q lies in PλQλ. The contrapositive gives a transposition t in Pλ whose conjugate g⁻¹tg lies in Qλ—the exact obstruction needed for the cancellation.

Chapter5/Discussion_lexicographic_orderi.title: Lexicographic order is not dominance order
explanation: Lean compares the decreasing row-length lists after padding them with zeros. Its hypothesis LexLt μ λ means μ < λ, or λ > μ in the book's notation.

The proof also uses dominance: λ dominates μ when every initial row sum for λ is at least the corresponding sum for μ. Dominance implies lexicographic comparison, but the converse fails; for example (4,1,1) is lexicographically larger than (3,3), although neither dominates the other. The second result below is the implication needed next: μ < λ prevents μ from dominating λ.

Chapter5/Lemma5.13.2.title: Why unequal shapes force the sandwich to vanish
explanation: The checked theorem assumes LexLt μ λ and proves rλxsμ = 0 for every x, where rλ is the unnormalized row sum and sμ the unnormalized signed column sum. Dividing by the two nonzero subgroup orders gives the book's aλxbμ = 0.

The implementation proves a stronger statement first: vanishing whenever μ does not dominate λ. If no row/column collision existed, counting entries in the first k rows column by column would give every dominance inequality for μ over λ. A collision therefore exists, and its transposition makes the sandwich equal its negative. Linearity extends the cancellation from permutation basis elements to all x.

Chapter5/Lemma5.13.3.title: The scalar is determined by the trace
explanation: The checked coefficient is the book's n!/(|Pλ||Qλ| dim Vλ), for the normalized cλ. The type writes the dimension using the reversed-product ideal from the classification, whose group-algebra-linear equivalence to Vλ was explained in the preceding section.

The proof starts with cλ² = γcλ and γ ≠ 0. Right multiplication by γ⁻¹cλ is then a projection onto the left ideal ℂ[Sₙ]cλ, so its trace is dim Vλ. Right multiplication by any group-algebra element has trace n! times its identity coefficient. Applying that formula to cλ and comparing the two traces determines γ. Thus γ⁻¹cλ is idempotent; cλ itself need not be.

Chapter5/Lemma5.13.4.title: A map out of Ae is determined by its value at e
explanation: The checked equivalence sends an A-linear map f to f(e), which satisfies e·f(e) = f(e). Conversely, a fixed element m gives the A-linear map x ↦ x·m on Ae. The fixed-point set equals eM: every e·m is fixed, and a fixed m is already e·m.

The result works for any ring and left module, with no finite-dimensional hypothesis. Its outer type uses ≃, a bijection between underlying types, rather than a bundled linear equivalence between Hom and an image submodule. The inverse values are nevertheless bundled A-linear maps.

explanation: The source reaches the same three conclusions through the group algebra. For exhaustion, it counts simple group-algebra blocks using conjugacy classes and partitions, then constructs a nonzero map from a Specht module to any remaining simple module.

explanation: Mathlib stores a partition as a multiset of positive integers summing to n. Sorting those parts in decreasing order recovers the book's row lengths. The diagram is represented by its cells (row, column), rather than by rectangles in the real plane.

A tableau is a bijection from these cells to Fin n, whose labels are 0,…,n − 1 instead of 1,…,n. The canonical filling assigns consecutive labels left to right, top to bottom. The source also checks that this filling increases along rows and columns; arbitrary tableaux are only required to be bijective.

Chapter5/Discussion_Young_projectors.title: Why the classification's reversed product represents the same module
explanation: Put r = ∑ₚ∈Pλ p and s = ∑q∈Qλ sign(q)q. The book uses cλ = rs/(|Pλ||Qλ|). The classification proofs instead use the left ideal generated by the unnormalized product sr. These products are not being identified as equal.

The checked equivalence maps the ideal generated by sr to the one generated by rs by right multiplication by s. Right multiplication by r goes back; the composites are nonzero scalar multiples of the identity. Removing the nonzero normalization factor leaves the generated ideal unchanged. Thus the equivalence is linear over ℂ[Sₙ], not merely an equality of dimensions.

The final result below checks that the book's normalized cλ is nonzero. In this implementation it follows by transferring simplicity across the equivalence; the identity-coefficient argument is used in establishing the underlying simple module.

declarations.documentation: The left ideal generated by the unnormalized column-then-row product is group-algebra-linearly equivalent to the ideal generated by the book's normalized row-then-column product.

declarations.documentation: For every partition, the normalized row-then-column Young symmetrizer does not vanish.

Chapter5/Theorem5.12.2.title: Simplicity, distinctness and completeness
explanation: The three statements below check the three parts of the classification over ℂ. First, the Young-symmetrizer left ideal is simple. Second, different partitions give nonisomorphic group-algebra modules. Third, every simple ℂ[Sₙ]-module is isomorphic to one of them.

Here partitionSubmodule is the ideal generated by the unnormalized column-then-row product. The checked comparison on the preceding page transfers the classification to the book's Vλ = ℂ[Sₙ]cλ. A linear equivalence over ℂ[Sₙ] respects every permutation's action; IsEmpty in the distinctness result rules out such an equivalence, not an ordinary complex-linear change of basis.

The existence proof uses the simple blocks of the group algebra and the bound from conjugacy classes to partitions. It then finds a Young symmetrizer acting nontrivially on a given simple module; the resulting nonzero map between simple modules is an isomorphism. No chosen basis or matrix realization is part of this theorem.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PartitionAuxiliary.partitionSubmodule_isSimpleModule
declarations.label: Each partition gives an irreducible module
declarations.documentation: The left ideal generated by a partition's column-then-row Young symmetrizer is a simple module over the complex symmetric-group algebra.

declarations.documentation: For distinct partitions of n there is no group-algebra-linear equivalence between their Young-symmetrizer modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SimpleModule.SubtypeRepresentation.exists_linearEquiv_to_subtype
declarations.label: Every irreducible occurs for some partition
declarations.documentation: Every simple module over ℂ[Sₙ] is group-algebra-linearly equivalent to the Young-symmetrizer module of a partition of n.

Chapter5/Example5.12.3.title: One row gives trivial action; one column gives sign action
explanation: For (n), every permutation fixes every vector in the checked module. For (1,…,1), each permutation acts on every vector by its sign. The source also establishes that each module has dimension one, so these are the trivial and sign representations, not just statements about one distinguished generator.
These two constructions assume n > 0. At n = 0 there is only the empty partition; the general classification still applies, but the positive-size definitions used in these examples do not.

declarations.label: One column: σ acts by sign(σ)
declarations.documentation: For every positive n, each permutation acts on the one-column module by multiplication by its sign.

Chapter5/Example5.12.3.title: The (2,1) module is the standard representation
explanation: The checked module for (2,1) has dimension two. The proof evaluates the hook-length product as 3 and obtains 3!/3 = 2.

The earlier S₃ catalogue has dimensions 1, 1 and 2. Since this Specht module is simple and has dimension two, it is isomorphic to the standard representation. The statement below checks the dimension; the linked catalogue supplies the identification.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SymmetricGroup.PartitionSubspaceAuxiliary.finrank_partitionThreeAuxiliary_eq_two

links.label: The three S₃ irreducibles

Chapter5/Example5.12.3.title: Four letters: dimensions and the two three-dimensional models
explanation: For (2,2), the hook-length product is 12, so the checked dimension is 4!/12 = 2. The earlier S₄ catalogue has just one two-dimensional irreducible, the representation obtained from the action on the three pair partitions. Simplicity and the dimension therefore identify this Specht module with that model.

For (3,1) and (2,1,1), the results below are actual representation isomorphisms: the first is the untwisted sum-zero subspace of ℂ⁴, the book's ℂ³₋; the second is its sign twist, ℂ³₊. The proof distinguishes them using a nonzero vector fixed by two adjacent transpositions, rather than relying on their equal dimensions.
All these comparisons use the column-then-row module; the preceding checked equivalence relates it to the book's Vλ.

declarations.label: The (2,1,1) module is the sign-twisted ℂ³₊
declarations.documentation: The representation for (2,1,1) is isomorphic to the sign twist of the four-coordinate sum-zero representation.

Chapter5/Corollary5.12.4.title: A rational representation whose complexification is the given irreducible
explanation: The construction starts with the same unnormalized Young symmetrizer over ℚ, where its coefficients are integers, and takes the left ideal it generates in ℚ[Sₙ]. Extending scalars produces ℂ ⊗ℚ Wλ. The checked map is bijective and intertwines every permutation with the action on the complex Specht module.

The second statement combines this scalar-extension equivalence with the classification: every complex irreducible has such a simple rational model. Choosing a ℚ-basis of that model gives rational matrices. The theorem checks the model and its equivariant complexification; it does not choose or print a particular matrix basis.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PartitionModels.exists_perm_equivariant_complexification
declarations.label: The rational Specht module complexifies equivariantly
declarations.documentation: For each partition, the complex scalar extension of its rational Young-symmetrizer module is complex-linearly equivalent to its complex module, compatibly with every permutation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PartitionModels.exists_partition_model_with_equivariant_complexification
declarations.label: Every complex irreducible has a simple rational model
declarations.documentation: Every simple complex symmetric-group algebra module is isomorphic to a partition module with a simple rational model and permutation-equivariant complexification.

Chapter5/Problem5.12.5.title: The answer counts involutions, including the identity
explanation: The checked answer is ∑ dim V = #{σ ∈ Sₙ : σ² = 1}, summing once over each irreducible. The identity is included: the condition is square equal to 1, not order exactly two.

The proof follows the hint. A real-coefficient Young symmetrizer supplies a nonzero invariant symmetric bilinear form on each irreducible, so its Frobenius–Schur indicator is +1. The indicator-weighted involution formula then becomes the unweighted sum of dimensions. The hypotheses in the statement ensure that the finite family is simple, has no repeated isomorphism classes and contains every irreducible.

For an explicit count, an involution has r disjoint transpositions and n − 2r fixed points. Choosing and pairing those letters gives n!/(2ʳ r! (n − 2r)!) possibilities. Sum this expression for 0 ≤ r ≤ ⌊n/2⌋. This counting interpretation is an explanation of the answer; the checked theorem below states it as the cardinality of the involution set.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SymmetricGroup.SimpleDimensions.sum_finrank_simple_eq_card_involutions
declarations.label: The sum of irreducible dimensions is the number of σ with σ² = 1
declarations.documentation: For any finite, nonredundant and exhaustive family of simple finite-dimensional complex Sₙ representations, the sum of their dimensions equals the cardinality of the permutations squaring to the identity.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.SimpleSymmetricGroupRepresentations.simpleSymmetricGroupRepresentation_value_eq_one
links.label: Every symmetric-group irreducible has Frobenius–Schur indicator +1

Chapter5/Discussion_5.11_examples.title: The transposition subgroup: trivial and sign induction
explanation: The subgroup is generated by a transposition s. Frobenius reciprocity computes the multiplicity of an irreducible S as (dim S + χₛ(s))/2 for the trivial inducing character and (dim S − χₛ(s))/2 for the sign character. The S₃ character values at s are 1, −1 and 0 for the trivial, sign and standard representations.

The two results below are isomorphisms of complex representations. The two-dimensional summand is the sum-zero plane in the three-coordinate permutation representation; the other summand is trivial in the first result and sign in the second.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.induced_trivial_auxiliarySubgroupA_iso_biprod
declarations.label: Inducing the trivial ℤ₂ character gives standard ⊕ trivial
declarations.documentation: Induction from the transposition subgroup of S₃ sends the trivial character to the sum of the two-dimensional standard and trivial representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.induced_restrictedCharacter_iso_biprod
declarations.label: Inducing the sign ℤ₂ character gives standard ⊕ sign
declarations.documentation: Induction from the transposition subgroup of S₃ sends its nontrivial character to standard plus sign.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.finrank_hom_induced_auxiliarySubgroupA
links.label: The two-term multiplicity formula

Chapter5/Discussion_5.11_examples.title: The three-cycle subgroup: the two primitive characters induce alike
explanation: Here H is A₃, generated by a three-cycle. Both the trivial and sign representations of S₃ restrict trivially, whereas the standard plane has the two primitive cube-root characters. Thus the trivial H-character induces to trivial ⊕ sign, and each nontrivial H-character induces to the standard plane.

The source constructs ε = exp(2πi/3) and ε² as actual complex-unit-valued characters. The proofs use their root-of-unity equations in the three-term character average, then check all three irreducible multiplicities. The existence of the resulting isomorphisms is stronger than a dimension count.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.induced_trivial_auxiliarySubgroupB_iso_biprod
declarations.label: The trivial ℤ₃ character induces to trivial ⊕ sign
declarations.documentation: Induction of the trivial character from A₃ to S₃ is isomorphic to the sum of the trivial and sign representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.induced_auxiliaryCharacterOne_iso_auxiliaryRepresentation
declarations.label: The ε character induces to the standard plane
declarations.documentation: The character sending a generating three-cycle to exp(2πi/3) induces to the standard S₃ representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.induced_auxiliaryCharacterTwo_iso_auxiliaryRepresentation
declarations.label: The ε² character also induces to the standard plane
declarations.documentation: The other primitive cube-root character induces to the same standard S₃ representation.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.finrank_hom_induced_auxiliarySubgroupB
links.label: The three-term multiplicity formula

Chapter5/Discussion_5.11_examples.title: The point stabilizer in S₄
explanation: The checked S₃ subgroup fixes the fourth coordinate. Its trivial, sign and sum-zero-plane representations induce to the three direct sums in the book. The untwisted four-coordinate sum-zero representation is the book's ℂ³₋; its sign twist is ℂ³₊. The two-dimensional S₄ summand comes from the action on the three pair partitions.

The proofs average the restricted characters over the six subgroup elements, check multiplicities against all five S₄ irreducibles, and use those multiplicities to obtain isomorphisms. In Lean, ⊞ denotes the representation direct sum and Nonempty asserts that an isomorphism exists; no particular decomposition basis is chosen.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.SubgroupInductionAuxiliary.induced_auxiliary_trivial_iso_biprod
declarations.label: Trivial induction: ℂ₊ ⊕ ℂ³₋
declarations.documentation: Inducing the trivial representation of the point-stabilizer S₃ gives trivial plus the three-dimensional sum-zero representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.SubgroupInductionAuxiliary.induced_auxiliary_sign_iso_biprod
declarations.label: Sign induction: ℂ₋ ⊕ ℂ³₊
declarations.documentation: Inducing sign from the point-stabilizer S₃ gives sign plus the sign-twisted three-dimensional sum-zero representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.SubgroupInductionAuxiliary.induced_auxiliary_subrepresentation_iso_biprod
declarations.label: Standard induction: ℂ² ⊕ ℂ³₋ ⊕ ℂ³₊
declarations.documentation: Inducing the two-dimensional standard S₃ representation gives the three non-linear S₄ irreducibles, once each.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.SubgroupInductionAuxiliary.finrank_hom_induced_eq_character_average
links.label: The subgroup character average giving each multiplicity

Chapter5/Problem5.11.1.title: From ℤ₂: two different thirty-dimensional decompositions
explanation: Write 1 for the trivial A₅ representation, T₊ and T₋ for its two three-dimensional irreducibles, and V₄, V₅ for the four- and five-dimensional ones. The signs distinguish the golden-ratio character values at the conjugacy class of (12345): T₊ has (1 + √5)/2 and T₋ has (1 − √5)/2.
For the trivial ℤ₂ character, Ind 1 ≅ 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ 3V₅. For its nontrivial character η, Ind η ≅ 2T₊ ⊕ 2T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ 2V₅. A coefficient means that many copies of the irreducible.

The results hold for any subgroup of A₅ of order two over ℂ. The proof computes the induced character on the five conjugacy classes and matches it with the direct-sum character; character rigidity then gives an isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_character_one_card_two_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: ℤ₂ trivial: 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ 3V₅
declarations.documentation: For any order-two subgroup of A₅, inducing its trivial character gives these irreducible multiplicities.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_nontrivial_card_two_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: ℤ₂ nontrivial: 2T₊ ⊕ 2T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ 2V₅
declarations.documentation: For any order-two subgroup of A₅, inducing its nontrivial simple representation gives two copies of each nontrivial A₅ irreducible.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorSquareSpectralDecomposition.indexedSimpleRepresentations
links.label: The five checked A₅ representation models

Chapter5/Problem5.11.1.title: From ℤ₃: both nontrivial characters give the same sum
explanation: The trivial character gives Ind 1 ≅ 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ V₅. Either nontrivial character η gives Ind η ≅ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ 2V₅.

Each sum has dimension 20, the subgroup index. The nontrivial theorem quantifies over any simple subgroup representation whose character is not constantly one, so it covers both primitive cube-root characters, not just one chosen character.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_character_one_card_three_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: ℤ₃ trivial: 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ 2V₄ ⊕ V₅
declarations.documentation: The trivial representation of an order-three subgroup induces to this direct sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_nontrivial_card_three_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: Either ℤ₃ nontrivial character: T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ 2V₅
declarations.documentation: Every nontrivial simple representation of an order-three subgroup induces to this same direct sum.

Chapter5/Problem5.11.1.title: From ℤ₅: the chosen character selects one three-dimensional summand
explanation: The trivial character gives Ind 1 ≅ 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₅. A nontrivial character η gives either T₊ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅ or T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅. All have dimension 12.

Choose a generator a conjugate in A₅ to (12345) and put z = η(a). The proof distinguishes the two values of z + z⁻¹: (−1 + √5)/2 selects T₊, and (−1 − √5)/2 selects T₋. The inverse characters have the same choice; replacing a by its square exchanges the two five-cycle classes.

The checked theorem presents the two alternatives without imposing a generator convention in its statement. Its proof obtains the class values A, B with A + B = −1 and A² + A − 1 = 0, then resolves the two roots.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_character_one_card_five_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: ℤ₅ trivial: 1 ⊕ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₅
declarations.documentation: The trivial representation of an order-five subgroup induces to this direct sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_nontrivial_card_five_iso_auxiliaryBiprod_or
declarations.label: ℤ₅ nontrivial: T₊ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅ or T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅
declarations.documentation: Every nontrivial simple representation of an order-five subgroup induces to one of the two displayed direct sums.
