links.label: The fifth-root calculation underlying the two alternatives

Chapter5/Problem5.11.1.title: From A₄: the linear characters and the three-dimensional representation
explanation: For the trivial A₄ character, Ind 1 ≅ 1 ⊕ V₄. Each of the two nontrivial linear characters induces to V₅. The three-dimensional irreducible induces to T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅.

The statements apply to any order-twelve subgroup of A₅, with the inducing representation's dimension recorded explicitly as one or three. The dimensions of the outputs are 5, 5 and 15, as required by the index-five subgroup.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_character_one_card_twelve_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: A₄ trivial: 1 ⊕ V₄
declarations.documentation: The trivial one-dimensional representation of an order-twelve subgroup induces to trivial plus the four-dimensional irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.Auxiliary.simpleFinrankOneNontrivialIso
declarations.label: Either A₄ nontrivial linear character induces to V₅
declarations.documentation: Every nontrivial simple one-dimensional representation of an order-twelve subgroup induces to the five-dimensional A₅ irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_finrank_three_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: A₄ three-dimensional: T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅
declarations.documentation: Every simple three-dimensional representation of an order-twelve subgroup induces to this direct sum.

Chapter5/Problem5.11.1.title: From the Klein four subgroup
explanation: The trivial character gives Ind 1 ≅ 1 ⊕ V₄ ⊕ 2V₅. Each of the three nontrivial linear characters gives Ind η ≅ T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅.

Both sums have dimension 15. The results quantify over any subgroup of A₅ of order four; the nontrivial theorem covers every simple representation with nonconstant character. These are existence statements for representation isomorphisms, not just character-table equalities.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_character_one_card_four_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: Klein four, trivial: 1 ⊕ V₄ ⊕ 2V₅
declarations.documentation: Induction of the trivial character of an order-four subgroup gives trivial, the four-dimensional irreducible and two copies of the five-dimensional irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupDegreeFiveCharacters.auxiliary_construction_simple_nontrivial_card_four_iso_auxiliaryBiprod
declarations.label: Klein four, nontrivial: T₊ ⊕ T₋ ⊕ V₄ ⊕ V₅
declarations.documentation: Every nontrivial simple representation of an order-four subgroup induces to these four nontrivial A₅ irreducibles, once each.

Chapter5/Theorem5.10.1.title: Reciprocity for the book's function-space induction
explanation: The book's Ind W is the space of H-equivariant functions on G with right-translation action. In Lean this is Rep.coind H.subtype W. The equivalence below is between G-equivariant maps into that function space and H-equivariant maps from the restricted representation.

It is a k-linear equivalence, not just a bijection of sets. The checked statement works over any field, for arbitrary groups and subgroups and without finite-dimensionality or finite-index assumptions. Finite index is needed only if we replace this full function space by Lean's coinvariant Rep.ind.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Subgroup.HomAdjunction.ambientSubgroupHomEquiv
declarations.label: Frobenius reciprocity as a linear equivalence
declarations.documentation: G-equivariant maps V → Coind W are linearly equivalent to H-equivariant maps Res V → W.

links.name: Rep.coind
links.label: The equivariant-function representation

Chapter5/Theorem5.10.1.title: Evaluation at 1 and the inverse formula
explanation: The forward map sends α to the map v ↦ α(v)(1), as in the book. Its inverse sends β to v ↦ (x ↦ β(ρᵥ(x)v)). There is no inverse on x: this agrees with the book's right-translation convention.

The construction checks H-equivariance of the resulting functions, G-equivariance of the lifted map, linearity, and both inverse identities. The local evaluation lemma below exposes the first formula; the linked Mathlib construction exposes the inverse.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Subgroup.HomAdjunction.ambientSubgroupHomEquiv_apply
declarations.label: The forward map evaluates the function at the group identity
declarations.documentation: Applying the reciprocity equivalence to α and then to v returns α(v)(1).

links.name: Rep.resCoindToHom
links.label: The inverse: v is sent to the function x ↦ β(ρᵥ(x)v)

links.name: Rep.resCoindHomEquiv
links.label: The two maps and their inverse identities

Chapter5/Theorem5.10.1.title: Naturality means the correspondence respects composition
explanation: Precomposing an ambient-group map or postcomposing a subgroup map commutes with reciprocity. The checked Hom-functor isomorphism packages both compatibility laws, as well as the k-linear equivalences at each pair (V, W).

The opposite category in its type records that Hom is contravariant in V; the second argument is covariant. The categorical notation is packaging for these composition identities, not an additional assumption on the representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Subgroup.HomAdjunction.ambientSubgroupHomFunctorIso
declarations.label: The Hom-space equivalences are natural in both representations
declarations.documentation: A natural isomorphism of module-valued Hom functors packages the linear reciprocity equivalences and their compatibility with composition.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Subgroup.HomAdjunction.ambientSubgroupHomFunctorIso_app_apply
links.label: The natural-isomorphism component is the same evaluation map

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: Restriction through identity induction
explanation: The checked counterpart to k[G] ⊗ₖ₍G₎ V ≅ V is induction along the identity homomorphism. It sends the identity generator to v; the inverse sends v to the class represented by 1 ⊗ v. Restricting this isomorphism to H gives the statement below.

This uses Lean's coinvariant induction model. It checks the representation-level identity and the displayed generator formula; it does not identify a separately constructed two-sided group-algebra bimodule tensor product with that model.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.restrictIndIdIso
declarations.label: Identity induction, restricted to H, recovers the restricted representation
declarations.documentation: After restriction to H, induction along the identity of G is isomorphic to the original restricted representation.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.restrictIndIdIso_inv_apply
links.label: The inverse sends v to the identity tensor generator

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: The Hom model gives the same reciprocity correspondence
explanation: The identification of equivariant functions with H-equivariant maps k[G] → W is Rep.coindIso: extend a function linearly from the group-algebra basis, and recover it by evaluation on basis elements.

Composing this comparison with the restriction–coinduction Hom equivalence gives the representation-level result in (b). The checked proof constructs this equivalence directly; it does not derive it by specializing all the two-sided bimodule tensor calculus requested in Problem 2.11.6.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Subgroup.HomAdjunction.ambientSubgroupHomEquiv
declarations.label: Reciprocity for maps into the function-space model
declarations.documentation: The linear equivalence relates maps into coinduction to maps from restriction.

links.name: Rep.coindIso
links.label: The function-space–group-algebra Hom comparison

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: Evaluation at 1 recovers the representation
explanation: For identity coinduction, an equivariant function satisfies f(g) = ρᵥ(g)f(1), so evaluation at 1 determines it. The inverse sends v to g ↦ ρᵥ(g)v. The isomorphism checks the action as well as the two inverse identities.
Via the group-algebra Hom comparison, this is the counterpart of evaluating a k[G]-linear map at the algebra unit. Restricting to H keeps the same underlying evaluation map.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.restrictCoindIdIso
declarations.label: Identity coinduction, restricted to H, recovers the restricted representation
declarations.documentation: Evaluation at the group identity gives the restricted identity-coinduction isomorphism.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.restrictCoindIdIso_hom_apply
links.label: The evaluation-at-1 equation

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: The finite coset sum compares the two induction models
explanation: The comparison sends an equivariant function f to the sum of the generators ⟦g ⊗ f(g)⟧, one for each right H-coset. The subgroup-equivariance relation makes each summand independent of the representative, and finite index makes the sum finite.

Lean's generator ⟦g ⊗ w⟧ corresponds to the book's usual balanced tensor g⁻¹ ⊗ w. This explains the inverse in the book's displayed formula; the two conventions do not give different maps. The checked isomorphism includes both inverse identities and compatibility with the G-action.
The local wrapper assumes a finite ambient group and works over any field. Mathlib's underlying comparison only needs finite subgroup index and permits a general commutative coefficient ring.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.coindIsoIndOfFinite
declarations.label: The function-space model is isomorphic to coinvariant induction
declarations.documentation: For a finite ambient group over a field, coinduction from H is isomorphic to induction from H.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.coindIsoIndOfFinite_hom_apply
declarations.label: The inverse comparison is a sum over right cosets
declarations.documentation: The map from equivariant functions to induced vectors is the sum of representative-independent coset generators.

links.name: Rep.indCoindIso
links.label: The finite-index comparison over a commutative ring

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: The other direction of Frobenius reciprocity
explanation: Part (e) has induction in the source rather than the target: Hom_G(Ind W, V) ≅ Hom_H(W, Res V). Lean checks this for coinvariant induction, without any finite-group or finite-index assumption. It is the left-adjoint counterpart to the function-space reciprocity of Theorem 5.10.1.
The forward map evaluates an equivariant map on the identity generator ⟦1 ⊗ w⟧. From β : W → Res V, the inverse sends ⟦g ⊗ w⟧ to ρᵥ(g⁻¹)β(w), using the generator convention described above.
For the finite groups in this exercise, the comparison in (d) identifies these coinvariant generators with the book's function-space induction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.indResHomLinearEquiv
declarations.label: Maps from induction correspond linearly to maps into restriction
declarations.documentation: For any subgroup over a field, the morphisms Ind W → V are linearly equivalent to W → Res V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.indResAdjunction
declarations.label: Coinvariant induction is left adjoint to restriction
declarations.documentation: The linear Hom equivalences are natural in both representations and define an induction–restriction adjunction.

links.name: Rep.indResHomEquiv
links.label: The generator formulas and inverse identities

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: Duality is checked here by characters
explanation: The isomorphism below checks Ind(V*) ≅ (Ind V)* for finite-dimensional complex representations of a subgroup of a finite group. It is an isomorphism of representations, not just equality of their dimensions.

The proof applies the induced-character formula to g and g⁻¹, using χᵥ*(g) = χᵥ(g⁻¹). It then uses the theorem that equal characters determine finite-dimensional complex representations of finite groups up to isomorphism.
This is a different proof from the book's explicit bilinear pairing involving S(g) = g⁻¹. No particular pairing or canonical duality map is constructed by this character-rigidity argument.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.finiteGroupFDRepAuxiliaryDualIso
declarations.label: Induction commutes with duality over ℂ
declarations.documentation: For finite-dimensional complex representations of a subgroup of a finite group, induction of the dual is isomorphic to the dual of induction.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.character_finiteGroupFDRepAuxiliary_dual
links.label: The character equality for the two dual representations

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroups.CharacterRigidity.nonempty_iso_of_character_eq
links.label: Equal characters give an isomorphism

Chapter5/Discussion_Problem5.10.2_parts.title: What the checked counterparts do not cover
explanation: The representation-level results above do not supply all the explicit two-sided group-algebra bimodule identifications and their tensor–Hom derivation in (a)–(d). Related balanced-tensor and adjunction constructions exist elsewhere in the development, but a complete specialization to this exercise is not provided here.

The duality isomorphism is specialized to finite-dimensional complex representations. The book's more general coefficient-field statement and its specified nondegenerate bilinear pairing are not supplied by this proof.

Chapter5/Theorem5.6.1.title: Any characteristic, but still an algebraically closed field
explanation: The book's standing convention is that k is algebraically closed unless stated otherwise. The checked theorem retains IsAlgClosed k; ‘any characteristic’ does not remove that assumption. There is no assumption that the characteristic is coprime to either group order.

The action on the tensor is (g,h)(v ⊗ w) = ρ(g)v ⊗ σ(h)w. The irreducibility predicate used below means a nonzero space with no proper invariant k-subspace. Both factors are finite-dimensional. The tensor-simplicity theorem actually does not require the groups to be finite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryTensorProductRepresentations.isAuxiliary_tensorProductRepresentation
declarations.label: The external tensor product of irreducibles is irreducible
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field, the external tensor product of two finite-dimensional irreducible group representations is irreducible.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryTensorProductRepresentations.tensorProductRepresentation
links.label: The external tensor-product action

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryTensorProductRepresentations.IsAuxiliary
links.label: The irreducibility predicate

Chapter5/Theorem5.6.1.title: The two restricted actions commute and supply the factors
explanation: The source restricts a representation of G × H along g ↦ (g,1) and h ↦ (1,h). It extends these commuting actions to the two group algebras, then applies the simple-module factorization from Theorem 3.10.2.

The conclusion supplies finite-dimensional irreducible factors and a linear equivalence with their tensor product, together with an equation checking equivariance for every (g,h). Thus it classifies up to representation isomorphism, not equality of chosen vector spaces. This existence result also works for arbitrary groups when the given representation is finite-dimensional.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryTensorProductRepresentations.auxiliary_exists_tensorProduct
declarations.label: Every finite-dimensional irreducible of G × H has tensor factors
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field, a finite-dimensional irreducible product-group representation is equivariantly linearly equivalent to an external tensor product of irreducible representations.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.auxiliary
links.label: The module factorization used in the proof

Chapter5/Definition5.7.1.title: A finitely supported integer function on irreducible isomorphism classes
explanation: The type SimpleCharacter ℂ G →₀ ℤ assigns an integer to each isomorphism class of simple finite-dimensional complex representations, with only finitely many nonzero coefficients. The index type remembers representation isomorphism classes, rather than chosen names for their vector spaces.

Negative coefficients are allowed. This is formal additive data, not an ordinary vector space of negative dimension. Its character is the finite sum below; its virtual dimension is an integer, and evaluation of the character at 1 is that integer embedded into ℂ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.VirtualRepresentations.Basic.VirtualRepresentation
declarations.label: Virtual complex representations
declarations.documentation: A virtual representation is a finitely supported integer-valued function on irreducible representation isomorphism classes.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.VirtualRepresentations.Basic.VirtualRepresentation.character_apply
declarations.label: The virtual character is the coefficient-weighted sum
declarations.documentation: At g, the virtual character is the finite sum over the support of each integer coefficient times the corresponding irreducible character value.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.SimpleCharacters.SimpleCharacter.ofSimple_eq_iff_nonempty_iso
links.label: When two irreducibles define the same index

links.name: RepresentationTheory.VirtualRepresentations.Basic.VirtualRepresentation.character_one
links.label: Character at the identity and virtual dimension

Chapter5/Lemma5.7.2.title: The criterion singles out one coefficient equal to +1
explanation: The checked coefficient statement uses a finite family of pairwise nonisomorphic simple complex representations and integer coefficients. It assumes the normalized self-character sum is one and that the integer sum of coefficient times dimension is positive.
The second factor in the character sum is evaluated at g⁻¹, which gives the conjugate character value over ℂ. Positive degree is expressed as an inequality in ℤ, not an ordering on complex numbers.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.Character.Irreducibility.exists_singleton_of_character_selfInner_eq_one
declarations.label: Exactly one coefficient is +1 and all others are zero
declarations.documentation: An integer linear combination of distinct simple complex characters with self-inner product one and positive degree has one coefficient equal to one and every other coefficient zero.

Chapter5/Lemma5.7.2.title: Orthonormality proves the virtual representation itself is a simple class
explanation: The proof expands the two character sums and uses orthogonality to obtain the integer equality ∑ nᵢ² = 1. Nonnegative integer squares then force one coefficient to be ±1 and the others zero. The corresponding irreducible has positive dimension, so positive virtual degree excludes −1.

A further checked result applies this argument to the finite support of the virtual representation defined above. It proves that the virtual representation equals one copy of a simple representation, and consequently that its character is an irreducible character. The finite family need not contain every irreducible class; it only needs distinct classes containing the support.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.VirtualRepresentations.Basic.VirtualRepresentation.eq_simpleMultiple_one_of_character_norm_one
links.label: The equality of virtual representations

links.name: RepresentationTheory.VirtualRepresentations.Basic.VirtualRepresentation.character_eq_simple_of_character_norm_one
links.label: The resulting irreducible-character statement

Chapter5/Introduction_5.8.title: Restriction keeps the vector space and changes only the parameter group
explanation: Along the inclusion H.subtype : H →* G, restriction is composition of the action with that inclusion. Thus an element h of H acts by the original operator for its image in G.
Rep.res packages this construction in the category of representations. It keeps the underlying module and the same linear maps on morphisms. No finite-index condition is needed for restriction.

links.name: Rep.res
links.label: The restriction construction

Chapter5/Definition5.8.1.title: The book's functions are Lean's coinduced space
explanation: Representation.coindV H.subtype ρ is the submodule of functions satisfying exactly f(hx) = ρ(h)f(x). The action in the book is right translation: (g • f)(x) = f(xg), with no inverse on g.

The named wrapper below specializes to ℂ, while Mathlib's underlying function-space definition works over more general coefficients. Both the equivariance condition and this action make sense for arbitrary subgroups, including those of infinite index.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.coinduced
declarations.label: The action on subgroup-equivariant functions
declarations.documentation: The ambient group acts on H-equivariant complex-valued vector functions by right translation of the argument.

links.name: Representation.coindV
links.label: The underlying function-space definition

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.coinduced_apply
links.label: The right-translation evaluation equation

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.coinduced_equivariance
links.label: The subgroup-equivariance equation

Chapter5/Definition5.8.1.title: Finite index identifies this model with coinvariant induction
explanation: Lean reserves Representation.ind for a quotient of k[G] ⊗ₖ V by the subgroup-action relations. Its generators have finite support in the group-algebra factor; its ambient action right-translates that factor by g⁻¹.

For a finite-index subgroup, the isomorphism below sends a generator to an equivariant function supported on its right coset. Its inverse is a finite sum over coset representatives. It is this comparison—not an equality of definitions—that lets later statements about Lean's induction apply to the book's functions. At infinite index, the full function model and this induction model should not be identified.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.finiteIndexInducedIsoCoinduced
declarations.label: Induction and the book's function model agree at finite index
declarations.documentation: For a finite-index subgroup, the coinvariant induced complex representation is isomorphic to the equivariant-function representation.

links.name: Representation.ind
links.label: The coinvariant induction construction

links.name: Rep.indCoindIso
links.label: The comparison over a general commutative ring

Chapter5/Remark5.8.2.title: Extend an equivariant function linearly to the group algebra
explanation: An equivariant function f : G → V determines an H-equivariant linear map k[G] → V by sending the basis element x to f(x). Conversely, evaluate such a linear map on each basis element to recover the function. Right translation gives the compatible G-action on these maps.

Mathlib checks this function-to-Hom comparison as Rep.coindIso, without a finite-index assumption, over a commutative ring. At finite index it composes with the induction/coinduction comparison; the resulting functor isomorphism below also checks naturality in the subgroup representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.FiniteIndex.indFunctorIsoCoindFunctorOfFiniteIndex
declarations.label: The finite-index induction–Hom comparison is natural in V
declarations.documentation: For a finite-index subgroup over a commutative ring, induction is naturally isomorphic to the Hom-model coinduction functor.

links.name: Rep.coindIso
links.label: The function-space–Hom isomorphism without finite index

Chapter5/Discussion_verification_of_Ind.title: Right translation preserves equivariance and obeys the group law
explanation: The subgroup relation is built into the function submodule. Right translation preserves it because h(xg) = (hx)g. Thus the translated function stays in the same space.

With this convention, applying g after g′ evaluates f at (xg)g′ = x(gg′), matching the action of gg′. Lean packages these identities as the multiplication and identity laws of the representation; the statements below specialize those laws to the coinduced space.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.coinduced_mul
declarations.label: The translated action respects multiplication
declarations.documentation: Acting by gg′ is acting by g after acting by g′ on an equivariant function.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.coinduced_one
declarations.label: The identity fixes every equivariant function
declarations.documentation: The identity group element acts as the identity on the coinduced space.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionAndCoinduction.mem_coinducedSpace_iff
links.label: Membership is exactly the subgroup-equivariance condition

links.name: Representation.coind
links.label: The function-space action and its law proofs

Chapter5/Remark5.8.3.title: Values at right-coset representatives determine every function
explanation: The linear equivalence below sends f to the function q ↦ f(q.out), where q.out is a chosen representative of a right H-coset.

Conversely, given values φ(q), write x = hₓq.out with hₓ = x(q.out)⁻¹ in H and set f(x) = ρ(hₓ)φ(q). The source checks equivariance and both inverse identities. This linear equivalence needs no finiteness assumption; it is a description of the vector space, not by itself an equivariant identification with an untwisted permutation action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.FiniteIndexEquivalences.coindVEquivRightCosetFunctions
declarations.label: Equivariant functions are determined by their coset values
declarations.documentation: The complex coinduced space is linearly equivalent to arbitrary vector-valued functions on the right-coset quotient.

Chapter5/Remark5.8.3.title: The checked finite-dimensional formula assumes finite index
explanation: For finite-dimensional V and a finite-index subgroup H, the function space has one copy of V for each right coset, giving finrank ℂ V * H.index. The ambient group may be infinite; the hypothesis concerns the number of cosets.

The source proves the formula for the book's function space first and then transfers it across the finite-index induction/coinduction equivalence. These dimension statements are specialized to ℂ and finite index; they are not statements about infinite-dimensional cardinal dimension at infinite index.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.FiniteIndexEquivalences.finrank_coindV
declarations.label: Dimension of the book's function space at finite index
declarations.documentation: For a finite-index subgroup and a finite-dimensional complex representation, the coinduced space has dimension dim V times the subgroup index.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InductionCoinduction.FiniteIndexEquivalences.finrank_indV
declarations.label: Dimension of coinvariant induction at finite index
declarations.documentation: Under the same hypotheses, the coinvariant induced space has dimension dim V times the subgroup index.

Chapter5/Problem5.8.4.title: Induction in stages is an equivariant linear equivalence
explanation: The theorem below returns a linear equivalence, not just an intertwining map. The source constructs forward and inverse maps on tensor/coinvariant generators, checks that they descend through both subgroup relations, proves both inverse identities, and checks the ambient action.

For K ≤ H ≤ G, K.subgroupOf H denotes the copy of K inside H. The representation is reindexed along the equivalence with K; the proof also identifies the corresponding quotient relations with direct induction from K. This result for complex coinvariant induction needs no finite-index hypothesis.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Induction.Transitivity.Representation.exists_induction_transitivity_intertwiner_of_le
declarations.label: Inducing through H is isomorphic to inducing directly from K
declarations.documentation: For nested subgroups, successive complex coinvariant induction is equivariantly linearly equivalent to direct induction.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Induction.Transitivity.Representation.exists_induction_transitivity_intertwiner
links.label: The construction along two general group homomorphisms

Chapter5/Problem5.8.4.title: Scope of the comparison with the book's function model
explanation: The checked transitivity theorem is for complex coinvariant induction. The finite-index comparison transfers it to the book's equivariant functions when both subgroup inclusions have finite index. The aligned sources do not provide a separate transitivity theorem for the full function-space model at infinite index.

Chapter5/Exercise5.8.5.title: The idempotent is embedded in the ambient group algebra
explanation: χ : K →* ℂˣ records that every character value is nonzero and multiplicative. The source forms eχ in ℂ[G] by the same normalized sum with inverse character values, embedding the subgroup elements into G.
submoduleOfSubgroupCharacter is the left ℂ[G]-span of that element: the vectors a eχ with a ∈ ℂ[G]. The proof checks that subgroup multiplication satisfies k eχ = χ(k)eχ and that eχ² = eχ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SubgroupCharacters.groupAlgebraElementOfSubgroupCharacter
declarations.label: The subgroup-character idempotent in ℂ[G]
declarations.documentation: The element |K|⁻¹∑ₖ χ(k)⁻¹k, with subgroup elements embedded in the ambient complex group algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SubgroupCharacters.submoduleOfSubgroupCharacter
declarations.label: The left ideal ℂ[G]eχ
declarations.documentation: The group-algebra submodule spanned by the subgroup-character idempotent.

Chapter5/Exercise5.8.5.title: The induced representation is isomorphic to that left ideal
explanation: The equivalence below has the correct G-action: on the target, g acts by left multiplication by its group-algebra basis element. The source proves both inverse identities, not just the existence of a map into the ideal.

In the coinvariant model's convention, a generator ⟦h ⊗ z⟧ maps to z·h⁻¹eχ. The inverse in h converts the model's right translation by g⁻¹ into left multiplication by g. Finite G ensures finite index, so the earlier comparison identifies this with the book's function-space induction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SubgroupCharacters.auxiliary_equivariant_map_of_subgroup_character
declarations.label: Induced subgroup character ≅ ℂ[G]eχ
declarations.documentation: The coinvariant induction of the one-dimensional subgroup-character representation is equivariantly linearly equivalent to the left ideal generated by its idempotent.

Chapter5/Theorem5.9.1.title: The coset sum uses zero for cosets that are not fixed
explanation: The checked formula below uses the chosen representative q.out for each right coset. Its summand is trace (ρ ⟨q.out * g * q.out⁻¹, h⟩) when that conjugate belongs to H, and zero otherwise; h is the proof of membership needed to regard it as an element of H.

This zero-extended sum is the book's sum restricted to fixed cosets. Separate source lemmas check that replacing a representative by h₀x preserves both membership and the trace, so the value does not depend on the representative choice.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.auxiliary_theorem
declarations.label: The Frobenius right-coset character formula
declarations.documentation: For a finite group and a finite-dimensional complex subgroup representation, the induced character is the sum of the subgroup character on conjugates from the fixed right cosets.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.auxiliary_additional_result
links.label: Changing a representative by a subgroup element

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.auxiliary_other_result
links.label: The summand depends only on the right coset

Chapter5/Theorem5.9.1.title: The formalized formula has narrower hypotheses
explanation: The available theorem assumes finite G and coefficients in ℂ. It does not cover the book's general ground field or an infinite ambient group with only finitely many H-cosets. In positive characteristic dividing |H|, the coset formula is still meaningful, but this source's averaging proof cannot be used as written.

Chapter5/Remark5.9.2.title: Each right coset contributes |H| identical summands
explanation: Define F(x) to be the subgroup character at xgx⁻¹ when that element lies in H, and zero otherwise. This is invariant under replacing x by h₀x, because characters are constant on subgroup conjugacy classes.

The normalization identity below groups the finite sum over G into right cosets. Each coset contributes |H| copies of its representative's value; division by the nonzero complex cardinality gives the coset sum. The linked induced-trace theorem is the resulting averaged Frobenius formula, not merely an identity for an unrelated function.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.inv_card_mul_sum_eq_sum_quotient
declarations.label: Normalized subgroup-invariant sums equal right-coset sums
declarations.documentation: For a finite group and a complex-valued function invariant under left multiplication by H, |H|⁻¹ times its group sum equals its sum over chosen right-coset representatives.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryUnavailableStatement.auxiliary_theorem
links.label: The averaged induced-character formula

Chapter5/Remark5.9.2.title: The positive-characteristic version is not supplied here
explanation: The book assumes the characteristic does not divide |H| so that division by |H| is valid in k. The checked identities here use ℂ; the corresponding theorem over other fields, including positive characteristic coprime to |H|, is not supplied by these aligned sources.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.9..title: The source first computes a trace on coinvariants
explanation: Instead of taking diagonal blocks of the book's function space, the source uses the coinvariant model (ℂ[G] ⊗ V)ₕ. An averaging projection identifies coinvariants with invariant vectors and expresses the induced trace as the average of traces on the tensor space.

For each h ∈ H, the group-algebra factor permutes its basis by x ↦ hxg⁻¹. Its trace counts fixed basis elements. The tensor-product trace then contributes the subgroup character χV(h); the fixed-point condition hxg⁻¹ = x says h = xgx⁻¹. Summing gives the averaged formula.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryUnavailableStatement.auxiliary_theorem
declarations.label: The trace computation gives the averaged Frobenius formula
declarations.documentation: For a finite group over ℂ, the induced character is |H|⁻¹ times the sum over x with xgx⁻¹ in H of the subgroup character at that conjugate.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationAveragingTrace.trace_coinvariantsMap_eq_average_trace
links.label: The averaging projection and coinvariant trace

links.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationAveragingTrace.trace_monoidAlgebra_mapDomain_eq_sum_fixedPoints
links.label: The permutation trace counts fixed basis elements

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.9..title: Regrouping gives the same right-coset formula
explanation: The source then groups the averaged sum into right cosets, using the bijection (h,q) ↦ h·q.out from H times the coset quotient to G. Subgroup-conjugation invariance makes the summand constant on each coset.

Canceling |H| yields the book's fixed-coset sum. The original block-trace proof remains above; the checked proof reaches its conclusion by averaging and regrouping, rather than formalizing each displayed diagonal block.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.inv_card_mul_sum_eq_sum_quotient
declarations.label: Regroup a normalized group sum by right cosets
declarations.documentation: For a finite group, normalizing a subgroup-invariant complex group sum by |H| gives the sum over right-coset representatives.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryQuotientSummation.auxiliary_theorem
links.label: The resulting right-coset theorem

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.9..title: Scope of this checked proof
explanation: The averaging/regrouping proof establishes the formula for finite groups over ℂ. The aligned sources do not check the full block-trace proof over arbitrary ground fields or for an infinite ambient group of finite subgroup index.

Chapter5/Theorem5.3.1.title: The dimension divides the order as a natural number
explanation: Here FDRep ℂ G is a finite-dimensional complex representation, and Simple V expresses irreducibility. The conclusion Module.finrank ℂ V ∣ Fintype.card G is divisibility of natural numbers, not just a quotient formed in ℂ.

The proof first shows that the dimension is positive. For each conjugacy class it forms the scalar λᵢ displayed above; Proposition 5.3.2 supplies the integrality needed to turn character orthogonality into this divisibility statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupCharacterArithmetic.finrank_dvd_card_of_simple
declarations.label: An irreducible dimension divides the group order
declarations.documentation: For a simple finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group, its dimension divides the group's cardinality.

Chapter5/Proposition5.3.2.title: The conjugacy-class factor makes the value integral
explanation: The class {h : G // IsConj g h} consists of all elements conjugate to g. The statement proves IsIntegral ℤ for its cardinality times V.character g, divided by the dimension.

The dimension is explicitly assumed positive in this helper. Irreducibility guarantees that condition when it is used in Frobenius's theorem. Integrality of χ(g) alone would not justify dividing by the dimension.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterIntegrality.isIntegral_card_conjClass_mul_character_div_finrank
declarations.label: The class-sum scalar is an algebraic integer
declarations.documentation: For a positive-dimensional simple complex representation, |C|χ(g)/dim V is integral over ℤ.

Chapter5/Proposition5.3.2.title: Centrality, Schur's lemma and the integer group algebra
explanation: The source reindexes the sum of the operators V.ρ h by conjugation to show that it commutes with the whole action. Schur's lemma makes this sum a scalar operator; taking its trace identifies the scalar as |C|χ(g)/dim V.

It then realizes the sum in the finite ℤ-module ℤ[G], where every element is integral. The representation maps its monic equation to an equation for the scalar operator. Because the representation space is nonzero, the scalar embedding into its endomorphisms is injective, so this also proves integrality of the scalar itself.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterIntegrality.isIntegral_card_conjClass_mul_character_div_finrank
links.label: The complete class-sum proof

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.3..title: Character values supply the other integral factor
explanation: For any finite-dimensional complex representation—not just an irreducible one—the source writes the trace as the sum of the characteristic-polynomial roots, counted with multiplicity. The finite-order equation for the action makes each root a root of unity and therefore an algebraic integer.

In the divisibility proof, χ(g⁻¹) supplies the book's conjugate character value. Multiplication and finite sums in the integral closure show that the entire class-weighted sum is integral; no division-closure assertion is used.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupCharacterArithmetic.character_isIntegral
declarations.label: Every finite-group character value is integral
declarations.documentation: The character of a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group takes values integral over ℤ.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.3..title: Orthogonality leaves a rational algebraic integer
explanation: The source regroups the sum over elements by conjugacy classes, using that the character is constant on each class. Irreducible character orthogonality then identifies the integral sum with |G|/dim V.

It forms this quotient in ℚ and embeds it into ℂ. The criterion below says that an integral rational number is an integer. Clearing the positive denominator and transferring the resulting integer divisibility back to natural numbers finishes the proof.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.NumberTheory.IntegralClosure.Rat.Rat.isIntegral_complex_iff
declarations.label: An integral rational number is an integer
declarations.documentation: A rational number embedded in ℂ is integral over ℤ exactly when it is an integer.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupCharacterArithmetic.finrank_dvd_card_of_simple
links.label: The class regrouping and final divisibility proof

Chapter5/Exercise5.3.3.title: Odd order rules out both real and quaternionic type
explanation: For a nontrivial irreducible representation, the odd-order character-sum argument from Exercise 5.1.7 rules out real type. Quaternionic type forces even dimension, while Frobenius divisibility makes that dimension a divisor of the odd group order.

Having excluded both possibilities, the checked conclusion is complex type: there is no equivariant linear equivalence with the dual representation. The nontriviality hypothesis is ∃ g, ρ g ≠ 1; it matters because the trivial irreducible is of real type.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.OddOrder.CharacterSums.auxiliary_of_odd_card_of_simple_of_nontrivial
declarations.label: Every nontrivial irreducible of an odd-order group has complex type
declarations.documentation: For a finite group of odd order, a nontrivial simple complex representation is not equivariantly equivalent to its dual.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.OddOrder.CharacterSums.auxiliary_not_of_odd_card_of_simple_of_nontrivial

Chapter5/Definition5.4.1.title: A subgroup series and the derived series give the same definition
explanation: The series predicate below writes the book's chain in descending order: H 0 = ⊤, H n = ⊥ and H (i+1) ≤ H i. Its condition ⁅H i, H i⁆ ≤ H (i+1) says that each step contains the preceding subgroup's commutators.

That condition makes H (i+1) normal in H i and the corresponding quotient abelian; it does not ask that every step be normal in the whole group. The equivalence below identifies such a finite series with Mathlib's IsSolvable G, defined by the derived series reaching the identity. No finiteness assumption on the group is needed.

declarations.label: A finite series with abelian successive quotients
declarations.documentation: There is a descending subgroup chain from G to the identity, with each step containing the commutator subgroup of the preceding step.

Chapter5/Theorem5.4.3.title: Burnside's theorem includes prime-power orders
explanation: The statement assumes a finite group, primality of p and q, and Fintype.card G = p ^ a * q ^ b. The exponents are natural numbers and may be zero; the primes are not required to be distinct.

The conclusion IsSolvable G is the derived-series property identified with the book's subgroup chain in Definition 5.4.1. Thus the theorem also covers groups of prime-power order and the trivial group.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupSolvability.isSolvable_of_card_eq_prime_pow_mul_prime_pow
declarations.label: A group of order pᵃqᵇ is solvable
declarations.documentation: Every finite group whose order is a product of powers of two primes is solvable, allowing zero exponents and equal primes.

Chapter5/Theorem5.4.4.title: Coprimality forces zero trace or scalar action
explanation: The hypothesis uses the cardinality of {h : G // IsConj g h} and the natural-number dimension of a simple finite-dimensional complex representation.

The two conclusions are V.character g = 0 or ∃ c : ℂ, V.ρ g = c • LinearMap.id. Scalar action on this representation does not itself say that g is central in the group: that further inference needs a faithful action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupCharacterCoprimality.character_eq_zero_or_action_eq_smul_id_of_conjClassCard_coprime_finrank
declarations.label: Coprime class size: zero character or scalar action
declarations.documentation: If the size of g's conjugacy class is coprime to the dimension of a simple complex representation, then its character vanishes at g or g acts as a scalar.

Chapter5/Lemma5.4.5.title: It is the average that must be integral
explanation: The family is indexed by Fin n, with 0 < n. Each entry has some positive power equal to one; repetitions are allowed, and the entries need not have the same order.

The important hypothesis is integrality of (∑ i, ε i) / n. The sum alone is always integral and would not force this alternative. The conclusion is that every pair of entries is equal or that their sum is zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RootsOfUnity.AverageIntegral.rootsOfUnity_all_eq_or_sum_eq_zero_of_average_integral
declarations.label: An integral average of roots of unity is constant or zero
declarations.documentation: A nonempty finite family of complex roots of unity with average integral over ℤ is constant or has zero sum.

Chapter5/Lemma5.4.5.title: The checked product is a number-field norm
explanation: The source adjoins all the roots to ℚ to obtain a number field containing their average α. Every complex embedding sends the roots to roots of unity, so every embedded average has absolute value at most one. If the original roots are not all equal, strict convexity gives |α| < 1 in the original embedding.

Assuming α ≠ 0, the product over all embeddings is a nonzero integral rational number, hence a nonzero integer. Its absolute value must be at least one, but the product bound makes it strictly less than one. This is the book's conjugate-product argument expressed as a field norm; embeddings account for any repeated conjugate values.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RootsOfUnity.AverageIntegral.rootsOfUnity_all_eq_or_sum_eq_zero_of_average_integral
links.label: The norm and strict-convexity proof

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.4..title: Bézout supplies an integral linear combination
explanation: The proof takes integer Bézout coefficients for the class size and dimension. Their identity writes χ(g)/n as an integer linear combination of |C|χ(g)/n and χ(g), both already known to be integral.

The checked proof establishes these ingredients internally, by the same class-sum and root-of-unity arguments as the linked results. It never assumes that arbitrary quotients of algebraic integers are integral.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.4..title: Equal eigenvalues imply scalarity because the action has finite order
explanation: After applying the average lemma, a zero sum gives the zero-character branch. For the other branch, equal eigenvalues alone would not exclude a nontrivial Jordan block.

The source uses the finite-order equation (V.ρ g) ^ orderOf g = 1. The polynomial Xᵐ−1 is separable over ℂ for m > 0, so the action's minimal polynomial is squarefree. With only one root c, that minimal polynomial is X−c, which forces the action to be c times the identity.

Chapter5/Theorem5.4.6.title: The conclusion exhibits a proper nontrivial normal subgroup
explanation: The hypothesis is that the entire conjugacy class of a chosen g has size p ^ k, with p prime and 0 < k. In particular, its size exceeds one and g ≠ 1.
The conclusion is ∃ N : Subgroup G, N.Normal ∧ N ≠ ⊥ ∧ N ≠ ⊤. The positive exponent is essential: singleton conjugacy classes do not force a group to have such a subgroup.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupNormalSubgroups.exists_nontrivial_proper_normalSubgroup_of_conjClassCard_eq_prime_pow
declarations.label: A prime-power conjugacy class forces a normal subgroup
declarations.documentation: A finite group with a conjugacy class of size pᵏ for a prime p and positive k has a nontrivial proper normal subgroup.

Chapter5/Theorem5.4.6.title: The regular character supplies the weighted sum
explanation: The source chooses one representative of each simple isomorphism class from a complete decomposition of the complex group algebra. At g ≠ 1, the regular character is zero, giving the displayed dimension-weighted identity.

The trivial representation contributes 1. The remaining indices split according to whether p divides their dimension, matching the book's sets D and N. Completeness of the family is needed here; a sum over an arbitrary collection of irreducibles would not suffice.

links.label: The dimension-weighted character identity

Chapter5/Lemma5.4.7.title: The nonvanishing representation is proved to exist
explanation: The statement below returns a simple complex representation that is not isomorphic to the trivial one, whose dimension is not divisible by p and whose character at g is nonzero. It includes the surrounding assumptions that the conjugacy class has size pᵏ, with p prime and k > 0.

To prove existence, assume that all the book's N terms vanish. The weighted character identity then says pS = −1, where S is a sum of character values with integer coefficients dim(V)/p. Thus S is integral, but S = −1/p is rational and cannot be an integer. This supplies the contradiction implicit in the book's last sentence.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.PrimePowerConjugacyClass.exists_simple_representation_of_conj_class_card_prime_pow
declarations.label: A nontrivial irreducible with nonzero character and p-free dimension
declarations.documentation: A positive prime-power conjugacy class admits a nontrivial simple complex representation with nonzero character at the element and dimension not divisible by that prime.

links.label: Why −1/p cannot be a rational algebraic integer

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.4..title: The existence theorem uses a simplicity contradiction
explanation: The source proves the same normal-subgroup existence conclusion, but does not construct the book's subgroup generated by ab⁻¹. It assumes no proper nontrivial normal subgroup exists and derives a contradiction.

Under that assumption, a nontrivial irreducible representation of this noncommutative group is faithful and has dimension at least two. If g acts as a scalar, faithfulness makes g central; a nonidentity central element in a simple group would make the group abelian, a contradiction. The coprimality theorem therefore makes every N character value vanish.

The source then repeats the weighted-character integrality argument: the remaining terms would give an integral value −1/p. This rules out simplicity and proves the existence statement. The separate existence lemma for the book's chosen V is checked too, but the normal-subgroup proof uses this direct contradiction rather than calling it.

declarations.documentation: A finite group with a conjugacy class of positive prime-power size has a proper nontrivial normal subgroup.

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.4..title: Lean uses induction on the group order
explanation: The checked proof uses strong induction on |G|, with the condition that every prime divisor is p or q. Once it finds a proper nontrivial normal subgroup N, the orders of N and G/N are smaller divisors of |G|, so the induction hypothesis makes both solvable.
The extension theorem then makes G solvable. This is the constructive induction counterpart of the book's smallest-counterexample reduction, with the trivial and abelian cases handled separately.

links.label: The complete induction and extension proof

Chapter5/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem5.4..title: A Sylow subgroup supplies the prime-power conjugacy class
explanation: The source does not use the book's final class-equation argument. If the noncommutative group has nontrivial center, that center already gives a proper nontrivial normal subgroup.

Otherwise choose a prime s dividing |G| and a nonidentity element g in the center of a Sylow s-subgroup. Its centralizer contains that Sylow subgroup, so its conjugacy-class size divides the Sylow index and is not divisible by s. It also divides |G| and exceeds one because the center of G is trivial.

With at most two prime divisors available, this class size is a positive power of the other prime. Theorem 5.4.6 gives the normal subgroup needed by induction. Thus the character-theoretic ingredient remains, while the last group-theoretic step differs from the printed proof.

Chapter5/Definition5.2.1.title: Algebraic over ℚ and integral over ℤ are different predicates
explanation: The two predicates are IsAlgebraic ℚ z and IsIntegral ℤ z. The notation aeval z p = 0 evaluates a polynomial at z, embedding its rational or integer coefficients into ℂ.

The algebraic predicate uses a nonzero rational polynomial, not necessarily a monic one. Over the field ℚ, dividing by the leading coefficient makes it monic without changing its roots. That normalization does not generally preserve integer coefficients, so the integer predicate explicitly requires monicity.

declarations.label: Algebraic integer: a root of a monic integer polynomial

Chapter5/Definition5.2.2.title: The matrix criterion is stated using characteristic-polynomial roots
explanation: Lean asks for a finite square matrix M over ℚ or ℤ, then embeds its entries into ℂ. The condition charpoly (M.map (algebraMap … ℂ)).IsRoot z says that its characteristic polynomial vanishes at z.

For a finite-dimensional complex endomorphism, being a characteristic-polynomial root is equivalent to being an eigenvalue with a nonzero eigenvector. Thus these statements express the book's eigenvalue criterion, not an extra condition on a chosen eigenvector. The quantified size permits zero, but a zero-sized matrix has characteristic polynomial 1 and cannot be a witness.

explanation: The integer statement below has the book's monic-polynomial formulation. The rational statement uses the equivalent nonzero-polynomial formulation. In the matrix-to-polynomial direction, the witness is the matrix's own monic characteristic polynomial.

Chapter5/Proposition5.2.3.title: The displayed companion matrix is multiplication by the adjoined root
explanation: The source defines the same matrix: ones immediately below the diagonal and the negated coefficients in the last column. For monic p, it identifies this matrix with multiplication by the distinguished root in R[x]/(p), in the basis 1,x,…,xⁿ⁻¹.

It then proves that the characteristic polynomial is p and transfers every root through coefficient embedding. These explicit companion-matrix results work over any nontrivial commutative ring. The existential rational proof also offers a smaller construction using multiplication in ℚ(z), whose power-basis characteristic polynomial is the minimal polynomial of z.

Chapter5/Discussion_after_Proposition5.2.title: The book's two sets are substructures of ℂ
explanation: Lean realizes the algebraic integers as integralClosure ℤ ℂ, a subalgebra, and the algebraic numbers as algebraicClosure ℚ ℂ, an intermediate field. These are subsets of the given complex field, not unrelated abstract copies. Their membership criteria are the predicates from Definition 5.2.1.

Chapter5/Proposition5.2.4.title: The algebraic numbers inside ℂ form an algebraic closure of ℚ
explanation: The subalgebra and intermediate-field structures already supply the ring and field operations on the two sets. The statement below proves more for the algebraic numbers: every element is algebraic over ℚ, and this field is algebraically closed. It does not assert that the algebraic integers form a field.

Chapter5/Proposition5.2.4.title: The source uses closure properties rather than the tensor-matrix proof
explanation: The exported closure statements below use membership in the integral closure and algebraic intermediate field. Their addition, multiplication and inverse laws come from Mathlib's general integrality and algebraicity results, rather than reconstructing the tensor matrices and reciprocal polynomial in this paragraph.

For the last assertion, the source applies the general theorem that the algebraic part of an algebraically closed field is an algebraic closure. This separates the checked conclusions from the book's particular proof route.

Chapter5/Proposition5.2.5.title: A rational number is integral over ℤ exactly when it is an integer
explanation: The statement below uses a rational q, embeds it into ℂ, and concludes that q equals an integer cast into ℚ. This is the book's set-intersection statement, including both inclusions.

The proof transfers integrality back through the injective embedding ℚ → ℂ, then uses that ℤ is integrally closed in its fraction field ℚ. The reverse direction is integrality of integer scalars. Thus it checks the conclusion without reproducing the denominator argument.

Chapter5/Discussion_after_Proposition5.2.title: Conjugacy is encoded by equality of minimal polynomials
explanation: For an algebraic α, Mathlib's minpoly ℚ α is the monic rational polynomial of least degree vanishing at α. It divides every rational polynomial vanishing there.

The predicate IsConjRoot ℚ α β means that α and β have the same minimal polynomial. Under algebraicity of α, this is equivalent to that polynomial vanishing at β. Thus “algebraic conjugate” here is not merely the complex-conjugation operation.

Chapter5/Discussion_after_Proposition5.2.title: An algebraic integer's rational minimal polynomial has integer coefficients
explanation: Mathlib proves the coefficient assertion through integrally closed domains: for α integral over ℤ, the polynomial minpoly ℚ α is minpoly ℤ α with its coefficients embedded into ℚ. This directly supplies the integer coefficients, rather than using a separate Vieta calculation.

Any rational-algebraic conjugate is therefore a root of that monic integer polynomial too, and is an algebraic integer. The change of coefficient ring matters: rational algebraicity alone is not integrality over ℤ.

Chapter5/Lemma5.2.6.title: One field embedding gives compatible conjugates of all the summands
explanation: The theorem treats an arbitrary finite sum at once. Given a conjugate β of the sum, it produces conjugates α′ᵢ whose sum is β. It does not claim that every independent choice of conjugates gives a conjugate of the original sum.

Instead of tensoring rational matrices, the proof adjoins all the summands to ℚ and extends the chosen image of their sum to a field embedding into ℂ. Applying that same embedding to each summand preserves its minimal-polynomial relation and the sum. The common embedding is what makes the choices compatible.

Chapter5/Problem5.2.7.title: One finite Galois field works for every representation of G
explanation: The quantifiers are important: Lean produces K first, then a suitable basis for each finite-dimensional complex representation. The field may depend on G, but not on the representation or its dimension. It is an actual intermediate field of ℂ, finite-dimensional and Galois over ℚ.
The predicate IsDefinedOver K V means that some complex basis makes every entry of every action matrix belong to K. It does not say that an arbitrary existing basis has that property.

declarations.documentation: For a finite group G, there is one finite Galois intermediate field of ℂ over ℚ such that every finite-dimensional complex representation of G has a basis with all action matrices over that field.

Chapter5/Problem5.2.7.title: A finite list of algebraic simple models supplies the common field
explanation: The proof decomposes the group algebra over the algebraic numbers into matrix blocks and extends scalars to ℂ. The resulting complete list of simple complex representations has algebraic action-matrix entries. It places the finitely many entries from these models in a common finite Galois extension.

Every finite-dimensional representation is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of those simple models. A block basis preserves the same field of entries, and transporting that basis through the isomorphism proves the assertion for all representations. No infinite collection of coefficients is adjoined.

Chapter5/Problem5.2.7.title: The character-zero theorem requires dimension greater than one
explanation: The checked conclusion is the requested existence of g with χ_V(g)=0, for a simple complex representation with 1 < dim V. The dimension restriction excludes character lines, whose values are nonzero scalars. Since χ_V(1)=dim V, the zero furnished here cannot occur at the identity.

declarations.documentation: For a finite group, every irreducible complex representation of dimension greater than one has a group element where its character is zero.

Chapter5/Problem5.2.7.title: Orthonormality and AM–GM give 0 < β < 1; the remark supplies the contradiction
explanation: If the character never vanishes, all factors in β=∏_{g≠1}|χ_V(g)|² are positive. Orthonormality gives Σ_g |χ_V(g)|²=|G|; removing the identity subtracts (dim V)². For dimension greater than one, the average of the remaining |G|−1 factors is less than one, so AM–GM gives β<1.

The checked vanishing proof does not proceed by Galois-conjugating the representation matrices in part (a). It uses the next remark's cyclotomic argument: β is rational and integral over ℤ, hence an integer, contradicting 0<β<1. In the algebraic part, the source writes each factor as χ(g)χ(g⁻¹), which equals the squared norm.

Chapter5/Remark5.2.8.title: Cyclotomic automorphisms permute the character factors
explanation: For N=|G|, each eigenvalue of ρ(g) satisfies μᴺ=1. The character is their sum, so it lies in ℚ(ζ). Sending ζ to ζʲ sends χ(g) to χ(gʲ); the source checks this with eigenvalue multiplicities and traces of powers.

When j is coprime to N, the power map is a bijection and preserves the nonidentity set. Reindexing the product therefore fixes ∏_{g≠1}χ(g)χ(g⁻¹). This argument needs a bijection of the underlying set, not a group homomorphism or an assumption that the group is abelian.

Chapter5/Remark5.2.8.title: A rational algebraic integer cannot lie strictly between zero and one
explanation: The proof constructs the product inside the finite Galois cyclotomic field and proves that every automorphism fixes it. The fixed-field theorem supplies a rational value. Each character value is an algebraic integer, so the finite product is integral over ℤ as well.

Proposition 5.2.5 now makes this rational value an integer. The contradiction below does not itself need irreducibility or a dimension hypothesis; those are used in Problem 5.2.7 to force the strict inequalities. Thus the cyclotomic proof avoids the field-of-definition theorem in part (a).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.CharacterArithmetic.character_pairing_product_not_rat_between_zero_one
declarations.label: The character product cannot be a rational value in (0,1)
declarations.documentation: For any finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group, the character product paired with inverses over nonidentity elements cannot equal a rational number strictly between zero and one.

Chapter5/Definition5.1.1.title: The real and quaternionic types use complex bilinear forms
explanation: The type V →ₗ[ℂ] V →ₗ[ℂ] ℂ means linearity over ℂ in both arguments. These are not Hermitian forms: there is no conjugation in either scalar rule. The real-type predicate asks for symmetry; the quaternionic-type predicate asks for B(v,w) = −B(w,v).

Both definitions require B(ρ(g)v,ρ(g)w) = B(v,w) and nondegeneracy, written as (∀ w, B(v,w)=0) → v=0. Symmetry or skew-symmetry gives the corresponding second-slot condition. Over ℂ, skew-symmetry also implies B(v,v)=0.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.Auxiliary.auxiliaryRepresentationConditionTwo
declarations.label: Real type: an invariant nondegenerate symmetric form
declarations.documentation: There exists a nondegenerate symmetric complex bilinear form preserved by the representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.Auxiliary.auxiliaryRepresentationConditionOne
declarations.label: Quaternionic type: an invariant nondegenerate skew form
declarations.documentation: There exists a nondegenerate skew-symmetric complex bilinear form preserved by the representation.

Chapter5/Definition5.1.1.title: Complex type means not isomorphic to the dual as a representation
explanation: A finite-dimensional vector space is always linearly isomorphic to its dual. What fails for complex type is an isomorphism commuting with the group actions. The definition below negates the existence of a complex-linear equivalence e : V ≃ V* satisfying e(ρ(g)v) = ρ*(g)e(v); the dual action uses g⁻¹.

The three predicates themselves can be applied to any finite-dimensional complex representation. The book's assumption of irreducibility matters when proving that exactly one type occurs. Lean proves the exhaustive alternatives and their incompatibility under that assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.Auxiliary.auxiliaryRepresentationProperty
declarations.label: Complex type: no equivariant isomorphism with the dual
declarations.documentation: There is no complex-linear equivalence from V to its complex dual intertwining the representation and its contragredient.

Chapter5/Discussion_after_Definition5.1..title: An odd-sized skew matrix cannot be nondegenerate
explanation: Choose a basis and let M be the Gram matrix of the skew form. Then Mᵀ = −M, so det M = (−1)ⁿ det M. For odd n, this forces det M = 0, contradicting nondegeneracy.

The checked theorem needs the skew-form predicate but not irreducibility. Thus the even-dimension conclusion holds for every representation satisfying that predicate, not just the irreducibles under discussion.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.InversionAndInvariantForms.even_finrank_of_auxiliary
declarations.label: A quaternionic-type representation has even complex dimension
declarations.documentation: A finite-dimensional complex representation admitting a nondegenerate invariant skew-symmetric bilinear form has even dimension.

Chapter5/Problem5.1.2.title: The real commutant has the three stated algebra types
explanation: Here V is the original complex representation regarded as a real vector space, not a chosen real form. Lean defines its real commutant as the subalgebra of real-linear endomorphisms commuting with every ρ(g). The conclusions are real-algebra equivalences, preserving addition, multiplication and real scalars—not just equal dimensions.
For a finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of a finite group, this algebra is ℂ, Mat₂(ℝ) or ℍ, according to complex, real or quaternionic type.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RealEndomorphismCentralizer.Representation.nonempty_realEndomorphismCentralizer_algEquiv_complex
declarations.label: Complex type gives the algebra ℂ
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible representation of complex type, the commuting real-linear endomorphisms form a real algebra isomorphic to ℂ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RealEndomorphismCentralizer.Representation.nonempty_realEndomorphismCentralizer_algEquiv_matrixFinTwo
declarations.label: Real type gives Mat₂(ℝ)
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible representation of real type, the commuting real-linear endomorphisms form a real algebra isomorphic to Mat₂(ℝ).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RealEndomorphismCentralizer.Representation.nonempty_realEndomorphismCentralizer_algEquiv_quaternion
declarations.label: Quaternionic type gives ℍ
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible representation of quaternionic type, the commuting real-linear endomorphisms form a real algebra isomorphic to the real quaternions.

links.label: The real commutant definition

Chapter5/Problem5.1.2.title: The invariant forms produce the antilinear operator in the hint
explanation: This source uses a Hermitian form H linear in its first slot and conjugate-linear in its second, matching the relation B(v,w) = H(v,jw). It constructs H by averaging a positive coordinate form, then uses its conjugate-linear dual equivalence to construct the equivariant antilinear map j.

The square j² is complex-linear, so Schur's argument makes it a scalar. Positivity of H shows that the scalar is real and has the sign of the bilinear form's symmetry: positive for real type, negative for quaternionic type. Rescaling by the reciprocal square root of its absolute value gives j² = 1 or j² = −1.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RealEndomorphismCentralizer.Representation.exists_equivariantMap_sq_of_invariant_bilinearForm_swap
links.label: The construction of j and the sign of j²

links.label: The normalized quaternionic-type operator

Chapter5/Problem5.1.2.title: Splitting linear and antilinear parts gives the algebra equivalences
explanation: Rather than first computing the complexification in the hint, the proof splits any real-linear commuting map f using I(v)=iv: its complex-linear part is (f−IfI)/2, and its antilinear part is (f+IfI)/2.

Schur makes the complex-linear part a scalar. For complex type the antilinear part must vanish, since a nonzero such map would give an equivariant isomorphism with the dual. In the other cases, composing it with j makes it complex-linear, so every commuting map is in the real span of 1,I,j,Ij. The relations I²=−1, Ij=−jI and j²=±1 yield explicit surjective algebra maps from real matrices or quaternions; injectivity is also proved.
