Chapter5/Problem5.1.2.title: A real form is an invariant real subspace of the right dimension
explanation: The checked criterion describes a real form inside V: a real subspace W stable under G, spanning V over ℂ, and satisfying dimℝ W = dimℂ V. A real basis of W is then a complex basis of V, giving the book's complexification description without introducing a separate tensor-product carrier.

For real type, the proof takes W to be the fixed space of the normalized antilinear involution j. Its two real eigenspaces are complementary and exchanged by multiplication by i. Conversely, an invariant W lets the proof extend the real part of an invariant Hermitian form to a symmetric complex bilinear form on V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.RealEndomorphismCentralizer.Representation.auxiliaryCondition_iff_exists_invariantRealSubmodule
declarations.label: Real type is equivalent to existence of an invariant real form
declarations.documentation: An irreducible representation has real type exactly when it contains an invariant real subspace spanning the complex space and having the same real dimension as its complex dimension.

Chapter5/Example5.1.3.title: For a cyclic group, only the trivial and possible sign characters are real
explanation: The cyclic group is Multiplicative (ZMod n), with n > 0. Its irreducibles are represented by homomorphisms into ℂˣ. A nondegenerate invariant bilinear form on a character line forces ξ(g)²=1, so the character takes values in {±1}.

The source proves that this means the trivial character, or the sign character when 2 ∣ n. All other characters are of complex type. There is no quaternionic character line, since a nondegenerate skew form requires even dimension.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryCharacterCriterion_eq_one_or_eq_specifiedEvenOrder
declarations.label: The cyclic real-type criterion
declarations.documentation: A character representation of a positive-order cyclic group has real type exactly when the character is trivial or is the specified sign character for an even order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryCharacterCriterionForFiniteCyclicGroup
declarations.label: Every other cyclic character has complex type
declarations.documentation: A cyclic character representation has complex type exactly when it is neither the trivial character nor the sign character for any proof of even order.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.cyclicCharacterOfEvenOrder
links.label: The sign character m ↦ (−1)ᵐ

Chapter5/Example5.1.3.title: All irreducibles of S₃ and S₄ have real type
explanation: The statements cover arbitrary finite-dimensional irreducibles, not just the previously chosen coordinate models. For S₃, the proof uses a 3-cycle and a transposition to determine the possible dimensions and traces, then computes the average of χ(g²) as 1.

For S₄, the proof identifies the simple module with a Young-symmetrizer model in the group algebra. The symmetric coefficient pairing B(x,y)=Σ_g x_g y_g is preserved by left translation. The symmetrizer's real coefficients make its self-pairing nonzero; irreducibility then makes the pulled-back form nondegenerate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryPropertyOfSimpleSymmetricThreeRepresentation
declarations.label: Every S₃ irreducible has real type
declarations.documentation: Every finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of S₃ admits a nondegenerate invariant symmetric complex bilinear form.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryPropertyOfSimpleSymmetricFourRepresentation
declarations.label: Every S₄ irreducible has real type
declarations.documentation: Every finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of S₄ admits a nondegenerate invariant symmetric complex bilinear form.

Chapter5/Example5.1.3.title: For A₅, real-valued characters are not the whole argument
explanation: Lean checks that every element of A₅ is conjugate to its inverse. Thus an irreducible is self-dual, and its indicator is ±1; this alone does not exclude quaternionic type.

The proof also uses five irreducibles, squared dimensions summing to 60, and 16 elements squaring to one. If any indicator were −1, the signed dimension sum 16 would force the unsigned sum to be at least 18. But Cauchy–Schwarz gives (Σ d_i)² ≤ 5·60 = 300, contradicting 18² = 324. Therefore all indicators are +1.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryPropertyOfSimpleAlternatingFiveRepresentation
declarations.label: Every A₅ irreducible has real type
declarations.documentation: Every finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of A₅ admits a nondegenerate invariant symmetric complex bilinear form.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryTheoremE
links.label: The signed-dimension arithmetic ruling out −1

Chapter5/Example5.1.3.title: Q₈ has real character lines and one quaternionic two-dimensional type
explanation: For any representation of QuaternionGroup 2 on ℂ, the scalar action has values ±1, and B(z,w)=zw supplies the invariant symmetric form. This checks real type for the one-dimensional representations.

The two-dimensional model uses diag(i,−i) and [[0,1],[−1,0]]. Lean proves its irreducibility and invariance of B(v,w)=v₀w₁−v₁w₀, using determinant one. It also proves that every two-dimensional irreducible is isomorphic to this model. The sign of the second generator differs from one earlier matrix convention, without changing the representation type.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.auxiliaryPropertyForQuaternionRepresentationOnComplex
declarations.label: Every quaternion-group character line has real type
declarations.documentation: Every complex representation of Q₈ on ℂ admits a nondegenerate invariant symmetric bilinear form.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.existsSimpleQuaternionRepresentationWithAuxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: A two-dimensional irreducible with an invariant skew form
declarations.documentation: There exists an irreducible Q₈ representation on ℂ² admitting a nondegenerate invariant skew-symmetric complex bilinear form.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentationExamples.simpleQuaternionRepresentationOfFinrankTwoIso
links.label: Uniqueness of the two-dimensional irreducible

Chapter5/Definition5.1.4.title: The formal definition computes the indicator from the character
explanation: Lean defines the complex scalar |G|⁻¹ Σ_g χ_V(g²), rather than choosing a type label and assigning it a number. The trace of ρ(g*g) in the definition below is χ_V(g²).
This average is defined for every finite-dimensional complex representation. Irreducibility is needed for the next statements identifying its value with the book's 0,1,−1 classification.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.AuxiliaryScalar.auxiliaryRepresentationScalar
declarations.label: The character average defining the Frobenius–Schur indicator
declarations.documentation: The complex scalar |G|⁻¹ times the sum of the character evaluated at squares of group elements.

Chapter5/Definition5.1.4.title: The three character-average values match the three types
explanation: For an irreducible, Lean proves both directions of each correspondence: complex type if and only if the average is 0, real type if and only if it is 1, and quaternionic type if and only if it is −1. Thus the computed average agrees with the book's definition by types.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.AuxiliaryProperties.auxiliaryPredicate_iff_auxiliaryValue_eq_zero
declarations.label: Complex type ↔ indicator 0
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible complex representation, non-self-duality is equivalent to the Frobenius–Schur character average being zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.AuxiliaryProperties.auxiliaryPredicate_iff_auxiliaryValue_eq_one
declarations.label: Real type ↔ indicator +1
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible complex representation, existence of a nondegenerate invariant symmetric bilinear form is equivalent to the character average being one.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.AuxiliaryProperties.auxiliaryStatement'''
declarations.label: Quaternionic type ↔ indicator −1
declarations.documentation: For an irreducible complex representation, existence of a nondegenerate invariant skew-symmetric bilinear form is equivalent to the character average being minus one.

Chapter5/Theorem5.1.5.title: The count includes the identity
explanation: The condition in the checked count is g*g=1. It includes the identity as well as elements of order two, matching the book's explicit convention—not the narrower use of “involution” for order exactly two.

The indexed family consists of one representative of each irreducible isomorphism class. The parameter D supplies the number of classes through the group-algebra decomposition; the chosen family is required to be simple and pairwise nonisomorphic. Dimensions and the count are cast to ℂ in this statement, where the natural-number cast is injective.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.Auxiliary.card_sq_eq_one_eq_sum_representationInvariant_mul_finrank
declarations.label: The Frobenius–Schur weighted dimension count
declarations.documentation: The number of elements whose square is one equals the sum, over the complete irreducible family, of each dimension times its Frobenius–Schur indicator.

Chapter5/Theorem5.1.5.title: The checked proof uses the flip on invariant tensors and forms
explanation: The book separates symmetric and exterior squares. The source instead works with the flip τ(x⊗y)=y⊗x and the identity tr(τ∘(A⊗A))=tr(A²). Composing with the averaging projection identifies the character average with the trace of the flip on invariant tensors.

For a self-dual irreducible the invariant tensor space has dimension one, so the flip acts by +1 or −1. The bilinear-form argument identifies these signs with symmetric or skew forms; in the non-self-dual case the invariant tensor space is zero and its trace is zero. This implements the same symmetric/skew distinction without requiring the proof to pass through separate quotient constructions.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.AuxiliaryVanishing.auxiliaryStatement
links.label: The flip-trace argument in the self-dual case

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.AuxiliaryVanishing.auxiliaryValue_eq_zero_of_character_not_inversionInvariant
links.label: Vanishing in the non-self-dual case

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Representation.Character.InversionAndInvariantForms.exists_symmetric_ne_zero_invariant_bilinear_form_of_auxiliary_eq_one
links.label: Extracting a symmetric invariant form from indicator +1

Chapter5/Theorem5.1.5.title: The regular character turns the weighted sum into a count
explanation: The final step uses Σ_V dim(V)χ_V(h)=χ_reg(h). The regular character is |G| at the identity and 0 elsewhere. Substitute h=g², exchange the finite sums, and divide by |G|: exactly the elements satisfying g²=1 contribute.

The source also proves this character-average identity over an algebraically closed field whose characteristic does not divide |G|. That version is a field-valued cast identity; the interpretation of indicators as the three complex representation types belongs to the complex results explained above.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.Auxiliary.card_sq_eq_one_eq_sum_finrank_mul_auxiliaryInvariant
links.label: The algebraic-field character-average identity

Chapter5/Corollary5.1.6.title: It is enough that every irreducible has real type
explanation: The checked hypothesis asks that each member of the complete irreducible family admit an invariant nondegenerate symmetric complex bilinear form. The real-form criterion in Problem 5.1.2 connects this with the book's assumption about complexifying real representations.

Each indicator is then 1, so the preceding weighted sum becomes the unweighted sum of dimensions. The count still includes the identity. The displayed equality is cast to ℂ; injectivity of that cast recovers the equality of natural numbers.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InvolutionRankSum.complex_cast_card_sq_eq_one_eq_sum_finrank_of_auxiliary_condition
declarations.label: The dimension sum when every irreducible has real type
declarations.documentation: If all members of the complete irreducible complex family have real type, their dimensions sum to the number of elements whose square is one.

Chapter5/Exercise5.1.7.title: Squaring permutes an odd-order group, even when it is nonabelian
explanation: For odd |G|, the function g ↦ g² is a bijection, with inverse g ↦ g^((|G|+1)/2). It is a permutation of the underlying set, not generally a group homomorphism. Therefore Σ_g χ(g²)=Σ_g χ(g).

A nontrivial irreducible has no fixed vectors, so its ordinary character average is zero. Its indicator is consequently zero, excluding real type. The existence proof uses the group-algebra matrix-block decomposition: if every irreducible action were trivial, its faithful action on the group algebra would identify a nonidentity group element with the identity. The theorem thus supplies an irreducible with nontrivial action and no invariant symmetric form.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.OddOrderAuxiliary.oddCardinality_exists_simpleRepresentation_not_auxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: An odd-order nontrivial group has a non-real irreducible
declarations.documentation: Every nontrivial finite group of odd order has a finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation with nontrivial action and without an invariant nondegenerate symmetric complex bilinear form.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.OddOrder.CharacterSums.auxiliaryEquivOfOddCard
links.label: The bijection given by squaring

links.name: RepresentationTheory.OddOrder.CharacterSums.sum_character_square_eq_zero_of_odd_card
links.label: The vanishing character sum for a nontrivial irreducible

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: Irreducibility here is over the real numbers
explanation: The carrier Fin 2 → ℂ is treated as a four-dimensional real vector space. The checked statement concerns every real subspace stable under the matrices in SU(2), not just complex subspaces.

For a nonzero vector v, the proof uses D = diag(i,−i) and B = [[0,−1],[1,0]]. The four vectors v, Dv, Bv, DBv are real-linearly independent. Any invariant subspace containing v therefore contains a real basis and is the whole space.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.matrixAction_011564
declarations.label: Real irreducibility of the standard SU(2) action
declarations.documentation: A real subspace of ℂ² stable under every matrix in SU(2) is either zero or all of ℂ².

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: The commuting endomorphisms form a four-dimensional division algebra
explanation: The algebra is the centralizer of the action inside the real-linear endomorphisms of ℂ². Thus its elements satisfy f(Av) = A f(v) for every A ∈ SU(2); multiplication is composition. The subalgebra construction includes closure under addition, real scalars and composition.

A nonzero commuting map has invariant kernel and image. Real irreducibility makes it bijective, and its inverse also commutes with the action. Evaluation at (1,0) is a real-linear equivalence from this algebra to ℂ², proving dimension four. Surjectivity uses the identity, multiplication by i, the map (z₀,z₁) ↦ (−conj z₁, conj z₀), and their composite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.equivariantEndomorphismAlgebra
declarations.label: The algebra of commuting real-linear maps
declarations.documentation: The real subalgebra of endomorphisms of ℂ² commuting with the SU(2) action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.membershipCharacterization_011477
declarations.label: Every nonzero commuting map is invertible
declarations.documentation: Every nonzero element of the commuting-endomorphism algebra is a unit of that algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.cardinalityFormula_011488
declarations.label: The commuting algebra has real dimension four
declarations.documentation: Evaluation at (1,0) identifies the underlying real vector space with ℂ², giving dimension four.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.evaluationLinearMap
links.label: Evaluation at the first coordinate vector

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: Coordinates check the quaternion multiplication table
explanation: For Mathlib's real quaternion algebra ℍ[ℝ], Lean supplies the basis 1,i,j,k and checks all nine products in the displayed table. In particular, the three imaginary units square to −1, and reversing their order changes the sign.

The source also checks that the eight elements ±1, ±i, ±j, ±k have norm one and are closed under multiplication and conjugation. Conjugation is inversion on norm-one quaternions. These are the eight quaternion-group elements; the source's name realUnitQuaternions denotes this finite set, not the whole sphere of norm-one quaternions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.quaternionBasis
declarations.label: The real quaternion basis 1, i, j, k
declarations.documentation: The four coordinate quaternions form a real basis of ℍ[ℝ].

links.label: The relation i² = −1

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.valueFormula_011515
links.label: The relation ij = k

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.membershipCharacterization_011460
links.label: Closure of the eight-element set

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: The identification of the two quaternion models is missing
explanation: The book defines its quaternion algebra as the commuting endomorphisms in part (b). The coordinate multiplication table and the constructions below instead use Mathlib's ℍ[ℝ]. The source proves the dimension and division properties of the commuting algebra, but does not construct an algebra equivalence between it and the coordinate quaternions. Thus the checked coordinate table does not yet complete part (c) for the book's definition.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: Conjugation reverses products; the squared norm multiplies
explanation: Quaternion conjugation is Lean's star. The first identity below reverses the factors, as in the book. Quaternion.normSq is the squared norm a²+b²+c²+d², not the norm itself.

The second checked identity is multiplicativity of that squared norm. The book's norm identity follows by taking nonnegative square roots. Norm-one quaternions are represented by unitary ℍ[ℝ], whose membership condition is equivalent to normSq q = 1; their inverse is their conjugate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.valueFormula_011596
declarations.label: Conjugation reverses multiplication
declarations.documentation: The conjugate of q₁q₂ is the conjugate of q₂ times the conjugate of q₁.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.quaternionNorm_011503
declarations.label: Multiplicativity of the squared norm
declarations.documentation: The squared norm of a quaternion product is the product of the squared norms.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.quaternionNorm_011502
links.label: Norm one is the unitary membership condition

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: A norm-one quaternion gives an SU(2) matrix
explanation: Write α = a+bi and β = c+di. The map sends a+bi+cj+dk to [[α,β],[−conj β,conj α]]. Lean checks multiplication, unitarity and determinant one; the first row recovers the four real quaternion coordinates, proving injectivity and surjectivity.

The conclusion below is an isomorphism of groups. The norm-one coordinate equation is the equation of S³, but this source does not bundle a homeomorphism or a smooth-manifold identification with SU(2). The sphere parenthesis in the book is therefore not a separate checked topological theorem here.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.multiplicativeEquivalence_011606
declarations.label: Norm-one quaternions are isomorphic to SU(2)
declarations.documentation: There exists a multiplicative equivalence between the norm-one real quaternions and SU(2).

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.unitQuaternionToSpecialUnitary
links.label: The explicit quaternion-to-matrix homomorphism

Chapter4/Problem4.12.7.title: Conjugation gives a surjection onto SO(3) with kernel ±1
explanation: The rotation matrix has as its columns the imaginary coordinates of qiq⁻¹, qjq⁻¹, qkq⁻¹. Lean checks both orthogonality and determinant one, so the image is in SO(3), not just O(3).

Surjectivity uses a decomposition into rotations about the third, second and third axes, lifting each with its half-angle quaternion. The identity rotation occurs exactly for q = ±1. Transport through the preceding group isomorphism gives the checked homomorphism from SU(2) below. Its two-element kernel makes it two-to-one as a group map; no topological covering-space assertion is needed for this statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.Auxiliary011486
declarations.label: The surjective SU(2) → SO(3) homomorphism and its kernel
declarations.documentation: There exists a surjective homomorphism from SU(2) to SO(3), and a matrix belongs to its kernel exactly when it is the identity or minus the identity.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.unitQuaternionToRotation
links.label: The quaternion rotation homomorphism

links.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionRotationMaps.surjective_011572
links.label: The half-angle lift proving surjectivity

Chapter4/Problem4.12.8.title: Every finite rotation group has one of the five group types
explanation: The input is an actual finite subgroup of the real matrix group SO(3). The alternatives are cyclicity or a multiplicative equivalence to D_n, A₄, S₄ or A₅. Here DihedralGroup n has order 2n; Equiv.Perm (Fin 4) is S₄.

The proof treats the trivial group as cyclic and derives the other alternatives from the pole-count equation. Its dihedral branch has n ≥ 2, although that bound is not retained in the final existential statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteRotationGroups.finiteRotationGroupClassification_011800
declarations.label: The five abstract finite rotation-group types
declarations.documentation: Every finite subgroup of SO(3) is cyclic or isomorphic to a dihedral group, A₄, S₄ or A₅.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.8.title: The pole count is checked using orbit–stabilizer and Burnside
explanation: The source's set rotationAxes G consists of poles on the unit sphere, not unoriented axis lines. It proves that a nonidentity rotation fixes exactly two opposite poles and that each pole stabilizer is cyclic.

With n = |G| ≥ 2, Burnside's count gives kn = |P| + 2(n−1), where k is the number of pole orbits. Orbit–stabilizer gives |P| = Σ n/m_i. Dividing and rearranging produces the book's equation, checked over the rational numbers. A multiset records the stabilizer orders, so repeated orders such as 2,2,n are retained.

links.label: A nonidentity rotation has two opposite poles

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteRotationGroups.cyclicGroup_011643

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteRotationGroups.exists_stabilizer_cardMultiset
links.label: The checked pole-count equation and its possible orders

Chapter4/Problem4.12.8.title: Only two or three pole orbits are possible
explanation: Each m_i ≥ 2, so each summand is at least 1/2, while the left side is less than 2. The equation permits either two orders n,n or three orders 2,2,r, 2,3,3, 2,3,4 or 2,3,5.

These give respectively a cyclic group of order n, a dihedral group of order 2r, and the groups A₄, S₄, A₅ of orders 12,24,60. The source goes beyond the numerical possibilities: separate arguments construct the abstract group equivalences used in the classification theorem.

links.label: The complete rational-equation case analysis

Chapter4/Problem4.12.8.title: Abstract group types are checked, geometric realizations are not
explanation: The theorem identifies the abstract groups, but does not prove that the subgroup is conjugate inside SO(3) to the specified polygon or polyhedron rotation group. The regular polyhedra and their geometric symmetry groups are not constructed in this source. This is the remaining distinction between the checked classification and the book's geometric list.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.8.title: Finite SU(2) subgroups are cyclic or full binary lifts
explanation: Use the surjection h : SU(2) → SO(3) with kernel {±I}. If a finite subgroup H contains −I, then it is the full inverse image of its image and has twice the image's order. If it omits −I, the restriction of h is injective. Lean proves that −I is the only element of order two in SU(2); Cauchy's theorem then rules out the even-order noncyclic image types, making H cyclic. A subgroup with cyclic image is also proved cyclic when it contains −I.

The remaining possibilities are the full inverse images of D_n, A₄, S₄, A₅, with orders 4n,24,48,120. These are the binary dihedral, tetrahedral, octahedral and icosahedral groups. In the checked statement, H = Subgroup.comap h (H.map h) asserts the full-inverse-image property; the source does not give separate presentations or isomorphisms to named binary-group models.

declarations.label: Cyclic subgroups or binary lifts, with their orders
declarations.documentation: Every finite subgroup of SU(2) is cyclic or is the full inverse image of a dihedral, A₄, S₄ or A₅ image under a surjection with kernel ±I; in these cases its order is respectively 4n, 24, 48 or 120.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: The zero-sum function representation has dimension q−1
explanation: Lean represents an affine transformation by a nonzero slope a and a translation b. The action on functions is pullback by the inverse transformation: (g·f)(x) = f(g⁻¹x). It preserves the sum of function values, so it restricts to the space V in the hint.

This space is the kernel of the surjective summation map to ℂ, and therefore has dimension q−1. Constant functions give the complementary trivial representation in the full q-dimensional function space.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: Averaging and translations prove irreducibility
explanation: Start with a nonzero function in an invariant subspace of V, and translate a point where it is nonzero to 0. Summing its transforms under the nonzero slopes isolates a nonzero multiple of qδ₀ − 1.

Translations then put every qδ_t − 1 in the subspace. These functions span the zero-sum space. The checked theorem states that any invariant subspace contained in V is zero or all of V; the source also checks that V is nonzero for every finite field.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.membershipCharacterization_011454
declarations.label: Irreducibility of the zero-sum function model
declarations.documentation: A subspace of the zero-sum functions stable under the affine pullback action is either zero or the whole zero-sum space.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: For q ≥ 3, these are all the irreducibles
explanation: Every one-dimensional character is trivial on translations and has the form χ(a,b) = ψ(a), where ψ is a character of 𝔽_qˣ. There are q−1 of them. Alongside these is the single irreducible V of dimension q−1.

The squared dimensions add to (q−1) + (q−1)² = q(q−1) = |G|. The source proves both the dimension dichotomy below and the stronger isomorphism classification: every irreducible is a character representation or is isomorphic to V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.cardinalityFormula_011354
declarations.label: The q−1 linear characters when q ≥ 3
declarations.documentation: For a finite field with at least three elements, the affine group has q−1 complex one-dimensional characters.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.simpleRepresentation_011343
declarations.label: The irreducible dimension dichotomy
declarations.documentation: Every finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of the affine group has dimension 1 or q−1.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.simpleRepresentation_011340
links.label: The isomorphism classification for q ≥ 3

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: The character of V is the fixed-point count minus one
explanation: An affine transformation fixes all q points if it is the identity, no points if it is a nonzero translation, and one point if a ≠ 1. Removing the constant functions gives χ_V(1) = q−1, χ_V(1,b) = −1 for b ≠ 0, and χ_V(a,b) = 0 for a ≠ 1.

The proof identifies the full function action with permutation matrices, computes its trace by counting fixed points, and subtracts the trace of the complementary constant line. Together with χ(a,b) = ψ(a) for the linear characters, this supplies all character values when q ≥ 3.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.characterFormula_011257
declarations.label: The fixed-point character formula
declarations.documentation: The character of the zero-sum function representation is the number of fixed field elements minus one.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: Products of characters and character twists
explanation: One-dimensional representations tensor by multiplying their characters: χ ⊗ χ′ ≅ χχ′. The source constructs the scalar tensor isomorphism directly.

For q ≥ 3, every character twist of V is isomorphic to V. A linear character is trivial on translations, where χ_V can be nonzero, and χ_V vanishes on all other nonidentity slopes. Thus twisting leaves its character unchanged; character rigidity yields the isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.cardinalityFormula_011306
declarations.label: A linear character twist preserves V when q ≥ 3
declarations.documentation: Tensoring any complex one-dimensional character with the zero-sum representation gives an isomorphic representation, for q ≥ 3.

links.label: The explicit tensor isomorphism for two characters

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: V ⊗ V contains every linear character once and q−2 copies of V
explanation: For q ≥ 3, the decomposition is the direct sum of all q−1 linear characters, each once, together with q−2 copies of V. The dimension is (q−1) + (q−2)(q−1) = (q−1)².

The proof checks the character identity on the identity, nonzero translations and the remaining transformations, then obtains a representation isomorphism. The target in the checked statement bundles the character sum and the repeated copies of V as a binary product, which is their direct sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AffineGroupRepresentations.cardinalityFormula_011270
declarations.label: The tensor-square decomposition for q ≥ 3
declarations.documentation: The tensor square of the zero-sum representation is isomorphic to the sum of all linear characters and q−2 copies of the zero-sum representation.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.6.title: The field with two elements is a separate case
explanation: When q = 2, the slope is always 1, so the group consists of the two translations. Both irreducibles are one-dimensional: the trivial character and the character taking the nonidentity translation to −1. The zero-sum representation is the latter.

Their tensor products obey the two-element character group: the nontrivial character tensored with itself is trivial. The preceding q−1 character count and twist/tensor-square formulas assume q ≥ 3; the source has separate count, classification and tensor results for q = 2.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.10.title: A nonzero intertwiner gives the requested occurrence
explanation: The formal hypothesis for faithfulness is Function.Injective ρ. The checked statements assume that V and the irreducible representation W are finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. The degree n is a natural number; degree zero is allowed.

The symmetric-power result supplies a nonzero linear map W → SⁿV commuting with every group action. Its kernel is invariant, so simplicity of W forces that kernel to be zero. Thus the conclusion really gives a copy of the irreducible inside one symmetric power, not merely a map with unspecified image.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationPolynomialFunctions.exists_nonzero_symmetric_power_intertwiner
declarations.label: Every irreducible maps nontrivially into some symmetric power

Chapter4/Problem4.12.10.title: A covector with a free orbit
explanation: Faithfulness passes to the dual action. For each nonidentity group element, its fixed covectors form a proper linear subspace. There are only finitely many such subspaces, and they cannot cover a complex vector space. A covector outside their union has trivial stabilizer, as the hint requires.

The source evaluates homogeneous symmetric tensors on this covector’s orbit. On a pure symmetric tensor, evaluation is the product of the covector’s values on its factors; permutation of those factors does not change the value.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.10.title: Orbit evaluation reaches every function on G
explanation: Distinct orbit points are distinguished by some linear functional. Products of normalized separating functions then give a function equal to 1 at one orbit point and 0 at all the others. These delta functions span all functions on the finite group, proving surjectivity.

Lean presents the polynomial space as the direct sum of its homogeneous symmetric powers. The target of the theorem is MonoidAlgebra ℂ G, identified with functions on G by their coefficients. Its action corresponds to left translation, (g·F)(x) = F(g⁻¹x). The theorem checks equivariance as well as surjectivity; it is a linear map, not a claimed algebra homomorphism to the group algebra with its convolution product.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.10.title: Semisimplicity selects a homogeneous degree
explanation: Every irreducible embeds in the regular representation. Maschke’s theorem lets the surjective orbit-evaluation map split equivariantly, so this embedding lifts into the direct sum of symmetric powers.

A nonzero lifted map has a nonzero projection into at least one homogeneous summand. That projection still intertwines the group actions, and its irreducible source makes it injective. This is the step converting surjectivity for all polynomials into occurrence in a single degree.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.10.title: Tensor powers: an embedding and an independent character proof
explanation: In characteristic zero, symmetrization embeds SⁿV equivariantly into V⊗ⁿ. The source constructs and checks this lift, which explains the book’s “and hence”.

The tensor-power theorem below uses a different proof. Tensor characters are powers of the original character. If an irreducible never occurred, all corresponding character averages would vanish; polynomial interpolation on the finitely many character values contradicts this by isolating the identity value dim V. Faithfulness and unitarization show that no other group element has that value.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: The theorem assumes the elasticity map commutes with rotations
explanation: The formal action is matrix conjugation, M ↦ AMAᵀ, for real orthogonal matrices A with determinant 1. A candidate elasticity map is a real linear map from symmetric matrices to all matrices, and the hypothesis says that it intertwines this action for every rotation.
This rotational equivariance is an input to the theorem. The result classifies linear laws satisfying it; it does not derive the hypothesis from physical laws or assert it for every material.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: Scalar, skew-symmetric and trace-free symmetric parts
explanation: The three pieces of a real matrix M are (tr M/3)I, (M−Mᵀ)/2, and (M+Mᵀ)/2 − (tr M/3)I. They are, respectively, a scalar matrix, a skew-symmetric matrix and a trace-free symmetric matrix. The checked internal direct sum says that these invariant pieces span all matrices and have zero overlap.

Their dimensions are 1, 3 and 5. For symmetric matrices the skew part vanishes, leaving scalar matrices plus the trace-free symmetric space W. The formal model uses symmetric matrices directly rather than the abstract symmetric tensor power.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: Skew-symmetric matrices carry the standard vector action
explanation: The map taking a vector v to the matrix of w ↦ v × w is a linear equivalence from ℝ³ to skew-symmetric matrices. The source writes the entries of that matrix explicitly, constructs its inverse, and proves that rotating the vector corresponds to conjugating the matrix.
This supplies the identification of the three-dimensional summand with the standard representation V, not merely an equality of dimensions.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: Irreducibility over both real and complex coefficients
explanation: The source proves that an invariant subspace of the skew-symmetric space, or of the trace-free symmetric space, is zero or the whole space. It proves the same statements with complex matrix entries, still acted on by the real rotation group. These are the concrete complexified models relevant to the problem.

The proofs use explicit rotations: half-turns extract matrix coordinates, cyclic coordinate rotations move them, and 45-degree rotations connect off-diagonal symmetric entries with trace-free diagonal ones. Starting from any nonzero invariant vector forces all basis directions into the subspace.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: Two scalars determine the output, which is symmetric
explanation: The classification theorem gives real numbers K, μ such that f(x+y) = Kx + μy for a scalar matrix x and a trace-free symmetric matrix y. Every symmetric input has this unique decomposition, so no skew-symmetric output component is possible.
For a symmetric matrix d, the formula reads f(d) = K(tr d/3)I + μ(d − (tr d/3)I). The source proves existence of these scalars and symmetry of all outputs; it does not impose signs on them.

The final proof takes a real route to scalarity: maps from the irreducible five-dimensional space into the smaller scalar and skew spaces must vanish, and an endomorphism of that five-dimensional real space has a real eigenvalue because its characteristic polynomial has odd degree. Its nonzero invariant eigenspace must then be the whole space. Thus this source proof does not simply invoke complex Schur’s lemma after complexification.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixConjugationActions.auxiliaryUniversalResultA
declarations.label: The two scalar actions and symmetry of every output
declarations.documentation: An equivariant real linear map from symmetric matrices to all matrices acts by one scalar on scalar matrices and another on trace-free symmetric matrices, and all its outputs are symmetric.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixConjugationActions.auxiliaryUniversalResultC
declarations.label: The two-parameter formula for every symmetric input
declarations.documentation: There are real K and μ such that each symmetric input decomposes into a scalar part x and a trace-free symmetric part y, with output Kx + μy.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.after: In fact, it is clear from physics
Chapter4/Problem4.12.11.title: The physical motivation and positivity remain outside these results
explanation: These checked results concern representations on matrix spaces and equivariant linear maps. The aligned source does not formalize the deformation’s polar decomposition, the derivation of stress from forces, or the physical argument for positive moduli. In particular, K > 0 and μ > 0 are not conclusions of the classification theorem.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.1.title: One-dimensional representations: two for odd N, four for even N
explanation: Write r for a generating rotation and s for a reflection. A one-dimensional representation is determined by their values u and w. The relations require uᴺ = 1, u² = 1 and w² = 1.

For odd N, this forces u = 1, while w can be either sign. For even N, both signs are allowed independently. The checked equivalence below constructs the characters from these pairs and recovers the pair from any character.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.1.title: The remaining representations come in rotation-eigenvalue pairs
explanation: Choose a primitive N-th root ζ. In the representation ρⱼ, the rotation acts diagonally with eigenvalues ζʲ and ζ⁻ʲ, and the reflection swaps the two coordinate vectors. Distinct rotation eigenvalues, together with this swap, force any nonzero invariant subspace to contain both coordinates.

Take one index from each pair j, −j, using 0 < j < N/2. This gives (N−1)/2 two-dimensional irreducibles for odd N, and (N−2)/2 for even N. Their squared dimensions, together with those of the characters, add to 2N. The classification proof uses this count and pairwise nonisomorphism to show that no irreducibles are missing.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.1.title: The tensor square is trivial + reflection sign + ρ₂
explanation: For the coordinate representation ρ₁, the checked isomorphism gives ρ₁ ⊗ ρ₁ ≅ 1 ⊕ ε ⊕ ρ₂, where ε is trivial on rotations and changes sign on reflections. The proof computes the characters and uses the fact that equal complex characters imply isomorphic finite-group representations.
For a polygon with N ≥ 3 and N ≠ 4, the two-dimensional summand is irreducible: its simplicity condition is that 4 be nonzero modulo N.

declarations.documentation: The target is the direct sum of the trivial character, the reflection-sign character and the index-two matrix representation.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.1.title: The square and the geometric identification need an extra step
explanation: For N = 4, ρ₂ is not irreducible. Its rotation is −Id, and the reflection swaps coordinates, so the lines through (1,1) and (1,−1) split it into the other two one-dimensional characters. The tensor square therefore contains all four characters once. This further line-splitting is not supplied as a separate checked isomorphism here.

The source also does not construct the change of basis identifying ρ₁ with the complexified polygon-plane action named in the problem. The checked result concerns the explicit matrix model; that geometric identification remains to be formalized.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: Three coordinates describe the group
explanation: Write an upper-triangular matrix as (a,b,c), with a and b in the two adjacent off-diagonal positions and c in the upper-right corner. The multiplication law is (a,b,c)(a′,b′,c′) = (a+a′, b+b′, c+c′+ab′). Lean uses these triples over ZMod p, rather than storing the whole matrix.
The two prescribed generators are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0). Their commutator is (0,0,1); this accounts for the central coordinate and for the sign in the action formula below.

links.label: The generator normal form

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: The action of any group element
explanation: The action is (ρ_z(a,b,c)f)(t) = z^(bt−c) f(t−a). Exponents are residues modulo p; choosing an integer representative has no effect because zᵖ = 1. In particular, a central element (0,0,c) acts by z⁻ᶜ, not zᶜ.
The construction checks the multiplication law, and the uniqueness theorem says that this is the only representation on the specified function space with the two prescribed generator actions.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: Nontrivial z gives irreducibility; z = 1 does not
explanation: Because p is prime, every nontrivial p-th root has order p. The scaling generator then has distinct eigenvalues on the delta-function basis. The proof isolates a delta function from a nonzero invariant subspace, and the shift generator moves it to every other delta function.
When z = 1, the constant functions form a proper invariant line. The theorem proves both directions of the criterion, for any representation satisfying the two generator formulas.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ThreeCoordinateGroupRepresentations.shiftScaleRepresentation_simple_iff
declarations.label: R_z is irreducible exactly when z ≠ 1

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: The p² characters factor through the first two coordinates
explanation: A one-dimensional character kills commutators, hence kills the central coordinate. The quotient is the additive group 𝔽_p × 𝔽_p. With a fixed primitive root η, the characters are χ_(u,v)(a,b,c) = η^(ua+vb), with u,v ∈ 𝔽_p.
The checked equivalence identifies characters of the Heisenberg group with characters of this quotient, and the count is p².

declarations.label: Every character comes from the two-coordinate quotient

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: R₁ contains p of those characters, each once
explanation: The Fourier functions f_j(t) = η^(jt) span invariant lines in R₁. The shift acts on this line by η⁻ʲ, and the scaling generator acts trivially. These are the p characters with second parameter zero, not all p² characters of the group.
The decomposition theorem supplies invariant one-dimensional subspaces forming an internal direct sum of the whole function space, with distinct characters on distinct lines.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ThreeCoordinateGroupRepresentations.exists_invariant_line_decomposition
declarations.label: The multiplicity-free Fourier-line decomposition of R₁

Chapter4/Problem4.12.2.title: The sum of squares makes the list exhaustive
explanation: The irreducibles are the p² characters and the p−1 representations R_z for nontrivial p-th roots. Each R_z has dimension p. Their central characters are different, so these representations are pairwise nonisomorphic.

The dimension count is p² + (p−1)p² = p³ = |G|. The checked classification concludes that every irreducible is isomorphic to a character representation or to one of these shift-and-scale representations.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.3.title: Invariant subspaces are zero or the whole power
explanation: Both checked statements assume a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic zero. They are not restricted to ℂ and do not assume algebraic closedness. Invariance means stability under the induced map of every invertible linear transformation of V.

The conclusion is W = ⊥ ∨ W = ⊤. To call the representation irreducible, the ambient space must also be nonzero: ΛᵐV is nonzero in the book’s range m ≤ dim V, while SⁿV is nonzero when V ≠ 0 or n = 0. If V = 0 and n > 0, the symmetric power is zero; the subspace dichotomy still holds, but it is not a nonzero irreducible representation.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.3.title: Distinct eigenvalues let the proof extract basis vectors
explanation: For the symmetric power, scale the original basis vectors by distinct primes. The degree-n monomial basis then has distinct eigenvalues by unique prime factorization. For the exterior power, scale e_i by 2^(2^i); the weights of the subset-indexed wedge basis are distinct by uniqueness of binary expansion.

If a vector in an invariant subspace has a nonzero coordinate at one of these eigenvectors, polynomial interpolation in the diagonal operator extracts that eigenvector. This proves the first step of the hint without assuming that an arbitrary invariant subspace was already given by a subset of the basis.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.InvariantSubmodule.Eigenbasis.eq_bot_or_top_of_invariant_of_eigenbasis_connected
links.label: The eigenbasis extraction and propagation argument

Chapter4/Problem4.12.3.title: Moving one basis vector forces all the others
explanation: For the symmetric power, the proof follows the transvection step of the hint. The map 1 + E_ij is invertible for i ≠ j; expansion of a monomial, followed by eigenvector extraction, lets one replace an occurrence of e_j by e_i. The relevant integer coefficients are nonzero in characteristic zero. Repeated replacements connect all degree-n monomials.

For the exterior power, the source uses a shorter route: basis permutations take any m-element subset to any other. Once one wedge basis vector belongs to the subspace, invariance puts every wedge basis vector there. This differs from using transvections for both powers, as suggested in the book.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.SymmetricPower.BasisPairMaps.Submodule.mem_of_objectRelation
links.label: Propagation between symmetric-power monomials

links.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.ExteriorPower.InvariantSubmodules.eq_bot_or_eq_top_of_exteriorPower_invariant
links.label: The exterior-power proof using permutations

Chapter4/Problem4.12.4.title: Noncommuting graph symmetries force a repeated eigenvalue
explanation: The formal graph is a finite undirected simple graph, and the adjacency matrix has real entries. The hypothesis explicitly supplies two graph automorphisms that do not commute.

The conclusion says that the characteristic polynomial is not squarefree. Since this real symmetric matrix is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues, that means some eigenvalue is repeated. It is the spectral conclusion of the problem, not just a claim that a polynomial fails an unrelated algebraic test.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GraphSpectrumSymmetry.not_squarefree_charpoly_of_noncommuting_automorphisms
declarations.label: Nonabelian automorphisms imply repeated adjacency eigenvalues

Chapter4/Problem4.12.4.title: The checked proof uses the centralizer of the adjacency matrix
explanation: Suppose all eigenvalues were distinct. In an eigenbasis, every matrix commuting with the adjacency matrix would be diagonal, so any two such matrices would commute. Each graph automorphism gives a permutation matrix commuting with adjacency.

The permutation-matrix action is faithful, so commuting matrices would force the two automorphisms themselves to commute, a contradiction. The proof uses real symmetric diagonalization directly; it does not first decompose the permutation representation into irreducible blocks.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.GraphSpectrumSymmetry.not_squarefree_charpoly_of_noncommuting_automorphisms.commute_of_commute_hermitian_squarefree
links.label: The distinct-spectrum centralizer lemma

links.name: RepresentationTheory.GraphSpectrumSymmetry.not_squarefree_charpoly_of_noncommuting_automorphisms.adjMatrix_mul_automorphismMatrix
links.label: Automorphism matrices commute with adjacency

Chapter4/Problem4.12.5.title: The 12-point model contains 1, 3, 3′ and 5 once
explanation: The algebraic model is the action of A₅ on cosets of a cyclic subgroup of order 5. It has 60/5 = 12 points. Using the two inequivalent three-dimensional representations 3 and 3′ from the character table, its function representation decomposes as 1 ⊕ 3 ⊕ 3′ ⊕ 5.

The theorem supplies actual invariant irreducible subspaces forming an internal direct sum, not only a sum of dimensions. It also distinguishes the two three-dimensional summands by their characters. The proof computes permutation characters by counting fixed points, then uses character inner products to find multiplicities.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011198
declarations.label: The 12-point irreducible decomposition
declarations.documentation: Four invariant irreducible subspaces of dimensions 1, 3, 3 and 5 form an internal direct sum; the two three-dimensional characters are different.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.5.title: The 20- and 30-point decompositions
explanation: Cosets of cyclic subgroups of orders 3 and 2 give the 20- and 30-point models. Their decompositions are 1 ⊕ 3 ⊕ 3′ ⊕ 4 ⊕ 4 ⊕ 5 and 1 ⊕ 3 ⊕ 3′ ⊕ 4 ⊕ 4 ⊕ 5 ⊕ 5 ⊕ 5, respectively.

Thus the four-dimensional irreducible occurs twice in both, while the five-dimensional irreducible occurs once in the 20-point model and three times in the 30-point model. The dimensions add to 20 and 30, and both theorems give internal decompositions into invariant irreducible subspaces.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011082
declarations.label: The 20-point irreducible decomposition
declarations.documentation: Six invariant irreducible subspaces of dimensions 1, 3, 3, 4, 4 and 5 form an internal direct sum; the two three-dimensional characters are different.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011043
declarations.label: The 30-point irreducible decomposition
declarations.documentation: Eight invariant irreducible subspaces of dimensions 1, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5 and 5 form an internal direct sum; the two three-dimensional characters are different.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.5.title: The coset answer does not depend on the point labels
explanation: The comparison theorems apply to any transitive A₅-action on 12, 20 or 30 points whose point stabilizers have orders 5, 3 or 2, respectively. Each gives an equivariant bijection with the corresponding coset model. Pulling back functions along that bijection transfers the decomposition.
These hypotheses, rather than the names of the points, are what lets the algebraic calculation apply to a geometric action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011190
declarations.label: Every transitive 12-point action with stabilizers of order 5 has this model
declarations.documentation: An equivariant bijection identifies an action satisfying the stated transitivity and stabilizer hypotheses with the canonical 12-point coset action.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011070
links.label: The corresponding 20-point comparison

links.name: RepresentationTheory.CosetPermutationActions.cardinalityFormula_011031
links.label: The corresponding 30-point comparison

Chapter4/Problem4.12.5.title: The geometric bridge is not yet checked here
explanation: The aligned source does not construct the vertex, face or edge sets of a regular icosahedron and prove that their rotation actions are transitive with the required stabilizers. It proves the coset decompositions and the conditional comparison results above. Identifying those models with the actual geometric actions remains a formalization gap; the geometry should not be inferred from a 12-, 20- or 30-dimensional carrier alone.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.9.title: The p-dimensional characters are supported on the center
explanation: Use the coordinates and conventions of Problem 4.12.2. For z ≠ 1, the character of R_z is p z⁻ᶜ on (0,0,c), and zero when either of the first two coordinates is nonzero. A nonzero shift has no diagonal entries in the delta-function basis; a nontrivial scale has a vanishing root-of-unity sum.

The condition called AuxiliaryProperty in the checked statement is just the two generator action formulas from Problem 4.12.2, not an additional representation-theoretic assumption. The one-dimensional characters factor through (a,b) and are trivial on the center.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexCharacterIdentities.trace_eq_ite_of_auxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: The character formula for nontrivial R_z
declarations.documentation: Assuming the two specified generator actions, the trace is p times z to the negative central coordinate on the center, and zero elsewhere.

Chapter4/Problem4.12.9.title: Products of characters and twists of R_z
explanation: Two one-dimensional representations tensor by multiplying their characters: χ ⊗ χ′ ≅ χχ′. The proof constructs this isomorphism using scalar multiplication ℂ ⊗ ℂ → ℂ.

For z ≠ 1, every one-dimensional twist satisfies χ ⊗ R_z ≅ R_z. Their characters agree because χ is trivial on the center, where the character of R_z is supported. This isomorphism is obtained from character rigidity.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexCharacterIdentities.tensor_multiplicativeCharacter_iso_mul
declarations.label: Tensoring two one-dimensional characters

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexCharacterIdentities.tensor_multiplicativeCharacter_iso_self
declarations.label: A character twist preserves nontrivial R_z

Chapter4/Problem4.12.9.title: If zw ≠ 1, the tensor product contains p copies of R_(zw)
explanation: For nontrivial p-th roots z,w with zw ≠ 1, the answer is R_z ⊗ R_w ≅ R_(zw) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ R_(zw), with p summands. Both sides have dimension p².
Multiplying the character formulas gives χ_z χ_w = p χ_(zw). The theorem turns this equality into a representation isomorphism, with the finite direct sum indexed by Fin p.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexCharacterIdentities.tensor_iso_biproduct
declarations.label: The p-copy decomposition when zw is nontrivial

Chapter4/Problem4.12.9.title: If zw = 1, all p² one-dimensional characters occur once
explanation: For inverse nontrivial roots, R_z ⊗ R_w is the direct sum of every one-dimensional character of the Heisenberg group, once each. It is not p copies of R₁: those would repeat only the p characters appearing in the Fourier decomposition of Problem 4.12.2.

The tensor-product character is p² on the center and zero elsewhere. Character orthogonality on the two-coordinate quotient gives the same character for the sum of all p² linear characters; rigidity yields the checked isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexCharacterIdentities.tensor_iso_multiplicativeCharacterBiproduct
declarations.label: The multiplicity-free sum of all characters for inverse roots

Chapter4/Introduction_4.10.title: There is one independent polynomial variable for each group element
explanation: The polynomial ring is indexed directly by G: X(g) denotes the indeterminate x_g. An enumeration is needed to print the matrix, but not to define its variables. The definition accepts any commutative coefficient ring; the algebraically closed field and characteristic restriction enter the factorization theorem, not this setup.

links.name: MvPolynomial.X
links.label: The polynomial variable indexed by a group element

Chapter4/Definition4.10.1.title: The definition uses the book's product-indexed matrix, without an inverse
explanation: The checked definition is det(X(g·h)), with rows and columns indexed by G itself. Reordering G permutes rows and columns together, so it does not change this determinant. This is the book's convention, not the often-used det(X(g·h⁻¹)). Inverting the column labels relates those two determinants by the sign of the inversion permutation; the proof below retains that sign.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.IndexedPolynomial.groupIndexedPolynomial
declarations.label: The group determinant is det(X(g·h))
declarations.documentation: Over any commutative coefficient ring, form the square matrix whose (g,h) entry is the polynomial variable indexed by g·h, and take its determinant.

Chapter4/Theorem4.10.2.title: Each irreducible representation supplies a factor of degree equal to its dimension
explanation: Choose a decomposition of k[G] into square matrix algebras, with block sizes dᵢ. The i-th factor is the determinant of ∑g x_g ρᵢ(g) on its dᵢ-dimensional coordinate representation. The source proves that this polynomial is irreducible and has total degree dᵢ, that distinct factors are not scalar multiples, and that the number of blocks is the number of conjugacy classes.

These results hold over an algebraically closed field in which |G| is nonzero, including ℂ. They do not assert the same factorization in characteristic dividing |G|. The stored decomposition chooses bases and an ordering of the blocks; it is not a canonical ordering of polynomials.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.MvPolynomial.GroupIndexedFactorization.exists_irreducible_factorization_of_auxiliaryGroupPolynomial
links.label: The full checked factorization, including irreducibility, distinctness and factor count

Chapter4/Theorem4.10.2.title: The natural determinant factors give the book's formula up to a sign
explanation: With the factors defined as representation determinants, the checked identity has the extra scalar sign(g ↦ g⁻¹). This is the column permutation already mentioned in the book's proof, not an extra group-theoretic hypothesis. For example, inversion swaps the two nonidentity elements of a group of order three, so its sign can be −1.

The final existence theorem absorbs this sign into one factor: it chooses a nonzero scalar c with cᵈ equal to the sign, where d is that factor's degree, and replaces the factor by c times itself. Algebraic closedness supplies c. Degree, irreducibility and nonproportionality are unchanged, and the product then equals the book's determinant without an external sign.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryGroupPolynomial_eq_sign_smul_prod_auxiliaryPolynomial_pow
declarations.label: The product-indexed determinant is the sign of inversion times the block-factor product
declarations.documentation: For a chosen matrix-block decomposition over an algebraically closed field with |G| nonzero, the group determinant equals sign(g ↦ g⁻¹) times the product of each block determinant raised to its block dimension.

Chapter4/Lemma4.10.3.title: The checked proof uses cofactor induction, not the cyclic specialization
explanation: Here 'generic' means that all n² entries are independent variables. For n > 0, Lean proves irreducibility over ℂ. That condition matters: the determinant of a 0 × 0 matrix is 1, a unit, not an irreducible polynomial.

The Lean proof expands along the first row, viewing the result as A·y₀₀ + B. Induction makes the cofactor A irreducible. A specialization of the other first-row entries and a comparison of variables show that A cannot divide B, hence A and B are relatively prime. A polynomial linear in y₀₀ with these coefficients is then irreducible. This proves the same conclusion as the book, without formalizing its shorter cyclic-matrix argument.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryMatrixDeterminantIrreducibility.det_auxiliaryMatrix_irreducible_of_pos
declarations.label: The determinant of a positive-size generic complex matrix is irreducible
declarations.documentation: For every n > 0, the determinant of the n × n matrix of independent complex polynomial variables is irreducible.

Chapter4/Discussion_proof_Theorem4.10.2.after: So the matrix of the linear operator
Chapter4/Discussion_proof_Theorem4.10.2.title: Left multiplication accounts for the inverse and the permutation sign
explanation: For the group-algebra element a with coefficients x_g, the coefficient at g of a·h is the variable indexed by g·h⁻¹. The source proves this matrix-entry identity and the effect of the column permutation h ↦ h⁻¹. It then identifies the determinant of left multiplication with the algebra norm of a. Thus the sign is carried through the proof explicitly, rather than discarded when passing to polynomial identities.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryGroupPolynomial_eq_sign_smul_prod_auxiliaryPolynomial_pow
links.label: Proof of the matrix-entry, column-permutation and norm identities

Chapter4/Discussion_proof_Theorem4.10.2.title: A d × d matrix block contributes its determinant d times
explanation: The formal proof transports the algebra norm across k[G] ≃ ∏ᵢ Mat_(dᵢ)(k). The norm of a product is the product of its block norms. Left multiplication by a d × d matrix acts separately on its d columns, so its norm is det(M)ᵈ. This gives the exponent dᵢ in the formula without requiring a separately chosen regular-representation basis of irreducible summands.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryGroupPolynomial_eq_sign_smul_prod_auxiliaryPolynomial_pow
links.label: The checked product-of-block-norms argument

Chapter4/Discussion_proof_Theorem4.10.2.title: Independent matrix coordinates turn each factor into a generic determinant
explanation: The group-algebra equivalence supplies preimages of the matrix units in a single block. These define linear substitutions from the x_g coordinates to independent matrix-entry coordinates and back, whose composite fixes every entry variable. The generic determinant is irreducible over the coefficient field; the reverse substitution and degree bounds show that any factorization of Pᵢ has a constant unit factor.

The degree proof also checks that Pᵢ is homogeneous of degree dᵢ and nonzero: setting x₁ = 1 and all other x_g = 0 gives the identity matrix and determinant 1. Consequently deg(Pᵢ) = dᵢ, as required by the exponent in the theorem.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryPolynomial_irreducible
declarations.label: Every block determinant is an irreducible polynomial
declarations.documentation: For each positive-size matrix block, the determinant of its group-indexed linear matrix is irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.totalDegree_auxiliaryPolynomial
declarations.label: The degree of each block determinant is its representation dimension
declarations.documentation: The total degree of the i-th factor equals the size of the i-th matrix block.

Chapter4/Discussion_proof_Theorem4.10.2.title: Different blocks separate the factors; the center counts them
explanation: To distinguish Pᵢ and Pⱼ, evaluate at the group-algebra element whose i-th block is the identity and whose other blocks are zero. Then Pᵢ evaluates to 1 and Pⱼ to 0, ruling out a nonzero scalar multiple. The number of blocks is determined by the center: central elements of k[G] have coefficients constant on conjugacy classes, while the center of the matrix-block product has one scalar coordinate per block.

The final statement below packages this factor count, irreducibility, distinctness, degree exponents and the sign absorption into one existence theorem. Its explicit invertibility assumption on |G| is automatic over ℂ, but excludes modular characteristic dividing the group order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryPolynomial_not_associated
declarations.label: Factors from different matrix blocks are not scalar multiples
declarations.documentation: At distinct block indices, the corresponding determinant polynomials are not associated: no polynomial unit turns one into the other.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MvPolynomial.GroupIndexedFactorization.exists_irreducible_factorization_of_auxiliaryGroupPolynomial
declarations.label: The group determinant factors as in Theorem 4.10.2
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field with |G| invertible, there are as many pairwise nonassociated irreducible factors as conjugacy classes, and the group determinant equals their product with each factor raised to its total degree.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.after: The characters of all the irreducible representations
Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.title: Class sizes supply the weights in character-table orthogonality
explanation: The character pairing can be computed by summing over conjugacy-class representatives, weighting each term by its class size and dividing by |G|. Thus the number row is part of the calculation, not a decorative header. The column formula uses centralizer orders; dividing each character-table column by the square root of its centralizer order gives the unitary matrix discussed in Section 4.5.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.ConjugacyClassCharacterMatrix.auxiliaryConjugacyClassMatrix_mul_conjTranspose_eq_one
links.label: Checked row orthogonality of the normalized character matrix

Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.title: The standard S₃ row is fixed-point count minus one
explanation: On the three-coordinate permutation representation, trace counts fixed coordinates. Removing the constant line subtracts one, giving 2, 0, −1 at the identity, a transposition and a three-cycle. The other rows are the trivial and sign characters. These are traces of the constructed representations, not just numbers satisfying orthogonality.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeThree.character_reducedCoordinateRepresentation
declarations.label: The S₃ sum-zero representation has character fixed-point count minus one
declarations.documentation: The trace of the action on the sum-zero three-coordinate plane is the number of fixed coordinates minus one.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.title: The three linear characters factor through A₄/V₄; the fourth acts on the sum-zero space
explanation: The source constructs a surjective homomorphism A₄ → ℤ/3ℤ with kernel the Klein four subgroup. Its three characters send a quotient generator to 1, ε or ε², using the same ε = exp(2πi/3) as the book. The fourth representation permutes four coordinates with their sum constrained to zero, so its character is 3, 0, 0, −1.

The class sizes are checked as 1, 4, 4, 3. The fourth row has squared character norm (9 + 3)/12 = 1, proving simplicity; distinct character rows prove nonisomorphism. The four-class count then proves that this family exhausts the irreducibles.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AlternatingGroupFourRepresentations.conjugacyQuotientHom_surjective_and_ker
declarations.label: A₄ maps onto ℤ/3ℤ with kernel V₄
declarations.documentation: The constructed quotient homomorphism is surjective and its kernel is the Klein four subgroup.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AlternatingGroupFourRepresentations.alternatingGroupFourRepresentations_character
declarations.label: All four A₄ representations have the displayed character-table rows
declarations.documentation: At the four selected conjugacy-class representatives, the characters of the constructed representations equal the four rows in the table.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AlternatingGroupFourRepresentations.simpleRepresentation_iso_alternatingGroupFourRepresentation
declarations.label: Every complex irreducible of A₄ is one of these four representations
declarations.documentation: The trivial character, the two nontrivial quotient characters and the three-dimensional sum-zero representation exhaust the simple finite-dimensional complex representations of A₄.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.after: The last row can be computed
Chapter4/Introduction_4.8.title: The checked model is a coordinate action, not a constructed tetrahedral rotation action
explanation: The aligned source computes the same fourth row using the sum-zero four-coordinate model. It does not construct the tetrahedron's rotation action or an explicit equivalence from that geometric model to the coordinate representation. The character-table and classification results above do not assert that additional geometric identification.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The Q₈ table is checked on actual one-dimensional and matrix representations
explanation: The indexed family is ordered as the four sign choices (++), (+−), (−+), (−−), followed by the two-dimensional matrix action. Its selected group elements represent 1, −1, i, j and −k; the last lies in the same conjugacy class as k, so the displayed columns agree with the book's. The checked character formula gives every table entry, and the source also proves simplicity and pairwise nonisomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.SmallRepresentationData.character_quaternionGroupRepFamily_apply
declarations.label: Every Q₈ table entry is the trace of the corresponding constructed action
declarations.documentation: The characters of the five constructed quaternion-group representations at the five class representatives agree with the displayed table.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The two three-dimensional S₄ rows come from a sum-zero action and its sign twist
explanation: Here the five stored rows are ordered as trivial, sign, the two-dimensional pair-partition model, the sign-twisted sum-zero model ℂ³₊ and the untwisted model ℂ³₋. This is the book's table order. The last row is fixed-point count minus one; multiplying by sign gives the preceding row. The two-dimensional row is the reduced permutation character of the induced action on three pair partitions.

The checked table theorem computes all these traces. As explained in Section 4.3, the coordinate and sign-twist construction does not supply an explicit equivalence with the cube-rotation model used in the prose below.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.SmallRepresentationData.character_permFin4RepFamily_apply
declarations.label: The five constructed S₄ representations have the displayed character rows
declarations.documentation: All character values at the five selected conjugacy-class representatives match the S₄ table, in the book's order: trivial, sign, two-dimensional, three-dimensional plus and three-dimensional minus.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The A₅ table belongs to five constructed simple representations
explanation: The stored family has dimensions 1, 3, 3, 4 and 5, in the table's row order. The source proves each representation simple and distinguishes their characters; together with the five-conjugacy-class count, this accounts for all irreducibles. It checks the class sizes 1, 20, 15, 12, 12, rather than treating the two five-cycle classes as one.

For exact arithmetic, an intermediate pair (a,b) of rationals represents a + b√5. Thus the two entries represented by (1/2, ±1/2) become (1 ± √5)/2 in ℂ. The table theorem below is about traces of the constructed actions, not just formal arithmetic with a candidate table.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorSquareSpectralDecomposition.character_indexedSimpleRepresentations
declarations.label: Every A₅ character value equals its displayed table entry
declarations.documentation: The five constructed A₅ representations have the table's exact complex character values on the five conjugacy classes.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorSquareSpectralDecomposition.simple_indexedSimpleRepresentations
declarations.label: All five A₅ representations are simple
declarations.documentation: Simplicity is proved for the trivial, two three-dimensional, four-dimensional and five-dimensional representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorSquareSpectralDecomposition.indexedSimpleRepresentations_pairwise_nonisomorphic
declarations.label: Different rows represent nonisomorphic A₅ representations
declarations.documentation: Different dimensions distinguish most pairs; the unequal golden-ratio values distinguish the two three-dimensional representations.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.after: Finally, we explain how to obtain
Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The checked three-dimensional models are spectral summands of an alternating tensor square
explanation: Start with the four-dimensional sum-zero representation U on five coordinates. Its alternating tensor square has dimension six. The source sums the operators for conjugates of a selected five-cycle over all sixty conjugating elements, so each of its twelve conjugates appears five times. This operator commutes with the group action. Its eigenspaces for 10 + 10√5 and 10 − 10√5 are invariant and each has dimension three.

The traces on these two summands are obtained from their sum and the trace weighted by those two eigenvalues. Solving the resulting two equations gives the two golden-ratio rows. Character norms then prove simplicity. This constructs the representations algebraically, without assuming an icosahedron rotation representation.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.TensorSquareSpectralDecomposition.finrank_secondSpectralSubrepresentation
links.label: Checked dimension of the first three-dimensional spectral summand

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.after: Finally, we explain how to obtain
Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The rotation paragraph's (13254) is a typo for the other five-cycle class
explanation: The table uses (13245), but this paragraph prints (13254). Conjugation by the even permutation (23)(45) sends (12345) to (13254), so the latter cannot label the other A₅ five-cycle class. The checked table selects (12345) and its square, which lie in the two different classes. Its second choice is conjugate in A₅ to the table's (13245). The original prose is retained here; the table and formalization keep the two classes distinct.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: Conjugation by a transposition exchanges the two three-dimensional representations
explanation: The source constructs conjugation by (12) as an automorphism of A₅. It checks that the automorphism fixes the first three class indices and swaps the last two, and that it is not inner. Pulling back the plus representation along this automorphism exchanges the two golden-ratio character rows.

The isomorphism statement below follows from the checked equality of characters and character rigidity for finite-dimensional complex representations of a finite group. It asserts a representation isomorphism, without claiming an explicit change-of-basis matrix.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.OuterAutomorphismTwist.twistedRepresentation_iso
declarations.label: The outer-automorphism twist of ℂ³₊ is isomorphic to ℂ³₋
declarations.documentation: Pulling back the first three-dimensional A₅ model along conjugation by a transposition gives a representation isomorphic to the other three-dimensional model.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The four- and five-dimensional models are reduced permutation actions
explanation: The four-dimensional model is the sum-zero subspace of functions on five letters. The five-dimensional model uses six objects instead: the six cyclic subgroups of order five, each stored as its four nonidentity permutations, with A₅ acting by conjugation. Removing the constant functions gives dimension five.

Their characters are fixed-point counts minus one. The source computes squared character norm one using the five class sizes, proving both irreducible. This checks the parenthetical irreducibility assertions, with an algebraic six-object action in place of geometric vertex pairs.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IndexedPermutationFinsetAction.auxiliaryRepresentationOne
declarations.label: The four-dimensional A₅ model is the sum-zero action on five letters
declarations.documentation: The reduced permutation representation of A₅ on its five-letter action.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.IndexedPermutationFinsetAction.auxiliaryRepresentationTwo
declarations.label: The five-dimensional A₅ model is the sum-zero action on six cyclic subgroups
declarations.documentation: The reduced permutation representation of the conjugation action on the six order-five cyclic subgroups, represented by their nonidentity-element sets.

Chapter4/Example4.8.1.title: The icosahedron-to-algebraic-model identifications are not constructed here
explanation: These aligned sources do not identify the spectral three-dimensional representations with rotations of an icosahedron, or the six-subgroup action with its pairs of opposite vertices. The algebraic models, their traces and their simplicity are checked; the extra geometric equivalences in the prose are not part of these results.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.9.title: Multiplicity is a natural-number dimension of equivariant maps
explanation: Lean defines the multiplicity attached to X, Y and S as dimℂ Hom_G(S, X ⊗ Y). For a simple S, Schur's lemma makes this the number of copies of S in the semisimple decomposition. The definition also accepts a nonsimple S, but then this Hom dimension is not a single irreducible multiplicity.
