The normalized character pairing computes its complex cast: |G|⁻¹ ∑g χX(g)χY(g)χS(g⁻¹). Over ℂ the inverse argument is complex conjugation, recovering the book's formula. The theorem needs a finite group, but does not require X or Y to be irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupTensorProductDecomposition.cast_tensorProductMultiplicity_eq_character_average
declarations.label: The character average equals the dimension of Hom_G(S, X ⊗ Y)
declarations.documentation: For finite-dimensional complex representations of a finite group, the normalized product-character average is the complex cast of the natural-number Hom dimension.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.9.title: The displayed sum means an isomorphism to a direct sum of repeated irreducibles
explanation: Choose a simple, pairwise nonisomorphic family containing every irreducible isomorphism class. The source repeats its member Sₖ exactly dimℂ Hom_G(Sₖ, X ⊗ Y) times and forms a finite direct sum. It proves that X ⊗ Y is isomorphic to this sum, and also proves that an appropriate complete family can be chosen.
Thus the displayed equality is a representation-level decomposition, not an equality of carrier types or only a formal identity of characters.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupTensorProductDecomposition.tensorProduct_iso_auxiliaryDecomposition
declarations.label: A tensor product is isomorphic to its direct sum with the computed multiplicities
declarations.documentation: For a complete pairwise nonisomorphic simple family, the tensor product is isomorphic to the direct sum containing each family member with multiplicity given by its Hom dimension.

Chapter4/Example4.9.1.title: For S₃, the standard tensor square is trivial ⊕ sign ⊕ standard
explanation: For the standard character (2,0,−1), the class-weighted pairing with each of the three irreducible characters gives one. Hence its tensor square contains all three once, with dimensions 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.

The source checks every product in the full 3 × 3 multiplication table, not just this cell. It proves the corresponding character identities and then uses character rigidity to obtain the representation isomorphisms below. Blank lower-triangle cells in the printed table are omitted symmetric entries, not zero products.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationTensorDecompositions.representationFamily_tensor_iso_multiplicitySum
declarations.label: Every S₃ tensor product has the multiplicities in this table
declarations.documentation: The three-entry family is ordered as trivial, sign and standard; each tensor product is isomorphic to the finite sum specified by its multiplicity vector.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationTensorDecompositions.reducedPermutationRepresentation_tensor_sq_iso
declarations.label: The S₃ standard tensor square is the sum of all three irreducibles
declarations.documentation: The two-dimensional reduced permutation representation tensored with itself is isomorphic to trivial ⊕ sign ⊕ standard.

Chapter4/Example4.9.1.title: The S₄ calculation yields actual direct-sum decompositions for all 25 pairs
explanation: The source's five-entry S₄ family has the table order trivial, sign, two-dimensional, three-dimensional plus and three-dimensional minus. Each stored multiplicity vector has those five output positions. For example, ℂ³₊ ⊗ ℂ³₊ contains trivial, ℂ², ℂ³₊ and ℂ³₋ once each, giving dimension 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9.

The proof checks the integer character-table product identity in every class, extends it to each group element by conjugacy, and uses equality of characters to prove the isomorphism to the indicated sum. In the expanded statement, 'secondFive' names this S₄ family; it is not another A₅ family.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationTensorDecompositions.secondFiveRepresentationFamily_tensor_iso_multiplicitySum
declarations.label: Every S₄ tensor product is isomorphic to the sum in its table cell
declarations.documentation: All pairs in the five-member S₄ family have the checked natural multiplicity vectors of the displayed table, realized as representation-level finite sums.

Chapter4/Example4.9.1.title: The A₅ products are checked exactly, including repeated summands
explanation: The A₅ family is ordered as trivial, ℂ³₊, ℂ³₋, ℂ⁴ and ℂ⁵. For example, ℂ⁵ ⊗ ℂ⁵ has multiplicities (1,1,1,2,2), so its dimension is 1 + 3 + 3 + 2·4 + 2·5 = 25. The repeated fours and fives in the last cell are genuine multiplicities.

The source checks all table-product identities in exact rational √5 arithmetic, maps them into ℂ, and applies character rigidity. The biproduct below is indexed by a representation label and a copy number, so it records repetitions explicitly. 'firstFive' in its Lean identifier denotes A₅.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RepresentationTensorDecompositions.firstFiveRepresentationFamily_tensor_iso_biproduct
declarations.label: Every A₅ tensor product has the displayed irreducible direct-sum decomposition
declarations.documentation: All tensor products in the complete five-member A₅ family are isomorphic to the finite biproduct indexed by the table's multiplicities, including multiple copies of an irreducible.

Chapter4/Definition4.6.1.title: A unitary action preserves a chosen inner product
explanation: The structure below packages a representation together with the equation ⟨ρ(g)v, ρ(g)w⟩ = ⟨v,w⟩. The complex inner-product-space structure and finite-dimensionality are supplied on the vector space; the group need not be finite.

Mathlib's inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, the reverse of the convention in the book's footnote. Writing the book's form as B(v,w) = ⟨w,v⟩ reconciles the conventions. Positivity and invariance are unchanged.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.UnitaryRepresentations.UnitaryRepresentation
declarations.label: Package a finite-dimensional complex action preserving its inner product
declarations.documentation: A representation on a complex inner-product space with an explicit proof that every group operator preserves the inner product. No finiteness hypothesis on the group is imposed.

Chapter4/Theorem4.6.2.title: The finite sum is positive definite and invariant
explanation: The source first chooses a basis and transports the ordinary Euclidean inner product to V. It then uses the same unnormalized sum as the book. Every self-inner-product summand is nonnegative, and the identity summand is positive for a nonzero vector, so the sum is positive definite. Right multiplication g ↦ gh permutes the summation index, proving invariance.

The result returns an InnerProductSpace.Core: the positive-definite sesquilinear form itself, before choosing a compatible norm. Thus the theorem applies to a finite-dimensional complex module without requiring an inner product in advance.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.InvariantInnerProduct.Representation.exists_invariantInnerProductCore
declarations.label: Every finite-group action on a finite-dimensional complex space admits an invariant inner product
declarations.documentation: Construct a positive-definite complex inner-product core invariant under the given action by summing a basis-induced Euclidean form over the finite group.

Chapter4/Theorem4.6.2.after: If V is an irreducible representation
Chapter4/Theorem4.6.2.title: Irreducibility forces two invariant forms to differ by a positive real scalar
explanation: The source uses the two forms to identify V conjugate-linearly with its dual; composing one identification with the inverse of the other produces a complex-linear endomorphism A. Invariance makes A commute with the group action. Its nonzero eigenspace is invariant, so irreducibility forces it to be all of V and A to be scalar.

Evaluating both forms on a nonzero vector identifies their ratio as a strictly positive real number. The statement includes nontriviality of V and the condition that every invariant subspace is zero or all of V; together these express irreducibility. The order of the two forms is reversed relative to the book's displayed comparison, with the reciprocal positive scalar.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Complex.InvariantInnerProduct.Representation.auxiliaryInvariantInnerProductResult
declarations.label: Two invariant positive-definite forms on an irreducible differ by a positive real factor
declarations.documentation: For a nonzero irreducible complex action, any two invariant inner-product cores satisfy c₂(v,w) = λ c₁(v,w) for some real λ > 0.

Chapter4/Discussion_after_Theorem4.6.2.title: Conjugating scalars makes the inner-product map complex-linear
explanation: The conjugate module has the same additive group as V, but z acts as the old scalar conjugate(z). The group operators themselves are unchanged. With Mathlib's convention, v maps to the functional w ↦ ⟨v,w⟩; this is conjugate-linear on V and therefore complex-linear on its conjugate module.

Positive definiteness makes this map injective, and equal finite dimensions make it surjective. Invariance gives ⟨ρ(g)v,w⟩ = ⟨v,ρ(g⁻¹)w⟩, exactly the equation intertwining it with the dual action. The checked result below is an actual linear equivalence plus this intertwining equation, not just equality of characters.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.ConjugateDuality.conjugateLinearEquivDual
declarations.label: An inner product identifies the conjugate module with the linear dual
declarations.documentation: The complex-linear equivalence sending a vector of the conjugate module to its inner-product functional.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.ConjugateDuality.conjugateLinearEquivDual_intertwines
declarations.label: The equivalence intertwines the conjugate and dual actions
declarations.documentation: An invariant inner-product core makes the conjugate-to-dual equivalence respect every group operator.

Chapter4/Theorem4.6.3.after: Proof. Let W be a subrepresentation
Chapter4/Theorem4.6.3.title: The orthogonal complement is invariant, even for an infinite group
explanation: If w is orthogonal to W and u belongs to W, then ρ(g⁻¹)u also belongs to W. Inner-product invariance gives ⟨u,ρ(g)w⟩ = ⟨ρ(g⁻¹)u,w⟩ = 0. Hence ρ(g)w stays in W⊥.

The source chooses W⊥ itself and uses the finite-dimensional orthogonal-complement theorem to prove that W and W⊥ are complementary. This checks the splitting step used in the book's complete-reducibility argument. Finiteness of G is unnecessary here; it was needed only to construct a unitary structure by averaging.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.InvariantComplements.exists_invariant_isCompl_of_preserves_inner
declarations.label: Every invariant subspace of a finite-dimensional unitary action has an invariant complement
declarations.documentation: For any group, an inner-product-preserving complex action admits an invariant complementary submodule to every invariant submodule; the proof takes its orthogonal complement.

Chapter4/Remark4.6.4.title: A nontrivial Jordan block gives the obstruction for ℤ
explanation: The source lets 1 ∈ ℤ act on ℂ² by Id + N, where N is a nonzero square-zero Jordan operator; its inverse is Id − N. Integer powers give an action of the whole group. Multiplicative ℤ in the statement is simply ℤ with its additive group written multiplicatively.

The fixed eigenline is a nonzero proper invariant subspace, so the action is not irreducible. Every nonzero invariant subspace contains that line, so two nonzero invariant subspaces cannot be complementary. The predicate appearing in the expanded statement records this absence of a nontrivial direct-sum decomposition. Combined with the preceding invariant-complement theorem, this rules out a unitary structure; the displayed theorem checks the indecomposable, nonirreducible example, rather than separately stating non-unitarizability.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MultiplicativeIntAuxiliaryExample.multiplicativeInt_infinite_and_exists_auxiliary_nonirreducible_representation
declarations.label: The infinite cyclic group has a two-dimensional indecomposable, nonirreducible complex action
declarations.documentation: Construct the integer-power action of a unipotent Jordan block, prove its eigenline is a proper invariant subspace, and show that no decomposition into two nonzero subrepresentations is possible.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.7.after: Let V be an irreducible representation
Chapter4/Introduction_4.7.title: Matrix entries use output-row, input-column indices
explanation: For a basis b, Lean's matrix entry Aᵢⱼ(g) is the coefficient of bᵢ in ρ(g)bⱼ. The book instead defines tᵢⱼ(g) by applying ρ(g) to the first-index vector and pairing with the second, so tᵢⱼ(g) = Aⱼᵢ(g) in an orthonormal basis. This index swap explains the crossed equalities in the checked formulas on the following page.

The source proves algebraic identities for arbitrary chosen bases, using inverse group arguments. For a unitary complex action in an orthonormal basis, Aₚq(g⁻¹) = conjugate(Aqₚ(g)); this turns those identities into the Hermitian orthogonality formulas in the book.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.orthogonalitySum_eq_ite
links.label: Proof of the matrix-entry orthogonality identity

Chapter4/Proposition4.7.1.after: Thus, matrix elements of irreducible representations
Chapter4/Proposition4.7.1.title: The inverse-argument identities recover the complex Hermitian formulas
explanation: For nonisomorphic simple V and W, the normalized sum of Aᵥᵢⱼ(g)Awₚq(g⁻¹) is zero. Within one simple representation it is 1/dim(V) if i = q and j = p, and zero otherwise. Use the index swap and inverse/conjugate identity explained on the preceding page to obtain the book's δᵢᵢ′δⱼⱼ′/dim(V).

The checked identities work over any algebraically closed field with invertible group order; the same-representation formula additionally assumes its dimension is invertible in the field. This assumption is automatic over ℂ, but is retained explicitly in the general statement. No orthonormal-basis hypothesis is needed for the algebraic inverse-argument formulas.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.orthogonalitySum_eq_zero_of_not_iso
declarations.label: Coefficients of nonisomorphic irreducibles have zero inverse-argument pairing
declarations.documentation: For arbitrary bases of two nonisomorphic simple representations, the normalized sum of their matrix entries at g and g⁻¹ is zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.orthogonalitySum_eq_ite
declarations.label: Within one irreducible, the pairing is δᵢqδⱼp/dim(V)
declarations.documentation: For a simple representation with invertible dimension, the normalized inverse-argument matrix-entry sum is the inverse dimension when the crossed indices match, and zero otherwise.

Chapter4/Proposition4.7.1.title: The proof averages a rank-one map and determines its scalar by trace
explanation: The source works on Hom(W,V), the linear-map version of V ⊗ W*. It averages T ↦ ρᵥ(g)Tρw(g⁻¹), starting with a rank-one coordinate map. The average is equivariant. Schur's lemma makes it zero for nonisomorphic simples, and a scalar multiple of Id when V = W.

Conjugation preserves trace, so averaging does too. The rank-one map has trace either one or zero according to its indices; since trace(Id) = dim(V), the scalar is that trace divided by dim(V). Evaluating a matrix entry supplies the remaining Kronecker delta. This is the checked counterpart of the book's projection onto the scalar summand.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.auxiliaryLinearMap
declarations.label: Average a linear map by conjugating with the two group actions
declarations.documentation: The operator |G|⁻¹ ∑g ρᵥ(g)Tρw(g⁻¹), whose values are equivariant maps W → V.

Chapter4/Proposition4.7.1.title: All irreducible matrix coefficients form a checked basis of G → k
explanation: Choose one representative of each irreducible isomorphism class and a basis of each representation. The coefficient functions are indexed by a representation and a pair of basis indices. Pairing a proposed linear relation with the inverse-argument coefficient having reversed indices isolates its corresponding scalar, proving linear independence.

There are ∑ᵢ dim(Vᵢ)² = |G| such functions, which is the dimension of G → k. The source uses this equality to construct the basis below. Its hypotheses require a simple, pairwise nonisomorphic, exhaustive family and nonzero dimensions in the field. Over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, a further theorem chooses all this data automatically.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.functionSpaceBasis
declarations.label: Construct the function-space basis from a complete irreducible family
declarations.documentation: A basis of all field-valued functions on the finite group, consisting of every matrix coefficient of a complete pairwise nonisomorphic simple family with chosen bases and nonzero dimensions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.MatrixCoefficientOrthogonality.auxiliaryUnavailableStatementOne
declarations.label: In characteristic zero, a complete matrix-coefficient basis exists
declarations.documentation: Over any algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, choose a complete simple family, its vector-space bases and the resulting function-space basis, together with the inverse-argument orthogonality identities.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S3.title: The class count and dimension identity are finite computations
explanation: Lean represents S₃ as permutations of Fin 3. It computes that there are three conjugacy classes and that 1² + 1² + 2² = |S₃|. These two finite checks support the dimension argument here; by themselves they neither construct the representations nor prove irreducibility.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeThree.card_conjClasses_perm_fin_three
declarations.label: S₃ has three conjugacy classes
declarations.documentation: The finite permutation group on three elements has exactly three conjugacy classes.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeThree.one_sq_add_one_sq_add_two_sq_eq_card_perm_fin_three
declarations.label: 1² + 1² + 2² equals the order of S₃
declarations.documentation: The proposed irreducible dimensions have squared sum six, the cardinality of the permutation group.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S3.title: The checked standard representation is the sum-zero plane in ℂ³
explanation: The source uses coordinate permutations, (σ · f)(r) = f(σ⁻¹r), restricted to f(0) + f(1) + f(2) = 0. Its character is the number of fixed coordinates minus one: 2 at the identity, 0 at a transposition and −1 at a three-cycle. The normalized squared character sum is (4 + 3·0 + 2·1)/6 = 1, proving irreducibility by the criterion in Section 4.5.

It constructs the trivial and sign representations as well, distinguishes all three, and uses the sum-of-squares theorem to exclude another irreducible. The statement below is this exhaustive classification up to equivariant isomorphism. Its three stored objects, in order, are trivial, sign and the sum-zero representation. The book's triangle matrices are a different coordinate model; no triangle-coordinate change of basis is asserted by this statement.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.AuxiliaryRepresentationComputations.simple_iso_one_of_three_auxiliary_representations
declarations.label: Every complex irreducible of S₃ is trivial, sign or the sum-zero representation
declarations.documentation: Every simple finite-dimensional complex representation of S₃ is isomorphic to one of the explicitly constructed trivial, sign and two-dimensional sum-zero representations.

Chapter4/Example4.3_Q8.title: The four one-dimensional characters choose independent signs for i and j
explanation: The source constructs χ(i) = α and χ(j) = β with α² = β² = 1. Over ℂ the four choices (α, β) ∈ {1, −1}² give the four one-dimensional representations. In each of them −1 in Q₈ acts trivially, as expected from the quotient by the center. The construction checks the homomorphism laws directly, rather than first supplying an isomorphism of the quotient with the Klein four group.
In the checked statements QuaternionGroup 2 is Q₈; its elements a 1, xa 0 and a 2 are i, j and −1 respectively. The center statement below identifies its two central elements.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.linearCharacter
declarations.label: Choose a one-dimensional character by two signs α and β
declarations.documentation: The multiplicative complex character of Q₈ sending i to α and j to β, for scalars whose squares are one.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.mem_center_iff
declarations.label: The center of Q₈ consists of 1 and −1
declarations.documentation: A quaternion-group element is central exactly when it is a 0 or a 2, representing 1 and −1.

Chapter4/Example4.3_Q8.title: The displayed matrices satisfy the quaternion multiplication laws
explanation: The source uses these same matrices. It checks that the first two square to −Id, anticommute and have product equal to the third. From these identities it builds a homomorphism on all eight group elements, then turns matrix multiplication into a linear action on ℂ².

The formulas below identify the images of i, j and k. The element xa 3 is k, since the source writes the second coset in the form jiᵐ. Complex.I in the second matrix is the scalar imaginary unit, not the quaternion-group element i.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.standardMatrixRepresentation_a_one
declarations.label: The matrix of i is the first displayed matrix
declarations.documentation: Evaluation of the quaternion matrix representation at a 1 gives the matrix with rows (0,1) and (−1,0).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.standardMatrixRepresentation_xa_zero
declarations.label: The matrix of j is diag(√−1, −√−1)
declarations.documentation: Evaluation at xa 0 gives the second displayed matrix.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.standardMatrixRepresentation_xa_three
declarations.label: The matrix of k is the product of the matrices of i and j
declarations.documentation: Evaluation at xa 3 gives the third displayed matrix, with off-diagonal entries −√−1.

Chapter4/Example4.3_Q8.title: Simplicity and completeness are checked, not inferred from the dimension list
explanation: The two-dimensional character has values 2 at 1, −2 at −1 and zero at the other six elements. Its normalized squared sum is (4 + 4)/8 = 1, proving simplicity. The four sign characters are simple and pairwise distinct; dimensions separate them from the two-dimensional representation.

The source then uses the five-conjugacy-class count to prove that these five representations exhaust all complex irreducibles. The classification below is up to equivariant isomorphism, with the four one-dimensional choices followed by the matrix representation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.standardRepresentation_simple
declarations.label: The two-dimensional quaternion representation is irreducible
declarations.documentation: The matrix representation of Q₈ on ℂ² is simple, as verified by its character norm.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupRepresentation.QuaternionGroup.ComplexIrreducibles.simpleRepresentation_iso_standard_or_linear
declarations.label: Every complex irreducible of Q₈ is one of the four sign characters or this matrix representation
declarations.documentation: The four constructed one-dimensional representations and the two-dimensional matrix representation exhaust the simple finite-dimensional complex representations of Q₈.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S4.title: The two-dimensional model comes from the action on three pair partitions
explanation: A permutation of four points permutes the three partitions 01|23, 02|13 and 03|12. The source encodes this as a homomorphism S₄ → S₃. Pulling back the three-coordinate permutation action and removing its constant line gives a two-dimensional representation, with character equal to the number of fixed pair partitions minus one.

The word 'induced' in the expanded definition's name refers to this induced action on partitions: this construction is pullback along a homomorphism, not induction from a subgroup. Its simplicity is checked by summing its squared character over all 24 permutations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeFour.inducedPermutationHom
declarations.label: S₄ acts on the three partitions into two pairs
declarations.documentation: The homomorphism from permutations of four points to permutations of their three pair partitions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeFour.inducedReducedCoordinateRepresentation
declarations.label: Define the two-dimensional sum-zero pair-partition representation
declarations.documentation: The pullback of the sum-zero three-coordinate representation along the pair-partition action homomorphism.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S4.title: The sum-zero model is ℂ³₋; its sign twist is ℂ³₊
explanation: The source starts with the sum-zero subspace of functions on four points. This is the book's final model for ℂ³₋, not the cube-rotation model ℂ³₊. Its character is fixed-point count minus one. Multiplying each action operator by the permutation sign gives the other three-dimensional irreducible, with character sign(σ) times that value.

At a transposition these characters are 1 and −1, proving that the models are not isomorphic. Both are proved simple by their character norms. The definitions below expose the coordinate model and the character-twist operation; the latter makes sense for any complex representation and any unit-valued character.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeFour.reducedCoordinateRepresentation
declarations.label: ℂ³₋ is the sum-zero four-coordinate representation
declarations.documentation: The representation of S₄ on functions on four points whose coordinate sum is zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.PermutationDegreeFour.twistRepresentationByCharacter
declarations.label: Multiply each action operator by a one-dimensional character
declarations.documentation: Given χ : G → ℂ× and an action ρ, the twisted action at g is χ(g) times ρ(g). Using the sign character exchanges the two three-dimensional S₄ models.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S4.title: The five constructed irreducibles exhaust the classification
explanation: The expanded alternatives are, in order, trivial, sign, the two-dimensional pair-partition model, the three-dimensional sum-zero model and its sign twist. The source proves simplicity and pairwise nonisomorphism before using 1² + 1² + 2² + 3² + 3² = 24. Any additional irreducible would have positive dimension and force a larger sum, so none remains.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroupRepresentations.SubgroupInductionAuxiliary.simple_iso_auxiliary_cases
declarations.label: Every complex irreducible of S₄ is isomorphic to one of these five models
declarations.documentation: Exhaustive classification of simple finite-dimensional complex S₄ representations by the explicitly constructed trivial, sign, pair-partition, sum-zero and sign-twisted sum-zero representations.

Chapter4/Example4.3_S4.title: The polyhedron realizations are not checked here
explanation: The coordinate representations and their complete classification are checked. These sources do not construct a geometric cube, octahedron or tetrahedron, or an explicit intertwiner identifying their symmetry actions with the coordinate models. Those geometric descriptions remain book explanations rather than additional formalized constructions.

Chapter4/Introduction_4.5.title: The Hermitian character pairing is an inverse-argument sum in Lean
explanation: For a complex finite-group character, conjugating χ(g) gives χ(g⁻¹). Lean therefore writes the normalized pairing as |G|⁻¹ ∑g χᵥ(g)χw(g⁻¹). This formula also makes sense over any field with invertible group order, where there need not be a complex conjugation or a Hermitian inner product.

Row orthogonality is checked in the following theorem. Together with the spanning statement below, it gives the claimed orthonormal basis of complex class functions. The source statements express these algebraic identities and spanning directly; they do not introduce a new bundled Hermitian-space structure on the class-function type.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.ClassFunctions.FiniteGroup.span_simple_characters_eq_auxiliarySubmodule
declarations.label: The irreducible characters span all class functions
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order, the irreducible characters span exactly the subspace of conjugation-invariant functions.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterOperations.character_inv_eq_conj
links.label: Read why inverse evaluation equals complex conjugation

Chapter4/Theorem4.5.1.title: The order of the characters fixes the direction of the Hom space
explanation: The pairing χᵥ(g)χw(g⁻¹) computes the dimension of equivariant maps W → V, not V → W by definition. The first statement below works over any field with invertible group order; the natural-number dimension is cast into that field. Algebraic closedness is needed for the second statement, where Schur's lemma makes the Hom dimension one or zero for simple representations.
Over ℂ inverse evaluation is conjugation, recovering the displayed Hermitian formula. No characteristic-zero hypothesis is required for the two inverse-argument identities themselves.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.CharacterPairing.FiniteGroup.normalized_characterPairing_eq_finrank_hom
declarations.label: The normalized pairing is dim Hom₍G₎(W,V)
declarations.documentation: For finite-dimensional representations over a field with invertible finite-group order, the normalized inverse-argument character pairing equals the cast dimension of equivariant maps from W to V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.CharacterPairing.FiniteGroup.normalized_characterPairing_of_simple
declarations.label: Simple characters pair to one for isomorphic representations and zero otherwise
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order, the normalized character pairing of two simple representations is the isomorphism-class Kronecker delta.

Chapter4/Theorem4.5.1.title: Averaging on Hom(W,V) projects onto equivariant maps
explanation: On a linear map T : W → V, g acts by T ↦ ρᵥ(g) ∘ T ∘ ρw(g⁻¹). Its invariant vectors are exactly the equivariant maps. Averaging this action over G fixes those invariants and sends every map into the invariant subspace, so it is a projection. The trace of a projection is the dimension of its image.

The character of this Hom action is χᵥ(g)χw(g⁻¹). Taking the trace of the average therefore gives the first formula. Mathlib carries out this argument on the linear-map representation, using its invariant-space equivalence with categorical Hom; this is the same mechanism as the book's tensor-dual presentation.

links.name: Representation.isProj_averageMap
links.label: Read the two identities proving that averaging projects onto invariants

links.name: FDRep.scalar_product_char_eq_finrank_equivariant
links.label: Read the Hom-action character and averaging proof

Chapter4/Discussion_after_Theorem4.5.1.title: Norm one means the equivariant endomorphism space has dimension one
explanation: Maschke gives a semisimple category, in which a representation is simple exactly when its equivariant endomorphisms have dimension one. The preceding pairing theorem computes that dimension from the character. The source uses this criterion, rather than choosing a decomposition and summing squared multiplicities.

The checked result works over any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Characteristic zero is important for the converse: equality of a dimension's cast with 1 must imply that the natural-number dimension itself is 1. In positive characteristic the pairing alone may lose that information.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.SimpleCharacterCriterion.simple_iff_characterInner_eq_one
declarations.label: V is irreducible exactly when its normalized character self-pairing is one
declarations.documentation: The norm-one irreducibility criterion for finite-dimensional representations of a finite group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

links.name: FDRep.simple_iff_end_is_rank_one
links.label: Inspect the semisimple endomorphism-dimension criterion

Chapter4/Problem4.5.2.title: The character formula selects a single irreducible block
explanation: For a simple representation V of dimension d, the source defines ψᵥ = (d/|G|)∑g χᵥ(g)g⁻¹, exactly as in the book. Conjugacy invariance makes it central. Its action on a simple W is therefore scalar; orthogonality determines the scalar by taking its trace. It is the identity on V and zero on a nonisomorphic W.

The definition below can be applied to any finite-dimensional representation, but the identity and zero-action theorems require the specified representations to be simple. Nonisomorphism is expressed by the absence of a representation isomorphism, not inequality of the chosen carrier types.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexRepresentationAuxiliaryElements.auxiliaryElement
declarations.label: Define ψᵥ by the dimension-weighted character sum
declarations.documentation: The element (dim(V)/|G|)∑g χᵥ(g)g⁻¹ of the complex group algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexRepresentationAuxiliaryElements.map_auxiliaryElement_eq_id
declarations.label: ψᵥ acts as the identity on its simple representation V
declarations.documentation: The algebra action of a simple complex representation sends its associated character element to the identity endomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexRepresentationAuxiliaryElements.map_auxiliaryElement_eq_zero_of_not_iso
declarations.label: ψᵥ acts by zero on a nonisomorphic simple representation
declarations.documentation: If V and W are simple and not isomorphic, the action of ψᵥ on W is zero.

Chapter4/Problem4.5.2.title: The product identities are equalities in the group algebra
explanation: The source expands the products as character convolutions. Composing a group operator with the action of ψ and taking its trace supplies the diagonal and off-diagonal convolution identities. These give ψᵥ² = ψᵥ and ψwψᵥ = 0 for nonisomorphic simple V and W.

Thus the checked conclusion is idempotence and orthogonality of the group-algebra elements themselves, not merely a statement that their actions agree on the displayed representations. This proof uses coefficient calculations rather than an unstated faithfulness argument.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexRepresentationAuxiliaryElements.auxiliaryElement_mul_self
declarations.label: ψᵥ is an idempotent
declarations.documentation: For a simple complex representation V, its character element satisfies ψᵥψᵥ = ψᵥ in the group algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ComplexRepresentationAuxiliaryElements.auxiliaryElement_mul_eq_zero_of_not_iso
declarations.label: The character idempotents of nonisomorphic irreducibles have zero product
declarations.documentation: For nonisomorphic simple complex representations V and W, the product ψwψᵥ is zero in the group algebra.

Chapter4/Remark4.5.3.title: Group-algebra coefficients carry the convolution product
explanation: For finite G, every function G → ℂ has finite support and can be viewed as a group-algebra coefficient function. Multiplication then has coefficient (f*g)(z) = ∑x f(x)g(x⁻¹z), the single-sum version of the displayed condition xy = z. The unit has coefficient 1 at the identity and zero elsewhere.

A coefficient function is conjugacy-invariant exactly when its group-algebra element is central. The class-function convolution algebra is therefore represented as the center subalgebra, which is commutative even when G is not. This is not the pointwise multiplication of functions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterCoefficientAlgebra.coeff_mul_eq_sum_coeff_mul_coeff_inv_mul
declarations.label: The coefficient of a product is ∑x f(x)g(x⁻¹z)
declarations.documentation: The convolution formula for complex group-algebra coefficients over a finite group.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterCoefficientAlgebra.auxiliaryComplexGroupSubalgebra
declarations.label: Class functions with convolution form the center of ℂ[G]
declarations.documentation: The center subalgebra of the complex group algebra; its coefficient functions are exactly the class functions.

Chapter4/Remark4.5.3.title: Primitive idempotents must be nonzero, and they exhaust the normalized characters
explanation: The checked primitive-idempotent condition includes e ≠ 0, in addition to e² = e and the prohibition on splitting into two nonzero idempotents. The nonzero condition is needed: zero is also a solution of the printed idempotent equation. The source proves both that every simple character gives a primitive idempotent and that every primitive idempotent of the center arises this way.

Its coefficient at g is χᵥ(1)χᵥ(g)/|G|. Notice the argument g, not g⁻¹: compared with ψᵥ in the preceding problem, this convention labels the block of the dual representation. The distinction does not change the collection of all primitive central idempotents.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterCoefficientAlgebra.auxiliaryRingElementPredicate_iff_exists_simple_representationElement
declarations.label: The primitive central idempotents are exactly the normalized simple characters
declarations.documentation: An element of the complex class-function convolution algebra is a nonzero primitive idempotent exactly when it is the normalized coefficient element associated with some simple representation.

Chapter4/Remark4.5.3.title: The square-root normalization is the positive scalar |G|/dim(V)
explanation: If d = dim(V), the normalized character has value d²/|G| at the identity. The positive square root in the book is therefore |G|/d. Lean recovers χᵥ(g) by this explicit nonzero scalar ratio, avoiding an ambiguous choice of a complex square root. The source also checks that this scalar's square equals the book's ratio.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CharacterCoefficientAlgebra.character_eq_card_div_finrank_mul_coefficient
declarations.label: Multiply the normalized coefficient function by |G|/dim(V) to recover χᵥ
declarations.documentation: For a simple complex representation, the character value at g is the coefficient of its normalized character element times the group cardinality divided by the representation dimension.

Chapter4/Theorem4.5.4.title: The sum uses one representative of each irreducible isomorphism class
explanation: The checked statement takes a finite family of simple representations, together with hypotheses that it is pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaustive. This is the precise meaning of summing over 'all irreducible representations': isomorphic copies must not be counted again.

It proves ∑ᵢ χᵢ(g)χᵢ(h⁻¹) = |Zg| when g and h are conjugate, and zero otherwise, over any algebraically closed field in which |G| is nonzero. The centralizer cardinality is cast into the field. Over ℂ, inverse evaluation gives the conjugated character in the book. The proof transports the left-right multiplication operator through the matrix-block decomposition and computes its trace on matrix units.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.CharacterColumnOrthogonality.FiniteGroup.sum_complete_simple_characters_mul_inv
declarations.label: Character columns pair to the centralizer order on a class, and to zero off it
declarations.documentation: Column orthogonality for a complete pairwise nonisomorphic simple family over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order.

Chapter4/Remark4.5.5.after: If g and h are not conjugate,
Chapter4/Remark4.5.5.title: The remaining trace computation counts conjugating elements
explanation: On the group-element basis, x ↦ gxh⁻¹ is a permutation, so its trace counts the fixed elements. The source checks that this count equals the number of conjugators between g and h. It is zero if they are not conjugate; if a conjugator is chosen, multiplying it by centralizer elements gives a bijection with all conjugators, so the count is |Zg|.
This paragraph finishes the proof begun on the preceding page. The linked source includes the fixed-point reindexing, centralizer/conjugator equivalence and both trace computations.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.CharacterColumnOrthogonality.FiniteGroup.sum_complete_simple_characters_mul_inv
links.label: Read the group-basis trace and conjugator-counting proof

Chapter4/Remark4.5.5.title: The normalized character table is square, so row orthogonality gives column orthogonality
explanation: Reindex the irreducibles by a set of the same size as the conjugacy classes; this is bookkeeping, not a canonical pairing of classes with representations. The source uses the conjugacy-class type for both matrix indices and chooses a group representative for each column. Each entry is divided by the positive real square root of the centralizer order.

Orbit–stabilizer converts the group sum to a weighted class sum, proving UUᴴ = Id from row orthogonality. Since U is square, the same conjugate transpose is also a left inverse: UᴴU = Id. Expanding this second equality gives column orthogonality. Both inverse identities are checked below, including nonvanishing of the normalizing square roots.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ConjugacyClassCharacterMatrix.auxiliaryConjugacyClassMatrix_mul_conjTranspose_eq_one
declarations.label: The normalized character table satisfies UUᴴ = Id
declarations.documentation: Row orthogonality of the square normalized complex character matrix for pairwise nonisomorphic simple representations indexed by conjugacy classes.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ConjugacyClassCharacterMatrix.conjTranspose_auxiliaryConjugacyClassMatrix_mul_eq_one
declarations.label: It also satisfies UᴴU = Id
declarations.documentation: The conjugate transpose is a left inverse as well as a right inverse of the square normalized complex character matrix.

Chapter4/Example4.3_FiniteAbelianGroups.title: One-dimensional representations are homomorphisms into ℂ×
explanation: For an abelian group the group algebra is commutative, so a finite-dimensional simple module over an algebraically closed field has dimension one. This dimension statement does not need the characteristic to be prime to the group order. The character group used here, however, is specifically the complex-valued group of multiplicative homomorphisms G → ℂ×, with pointwise multiplication and inversion.

Distinguish this multiplicative character group from the vector space of class functions in Section 4.2. For a one-dimensional representation its trace character is the same scalar-valued function, but the two spaces have different operations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterDuality.finrank_eq_one_of_isSimpleModule
declarations.label: An irreducible representation of a finite abelian group has dimension one
declarations.documentation: A finite-dimensional simple representation of a finite commutative group over an algebraically closed field has dimension one, in any characteristic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterDuality.characterGroup
declarations.label: The complex character group is G →* ℂ×
declarations.documentation: The group of homomorphisms from a commutative group to the multiplicative group of nonzero complex numbers.

Chapter4/Example4.3_FiniteAbelianGroups.title: Product characters are determined by their restrictions to the factors
explanation: A character of G₁ × G₂ restricts to one character on each factor. Conversely, the pair (χ₁, χ₂) gives (g₁, g₂) ↦ χ₁(g₁)χ₂(g₂). The source checks these inverse maps as a multiplicative equivalence, and also supplies the finite-indexed-product version. The factors need not themselves be finite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterDuality.characterGroupProdEquiv
declarations.label: The character group of a product is the product of the character groups
declarations.documentation: Restriction to the two factors and multiplication of their values are inverse group homomorphisms.

Chapter4/Example4.3_FiniteAbelianGroups.title: The double dual has a specified evaluation map; the single dual does not
explanation: For a finite abelian group the source proves existence of an isomorphism G ≃ G∨, without choosing a preferred one. By contrast, its double-dual equivalence is explicitly g ↦ (χ ↦ χ(g)). The second statement below verifies this evaluation formula. Thus 'canonical' here refers to a concrete, choice-free formula for the map, not merely existence of some isomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterDuality.nonempty_characterGroupEquiv
declarations.label: A finite abelian group is isomorphic to its character group
declarations.documentation: Existence of a multiplicative equivalence between a finite commutative group and its complex character group, without selecting a canonical equivalence.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterDuality.characterGroupDualEquiv_apply
declarations.label: The double-dual map evaluates characters at g
declarations.documentation: Evaluation of the double-character equivalence at g and χ is χ(g).

Chapter4/Exercise4.3.1.title: A side correction is needed for the function space to be invariant
explanation: As printed, the condition f(gi) = √−1 f(g) is not preserved by the stated right-translation action. The checked construction corrects the condition to f(ig) = √−1 f(g), keeping (h · f)(x) = f(xh). Left multiplication by i commutes with right translation: f(i(xh)) = √−1 f(xh). This is the condition used by the invariance theorem below; it is not a proof of the right-sided condition printed in the book.
In the expanded Lean statement the quaternion group is QuaternionGroup 2, which has order eight, and its element a 1 is i. The scalar Complex.I is the imaginary unit, not a group element.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionFunctionSubmodule.auxiliaryFunctionSubmodule_invariant
declarations.label: Right translations preserve the corrected left-equivariant function space
declarations.documentation: The subspace defined by f(ig) = √−1 f(g) is invariant under the action (h · f)(x) = f(xh).

Chapter4/Exercise4.3.1.title: Two function values determine the representation, and there is no invariant line
explanation: The corrected condition determines every function from its values at 1 and j, giving an explicit linear equivalence with ℂ². To prove irreducibility, the source starts with a nonzero function in an invariant subspace and finds a translate whose two coordinates are linearly independent from its own. The subspace must therefore have dimension two and be the whole function space.

Both dimension and irreducibility are checked below. The second result is stated as a bottom-or-whole condition on invariant subspaces of the ambient function space, rather than as a separately bundled isomorphism to the preceding matrix model.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionFunctionSubmodule.finrank_auxiliaryFunctionSubmodule
declarations.label: The corrected function space has complex dimension two
declarations.documentation: Evaluation at 1 and j gives two independent complex coordinates on the left-equivariant quaternion function space.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.QuaternionFunctionSubmodule.invariant_submodule_eq_bot_or_auxiliaryFunctionSubmodule
declarations.label: Every invariant subspace of this function space is zero or the whole space
declarations.documentation: A complex subspace contained in the corrected function space and invariant under every right translation is bottom or the whole corrected function space.

Chapter4/Discussion_4.4.title: The dual action pulls a functional back along ρ(g⁻¹)
explanation: For a functional ℓ : V → k, the dual action is (g · ℓ)(v) = ℓ(ρ(g⁻¹)v). The inverse is essential: ordinary pullback reverses composition, and inversion restores the group-action law. Trace of the dual linear map equals trace of the original map, giving χᵥ*(g) = χᵥ(g⁻¹). This identity works over any field for finite-dimensional V, with no finite-group assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterOperations.character_dual
declarations.label: The dual character at g is the original character at g⁻¹
declarations.documentation: For a finite-dimensional representation over any field, the character of its contragredient representation is obtained by evaluating the original character on the inverse group element.

Chapter4/Discussion_4.4.title: For complex finite-group representations, self-duality is detected by real character values
explanation: The source proves χᵥ(g⁻¹) = conjugate(χᵥ(g)) by averaging a positive-definite Hermitian matrix H over G. Invariance gives ρ(g)ᴴ = Hρ(g)⁻¹H⁻¹, and taking traces gives the identity. This replaces the book's roots-of-unity argument with an invariant-inner-product argument.

Combining it with the preceding character-isomorphism theorem proves that V is isomorphic to its dual exactly when its character is fixed by complex conjugation. This does not say that the chosen action matrices are real, or provide a real form of V. The finiteness of G and the complex field are hypotheses of these two statements.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterOperations.character_inv_eq_conj
declarations.label: Evaluating a complex character at g⁻¹ conjugates its value
declarations.documentation: For a finite group and a finite-dimensional complex representation, the character at g⁻¹ is the complex conjugate of the character at g.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterOperations.dual_iso_iff_character_star_eq
declarations.label: V is self-dual exactly when all of its character values are real
declarations.documentation: A finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group is isomorphic to its contragredient exactly when every character value is fixed by complex conjugation.

Chapter4/Discussion_4.4.title: The diagonal tensor action multiplies characters pointwise
explanation: Both factors are acted on by the same group element: g(v ⊗ w) = ρᵥ(g)v ⊗ ρw(g)w. The trace of a tensor product of linear maps is the product of their traces. Hence the tensor-product character is the pointwise product χᵥχw, over any field and for any group, provided both representations are finite-dimensional. It does not assert that the tensor product is irreducible.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterOperations.character_tensor
declarations.label: The character of V ⊗ W is χᵥ(g)χw(g)
declarations.documentation: The diagonal tensor product of finite-dimensional representations has the pointwise product of their character functions, over any field and without a finite-group assumption.

Chapter4/Introduction.title: A group action extends linearly to the group algebra
explanation: Lean stores a representation as a multiplicative map ρ : G → Endₖ(V). Every ρ(g) is invertible because ρ(g⁻¹) is its inverse. Extending by linearity sends a group-algebra element ∑g c(g)g to ∑g c(g)ρ(g), giving the algebra action described here.

The representation-to-module construction uses a type copy of V so that the new k[G]-action does not conflict with existing instances; the vector space itself is unchanged up to the supplied linear equivalence. The inverse construction restricts a k[G]-module action to the group elements. The linked categorical equivalence also transports equivariant maps and isomorphisms. None of these constructions requires G or V to be finite.

Chapter4/Theorem4.1.1.title: Semisimplicity needs an invertible group order, not algebraic closedness
explanation: The checked hypothesis IsUnit (|G| : k) says that the group order is invertible in k. Over a field, this is equivalent to the characteristic not dividing |G|. Maschke's semisimplicity conclusion works over any such field. Algebraic closedness is needed for the split endomorphism-algebra decomposition in part (ii), not for part (i).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.RegularRepresentationDecomposition.MonoidAlgebra.isSemisimpleRing_of_isUnit_card
declarations.label: k[G] is semisimple when |G| is invertible in k
declarations.documentation: Maschke's theorem for a finite group over any field in which the group order is a unit.

Chapter4/Theorem4.1.1.title: The algebra equivalence evaluates each group element on every irreducible
explanation: Over an algebraically closed field, the source chooses a finite family Vᵢ of simple representations, proves that they are pairwise nonisomorphic and exhaust all simple finite-dimensional representations, and identifies k[G] with the product of their endomorphism algebras. For this finite family the product is also the vector-space direct sum in the book.

The second statement checks the map on the basis: g goes to ρᵢ(g) in the i-th component. Thus this is the action map in the book, not just an abstract algebra isomorphism. The additional IsAlgClosed hypothesis matters: over a nonsplitting field, the endomorphism blocks need not be full matrix algebras over k.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.RegularRepresentationDecomposition.FiniteGroup.exists_complete_simple_family_with_groupAlgebra_equiv
declarations.label: Choose all irreducibles and decompose k[G] into their endomorphism algebras
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order, a complete pairwise nonisomorphic finite family of simple representations gives an algebra equivalence with the product of its endomorphism algebras and the sum-of-squares identity.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FDRep.GroupAlgebraDecomposition.DecompositionData.auxiliaryMap_apply_single
declarations.label: The component of the image of g is its action on Vᵢ
declarations.documentation: The chosen group-algebra equivalence sends the basis element at g to the representation map ρᵢ(g) in every endomorphism component.

Chapter4/Theorem4.1.1.title: Each endomorphism block contributes dim(Vᵢ) copies of Vᵢ
explanation: Under left multiplication, g acts on Endₖ(Vᵢ) by postcomposition F ↦ ρᵢ(g) ∘ F. Evaluating F on a basis of Vᵢ identifies this with dim(Vᵢ) independent columns, each carrying the action on Vᵢ. The source checks the resulting equivariant decomposition of the regular representation, not merely an equality of dimensions.
Taking dimensions gives |G| = ∑ᵢ dim(Vᵢ)² as an equality of natural numbers. The positive dimensions in the second statement come from the same decomposition data.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.RegularRepresentationDecomposition.FiniteGroup.exists_complete_simple_family_coordinateRepresentation
declarations.label: The regular representation has dim(Vᵢ) copies of each irreducible Vᵢ
declarations.documentation: A complete simple family and an equivariant isomorphism from the left regular representation to the corresponding family of coordinate copies, over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.RegularRepresentationDecomposition.FiniteGroup.exists_positive_dimensions_sum_sq_eq_card
declarations.label: The positive irreducible dimensions satisfy the sum-of-squares formula
declarations.documentation: The chosen positive natural-number dimensions have squared sum equal to the cardinality of the finite group.

Chapter4/Theorem4.1.1.title: Averaging turns a linear retraction into an equivariant one
explanation: The Mathlib construction starts with a linear retraction onto W and averages its conjugates. It writes the summands in the order g⁻¹Pg rather than gPg⁻¹; reindexing the finite sum by inversion gives the same average. The normalization by |G| makes the restriction to W the identity. Equivariance then makes its kernel an invariant complement.

The averaging construction itself works over a commutative ring when |G| is a unit and a linear retraction is supplied. Over a field, every subspace has such a retraction. Consequently the checked complement theorem applies to all k[G]-modules, without the finite-dimensionality restriction used in this book proof.

links.label: Read the verification that the averaged map remains a retraction

links.name: MonoidAlgebra.Submodule.exists_isCompl
