Chapter4/Proposition4.1.2.title: The checked converse uses the central element ∑g g
explanation: The source proves the same converse by a different argument. If |G| = 0 in k, put Λ = ∑g g in k[G]. Its coefficient at the identity is 1, so Λ ≠ 0. Translation permutes the summands, making Λ central, while Λ² = |G|Λ = 0. The ideal it generates therefore has square zero.

In a semisimple ring this ideal is generated by an idempotent. Because that idempotent lies in a square-zero ideal, it must be zero, contradicting Λ ≠ 0. Centrality and the ideal argument are essential: a matrix algebra can contain nonzero nilpotent elements. The conclusion holds over any field, with no algebraic-closedness assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.SemisimpleGroupAlgebraCardinality.isUnit_card_of_isSemisimpleRing
declarations.label: If k[G] is semisimple, then |G| is invertible in k
declarations.documentation: The converse to Maschke's theorem for a finite group over an arbitrary field, proved using the central square-zero ideal generated by the sum of the group elements.

Chapter4/Example4.1.3.title: A commuting nilpotent operator must vanish on an irreducible module
explanation: For g in the cyclic group of prime order p, characteristic p gives (ρ(g) − 1)ᵖ = ρ(g)ᵖ − 1 = 0. Since the group is abelian, ρ(g) − 1 is an intertwiner. On a simple module an intertwiner is either zero or injective; a nilpotent operator on a nonzero space cannot be injective. Hence every group element acts as the identity.

The statement below proves this identity for finite-dimensional simple representations over any field of characteristic p, without assuming algebraic closedness. Once the action is trivial, simplicity forces dimension one. The next problem has a stronger checked result that does not require finite-dimensionality.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CyclicPrimeRepresentation.apply_eq_id_of_isSimpleModule
declarations.label: Every element of the cyclic group of order p acts trivially
declarations.documentation: In a finite-dimensional simple representation of the cyclic group of prime order p over a field of characteristic p, every group element acts by the identity.

Chapter4/Problem4.1.4.title: Every nonzero representation of a finite p-group has a fixed vector
explanation: The source first proves the stronger fixed-vector assertion. Induct on the group order, choosing a nonidentity central element z of p-power order. The nilpotent operator ρ(z) − 1 has a nonzero, G-invariant kernel. On that kernel the action factors through the smaller p-group G/⟨z⟩, so induction supplies a nonzero vector fixed by all of G.

In a simple representation the line through that fixed vector is the whole module, and all group elements act as the identity. The checked hypotheses are a finite group of order pⁿ, prime p, a field of characteristic p, and simplicity. Neither finite-dimensionality nor algebraic closedness is required.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ModularPGroup.eq_id_of_isSimpleModule_of_card_eq_primePow
declarations.label: A simple representation of a finite p-group in characteristic p is trivial
declarations.documentation: Every group element acts by the identity on a simple representation over a field of characteristic p when the finite group has p-power order; no finite-dimensionality assumption is imposed.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.ModularPGroup.eq_id_of_isSimpleModule_of_card_eq_primePow.exists_ne_zero_fixedVector
links.label: Read the induction that constructs a nonzero common fixed vector

Chapter4/Introduction_4.2.after: If V is a finite dimensional
Chapter4/Introduction_4.2.title: The group character is the trace functional restricted to the basis G
explanation: Lean defines χᵥ(g) as the linear-map trace of ρ(g). Trace is invariant under conjugation, so conjugate elements have the same value. Linearity recovers the character of the group-algebra action from these values: χᵥ(∑g c(g)g) = ∑g c(g)χᵥ(g). The statement below checks agreement of the two character constructions on each basis element g.

These identities require a finite-dimensional representation over a field, but not a finite group or an algebraically closed field. Group-algebra elements always have finite support, so the extension formula remains a finite sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ConjugationInvariantCharacters.character_eq_auxiliaryMap_apply
declarations.label: The group character equals the group-algebra trace character at g
declarations.documentation: For a finite-dimensional representation, evaluation of its group character at g agrees with evaluation of the linear trace character of the associated group-algebra module on the basis element g.

links.name: FDRep.character
links.label: Inspect the trace definition of a representation character

links.name: FDRep.char_conj
links.label: Read the proof of conjugacy invariance

Chapter4/Introduction_4.2.title: Class functions form a linear subspace of the function space
explanation: The function space F(G, k) is simply G → k, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. Its class-function submodule consists of the functions satisfying f(hgh⁻¹) = f(g) for every g and h. This definition makes sense even for an infinite group and over a semiring; the membership statement below exposes the condition without needing the implementation's type alias.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.ConjugationInvariantCharacters.mem_conjugationInvariantSubmodule_iff
declarations.label: A class function is a function invariant under conjugation
declarations.documentation: A function belongs to the class-function submodule exactly when f(hgh⁻¹) = f(g) for every pair of group elements.

Chapter4/Theorem4.2.1.title: A class function extends to a trace on the group algebra
explanation: Extend f : G → k linearly to φ : k[G] → k. Conjugacy invariance of f is equivalent to φ(ab) = φ(ba): on basis elements gh and hg are conjugate, and conversely hgh⁻¹ and g arise by swapping two factors. Thus class functions identify with the linear functionals annihilating commutators.

The general algebra theorem below proves that such functionals are spanned by simple-module trace characters for a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra over an algebraically closed field. Its proof uses matrix units in each matrix block to show that a functional vanishing on commutators is a scalar multiple of the ordinary trace in that block. This supplies the spanning argument in the book.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.Dual.SimpleFamilies.mem_span_moduleDualElement_of_commutes_mul
declarations.label: Every trace functional on a split semisimple algebra is spanned by simple characters
declarations.documentation: A linear functional φ satisfying φ(ab) = φ(ba) belongs to the span of the chosen simple-module trace characters, for a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra over an algebraically closed field.

Chapter4/Theorem4.2.1.title: The group proof also constructs the coefficients by character pairing
explanation: For one representative Vᵢ of each irreducible isomorphism class, the source proves linear independence of the character functions and equality of their span with the class-function subspace. It also gives the expansion coefficients cᵢ = |G|⁻¹ ∑g f(g)χᵢ(g⁻¹), using character orthogonality to show that the remaining class function is zero.

The hypotheses are a finite group, an algebraically closed field, and invertible group order. The two statements below are the independence and spanning assertions underlying 'form a basis'; they do not require the reader to interpret a subtype's name as a mathematical definition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.ClassFunctions.FiniteGroup.auxiliarySubtypeValLinearIndependent
declarations.label: The distinct irreducible characters are linearly independent
declarations.documentation: The underlying functions of the simple-representation characters are linearly independent over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FiniteGroup.ClassFunctions.FiniteGroup.span_simple_characters_eq_auxiliarySubmodule
declarations.label: Their span is exactly the class-function subspace
declarations.documentation: The span of the irreducible character functions equals the submodule of functions invariant under conjugation, under the same finite-group and field hypotheses.

Chapter4/Corollary4.2.2.title: Count irreducible isomorphism classes, not chosen module carriers
explanation: The statement below chooses a complete family of pairwise nonisomorphic simple finite-dimensional representations whose size is the number of conjugacy classes. The source proves the count through the center of k[G]: its coefficients are constant on conjugacy classes, whereas each matrix block contributes a one-dimensional center. This is a different route to the same count as the character-basis argument in the book.
As with the preceding basis theorem, the checked assumptions are algebraic closedness and invertible group order. They ensure that each simple block is a full matrix algebra over k.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.SimpleRepresentations.exists_simpleReps_card_eq_conjClasses
declarations.label: A complete family of irreducibles has one member per conjugacy class
declarations.documentation: For a finite group over an algebraically closed field with invertible group order, there exists a complete pairwise nonisomorphic simple family of size equal to the number of conjugacy classes.

Chapter4/Exercise4.2.3.title: The modular case forces all irreducible traces into a proper hyperplane
explanation: Let P = ∑g g. When |G| = 0 in k, P is central and P² = 0, so it acts by zero on every simple module. Every simple trace character therefore vanishes on P. But P has nonzero image in k[G] modulo commutators: summing the coefficients in the identity conjugacy class gives 1 on P and zero on every commutator.

Over an algebraically closed field, the simple trace characters are linearly independent. Since they all annihilate that nonzero quotient vector, their number is strictly less than the dimension of the quotient, which is the number of conjugacy classes. The statement below checks this strict inequality, including the nonzero-vector and independence arguments.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupTheory.CardinalityBounds.auxiliaryCard_lt_conjClasses_of_card_cast_eq_zero_algClosed
declarations.label: In the modular case there are fewer irreducibles than conjugacy classes
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field in which the finite group order is zero, the number of simple finite-dimensional representation isomorphism classes is strictly less than the number of conjugacy classes.

Chapter4/Exercise4.2.3.title: Extension to an algebraic closure gives the arbitrary-field result
explanation: The formalization also proves the exercise for an arbitrary field. It bounds the number of irreducible isomorphism classes over k by the number over an algebraic closure and then applies the strict inequality above. The comparison uses the radical quotient and scalar extension; it does not assume that an irreducible representation stays irreducible after extending scalars.

In the expanded statement, SimpleCharacter is the quotient of simple finite-dimensional representations by isomorphism. Its cardinality counts irreducible isomorphism classes, not just distinct trace functions. This distinction matters in positive characteristic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupTheory.CardinalityBounds.auxiliaryCard_lt_conjClasses_of_card_cast_eq_zero
declarations.label: The strict inequality holds over any field in which |G| = 0
declarations.documentation: For any field and finite group whose order is zero in that field, there are strictly fewer simple finite-dimensional representation isomorphism classes than conjugacy classes.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.GroupTheory.ConjugacyClassCardinalityBounds.auxiliaryCard_le_auxiliaryCard_of_algebra
links.label: Read the scalar-extension comparison of irreducible counts

Chapter4/Corollary4.2.4.title: Characteristic zero lets character values recover integer multiplicities
explanation: For finite-dimensional representations of a finite group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, χᵥ = ∑ᵢ mᵢχᵢ records each irreducible multiplicity mᵢ. Characteristic zero makes the map from these natural-number multiplicities into k injective. In characteristic p, p copies of the trivial representation already have zero character, so equality of character values alone cannot recover dimension.

The checked proof below first recovers dimensions of equivariant Hom spaces from character pairings, then splits off common simple summands and inducts on dimension. Its conclusion is an actual representation isomorphism, not only matching multiplicities in a chosen list. The source has both this algebraically closed characteristic-zero theorem and its specialization to complex representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Group.CharacterAuxiliary.iso_of_character_eq
declarations.label: Equal characters give an equivariant isomorphism in characteristic zero
declarations.documentation: Finite-dimensional representations of a finite group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero are isomorphic when their character functions agree.

Chapter3/Introduction_to_3.10.title: The tensor product carries componentwise multiplication
explanation: The same tensor-product type used for vector spaces carries an algebra structure: multiplication is the bilinear extension of (a₁ ⊗ b₁)(a₂ ⊗ b₂) = a₁a₂ ⊗ b₁b₂, and its unit is 1 ⊗ 1. The Mathlib theorem below checks the displayed multiplication rule directly. The factors need not be commutative or finite-dimensional.

links.name: Algebra.TensorProduct.tmul_mul_tmul
links.label: Read the checked multiplication rule for pure tensors

Chapter3/Exercise3.10.1.title: The isomorphism is the Kronecker product of matrices
explanation: A tensor M ⊗ N maps to the matrix indexed by pairs, with entry MᵢⱼNₐᵦ at row (i, a), column (j, b). In particular, Eᵢⱼ ⊗ Eₐᵦ maps to E₍ᵢ,ₐ₎₍ⱼ,ᵦ₎. The proof composes the Kronecker algebra equivalence, the scalar-tensor identification k ⊗ k ≃ k, and the reindexing of pairs by Fin(mn).

The checked result is an algebra equivalence, so it preserves multiplication and the unit as well as the vector-space structure. It works over any commutative ring k, including zero matrix sizes; no field or algebraic-closedness assumption is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.TensorProduct.matrixTensorProduct_algEquiv
declarations.label: Matₘ(k) ⊗ Matₙ(k) is algebra-isomorphic to Matₘₙ(k)
declarations.documentation: Existence of the Kronecker-product algebra equivalence over a commutative ring, with the paired row and column indices reindexed by Fin(m*n).

links.name: Matrix.kroneckerTMulAlgEquiv
links.label: Inspect the underlying Kronecker algebra equivalence

Chapter3/Theorem3.10.2.title: The tensor of two finite-dimensional simple modules is simple
explanation: The action is (a ⊗ b)(v ⊗ w) = av ⊗ bw. Lean states simplicity by saying that a k-subspace stable under every such action is either zero or the whole tensor product. Simplicity of V and W also ensures that the tensor product is nonzero.

The checked hypotheses are a field k that is algebraically closed, finite-dimensional V and W, and compatible A- and B-module structures. The algebras themselves need not be finite-dimensional. The proof uses density to replace the two algebra actions by arbitrary linear endomorphisms, then extracts every pure tensor from any nonzero invariant subspace.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.submodule_eq_bot_or_top_of_tensorActions
declarations.label: Every subspace stable under the two factor actions is zero or everything
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field, for finite-dimensional simple A- and B-modules, every k-subspace of V ⊗ W stable under the tensor-factor actions is bottom or top.

Chapter3/Theorem3.10.2.title: Existence gives both factors and equivariance; uniqueness is up to isomorphism
explanation: A module for A ⊗ B is treated as a vector space with commuting A- and B-actions. For a finite-dimensional nonzero module having no proper subspace stable under both actions, the source constructs finite-dimensional simple factors V and W and a linear equivalence M ≃ V ⊗ W. Separate equations check that this equivalence respects both actions.

If two such tensor products are equivariantly isomorphic, the uniqueness theorem produces an A-module isomorphism between their first factors and a B-module isomorphism between their second factors. This is the meaning of 'unique' here, not equality of chosen carriers. Existence uses algebraic closedness; the factor-uniqueness theorem works over any field.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.auxiliary
declarations.label: Construct simple factors and an equivalence respecting both actions
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field, a finite-dimensional nonzero module with commuting A- and B-actions and no proper common invariant subspace is equivariantly equivalent to V ⊗ W for finite-dimensional simple factors.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.nonempty_linearEquiv_factors_of_tensorEquiv
declarations.label: An equivariant tensor-product isomorphism determines both simple factors
declarations.documentation: Over any field, an isomorphism between tensor products of finite-dimensional simple factors that respects both factor actions yields module isomorphisms of the respective factors.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.10.title: The finite-dimensional reduction uses the images of the actions
explanation: Although A and B may be infinite-dimensional, their images A′ and B′ lie in Endₖ(M), which is finite-dimensional when M is. Commutation of the actions gives an algebra homomorphism A′ ⊗ B′ → Endₖ(M), sending a pure tensor to the product of the corresponding endomorphisms. The source constructs this map and the induced module structure, and proves the radical formula for these image algebras.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.JacobsonRadical.TensorProduct.tensorProductRangeAction
declarations.label: The two commuting image algebras act through their tensor product
declarations.documentation: The algebra homomorphism from the tensor product of the two action ranges to Endₖ(M), constructed from commutation of the actions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.JacobsonRadical.TensorProduct.jacobson_tensorProduct_actionRange_eq_aux3
declarations.label: The radical formula applies to the finite-dimensional image algebras
declarations.documentation: For actions on a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field, the Jacobson radical of the tensor product of their ranges is the ideal generated by the radicals of those ranges.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.10.title: The two radical inclusions and the quotient are checked
explanation: The ideal J is the sum of the ideals generated by rad(A) ⊗ 1 and 1 ⊗ rad(B); over a field these identify with the tensor subspaces in the book's formula. The source proves that each summand is nilpotent and hence lies in rad(A ⊗ B). It constructs the quotient by J as (A/rad A) ⊗ (B/rad B).

Over an algebraically closed field, finite-dimensional semisimple algebras are products of matrix algebras; their tensor product is again semisimple by the Kronecker equivalence. This gives the reverse inclusion rad(A ⊗ B) ⊆ J. The resulting equality and quotient equivalence below assume both algebras finite-dimensional. The source derives nilpotence of the sum from its inclusion in the Artinian ring's radical, rather than assuming a commutative binomial expansion of ideals.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.JacobsonRadical.TensorProduct.jacobson_tensorProduct_eq_aux3
declarations.label: rad(A ⊗ B) = rad(A) ⊗ B + A ⊗ rad(B)
declarations.documentation: For finite-dimensional algebras over an algebraically closed field, the Jacobson radical of the tensor product equals the ideal generated by the radicals of both factors.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.RingTheory.JacobsonRadical.TensorProduct.quotientJacobsonTensorProductAlgEquiv
declarations.label: The semisimple quotient is the tensor product of the factor quotients
declarations.documentation: An algebra equivalence (A ⊗ B)/rad(A ⊗ B) ≃ (A/rad A) ⊗ (B/rad B), under the same field and finite-dimensionality hypotheses.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.10.title: The factor-existence proof also gives a direct evaluation construction
explanation: The source proves existence independently of the radical reduction: choose a simple A-submodule V of M, let W = Hom_A(V, M), and evaluate v ⊗ f ↦ f(v). Commutation gives W its B-action. Joint simplicity makes evaluation surjective; density on V proves injectivity. A dimension argument then proves W is simple.

For uniqueness, contract a proposed tensor-product equivalence against a nonzero vector and a suitable linear functional to obtain a nonzero A-linear map between the first factors. Simplicity makes it an isomorphism; exchanging the tensor factors gives the B-linear isomorphism. The separate radical results above validate the book's displayed identities, while these arguments prove the factorization and uniqueness themselves.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.auxiliary
links.label: Read the evaluation-map construction of the two factors

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductSimplicity.nonempty_linearEquiv_factors_of_tensorEquiv
links.label: Read the contraction proof of uniqueness

Chapter3/Remark3.10.3.title: A simple Weyl-algebra tensor module need not split into simple factors
explanation: The counterexample uses ℂ[x, y]. The first Weyl algebra acts by X ↦ multiplication by x and D ↦ ∂/∂x + y; the second acts by X ↦ multiplication by y and D ↦ ∂/∂y + x. Each pair satisfies DX − XD = 1, and the two pairs commute, giving an action of A ⊗ A.

This joint module is simple: subtracting the cross multiplication terms recovers both ordinary partial derivatives, which reduce any nonzero polynomial to a nonzero constant; multiplication then recovers every polynomial. Yet its restriction to the first A is the regular module A, which has no simple submodules. A factorization with a simple first factor would embed that factor into the restriction, a contradiction. Lean proves both simplicity and the nonexistence of such an equivariant tensor-product factorization, without assuming finite-dimensional factors.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.AuxiliaryRepresentations.auxiliaryTensorProductModule_isSimpleModule
declarations.label: The coupled action on ℂ[x, y] is a simple A ⊗ A-module
declarations.documentation: The polynomial carrier with the two commuting Weyl actions is a simple module over the tensor product algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.AuxiliaryRepresentations.not_equivariant_tensorProductEquiv
declarations.label: This module is not an equivariant tensor product with a simple first factor
declarations.documentation: No tensor product V ⊗ W with V simple and W nonzero can be equivariantly equivalent to this polynomial module, even allowing infinite-dimensional factors.

Chapter3/Remark3.10.3.title: The rational-function example has a nonzero, noninvertible tensor
explanation: Put K = ℂ(x). In K ⊗ℂ K, the element t = x ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ x maps to zero under multiplication into K. But it is not zero: applying x ↦ x + 1 in the first factor and the identity in the second sends it to 1. Therefore t cannot be invertible, and the tensor product is not a field.

Each factor K is simple over itself, whereas the tensor of their regular modules is the regular module of K ⊗ℂ K. For a commutative ring, that module is simple only when every nonzero element is a unit. The checked non-field result and this general criterion establish the failure of part (i); the criterion is linked separately below.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.AuxiliaryRepresentations.not_isField_tensorProduct_ratFunc_self
declarations.label: ℂ(x) ⊗ℂ ℂ(x) is not a field
declarations.documentation: The nonzero element x ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ x lies in the kernel of the multiplication homomorphism, so it cannot have an inverse.

links.name: isSimpleModule_self_iff_isUnit
links.label: A ring's regular module is simple exactly when every nonzero element is a unit

Chapter3/Problem3.9.3.title: The simple representations are concentrated at one vertex
explanation: For each vertex i, let Sᵢ have carrier k at i, zero at every other vertex, and zero arrow maps. The source proves Sᵢ is simple. For a finite quiver without oriented cycles it also proves every simple quiver representation is isomorphic to some Sᵢ, without assuming finite-dimensional carriers or an algebraically closed field.

The path-algebra interpretation uses the earlier correspondence: vertex spaces are the images of the vertex idempotents, arrows act between those images, and a quiver representation gives an action on the direct sum of its vertex spaces. The forward-composition version below uses the book's path multiplication convention.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryConstructions.hasAuxiliaryProperty_vertex
declarations.label: The representation Sᵢ at a vertex is simple
declarations.documentation: The representation with a one-dimensional carrier at i, zero elsewhere and zero arrow maps is nonzero and has no proper nonzero subrepresentation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryConstructions.exists_vertex_nonempty_auxiliaryObject
declarations.label: Every simple representation of a finite acyclic quiver is some Sᵢ
declarations.documentation: For a finite quiver without oriented cycles, any simple quiver representation is isomorphic to a representation concentrated at one vertex.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.representationOfModule
links.label: Recover the vertex spaces and arrow maps from a path-algebra module

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.directSumActionAlgHom
links.label: Construct the book's path-algebra action from a quiver representation

Chapter3/Problem3.9.3.title: Ext¹ counts arrows, with their direction preserved
explanation: The explicit model takes arrow-indexed maps Vᵢ → Wⱼ modulo the image of the vertex-indexed differential dX(e : i → j) = W(e) ∘ Xᵢ − Xⱼ ∘ V(e). For V = Sᵢ and W = Sⱼ the differential is zero. Only the components at arrows i → j survive, so this quotient has one scalar coordinate for each such arrow.

With finitely many vertices and arrows, Lean checks that its dimension is the number of arrows i → j. The separate vanishing criterion says the quotient is zero exactly when there are no arrows in that direction. This is the arrow-cokernel construction of Ext¹(Sᵢ, Sⱼ); these results do not identify it with a separately bundled categorical Ext functor. No algebraic-closedness hypothesis is needed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryConstructions.finrank_homObject
declarations.label: The dimension of Ext¹(Sᵢ, Sⱼ) is the number of arrows i → j
declarations.documentation: For a finite quiver with finite arrow types, the explicit arrow-cokernel quotient between the vertex representations has dimension equal to the cardinality of i → j.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryConstructions.auxiliaryRelation_iff_isEmpty_hom
declarations.label: Ext¹(Sᵢ, Sⱼ) vanishes exactly when there is no arrow i → j
declarations.documentation: Surjectivity of the vertex-to-arrow differential for these representations is equivalent to emptiness of the arrow type i → j. Since that differential is zero, this is the vanishing criterion for its cokernel.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.3.title: Two-dimensional means the sum of all vertex dimensions is two
explanation: The exhaustive normal form is either Sᵢ ⊕ Sⱼ, allowing i = j, or a representation supported at distinct vertices i and j with a one-dimensional space at each. In the latter case each arrow e : i → j acts by a scalar c(e), and all other arrow maps vanish. A nonsplit form has at least one nonzero c(e). This is a classification over any field for a finite acyclic quiver.

The displayed normal-form theorem uses total dimension ∑ᵥ dim Vᵥ = 2, not dimension two at each vertex. Its coefficient function is stored on all arrows, but only the i → j entries affect the action. With zero coefficients the checked isomorphism below gives Sᵢ ⊕ Sⱼ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.exists_equiv_auxiliaryDefinition5_of_totalDimension_eq_two
declarations.label: Every representation of total dimension two has one of these normal forms
declarations.documentation: For a finite acyclic quiver with finite-dimensional vertex spaces, every representation of total dimension two is isomorphic to a two-vertex model: either zero arrow coefficients, or distinct vertices with a nonzero coefficient on an arrow between them.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.zeroAuxiliaryEquivalenceData
declarations.label: The zero-arrow model is Sᵢ ⊕ Sⱼ
declarations.documentation: An explicit quiver-representation isomorphism from the zero-coefficient two-vertex model to the direct sum of the two vertex representations, including repeated vertices.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.3.title: Nonzero arrow vectors are classified up to common scaling
explanation: For fixed distinct i and j, changing the bases of the two one-dimensional vertex spaces multiplies every c(e), e : i → j, by the same nonzero scalar. The source constructs this rescaling isomorphism and proves the converse. Thus the nonsplit classes with these endpoints are nonzero arrow-coefficient vectors modulo common scaling.

A nonzero coefficient makes the model indecomposable: any attempted complementary decomposition must put the two endpoint lines in the same summand. Zero coefficients instead give a decomposable direct sum. Isomorphisms preserve the unordered pair of support vertices; acyclicity rules out simultaneous arrows in both directions, while the split form has no preferred ordering of its summands.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.auxiliaryFact3
declarations.label: An isomorphism forces common nonzero scaling of the arrow coefficients
declarations.documentation: For models on the same distinct vertices i and j, an isomorphism implies c′(e) = t c(e) on every arrow i → j for some nonzero scalar t.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.auxiliaryDefinition6
declarations.label: Rescaling the coefficients constructs an isomorphism
declarations.documentation: The vertexwise change of basis giving an isomorphism from the model with coefficients c to the model with coefficients t c, for t nonzero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.auxiliaryFact21
declarations.label: An isomorphism preserves the unordered pair of support vertices
declarations.documentation: Isomorphic two-vertex models have the same two distinguished vertices, up to exchanging their order.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.TwoDimensionalRepresentations.auxiliaryFact14
declarations.label: A nonzero arrow coefficient makes the model indecomposable
declarations.documentation: For distinct vertices i and j, a nonzero coefficient on an arrow i → j prevents any decomposition into two nonzero subrepresentations.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: The quadratic relation specializes to the exterior algebra
explanation: The input to Lean's Clifford algebra is the quadratic form Q(v) = B(v, v), where B is the symmetric bilinear form in the problem. Its generator satisfies ι(v)² = Q(v)1. Expanding the square of ι(v + w) gives the relation ι(v)ι(w) + ι(w)ι(v) = 2B(v, w)1 over ℂ.

For the zero bilinear form, the checked result is an algebra equivalence with the exterior algebra, not just agreement of dimensions. For a general form the later exterior-space comparison is only a linear equivalence; its multiplication is different.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.nonempty_algEquiv_exterior_of_zero
declarations.label: The zero-form Clifford algebra is the exterior algebra
declarations.documentation: If B is identically zero, its Clifford algebra is ℂ-algebra equivalent to the exterior algebra of V.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: The algebra classification proves the claimed matrix sizes
explanation: For a symmetric nondegenerate form on a finite-dimensional complex space, the source constructs an algebra equivalence with one full matrix algebra of size 2ⁿ in dimension 2n, and with a product of two such matrix algebras in dimension 2n + 1. These are whole-algebra equivalences, stronger than merely producing one or two representations.

The proof first establishes semisimplicity and computes the center. The even center has dimension one, forcing one matrix factor. The odd center has dimension two; the grading involution exchanges the two factors, forcing equal sizes. The dimension 2^dim V then determines their sizes. The hypotheses here are specifically symmetry, nondegeneracy, finite dimension and the complex field.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.exists_algEquiv_end_of_finrank_even
declarations.label: In dimension 2n, the algebra is one matrix algebra of size 2ⁿ
declarations.documentation: A symmetric nondegenerate complex form of dimension 2n gives an algebra equivalence between its Clifford algebra and the endomorphism algebra of Fin (2^n) → ℂ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.exists_algEquiv_prod_end_of_finrank_odd
declarations.label: In dimension 2n + 1, the algebra is a product of two matrix algebras of size 2ⁿ
declarations.documentation: A symmetric nondegenerate complex form of dimension 2n + 1 gives an algebra equivalence with the product of two copies of the endomorphism algebra of Fin (2^n) → ℂ.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: The even spin representation uses wedge multiplication and contraction
explanation: On S = ∧ℂⁿ, a vector u acts by left wedge multiplication, and a covector f acts by contraction. Each squares to zero; their anticommutator is f(u) times the identity. On the hyperbolic space (ℂⁿ)* × ℂⁿ with Q(f, u) = f(u), this gives exactly the δᵢⱼ/2 normalization of the bilinear form in the hint.

An isometry transports this construction to any symmetric nondegenerate form of dimension 2n. The resulting algebra homomorphism onto Endℂ(S) is bijective. Unlike the order suggested in the hint, the source uses the abstract matrix-algebra classification first: simplicity gives injectivity, and equal dimensions give surjectivity. It then deduces that S is simple and that every simple module is isomorphic to it.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.AuxiliaryRepresentation.vectorAction
declarations.label: A vector acts by wedge multiplication
declarations.documentation: The endomorphism of the exterior algebra given by left multiplication by its degree-one generator ι(u).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.AuxiliaryRepresentation.dualAction
declarations.label: A covector acts by contraction
declarations.documentation: The contraction endomorphism associated with a linear functional, serving as differentiation on the exterior algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.EvenDimensionalModules.standardCliffordRepresentation_bijective
declarations.label: The transported spin action identifies the Clifford algebra with Endℂ(S)
declarations.documentation: For a symmetric nondegenerate complex form of dimension 2n, the explicit exterior-space representation is a bijective algebra homomorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.EvenDimensionalModules.simpleModule_linearEquiv_evenCliffordModule
declarations.label: Every simple module is isomorphic to the even spin module
declarations.documentation: Every simple module over this even-dimensional Clifford algebra is module-linearly equivalent to the transported exterior-space spin module. No separate finite-dimensionality assumption on the simple module is required.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: The two odd spin modules differ by the sign of parity
explanation: Let P act on the exterior algebra by (−1)^degree. Then P² = 1, and P anticommutes with wedge multiplication and contraction. The extra orthogonal unit vector therefore acts by either +P or −P. Both choices give simple modules of dimension 2ⁿ.

They cannot be isomorphic. An intertwiner must commute with P because the even Clifford algebra acts as all of Endℂ(S), but it must also anticommute with P because the extra generator has opposite signs. Over ℂ this forces the intertwiner to be zero. The classification theorem proves that every simple module belongs to one of these two isomorphism classes; finite-dimensionality of that module is a consequence, not an extra assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.OddDimensionalModules.positiveSpinRepresentationOfBilin
declarations.label: Construct S₊, where the extra generator acts by +P
declarations.documentation: The exterior-space spin action transported to a general symmetric nondegenerate odd-dimensional complex form, choosing positive parity for the extra generator.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.OddDimensionalModules.negativeSpinRepresentationOfBilin
declarations.label: Construct S₋, where the extra generator acts by −P
declarations.documentation: The corresponding spin action choosing negative parity for the extra generator.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.OddDimensionalModules.isEmpty_linearEquiv_secondOddCliffordModule_firstOddCliffordModule
declarations.label: The two odd spin modules are not isomorphic
declarations.documentation: There is no module-linear equivalence between the positive and negative exterior-space spin modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.OddDimensionalModules.simpleModule_equiv_first_or_second
declarations.label: Every simple module is isomorphic to S₊ or S₋
declarations.documentation: Every simple module over a symmetric nondegenerate complex Clifford algebra of dimension 2n + 1 is isomorphic to one of the two spin modules.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: Ordered subset monomials give a basis of size 2^dim V
explanation: For an orthogonal basis of V, take the products of distinct basis generators in increasing order, including the empty product 1. The source proves these products span and constructs the resulting basis indexed by subsets. There are 2^dim V such subsets.

The dimension formula holds even when the form is degenerate. Its proof uses the linear equivalence between Clifford and exterior spaces; it does not assert that their algebra structures agree. Together with the matrix-algebra classification and the explicit spin actions, this rules out further simple-module classes in the nondegenerate case.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.finsetMonomialBasis
declarations.label: The increasing products indexed by subsets form a basis
declarations.documentation: An orthogonal basis of V induces a basis of its Clifford algebra indexed by finite subsets of the basis index set, using increasing generator products.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.finrank_eq_two_pow
declarations.label: The Clifford algebra has dimension 2^dim V, including degenerate forms
declarations.documentation: For a finite-dimensional complex vector space with bilinear form B, the associated Clifford algebra has dimension 2^dim V.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: Degeneracy produces radical elements, not merely nilpotents
explanation: In the nondegenerate case the trace pairing of left multiplication is nondegenerate: orthogonal subset monomials have zero off-diagonal pairings and nonzero diagonal pairings. An element of the Jacobson radical pairs to zero with everything, so the radical vanishes; finite-dimensionality then gives semisimplicity.

If 0 ≠ v lies in the radical of B, its Clifford generator a is nonzero, a² = 0, and a r a = 0 for every algebra element r. The source uses this stronger property to put a in the Jacobson radical. Merely exhibiting a nonzero square-zero element would not suffice: matrix algebras also contain such elements. This proves the converse without that mistaken shortcut.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.isSemisimpleRing_iff_nondegenerate
declarations.label: The Clifford algebra is semisimple exactly when the form is nondegenerate
declarations.documentation: For a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional complex vector space, semisimplicity of its Clifford algebra is equivalent to nondegeneracy of the form.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.5.title: The radical quotient is the Clifford algebra of V/rad B
explanation: Let R be the radical of B. The induced form on V/R is nondegenerate. The map on Clifford algebras is surjective, and the source proves its kernel is exactly the Jacobson radical: the two-sided ideal generated by the degree-one elements coming from R. Thus the formalization answers the quotient question, not just the existence of a map to some nondegenerate Clifford algebra.

Write r = dim(V/R), the rank of B. The quotient is one matrix algebra of size 2ⁿ if r = 2n, or a product of two such matrix algebras if r = 2n + 1. In particular, the zero form has rank zero and quotient ℂ. Lean expresses V/R in finite coordinates in the displayed existence theorem; the source constructs it from the actual quotient space.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.exists_surjective_algHom_nondegenerate_quotient_of_degenerate
declarations.label: The map to the nondegenerate quotient has kernel equal to the Jacobson radical
declarations.documentation: For a symmetric degenerate form, there is a surjective algebra homomorphism to the Clifford algebra of the induced nondegenerate quotient form, with kernel exactly the Jacobson radical.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.CliffordAlgebra.ComplexClassification.radicalIdeal_eq_jacobson
links.label: Read the proof identifying the radical with the ideal generated by R

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: The cocycle defines an actual extension module
explanation: The carrier is V × W, but its A-action is twisted: a acts on (v, w) as (a • v + f(a)(w), a • w). This is a vector-space direct sum; it need not be a direct sum of A-modules. The source constructs the module instances, rather than recording only a block-matrix formula.

The maps v ↦ (v, 0) and (v, w) ↦ w are A-linear, the first is injective, the second is surjective, and the image of the first is the kernel of the second. The quotient by that image is A-linearly equivalent to W. These are the checked extension data.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule
declarations.label: The product vector space with the twisted A-action
declarations.documentation: The representation on V × W associated with a linear cocycle f : A → Hom_k(W, V).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.exact_inclusion_projection
declarations.label: The inclusion and projection form an exact sequence
declarations.documentation: The image of the A-linear inclusion of V is the kernel of the A-linear projection onto W.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.quotientRangeInclusionEquiv
declarations.label: The quotient of the extension by V is isomorphic to W
declarations.documentation: An A-linear equivalence from the quotient by the image of the inclusion to W.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: The off-diagonal block gives the cocycle equation
explanation: Multiplying the two block matrices gives f(ab) = ρ_V(a) ∘ f(b) + f(a) ∘ ρ_W(b). The formalization proves that this equation is equivalent to multiplicativity of the displayed action. Because f is already bundled as a k-linear map, linearity is not an additional obligation hidden in the predicate.

Putting a = b = 1 gives f(1) = f(1) + f(1), hence f(1) = 0. Thus the cocycle equation also supplies the unit condition for the extension action. This works over any field, without finite-dimensionality or algebraic closedness. The submodule below is Z¹(W, V).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.extensionAction_mul_iff
declarations.label: Multiplicativity is equivalent to the cocycle equation
declarations.documentation: The triangular action preserves products if and only if f satisfies the extension-cocycle identity.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.auxiliaryMapSubmodule
declarations.label: The vector space Z¹(W, V) of linear cocycles
declarations.documentation: The k-submodule of linear maps A → Hom_k(W, V) satisfying the cocycle identity.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: Coboundaries measure failure to intertwine the action
explanation: The linear map X ↦ dX has kernel exactly the maps commuting with the A-action, namely Hom_A(W, V). Its range is B¹(W, V). The checked kernel and range descriptions give the first-isomorphism-theorem interpretation in the book.

Ext¹(W, V) is encoded here as the quotient of the cocycle submodule by the coboundary submodule inside it. This is the explicit cocycle construction, not an identification with a separately defined categorical Ext functor. In the Lean parameters V precedes W even though the book writes Ext¹(W, V), so f still maps W to V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.coboundary_eq_zero_iff
declarations.label: The kernel of d consists of A-linear maps
declarations.documentation: The coboundary of a k-linear map W → V is zero exactly when it intertwines the A-actions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.coboundaries_eq_range
declarations.label: B¹(W, V) is the range of the coboundary map
declarations.documentation: The span used to define coboundaries equals the range of the linear map X ↦ dX.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.AuxiliaryData
declarations.label: Ext¹(W, V) as cocycles modulo coboundaries
declarations.documentation: The quotient vector space Z¹(W, V)/B¹(W, V), with the denominator regarded as a submodule of Z¹.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: A shear identifies extensions while fixing both ends
explanation: If f − f′ = dX, the proof constructs the isomorphism (v, w) ↦ (v + Xw, w), with inverse (v, w) ↦ (v − Xw, w). It is the identity on the included V and the quotient W. Conversely, the same intertwining equation for a shear forces f − f′ to be a coboundary.

The printed B¹(V, W) in the converse has its arguments reversed: both cocycles take values in Hom_k(W, V), so the conclusion belongs to B¹(W, V). The checked statement uses this consistent direction. An arbitrary A-module isomorphism is not required to fix the two end terms; that is the different question in part (d).

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.nonempty_linearEquiv_of_sub_mem_coboundaries
declarations.label: A coboundary difference gives an A-module isomorphism
declarations.documentation: The proof constructs an invertible shear between the two extension modules when their cocycles differ by a coboundary.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.sub_mem_coboundaries_of_shear_linearEquiv
declarations.label: An A-linear shear forces a coboundary difference
declarations.documentation: An isomorphism acting as (v, w) ↦ (v + Xw, w) implies that f − f′ belongs to B¹(W, V).

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: Underlying module isomorphisms allow a nonzero scalar
explanation: For finite-dimensional simple V and W over an algebraically closed field, the checked criterion is existence of c ≠ 0 with f − c f′ ∈ B¹(W, V). Thus it is the quotient classes that differ by a nonzero scalar, not necessarily the chosen cocycle representatives. Algebraic closedness is an explicit hypothesis because Schur's lemma makes the endomorphisms of each simple module scalars.

The zero class gives the split representation V ⊕ W; nonzero classes give the projective-space description in the book. The source proves the isomorphism criterion and the split criterion directly. It does not separately package a bijection with projective space or construct a cocycle from every abstract short exact sequence.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.nonempty_linearEquiv_iff_exists_sub_smul_mem_coboundaries
declarations.label: Isomorphic extension modules correspond to nonzero scalar-related classes
declarations.documentation: Over an algebraically closed field, for finite-dimensional simple V and W, the extension modules are A-linearly isomorphic exactly when f − c f′ is a coboundary for some nonzero c.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.ExtensionModule.nonempty_linearEquiv_prod_iff_mem_coboundaries
declarations.label: The extension is split exactly when its class is zero
declarations.documentation: Under the same simplicity, finite-dimensionality and algebraic-closedness hypotheses, the extension module is isomorphic to V × W exactly when its cocycle is a coboundary.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.1.title: The proof also handles isomorphic end terms
explanation: An arbitrary isomorphism has four blocks. Its lower-left block V → W intertwines the A-actions. If this block is nonzero, Schur's lemma makes it invertible, and the block equations show that both cocycles are coboundaries. If it is zero, the diagonal blocks are nonzero scalars; the upper-right equation gives proportionality modulo a coboundary.
There is no extra assumption that V and W are nonisomorphic. The nonzero-block case is what prevents that omission from being a gap in the classification proof.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.ExtensionCocycles.exists_isExtensionEquiv_iff_exists_sub_smul_mem_coboundaries
links.label: Inspect the four-block proof of the classification criterion

Chapter3/Problem3.9.2.title: Ext¹ is zero at distinct points and ℂⁿ at a repeated point
explanation: The evaluation representation at a is realized as the quotient of ℂ[x₁, …, xₙ] by the ideal generated by xᵢ − aᵢ. Every polynomial acts by its value at a, and the quotient is one-dimensional over ℂ.

At the same point, coboundaries vanish and cocycles are derivations at a. A derivation is freely determined by its n values on the generators, giving a checked linear equivalence Ext¹(Va, Va) ≃ ℂⁿ. At distinct points, commutativity forces the cocycle's generator values to be proportional to the differences of the evaluation coordinates; choosing one nonzero difference constructs a coboundary. Lean expresses the resulting zero quotient as Subsingleton.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.PolynomialEvaluationModules.nonempty_auxiliaryType_linearEquiv
declarations.label: Self-extensions at a point form an n-dimensional vector space
declarations.documentation: The cocycle quotient for the evaluation module at a is ℂ-linearly equivalent to Fin n → ℂ.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.PolynomialEvaluationModules.auxiliaryType_subsingleton_of_ne
declarations.label: There are no nonsplit extensions between distinct evaluation points
declarations.documentation: For distinct a and b, the cocycle quotient Ext¹(V_a, V_b) is a subsingleton vector space, hence zero.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.2.title: Two-dimensional modules have explicit normal forms and isomorphism tests
explanation: Every two-dimensional module is either V<sub>a</sub> ⊕ V<sub>b</sub> with a ≠ b, or a copy of the dual-number vector space ℂ[ε]/(ε²) on which xᵢ acts by multiplication by aᵢ + cᵢ ε. The proof obtains a common eigenvector, completes it to a basis, and uses commutativity either to split distinct weights or to put equal weights in this form.

Two dual-number forms are isomorphic exactly when their a-tuples agree and their c-tuples differ by a nonzero scalar. This includes c = 0, the repeated split module V<sub>a</sub> ⊕ V<sub>a</sub>. Products of evaluation modules are isomorphic exactly when their two points agree up to exchange; a product at distinct points cannot be a dual-number form. The cards give exhaustiveness and the isomorphism criteria, not merely a list of examples.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwoDimensionalPolynomialModules.finrank_two_linearEquiv_prod_or_dualNumberModule
declarations.label: Every two-dimensional polynomial module has one of the two normal forms
declarations.documentation: A two-dimensional complex module is polynomial-linearly equivalent to a product of distinct evaluation modules or to a dual-number module with parameters a and c.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwoDimensionalPolynomialModules.nonempty_linearEquiv_iff
declarations.label: The exact isomorphism criterion for dual-number forms
declarations.documentation: Two such forms are polynomial-linearly isomorphic exactly when their evaluation parameters agree and their nilpotent parameters differ by a nonzero scalar.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwoDimensionalPolynomialModules.nonempty_prod_evaluationModule_linearEquiv_iff
declarations.label: Evaluation pairs are unordered isomorphism invariants
declarations.documentation: Two products of evaluation modules are isomorphic exactly when their evaluation points agree in the same or reversed order.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.2.title: A countably infinite family already proves the square-zero claim
explanation: The algebra B is the quotient of the free algebra by all relations xᵢxⱼ = 0. On ℂ² let N(z₀, z₁) = (0, z₀), so N² = 0. For each natural number r, let x₁ act by N, x₂ by rN, and the remaining generators by zero. Every required product is zero.

Every nonzero submodule contains the line generated by (0, 1), so two nonzero submodules cannot be complementary: the representation is indecomposable. An isomorphism between the r and s representations must intertwine both N and rN, forcing r = s because N is nonzero. The checked theorem produces this natural-number-indexed family of pairwise nonisomorphic indecomposables for n > 1; a classification of all B-modules is not needed. Lean numbers the generators from zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.PolynomialEvaluationModules.AuxiliaryAlgebra
declarations.label: The free-algebra quotient with all generator products zero
declarations.documentation: The complex algebra generated by Fin n with relations xᵢxⱼ = 0 for every pair of generators.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.PolynomialEvaluationModules.exists_pairwise_nonisomorphic_auxiliaryModules
declarations.label: Infinitely many pairwise nonisomorphic indecomposable representations
declarations.documentation: For n > 1, a natural-number-indexed family of nonzero indecomposable modules over the square-zero-generator algebra, with isomorphism implying equality of indices.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.4.title: Formal series are represented by their coefficients
explanation: A deformation stores k-linear maps ρₙ : A → End<sub>k</sub>(V), with ρ₀ equal to the given action. The product coefficient ρₙ(ab) is the sum of ρᵢ(a) ∘ ρⱼ(b) over i + j = n. Each sum is finite, so there is no convergence or analytic assumption.

The equivalence relation records coefficients of b(t) with b₀ = 1 and the coefficientwise identity bρ̃ = ρ̃′b. This is the intertwining form of the book's conjugation equation. The source constructs these coefficients directly; the relation does not store a separate inverse series. The canonical deformation has all positive-degree coefficients zero.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FormalDeformations.FormalRepresentationDeformation
declarations.label: A deformation is a sequence obeying the product convolution law
declarations.documentation: The sequence of k-linear action coefficients, its fixed zeroth term, and the finite convolution identity for every coefficient of a product.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FormalDeformations.AuxiliaryDeformationRel
declarations.label: A formal change of basis with constant term the identity
declarations.documentation: Existence of coefficients bₙ with b₀ = id satisfying bρ̃ = ρ̃′b coefficient by coefficient.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.4.title: Vanishing Ext¹ removes the obstruction at every order
explanation: The hypothesis Subsingleton for the cocycle quotient means Ext¹(V, V) = 0. After constructing the first n coefficients of b(t), the proof shows that the next error term is a cocycle. Vanishing Ext¹ makes it a coboundary dX, and choosing X supplies the next coefficient of b(t). Strong induction verifies the intertwining equation at every order.

Thus every formal deformation is equivalent to the constant action. The theorem works over any field and does not require V to be finite-dimensional, simple, or A to be finite-dimensional. The checked conclusion uses the coefficientwise relation just described.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FormalDeformations.auxiliaryDeformationProperty_of_auxiliaryType_subsingleton
declarations.label: Ext¹(V, V) = 0 implies formal rigidity
declarations.documentation: If the self-extension cocycle quotient is zero, every formal representation deformation admits a coefficientwise intertwiner to the canonical deformation with constant coefficient id.

Chapter3/Problem3.9.4.title: The converse fails: a first-order cocycle need not extend to a formal deformation
explanation: Take V = k with the dual-number generator ε acting by zero. In a formal deformation on this one-dimensional space, ε must act by a scalar series u(t) satisfying u(t)² = 0. The power-series ring over a field has no zero divisors, so u(t) = 0. The source proves more than equivalence: every deformation equals the constant one.

Yet f(a + bε) = b · id is a nonzero self-extension cocycle, and every coboundary is zero because the original action is scalar. Hence its Ext¹ class is nonzero. Both halves of this counterexample are checked in the source and linked below, over any field. This separates formal rigidity from vanishing of all first-order extension classes.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FormalDeformations.eq_canonicalDeformation_dualNumber
links.label: Checked proof that every deformation of this dual-number module is constant

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FormalDeformations.auxiliaryType_not_subsingleton_dualNumber
links.label: Checked proof that its self-extension space is nonzero

Chapter3/Theorem3.8.1.title: An internal direct sum, unique up to matching isomorphic summands
explanation: Lean chooses finitely many nonzero indecomposable submodules W : Fin n → Submodule A V. The condition iSup W = ⊤ says they span V; iSupIndep W says each has zero intersection with the sum of the others. Together these express an internal direct sum, not just pairwise disjointness.

For two such decompositions, the uniqueness theorem gives equal numbers of summands and a bijection of their index sets with an A-linear equivalence on every matched pair. It does not make the chosen submodules literally equal or select a canonical decomposition. Both statements work over any field, without finite dimension of A. The zero representation has the empty decomposition.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.IndependentSpanningFamilies.exists_iSupIndep_eq_top
declarations.label: Existence of a finite internal sum of indecomposable submodules
declarations.documentation: A finite-dimensional representation over any field admits an independent spanning family of nonzero indecomposable submodules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.IndependentSpanningFamilies.eq_card_and_exists_equiv_of_iSupIndep
declarations.label: Equal numbers of summands and matching A-linear isomorphisms
declarations.documentation: Two finite internal decompositions into nonzero indecomposable submodules have the same number of summands, with corresponding summands isomorphic after a bijection of indices.

Chapter3/Lemma3.8.2.title: Kernel and range stabilization replaces eigenvalues
explanation: The formal proof does not assume algebraic closedness. Finite dimension makes the ascending kernels and descending ranges of powers of θ stabilize. Fitting's decomposition makes their stable values complementary A-submodules of W. Indecomposability forces one to vanish.

If the stable kernel is zero, θ is injective and hence bijective by finite dimension. If the stable range is zero, a sufficiently high power of θ is zero. Thus the checked conclusion is Function.Bijective θ ∨ IsNilpotent θ, over any field. Bijectivity of an A-linear map supplies an A-linear inverse.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.EndomorphismDichotomy.bijective_or_nilpotent_of_auxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: An endomorphism of a finite-dimensional indecomposable is bijective or nilpotent
declarations.documentation: For a nonzero indecomposable finite-dimensional representation over any field, each intertwining endomorphism is either bijective or has a zero power.

links.name: LinearMap.isCompl_iSup_ker_pow_iInf_range_pow
links.label: The Fitting decomposition used in the source proof

Chapter3/Lemma3.8.2.title: The nilpotent-sum result depends on indecomposability
explanation: A finite sum of nilpotent endomorphisms of this W is nilpotent; the summands need not commute. This is not a general assertion about nilpotent matrices. The proof uses the bijective-or-nilpotent alternative for every endomorphism of W.

If the sum were invertible, multiplying by its inverse would express 1 as the sum of two nilpotent endomorphisms, using induction for the remaining terms. But 1 minus a nilpotent is a unit, contradicting nilpotence of the other term. The source checks that the normalized terms are nilpotent through the same dichotomy; it does not assume that multiplying an arbitrary nilpotent by a unit preserves nilpotence.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.EndomorphismDichotomy.sum_nilpotent_of_auxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: Finite sums of nilpotent endomorphisms remain nilpotent on this indecomposable
declarations.documentation: For a nonzero indecomposable finite-dimensional representation, any finite sum of nilpotent A-linear endomorphisms is nilpotent, without a commutativity hypothesis.

Chapter3/Lemma3.8.2.title: An identity sum finds a matching summand
explanation: The uniqueness proof constructs the inclusion/projection composites from the two internal decompositions and verifies that their sum is the identity on the first summand. They cannot all be nilpotent: their sum would then be nilpotent, whereas the identity on a nonzero module is not. The dichotomy therefore makes one composite invertible.

The source helper then proves that the maps between the selected summands are isomorphisms and that the selected summand of the second decomposition complements the remaining summands of the first. This is the step needed to continue the induction, not merely a count of dimensions.

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.IndependentSpanningFamilies.eq_card_and_exists_equiv_of_iSupIndep
links.label: Inspect the uniqueness proof and its summand-matching helper

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.8..title: The source compares complements through a common quotient
explanation: After matching a summand, the source proves that both remaining sums complement that same selected submodule. Each complement is A-linearly isomorphic to the quotient by the common submodule, so composing these quotient equivalences identifies the two remaining sums.

It transports one remaining decomposition across that equivalence and applies induction in strictly smaller dimension, then extends the matching by the already chosen summand. This verifies the same uniqueness conclusion as the book, but uses common-complement quotient equivalences rather than the particular projection map h in the preceding paragraph.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.IndependentSpanningFamilies.eq_card_and_exists_equiv_of_iSupIndep
declarations.label: The completed Krull–Schmidt uniqueness proof
declarations.documentation: The two indecomposable internal decompositions have equal cardinality and A-linearly isomorphic summands after a bijection of their finite index sets.

Chapter3/Problem3.8.3.title: The checked results already allow an arbitrary field
explanation: The proofs available here use Fitting's kernel/range decomposition, not generalized eigenspaces. Their assumptions say [Field k], with no [IsAlgClosed k]. The endomorphism dichotomy, finite-sum lemma, decomposition existence and Krull–Schmidt uniqueness therefore apply to the field requested in this problem.

The statements below are exported versions of the same results used in the preceding theorem and lemma. Indecomposability includes that the module is nonzero; existence still allows the empty decomposition for the zero module.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FiniteDecompositions.bijective_or_nilpotent_of_auxiliaryProperty
declarations.label: The endomorphism dichotomy over any field
declarations.documentation: Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional indecomposable representation is bijective or nilpotent, without algebraic closedness.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FiniteDecompositions.internal_families_equal_length_and_corresponding_equiv
declarations.label: Krull–Schmidt uniqueness over any field
declarations.documentation: Finite internal decompositions into nonzero indecomposables have equal cardinality and matching isomorphic summands over an arbitrary field.

Chapter3/Problem3.8.4.title: An isomorphism after scalar extension descends
explanation: Lean writes the extended module as L ⊗[K] V and the acting algebra as L ⊗[K] A, reversing the factor order used in the book. The hypothesis is a linear equivalence over that extended algebra, not merely an isomorphism of L-vector spaces.

The conclusion is existence of an A-linear equivalence V ≃ₗ[A] W. V and W must be finite-dimensional over K, but neither finite dimension of A nor finite degree of L/K is assumed in this theorem. No algebraic-closedness hypothesis is used.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorEquivDescent.exists_equiv_of_tensorEquiv
declarations.label: Scalar extension reflects isomorphisms of finite-dimensional representations

Chapter3/Problem3.8.4.title: The finite-extension step uses a residue field
explanation: The proof first collects the finitely many matrix coefficients of an isomorphism and its inverse in a finitely generated K-subalgebra R of L. It then specializes the maps to R/m for a maximal ideal m. This residue field is a finite extension of K; it need not be a subfield of L.

Choosing a basis of that finite extension identifies its scalar-extended module, after restriction to A, with Fin n → V, where n is the positive extension degree. Krull–Schmidt compares the multiplicities of indecomposable summands in n copies of V and W and cancels n as a natural-number count. This works in positive characteristic too: it does not divide by the image of n in K.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorProductCoordinates.nonempty_linearEquiv_fin_fun
declarations.label: Restriction of scalars gives n copies of the original module

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.EquivalenceTransfers.exists_equiv_of_fin_fun_equiv
declarations.label: An isomorphism of n copies descends when n is positive

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FinitelyGeneratedSubalgebraDescent.exists_fgSubalgebra_equiv
links.label: The finite-coefficient subalgebra reduction

Chapter3/Problem3.8.4.title: A direct summand is expressed by inclusion and retraction maps
explanation: The formal hypothesis supplies extended-algebra-linear maps i and p with p.comp i = LinearMap.id. The conclusion supplies A-linear maps with the same identity before extension. This says V is a direct summand of W, with W decomposing into the image of i and the kernel of p; it is stronger than the existence of an injection alone.

The proof again reduces the finite coefficients to a finitely generated subalgebra, specializes to a finite residue-field extension, and cancels repeated indecomposable summands. The original L/K may have arbitrary degree.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TensorSplitDescent.exists_retract_of_tensorRetract
declarations.label: A split inclusion after scalar extension descends to a split inclusion

Chapter3/Problem3.8.5.title: Connectedness rules out nontrivial projections
explanation: The source defines exactly the book's algebra A of continuous 1-periodic real functions and its module M of continuous 1-antiperiodic functions, with pointwise multiplication as the action. An idempotent continuous real function takes only the values 0 and 1. Connectedness of ℝ forces it to be constant, so A has no nontrivial idempotents and its regular module is indecomposable.

For M, set c(x) = cos(πx) and s(x) = sin(πx). These belong to M and satisfy c² + s² = 1. They generate M over A, since f = (cf)c + (sf)s. The proof uses this formula to show that any A-linear projection on M is multiplication by an idempotent in A, hence is zero or the identity. Both indecomposability statements include nonzero modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.ContinuousMap.StableModuleEquivalence.auxiliaryProperty_auxiliaryFunctionAlgebra
declarations.label: The periodic-function algebra is indecomposable as its regular module
declarations.documentation: The regular module of the real algebra of continuous 1-periodic functions is nonzero and indecomposable.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.ContinuousMap.StableModuleEquivalence.auxiliaryProperty_auxiliaryFunctionModule
declarations.label: The antiperiodic-function module is indecomposable
declarations.documentation: Continuous real 1-antiperiodic functions form a nonzero indecomposable module over the periodic-function algebra.

Chapter3/Problem3.8.5.title: An antiperiodic function cannot generate M
explanation: An A-linear isomorphism A → M would send 1 to a generator u, making every f in M a periodic-function multiple of u. But u(1) = −u(0), so continuity gives a zero x₀ in [0,1]. Every such multiple would vanish at x₀. The antiperiodic function cos(π(x − x₀)) has value 1 there, a contradiction. The checked proposition excludes any A-linear equivalence, not just a chosen candidate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.ContinuousMap.StableModuleEquivalence.isEmpty_linearEquiv_auxiliaryFunctionModule
declarations.label: There is no A-linear isomorphism between A and M
declarations.documentation: The regular periodic-function module is not isomorphic to the antiperiodic-function module.

Chapter3/Problem3.8.5.title: A sine/cosine matrix identifies the doubled modules
explanation: With c(x) = cos(πx) and s(x) = sin(πx), the forward map sends (p,q) in A × A to (pc + qs, −ps + qc) in M × M. Its inverse sends (f,g) to (cf − sg, sf + cg). Products of two antiperiodic functions are periodic, so the inverse lands in A × A.

The source checks A-linearity and both inverse equations using c² + s² = 1. Binary products here represent binary direct sums. Thus A ⊕ A and M ⊕ M have different indecomposable summand types despite being isomorphic: finite-dimensional Krull–Schmidt uniqueness cannot be extended to arbitrary modules.

Chapter3/Remark3.8.6.title: Finite module length is the general hypothesis
explanation: The checked existence and uniqueness statements assume [IsNoetherian A V] and [IsArtinian A V]. Together these are equivalent to finite module length: ascending and descending submodule chains both terminate, and there is a finite bound on the lengths of strict chains. There is no base field or vector-space dimension in these statements.

The proof uses Fitting decomposition for endomorphisms and induction on Module.length A V in place of induction on vector-space dimension. It again returns a finite internal sum of nonzero indecomposables and a bijection matching the summands of any two such decompositions. Infinite vector-space dimension alone does not force failure; the preceding example shows why an unrestricted statement is false.

declarations.label: Krull–Schmidt uniqueness for modules of finite length

Chapter3/Introduction_to_3.6.title: A character is the trace of the action
explanation: The action homomorphism sends a to its linear operator on V; composing with LinearMap.trace k V gives the character. Lean stores this linear function as Module.Dual k A, meaning A →ₗ[k] k. The construction also works for a finite free module over a commutative base ring, without requiring A to be finite-dimensional.

Chapter3/Introduction_to_3.6.title: The commutator quotient is a vector-space quotient
explanation: Cyclic invariance of trace gives χ(xy) = χ(yx), so the character vanishes on the linear span of all xy − yx. That span is recorded as a Submodule k A, not a two-sided ideal. Consequently A/[A,A] here is a quotient vector space; the construction does not give it an algebra multiplication.
The descended map is well-defined because this subspace lies in the character's kernel. Evaluating it on the class of a recovers χ(a).

Chapter3/Exercise3.6.1.title: Additivity does not require a split representation
explanation: The checked equality is between linear functions on A: the character of V is the sum of those of W and V/W. It holds over any field, in every characteristic, without semisimplicity or finite dimension of A.

The proof chooses a k-linear section of the quotient map, not an A-linear section. This supplies vector-space coordinates in which each action is block triangular; trace sees only the two diagonal blocks. In the source, the same computation uses inclusion, quotient and projection maps together with cyclic invariance of trace. It does not assert that V is the direct sum of W and V/W as representations.

Chapter3/Theorem3.6.2.title: Independence holds in positive characteristic too
explanation: Lean assumes an algebraically closed field and a finite family of finite-dimensional, pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules. It does not assume that A is finite-dimensional or that the field has characteristic zero. Checking every finite subfamily gives the usual independence assertion for all irreducible characters.

Joint density lets the proof prescribe a rank-one operator of trace 1 on one module and the zero operator on all the others. Evaluating a character relation on the realizing algebra element isolates one coefficient. Using a rank-one operator rather than the identity avoids division by the module's dimension, which could vanish in the field.

Chapter3/Theorem3.6.2.title: Traceless matrices are spanned by commutators over any commutative ring
explanation: The checked matrix identity is stronger than the field case used here: it holds over any commutative ring and for any finite matrix index type, including the empty type. The reverse inclusion expresses a traceless matrix using off-diagonal matrix units and differences of diagonal matrix units. Each is a commutator; the trace-zero equation removes the remaining diagonal correction. No division by d is used, even when d vanishes in the base ring.

Chapter3/Theorem3.6.2.title: How the checked statements express the basis conclusion
explanation: A linear functional on A descends to A/[A,A] exactly when f(ab) = f(ba) for every a and b. For a complete, pairwise nonisomorphic finite family of simple modules of a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra, the theorem below proves that every such functional is in the span of their characters. Together with independence and the quotient construction above, this supplies the basis assertion. The source states these ingredients separately, rather than packaging them as a Basis object on the quotient dual.

The spanning proof identifies A with the product of its simple-module endomorphism algebras using density and radical zero. It then uses matrix units to show that a functional with f(ab) = f(ba) on each block is a scalar multiple of trace. Algebraic closedness is needed for these full k-endomorphism blocks; characteristic zero is not.

declarations.label: Every functional vanishing on commutators is a linear combination of simple characters

Chapter3/Theorem3.7.1.title: A bijection matches the simple quotient modules
explanation: A CompositionSeries (Submodule A V) is a finite chain whose adjacent steps are maximal inclusions. For submodules, that says each successive quotient is simple. The endpoint hypotheses require the chain to run from zero to all of V.

The checked result gives a bijection Fin s₁.length ≃ Fin s₂.length and an A-linear equivalence between each pair of matched quotient modules. A companion theorem gives equality of the lengths. This is the permutation conclusion, not an assertion that the factors occur in the same order.

The proof uses Mathlib's general Jordan–Hölder theorem for the submodule lattice, with quotient-module isomorphisms supplied by the second isomorphism theorem. It works over any ring once the two full composition series are given. Finite dimension guarantees existence in the book's setting, but is not needed for this comparison of existing series.

Chapter3/Theorem3.7.1.title: Characters detect multiplicities only modulo the characteristic
explanation: Additivity and independence are checked separately. In characteristic zero, equality of character sums recovers the natural-number multiplicities because their images in k are distinct. In characteristic p > 0, the same argument recovers those multiplicities only modulo p; this does not contradict independence of the distinct simple characters.

The footnote's example is also checked: Fin p → V, with its componentwise action, represents p copies of V. Its character is p times χ_V and is therefore zero in characteristic p. More generally the source proves χ_(nV) = nχ_V for finite free modules over a commutative base ring. The main Jordan–Hölder result above uses the general lattice proof, not a separately formalized version of the entire character argument.
