Chapter3/Discussion_after_Theorem3.7.1.title: Length counts factors, not vector-space dimension
explanation: A chain V₀ ⊊ ⋯ ⊊ Vₙ has n steps and n successive factors, although it lists n + 1 submodules. Lean's series length counts those steps. The theorem below shows that a full composition series attains the greatest length among all finite strict submodule chains, not just among other composition series.

Mathlib's Module.length A V takes values in ℕ∞ to allow modules of infinite length. For a full composition series it equals the finite number of factors. This is not generally Module.finrank k V: a simple factor can have dimension greater than one. The factor order depends on the series; Jordan–Hölder makes the factors with their multiplicities invariant.

Chapter3/Definition3.5.1.title: The radical is the common annihilator of all simple modules
explanation: Lean identifies the book's radical with Ideal.jacobson ⊥, the Jacobson radical of A. The checked equivalence says that a belongs to it exactly when a • v = 0 for every vector in every simple A-module. This characterization works for any unital ring; finite-dimensionality and algebraic closedness are not needed here.

The converse tests quotient modules A/I for maximal left ideals I. The displayed quantifier uses modules at A's type-size level, which already includes these quotients; a separate forward lemma proves annihilation of simple modules at any type size. This is not the set of individually nilpotent elements: a nonzero nilpotent matrix can still act nontrivially on the simple column module.

Chapter3/Proposition3.5.2.title: Both left and right multiplication preserve the radical
explanation: For a ∈ Ideal.jacobson ⊥ and any r, the checked conclusion includes both r * a ∈ Ideal.jacobson ⊥ and a * r ∈ Ideal.jacobson ⊥. Lean's Ideal A is a left-ideal type even for a noncommutative ring, so IsTwoSided supplies the extra right-multiplication closure. Neither finite dimension nor a field is required.

Chapter3/Proposition3.5.3.title: A nilpotent ideal lies in the radical without a dimension hypothesis
explanation: The hypothesis IsNilpotent I means that one power of the entire ideal is zero, not merely that selected elements are nilpotent. Lean proves containment for a left ideal in any ring, hence in particular for the book's two-sided ideal. Its proof uses the Jacobson membership criterion: y·x lies in I and is nilpotent, so 1+y·x is a unit. This replaces the book's argument through a simple module.

Chapter3/Proposition3.5.3.title: Finite dimension supplies nilpotence of the radical itself
explanation: A finite-dimensional algebra over any field is Artinian as a ring. Lean applies the general theorem that an Artinian ring's Jacobson radical is nilpotent, rather than constructing the regular-module filtration displayed below. Together with the preceding containment, this proves that the radical is the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal. The checked statement gives some vanishing power; it does not specify the filtration length as an exponent.

Chapter3/Theorem3.5.4.title: Simplicity makes one nonzero vector a cyclic generator
explanation: The A-linear map a ↦ a • v is surjective for any nonzero vector v in a simple module. Restricting scalars makes V a k-linear quotient of A, so finite-dimensional A forces finite-dimensional V. This first step works over any field and does not assume V finite-dimensional in advance.

Chapter3/Theorem3.5.4.title: A bounded family of simple quotients gives a complete finite list
explanation: Density bounds the size of any finite family of pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules by finrank k A. Lean then chooses a largest such family among quotients A/M, where M is a maximal proper submodule of the regular module. A missing simple type would enlarge it, contradicting the bound. Every simple module is isomorphic to one of these quotients, so the list is complete without forming a collection of all possible module types.

The finite list is a choice of representatives up to A-linear isomorphism, not a canonical list or an algorithm for finding them. This density argument uses the section's algebraically closed base field.

Chapter3/Theorem3.5.4.title: The joint action has kernel Rad(A), giving an algebra equivalence
explanation: For a complete finite family Vᵢ, the checked map A →ₐ[k] (∀ i, Module.End k (V i)) is surjective by density. Its kernel is the radical: elements killing every listed simple kill every simple quotient A/M, and testing the class of 1 puts them in every maximal left ideal. The first isomorphism theorem then gives a k-algebra equivalence, preserving multiplication as well as the vector-space structure.

Completeness and pairwise nonisomorphism are explicit hypotheses of the displayed quotient theorem; the finite-family result above supplies them. The finite product is the book's finite direct sum. Algebraic closedness matters for these full k-endomorphism blocks; over a general field the structure theorem uses division-algebra blocks instead.

Chapter3/Corollary3.5.5.title: The inequality works for any finite selection of distinct simple types
explanation: Lean proves ∑ i, (finrank k (V i))² ≤ finrank k A for any finite pairwise nonisomorphic family; it need not already exhaust all simples. Joint density makes the product of the Endₖ(Vᵢ) a quotient of A, and each block has dimension (dim Vᵢ)².

For a complete family, the quotient equivalence above and the submodule dimension formula give the sharper identity ∑ᵢ (dim Vᵢ)² + dim Rad(A) = dim A. Its equality case is therefore Rad(A)=0, as used in Proposition 3.5.8. These dimension formulas retain the algebraically closed field hypothesis.

Lean proves that this ideal is the Jacobson radical and that every simple module is isomorphic to the one-dimensional residue-field module, on which x acts by zero. No algebraic closedness is needed.
The hypothesis 0 < n is essential: for n=0 the quotient is the zero algebra and has no nonzero simple module. The theorem's explicit positive-exponent assumption makes this convention visible.

Chapter3/Example3.5.6.title: Diagonal characters distinguish the simple triangular-matrix modules
explanation: Lean's matrix subalgebra consists of matrices with M i j = 0 when j<i. Its radical consists of those also zero on the diagonal. Each simple module is a copy of k with M • v = M i i * v at one index i; different indices give nonisomorphic modules. The classification covers all simple modules, without assuming their dimension in advance, and works over any field.

The diagonal matrix units are not central in the triangular algebra. Their commutators lie in the radical, which kills a simple module, so their actions become A-linear projections there. This explains the step that isolates a single diagonal character. The radical computation also checks that every strictly upper-triangular matrix has nth power zero; the n=0 algebra has no simple modules.

Chapter3/Definition3.5.7.title: Rad(A)=0 agrees with semisimplicity of the regular module
explanation: The book's predicate is encoded as simpleModuleAnnihilator A = ⊥. For a finite-dimensional algebra, Lean proves it equivalent to IsSemisimpleRing A, meaning that A is semisimple as its own left module. This bridge works over any field; algebraic closedness is needed only for the later classification by matrix algebras over k.

Finite-dimensionality matters to this equivalence: radical zero alone does not make an arbitrary ring semisimple. The zero algebra is allowed, as the footnote says; the empty matrix product in the following proposition represents it.

Chapter3/Proposition3.5.8.title: TFAE packages the same five equivalent conditions
explanation: The checked conclusion is a five-element list followed by .TFAE: all five statements are equivalent. They are radical zero, equality in the sum-of-squares formula, a k-algebra equivalence with a finite matrix product, semisimplicity of every finite-dimensional module, and semisimplicity of the left regular module. The supplied Vᵢ must form a complete finite family of pairwise nonisomorphic simples; positive block sizes are required, but the family may be empty.

The proof establishes the dimension equivalence through A/Rad(A), invokes Mathlib's Wedderburn–Artin theorem over the algebraically closed field for the matrix-product condition, and uses the ring/module semisimplicity bridge for complete reducibility. Thus it verifies the book's five conclusions without claiming to follow every displayed implication in the same order.

explanation: A subsingleton ring is semisimple, but not simple. Every unital module over it is zero and hence is not a simple module; it is not indecomposable either, since indecomposability requires nonzero. Lean supplies an algebra equivalence with the product indexed by Fin 0. Its lack of factors, rather than a positive-size matrix block, is what models the zero algebra.

Chapter3/Corollary3.2.1.title: One algebra element can prescribe several images at once
explanation: The input v : Fin n → V is any finite k-linearly independent family, not necessarily a basis of V. The target family w is arbitrary. Lean supplies a single a with a • v i = w i at every index. As in the book, V must be finite-dimensional and simple, and k algebraically closed; A itself need not be finite-dimensional.

The checked proof takes a different route from the displayed matrix argument: define a linear map on the span of the vᵢ, extend it to V, and apply the already-proved surjectivity of the algebra action. The density theorem below is established from Mathlib's general Jacobson density theorem, so this order does not use the corollary circularly.

Chapter3/Theorem3.2.2.title: Density here means surjectivity onto all k-linear operators
explanation: The map Algebra.lsmul k k V : A →ₐ[k] Module.End k V sends a to its action on V. Its surjectivity says that every k-linear endomorphism of V equals the action of some a. This is not a topological approximation statement, and it does not say the action is injective: different algebra elements can act identically.

Lean specializes the general Jacobson density theorem. That theorem describes operators commuting with Endₐ(V). Schur's lemma identifies Endₐ(V) with scalar operators in the present finite-dimensional, algebraically closed setting, so every k-linear operator is in that double commutant. Finite generation over the endomorphism ring then gives surjectivity on all of V. These hypotheses explain why the finite-dimensional conclusion is stronger than agreement on a finite set of vectors.

Chapter3/Theorem3.2.2.title: Pairwise nonisomorphic simples allow independent choices in every block
explanation: For a finite family Vᵢ, the target is ∀ i, Module.End k (V i), the product of the endomorphism algebras. Lean proves that one a realizes any family of operators chosen independently in these blocks. Finite products and finite direct sums agree here, as the footnote explains; this theorem is not a surjectivity claim for an infinite product.

The proof shows that A-linear maps on the sum have no off-diagonal components between nonisomorphic simples, and each diagonal component is scalar. A chosen blockwise k-linear operator therefore commutes with every A-linear endomorphism, and general density supplies a. If a simple type were repeated, intertwiners between its copies would impose compatibility; independent operators on those copies would not be arbitrary.

Chapter3/Introduction_to_3.3.title: A finite product of matrix algebras records the blocks separately
explanation: The Lean type MatrixProductAlgebra k d is ∀ i : Fin r, Matrix (Fin (d i)) (Fin (d i)) k. Addition and multiplication are componentwise. It represents the book's finite direct sum of matrix algebras; no algebraic closedness is required in this section.

The classification uses NeZero (d i) to require positive block sizes. A zero-size matrix block contributes no nonzero column module and can be omitted. The index family itself may be empty; then the algebra and its unital modules are trivial.

declarations.label: The product algebra with the stated matrix block sizes

Chapter3/Theorem3.3.1.title: A simple module is the column space of exactly one block
explanation: The i-th column module is Fin (d i) → k, with a • v = a i • v: only the i-th matrix block acts. Lean proves these modules simple and every finite-dimensional simple module is A-linearly isomorphic to one of them, over any field k.

Even when dᵢ=dⱼ, the modules for different blocks are not isomorphic as A-modules. The central idempotent eᵢ acts as the identity on the i-th column module and zero on the j-th, so an intertwining equivalence would force a nonzero vector to vanish. Thus the index, not just the vector-space dimension, distinguishes the simple types.

Chapter3/Theorem3.3.1.title: Every finite-dimensional module splits into finitely many column modules
explanation: The checked conclusion supplies multiplicities m : Fin r → ℕ and an A-linear equivalence X ≃ ⊕ᵢ (Fin (m i) → (Fin (d i) → k)). This is a decomposition up to isomorphism, not a distinguished choice of submodules or bases in X. The proof follows the dual-embedding argument in the later proof paragraph and then applies the submodule classification from Section 3.1.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.FiniteFamilySemisimplicity.exists_linearEquiv_directSum_columnModules
declarations.label: The column-module decomposition with finite multiplicities

Chapter3/Definition3.3.2.title: Precomposition makes the linear dual a right A-module
explanation: A functional is an element of Module.Dual k V. For a : Aᵐᵒᵖ, Lean defines (a • f)(v)=f(a.unop • v). This is the book's right action (f · a)(v)=f(av), expressed as a left action of the opposite ring. Reversing multiplication is what makes the module law hold.

This construction works over a commutative base ring, without finite-dimensionality. It requires the A-action to commute with k-scalars so that precomposition preserves k-linearity. There is no inverse, transpose or minus sign in this definition; transpose enters the matrix-algebra proof only when identifying A with its opposite.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.3..title: Transpose identifies A with its opposite and twists the dual action
explanation: Blockwise transpose gives A ≃+* Aᵐᵒᵖ, since it reverses matrix multiplication. Transporting the opposite-ring action along this equivalence makes X* a left A-module with (a • f)(x)=f(aᵀ • x), where transpose is applied in every block. This is the action used throughout the dual proof, not the original action on X.

The transpose map also respects k-scalars, so the transported action is compatible with the vector-space structure. Transposing twice is the identity, which makes the usual finite-dimensional evaluation map X→X** A-linear.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.3..title: The missing identification A* ≃ A is a matrix-entry pairing
explanation: The checked map sends a to the functional x ↦ ∑ᵢ trace((a i)ᵀ * x i). Testing against matrix units recovers every entry of a, proving injectivity; equal finite dimensions give surjectivity. With the transpose-twisted dual action above, it is an A-linear equivalence between the regular module A and A*.

This is a bilinear matrix-entry pairing, not a Hermitian pairing: it uses no complex conjugation and works over any field. The corresponding finite-product dual equivalence supplies the step (Aⁿ)* ≃ Aⁿ in the book.

Chapter3/Discussion_proof_of_Theorem3.3..title: Reading matrix columns gives the multiplicities in A and Aⁿ
explanation: Each dᵢ×dᵢ matrix has dᵢ columns, and left multiplication acts on each column separately. The checked equivalence reads M i j c as entry j of column c in block i. Thus the regular module contains dᵢ copies of the i-th column module, and Aⁿ contains n·dᵢ copies.

The full proof maps Aⁿ onto X* using a basis, dualizes to embed X in (Aⁿ)*, uses the self-duality and column equivalences, and classifies the resulting submodule. These are bundled A-linear constructions, so the embedding and decomposition preserve the action, not just dimensions.

Chapter3/Problem3.3.3.title: Central idempotents isolate exactly one factor in a simple module
explanation: Lean represents eᵢ=1ᵢ by Pi.single i 1 and the component eᵢV by the range of the A-linear projection v ↦ eᵢ • v. The eᵢ are orthogonal central idempotents and their finite sum is 1. A simple module therefore has exactly one nonzero component; on it the action factors through Aᵢ, and that component is simple as an Aᵢ-module.

The criterion works for any finite product of rings, without a field or finite-dimensionality assumption. Conversely, a simple module for one factor becomes a simple product-ring module by letting the other factors act as zero. The accompanying equivalence constructions show that this classification is up to module isomorphism, with the active factor uniquely determined.

Chapter3/Problem3.3.3.title: Matrix units build copies of the standard column module
explanation: Lean uses E₀₀ for the book's E₁₁. A basis of E₀₀V produces an explicit matrix-module map from copies of kᵈ to V: a column w and basis vector v contribute ∑ⱼ wⱼ • (Eⱼ₀ • v). Applying E₀ⱼ proves injectivity from basis independence; the identity ∑ⱼ Eⱼⱼ=1 proves surjectivity. The resulting number of copies is the dimension of E₀₀V, although the theorem's conclusion packages it existentially.

These elementary proofs of (a) and (b) do not use Proposition 3.1.4. The matrix result assumes d>0 and finite-dimensional V, over any field. For (c), the product-algebra classification above is also checked, but its recorded proof uses the dual/submodule route rather than a separately assembled combination of (a) and (b).

Chapter3/Remark3.3.4.title: Basis expansion presents X as a quotient of a finite free module
explanation: For a finite k-basis b of X, basisExpansion A b sends a : ι → A to ∑ᵢ aᵢ • bᵢ. It is A-linear and surjective: choose coefficients by mapping the k-coordinate values of x into A. The formula determines the map uniquely, and the first isomorphism theorem gives Aⁿ/ker ψ ≃ X. These constructions work even over a commutative base ring, whenever a finite basis and compatible actions are supplied.

For the matrix product, the column equivalence supplies the regular-module decomposition used in this paragraph. The final decomposition theorem is checked by the dual route described above; the library supplies the quotient construction here, but does not record a second proof of that theorem using Lemma 3.1.6.

Chapter3/Definition3.4.1.title: A filtration records the submodules, their order, and both endpoints
explanation: The finite-filtration structure stores a RelSeries of A-submodules with strict consecutive inclusions, plus proofs that its first term is ⊥ and its last term ⊤. Those lattice elements mean the zero submodule and all of V. A series of length n has n+1 terms, indexed from 0 through n.

This uses the strict-chain convention: repeated terms are not stored. It does not yet require the successive quotients to be irreducible; that is the additional conclusion of the next lemma. For the zero module, the one-term series has length zero and both endpoints agree.

Chapter3/Lemma3.4.2.title: Finite dimension gives a composition series, without semisimplicity
explanation: Finite-dimensional V is both Noetherian and Artinian over k, and these properties pass to its A-submodules through the compatible scalar action. Lean obtains a finite chain of invariant subspaces in which no intermediate submodule can be inserted. Each such maximal step has a simple quotient, giving the requested filtration over any field.

The quotient expression in the statement pulls Vᵢ₋₁ back along the inclusion of Vᵢ before forming the quotient, so both submodules live in the same ambient type. This is the Lean encoding of Vᵢ/Vᵢ₋₁. The proof uses the general finite-length construction rather than the book's induction on dimension; it makes no claim that the filtration splits or that V is a direct sum of its factors.

Chapter3/Definition3.1.1.title: Direct sums and invariant complements express the same condition
explanation: Lean uses IsSemisimpleModule A V: every A-submodule of V has an A-submodule complement. Mathlib proves this equivalent to a direct sum of simple modules, which is the definition in the book. The notation Π₀ in that equivalence means finitely supported families: an algebraic direct sum, not an unrestricted product.

The definition works over any ring and allows infinitely many summands. It does not need the algebraically closed field assumed at the start of this section. The zero module is semisimple, as the empty direct sum; simple modules themselves must be nonzero.

Chapter3/Example3.1.2.title: Evaluate k-linear operators on a basis—not A-linear endomorphisms
explanation: Here Module.End k V contains all k-linear maps V→V, not just the maps commuting with A. The A-action is (a • f)(v)=a • f(v): postcomposition by the action of a, not conjugation. Evaluation at the basis vectors gives the checked A-linear equivalence Endₖ(V) ≃ (ι → V).

For a finite basis, ι → V is a direct sum of copies of V. The equivalence needs no irreducibility or algebraic closedness; irreducibility is used only to deduce that this sum, and hence Endₖ(V), is semisimple. With ι=Fin (finrank k V), the number of copies is the dimension n. This identification depends on the chosen basis.

Chapter3/Remark3.1.3.title: Evaluation assembles the multiplicity spaces without choosing bases
explanation: The multiplicity space of a simple X in V is X →ₗ[A] V. Evaluation sends g ⊗ x to g(x). Over an algebraically closed field, Schur's lemma makes Endₐ(X) consist of scalars, so this evaluation is an isomorphism on a simple summand and then on a finite-dimensional semisimple V.

The checked construction chooses a finite family X i of pairwise nonisomorphic finite-dimensional simples. Its completeness hypothesis says that every simple submodule of V is isomorphic to one of them. Only the constituents of V are needed: the other simple types in the book's sum have zero multiplicity. Once these representatives are fixed, evaluation is canonical and involves no choice of bases.

The bundled equivalence below has type ≃ₗ[k], a k-linear equivalence. The evaluation formula is compatible with the A-action on the X factor, but this declaration does not package the result as an A-linear equivalence. The notation should not be read as claiming that stronger bundled type.

Chapter3/Proposition3.1.4.title: Submodules cannot introduce new simple types or increase multiplicities
explanation: The family V i consists of pairwise nonisomorphic simple A-modules. A block Fin (n i) → V i stores nᵢ copies of Vᵢ. For any A-submodule W of their finite direct sum, Lean supplies numbers rᵢ≤nᵢ and an A-linear equivalence from W to the sum with those smaller multiplicities.

This theorem works for any ring A: neither a base field nor finite-dimensionality of the simple modules is assumed. The proof separates the simple types into isotypic components and uses module length to bound the multiplicities. Thus it proves the book's decomposition and also the broader setting of the next remark, rather than following the displayed induction word for word.

Chapter3/Proposition3.1.4.title: The inclusion matrices are checked over endomorphism division rings
explanation: The coordinate theorem also describes the original inclusion of W. Its matrix entry X i a l lies in Module.End A (V i), and the l-th output coordinate is ∑ a, X i a l (e w i a). Rows are right-linearly independent over that endomorphism ring; Lean writes this as linear independence over its opposite ring.

For the finite-dimensional simples over the algebraically closed k in the book, Schur's lemma identifies each entry with scalar multiplication. Substituting those scalars gives the book's k-valued matrices. The checked theorem retains endomorphism-valued entries; it does not itself construct scalar matrices. The next remark explains why that generality is useful.

Chapter3/Proposition3.1.4.title: A nonzero finite-dimensional module has a simple submodule
explanation: The checked existence result applies over any field. Finite dimensionality makes the descending chain of invariant subspaces terminate, so a minimal nonzero invariant subspace is simple. The proof uses the corresponding Artinian property and an atom of the submodule lattice. For the infinite-dimensional simple summands allowed in the footnote, the finite-sum semisimple argument supplies the needed simple submodule instead.

Chapter3/Remark3.1.5.title: Over a division ring, composition order matters
explanation: For a simple A-module X, Schur's lemma gives a division ring D=Module.End A X. A map between r and n copies of X is represented by an r×n matrix with entries in D, acting by (φ v)ⱼ=∑ᵢ Xᵢⱼ(vᵢ). The checked correspondence is additive; no commutative base field is needed.

The injectivity test is: if ∑ᵢ Xᵢⱼ ∘ cᵢ=0 for every j, then all cᵢ vanish. The order of composition cannot be reversed when D is noncommutative. This is right-linear independence of the rows over D, expressed in Lean as left-linear independence over Dᵐᵒᵖ.

The block theorem allows arbitrary dimensions of the simple modules, but the family of simple types and each number of copies remain finite. It provides both the bounded multiplicities and injective inclusion maps for W.

Chapter3/Discussion_alternative_proof_of.title: A module map is a family of maps on multiplicity spaces
explanation: Lean takes the multiplicity spaces to be Mᵢ(V)=Homₐ(Xᵢ,V). An A-linear f:V→U induces fᵢ:g ↦ f ∘ g. The checked equivalence says that every family of k-linear maps Mᵢ(V)→Mᵢ(U) arises uniquely this way. Its inverse decomposes V by evaluation, applies fᵢ ⊗ id in each summand, and recombines U; the proof checks that this reconstructed map is A-linear.

Both V and U are assumed finite-dimensional and semisimple over an algebraically closed k. A finite pairwise nonisomorphic family Xᵢ must cover the simple constituents of both modules. These are explicit hypotheses of the equivalence, not assumptions of postcomposition itself.

Chapter3/Discussion_alternative_proof_of.title: Injectivity and surjectivity can be tested one simple type at a time
explanation: After the evaluation identifications, f is a direct sum of fᵢ ⊗ idₓᵢ. Each Xᵢ is nonzero, so tensoring over the field with Xᵢ detects injectivity and surjectivity. The finite direct sum then has either property exactly when all its components do. Lean checks both criteria and combines them into the bijectivity criterion.

Chapter3/Lemma3.1.6.title: Select original simple summands on which the given surjection is an isomorphism
explanation: The f in this lemma is the surjection V→U introduced in the preceding paragraph. Lean models the original summands by an internal family of simple submodules p i. It selects a subset J and an A-linear equivalence from their sum to U whose value at every vector is the original f. This is stronger than merely finding some isomorphic copy of U inside V.

The proof uses Zorn's lemma to choose a maximal selection disjoint from ker f. If it and ker f do not span V, another simple summand can be added without meeting the kernel, a contradiction. Surjectivity then makes the restriction onto U bijective. The construction allows infinitely many original summands and works over any ring; finite-dimensionality and algebraic closedness are not needed.

Chapter3/Discussion_after_Lemma3.1.6.title: The kernel is determined by the multiplicity-space kernels
explanation: Apply the multiplicity construction to the quotient map q:V→V/W. Lemma 3.1.6 supplies semisimplicity of the quotient, and finite-dimensionality passes to it. In evaluation coordinates, q acts in the i-th summand by qᵢ ⊗ idₓᵢ. Lean proves that v lies in ker q exactly when every such component vanishes.

This checked statement is a membership criterion, not a separately bundled equivalence ker q ≃ ⊕ᵢ ker(qᵢ) ⊗ Xᵢ. Together with the evaluation factorization and exactness of tensoring over a field, it gives the kernel description in the book. The inclusion and bounded-multiplicity theorems above provide the full submodule classification independently.

Chapter2/Discussion_after_Theorem2.1.1.title: A quiver representation stores vertex spaces and arrow maps
explanation: A Lean quiver assigns a type of arrows to each ordered pair of vertices. Separate arrows can have the same endpoints, and arrows from a vertex to itself are allowed. A representation then stores one module obj i per vertex and one linear map map h per arrow, in the direction shown in the book. The general structure does not require a finite quiver or finite-dimensional vertex spaces; those restrictions are imposed by later statements.

Chapter2/Discussion_after_Theorem2.1.1.title: Path-algebra modules recover the representation, with an orientation convention
explanation: The correspondence decomposes a module using the vertex idempotents: V=⊕ᵢ pᵢV. In the reverse direction it lets each path act on the direct sum of the vertex spaces by composing the arrow maps. Finite vertices make the sum of the idempotents equal to 1; neither finite-dimensional spaces nor finitely many arrows are required for this construction.

The checked equivalence below uses the reversed-composition path algebra and representations of Qᵒᵖ. With this multiplication, an original arrow i→j acts from pⱼV to pᵢV, hence the opposite quiver. This is the orientation-adjusted version of the book's correspondence, not a reversal of the representation maps defined above. The quotient types identify isomorphic modules and vertexwise-isomorphic representations; the equivalence is between their isomorphism classes.

Chapter2/Discussion_after_Theorem2.1.1.title: Finite type means finitely many isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional indecomposables
explanation: Lean makes the implicit qualifications explicit: for vertices Fin n, there must be a finite list of finite-dimensional indecomposable representations covering every such representation up to vertexwise linear equivalences that commute with the arrows. The definition does not require these listed representatives to be distinct. Indecomposability excludes the zero representation and nontrivial decompositions into two arrow-stable summands.

The finite list is not a list of all concrete types or all choices of matrices. Changing bases produces many descriptions of the same isomorphism class. This definition works over an arbitrary field; the hypotheses needed for Gabriel's classification belong to the next theorem.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryFiniteProperties.AuxiliaryQuiverProperty
declarations.label: A finite list covers the finite-dimensional indecomposable isomorphism classes
declarations.documentation: A finite quiver has finite representation type if a finite list of finite-dimensional indecomposable representations covers all such representations up to isomorphism.

Chapter2/Theorem2.1.1.title: Lie actions and enveloping-algebra actions describe the same representations
explanation: Here Lean uses the complex Lie algebra of traceless 2×2 matrices for sl(2). Its universal enveloping algebra is the basis-independent version of the three-generator algebra U introduced above. The checked equivalence sends a Lie action on V to a unital algebra homomorphism into Module.End ℂ V. It needs no finite-dimensionality assumption. Invariant subspaces and intertwining linear maps are unchanged by this correspondence, so the classification can be proved on the Lie-module side.

Chapter2/Theorem2.1.1.title: There is one irreducible of each positive finite dimension
explanation: The parameter d : ℕ+ excludes dimension zero. Existence is proved using the space Fin d → ℂ; uniqueness says that any two irreducible finite-dimensional complex modules of dimension d admit a linear equivalence commuting with the Lie action. This is an isomorphism classification, not equality of the underlying types, and it makes no assertion about infinite-dimensional irreducibles.

The proof chooses a nonzero highest-weight vector, then shows that its successive images under f form a basis. The highest weight must be d−1. Matching the two lowering bases produces the equivalence used in the uniqueness theorem.

Chapter2/Theorem2.1.1.title: The polynomial model includes all three differential operators
explanation: The basis vector indexed by i : Fin d corresponds to x^(d−1−i)y^i in the degree-(d−1) homogeneous subspace of MvPolynomial (Fin 2) ℂ. On this basis, h acts by d−1−2i, e sends the i-th monomial to i times the preceding one, and f sends it to (d−1−i) times the following one; the endpoint coefficients vanish. These are exactly the three differential formulas in the book.

The checked statement supplies a linear equivalence onto the homogeneous subspace and proves the three operator identities for every vector, by checking the monomial basis. It is not merely a dimension count.

Chapter2/Theorem2.1.1.title: Complete reducibility means every invariant subspace has an invariant complement
explanation: For every finite-dimensional complex sl(2) module, Lean proves that its lattice of invariant subspaces is complemented. Thus each invariant W has an invariant P with W∩P=0 and W+P=V. In finite dimension, splitting off irreducible submodules gives a finite direct sum of irreducibles. The checked lattice statement expresses the splitting property; it does not choose a canonical decomposition.

The accompanying definition of indecomposable requires a nonzero module and says that every such complementary pair has a zero member. Combining it with the complement theorem leaves no proper nonzero invariant subspace, proving part (ii). The finite-dimensional and complex-field hypotheses matter; this is not a complete-reducibility assertion for arbitrary Lie algebras or fields.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.5.title: The quantum algebra is presented over ℂ with the denominator cleared
explanation: The construction specializes the book's field to ℂ. Lean represents the nonzero parameter as q : ℂˣ. Four free generators e, f, K and L are subjected to KL=LK=1, the two weight-commutation relations, and (q−q⁻¹)(ef−fe)=K−L. Thus L is K⁻¹. The quotient is defined for every nonzero q, but it agrees with the book's divided commutator relation only when q²≠1, equivalently q≠±1. That hypothesis appears explicitly wherever division by q−q⁻¹ is needed.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.5.title: Structural results are checked; the exhaustive classification is intentionally omitted
explanation: The results below concern finite-dimensional modules over ℂ. The project intentionally omits the enumeration of all finite-dimensional irreducibles up to isomorphism, in both parameter cases. Highest weights, central scalars and dimension bounds are constraints on that classification, not a substitute for constructing every family and proving its isomorphism criteria. No classification of infinite-dimensional modules is supplied either.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.5.title: When q is not a root of unity, every nonzero finite-dimensional module has a highest-weight vector
explanation: Lean writes this parameter condition as ¬ IsOfFinOrder q. Applying e to a K-eigenvector of eigenvalue λ gives either zero or a vector of eigenvalue q²λ. Since K is invertible, λ≠0; infinite order makes the successive eigenvalues distinct. Finite-dimensionality forces the chain to stop, giving a nonzero vector killed by e. This existence result does not require irreducibility.

For an irreducible module of dimension d, the lowering ladder from such a vector spans the module. Its distinct weights make the nonzero ladder vectors independent, and its final raising coefficient forces λ=ε·q^(d−1) with ε²=1, so ε=±1 over ℂ. The checked theorem asserts existence of this vector and eigenvalue; it does not itself enumerate isomorphism classes.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.5.title: At a root of unity, the central powers control the weight operator
explanation: Let N=orderOf q>0. On a finite-dimensional irreducible, the central elements Kᴺ, eᴺ, fᴺ act by scalars. The K-scalar α is nonzero because K is invertible; the e- and f-scalars may vanish. The e- and f-power statements use q²≠1.

The identity Kᴺ=α·Id makes K satisfy the polynomial Xᴺ−α. Over ℂ this polynomial has distinct roots, so K is diagonalizable, its eigenspaces span V, and every eigenvalue λ satisfies λᴺ=α. The semisimplicity in the checked signature is semisimplicity of the single endomorphism K, not a claim that every module over the quantum algebra is completely reducible.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.5.title: The proved root-of-unity bound is dim V ≤ orderOf q
explanation: The proof separates the cases where eᴺ acts by zero, where fᴺ acts by zero, and where both act by nonzero scalars. In the first two cases it obtains a highest- or lowest-weight vector and an invariant ladder spanned by at most N iterates. In the remaining case it chooses a simultaneous eigenvector for K and fe and builds an invariant cyclic ladder. Irreducibility makes each nonzero invariant span all of V, yielding dim V≤N. This is a bound using the order of q itself; the statement is not an exact dimension formula or an isomorphism classification.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_irreducible_inde.title: Irreducibility rules out every submodule; indecomposability only rules out complementary pairs
explanation: Irreducibility is IsSimpleModule A V: V is nonzero and its submodule lattice has only zero and V. Indecomposability says that V is nonzero and, whenever IsCompl W₁ W₂, at least one submodule is zero. Here IsCompl includes both zero intersection and a sum equal to V. An irreducible module is therefore indecomposable: if one complementary summand is nonzero, it must be all of V, forcing the other to vanish. These definitions and the implication do not require finite-dimensionality.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_irreducible_inde.title: A size-two nilpotent Jordan block gives the converse counterexample
explanation: Let the polynomial variable act on k² by J=[[0,1],[0,0]]. The first coordinate line is a proper nonzero invariant subspace, so this representation of k[x] is not irreducible. But every nonzero invariant subspace contains the first basis vector: restricting the nilpotent operator gives a nonzero kernel vector, and the kernel is that line. Two nonzero invariant subspaces therefore cannot have zero intersection, so there is no nontrivial direct-sum decomposition. The checked counterexample works over every field, not only over ℂ.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_irreducible_inde.title: Solving the generator relations really does produce a representation
explanation: A compatible algebra action gives a homomorphism A →ₐ[k] Module.End k V. For a presented algebra, the checked lift extends proposed generator operators to such a homomorphism when every defining relation evaluates to zero; agreement on generators proves uniqueness. After choosing a basis of V, the endomorphisms become matrices with multiplication by composition. This establishes the reduction to matrix equations, rather than merely declaring that the relations are necessary.

For the three displayed sl(2) relations, the separately checked algebra equivalence identifies their generators-and-relations quotient with the basis-independent enveloping algebra. It sends e, f and h to the images of the corresponding Lie algebra generators.

Chapter2/Example2.2.4.title: These examples use existing algebra constructions
explanation: The scalar algebra is k itself. Polynomials in n commuting variables are MvPolynomial (Fin n) k; a monomial is encoded by its finitely supported exponent function. Endomorphisms form Module.End k V, where multiplication means (f*g)(v)=f(g(v)), with g applied first. The noncommutative free algebra is FreeAlgebra k (Fin n). The group algebra is MonoidAlgebra k G, whose coefficients have finite support even when G is infinite.

Mathlib constructs the free algebra by its universal property and proves an algebra equivalence with the monoid algebra on finite words. Transporting the single-word basis through that equivalence gives the book's word basis. In the group algebra the vector a_g is single g 1; the checked multiplication formula gives a_g*a_h=a_(gh). Neither construction requires a finite index set or a finite group.

Chapter2/Discussion_commutativity_exampl.title: Noncommutativity is witnessed by explicit pairs
explanation: For End(V), the proof chooses two basis vectors and maps one to the other in opposite directions, sending the remaining basis vectors to zero. Their two compositions act differently on the first basis vector. The hypothesis 2 ≤ Module.rank k V uses cardinal dimension, so V need not be finite-dimensional.

For the free algebra on more than one generator, the proof sends two distinct generators to E₀₁ and E₁₀ in 2×2 matrices. Their products are different diagonal matrix units; the free-algebra universal property therefore rules out commutation of those generators. This argument works over any nontrivial commutative ring.

Finally, group-algebra commutativity is equivalent to group commutativity by multiplying the basis vectors single g 1 and single h 1. The checked theorem applies more generally to a monoid over a nontrivial commutative semiring. Nontriviality of the coefficient semiring matters: over the zero semiring the monoid algebra cannot distinguish gh from hg.

Chapter2/Proposition2.2.3.title: Uniqueness does not require a unit to have been chosen
explanation: The hypotheses say that e and e′ each act as an identity on both sides of the same bilinear multiplication. Applying the right-identity property of e′ to e and the left-identity property of e to e′ gives e = e·e′ = e′. No distinguished unit is assumed. The proof only uses these two identity equations, although its ambient structure also includes associativity and bilinearity.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.1.title: A common eigenvector spans an invariant line
explanation: Mathlib supplies a nonzero common weight vector v: every x in the Lie algebra acts as χ(x)·v. The proof constructs the Lie submodule spanned by v. It is nonzero, so irreducibility makes it the whole module; the dimension of the span of one nonzero vector is one. In the checked statement, IsSimpleOrder (LieSubmodule ℂ L V) expresses that the only invariant subspaces are zero and V, while Nontrivial V excludes the zero representation.

The theorem specializes to the book's complex field, but does not assume that the Lie algebra itself is finite-dimensional. Mathlib first reduces the common-eigenvector argument to the finite-dimensional image of the Lie algebra in the module's endomorphisms.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.1.title: Characteristic zero enters through the trace argument
explanation: The underlying common-weight-space proof checks the same key step as the hint: on the finite cyclic subspace generated by x and a weight vector, the trace of the commutator is zero and also equals dim(U)·χ([x,a]). Since U is nonzero, its positive dimension is a nonzero scalar in characteristic zero, forcing χ([x,a])=0. Mathlib organizes the subsequent induction using codimension-one ideals. In characteristic p, the dimension can vanish as a scalar; the next problem gives actual higher-dimensional irreducible counterexamples.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.2.title: In characteristic zero the irreducibles are one-dimensional characters
explanation: The Lie algebra is realized inside 2×2 matrices with X=E₀₀ and Y=E₀₁, so [X,Y]=Y. Its second derived algebra is zero. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, every finite-dimensional irreducible module has X=μ·Id and Y=0, for a unique scalar μ. The character module below is k with that action. Algebraic closedness is an explicit hypothesis of the classification; this is not a classification over every characteristic-zero field.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.2.title: In characteristic p a nonzero cyclic shift gives p-dimensional irreducibles
explanation: Let p be prime and char k=p. For a scalar a and a nonzero scalar γ, the cyclic module has basis eᵢ indexed by i∈ℤ/pℤ, with X eᵢ=(a+i)eᵢ and Y eᵢ=γ eᵢ₊₁. Lean implements vectors as functions ZMod p → k, so the Y-action is (Yv)(i)=γ·v(i−1). The type kˣ records that γ is nonzero. Distinct X-eigenvalues isolate a coordinate of a nonzero invariant vector; repeated Y-actions then generate every basis vector. This proves irreducibility over any field of characteristic p, without algebraic closedness.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.2.title: Exhaustion needs algebraic closedness, and a is determined modulo the prime field
explanation: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, every finite-dimensional irreducible is either one of the one-dimensional characters or one of the cyclic modules. If Y acts nontrivially, its kernel would be an invariant proper subspace, so Y is invertible. The proof shows that Yᵖ is a nonzero scalar, takes its p-th root γ, and builds a cyclic basis from an X-eigenvector.

Two cyclic modules are isomorphic exactly when their γ parameters agree and a′=a+n for some n∈ℤ/pℤ embedded in k. Translating the basis indices gives the equivalence. A cyclic module is never isomorphic to a character module, since their dimensions are p and one. Thus the parameter a is a coset, not a unique scalar.

Chapter2/Problem2.16.2.title: Lie's one-dimensional conclusion fails in positive characteristic
explanation: Taking γ=1 and a=0 gives an irreducible module of dimension p for this solvable Lie algebra. Since p is prime, p>1. The checked theorem packages this as a counterexample over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p; the explicit family's construction and irreducibility proof above need only a field of characteristic p.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: Bilinear maps are curried linear maps, and the lift is an equivalence
explanation: The type V →ₗ[k] W →ₗ[k] U bundles a map linear in each input. The checked equivalence sends such a map f to the unique linear map on V ⊗[k] W with value f v w on v ⊗ₜ[k] w. Its construction uses the tensor product's universal property, with no choice of bases or finite-dimensionality assumptions.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: Pairs of basis indices index the tensor-product basis
explanation: Given bases b and c indexed by ι and κ, the resulting basis is indexed by ι × κ and takes (i,j) to b i ⊗ c j. A bundled Module.Basis certifies both linear independence and spanning. Neither input basis needs to be finite.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: A dual vector and a target vector define a rank-one operator
explanation: The equivalence sends f ⊗ w to the linear map v ↦ f(v) • w. Its finite-dimensionality assumption is on V, the space being dualized; W may be infinite-dimensional. The inverse recovers a finite sum of rank-one operators. The forward map is basis-free, and the result is a linear equivalence, not merely an injection into the linear maps.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: Multisets index symmetric powers; subsets index exterior powers
explanation: The types SymmetricPower k V n and ExteriorPower k V n implement the two quotients stated in the problem. For a chosen basis indexed by I, the symmetric basis is indexed by Sym I n, the multisets of n indices, allowing repetition. After choosing an order on I, the exterior basis is indexed by its n-element subsets and uses increasing indices. The latter quotient is proved equivalent to Mathlib's usual exterior power over every field, including characteristic two.

If dim V = m, the dimensions are (m+n-1).choose n and m.choose n. These formulas are checked without characteristic-zero assumptions. In degree zero both spaces have dimension one; the exterior power is zero when n exceeds m.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: Averaging explains the characteristic hypothesis
explanation: The maps average over all permutations: (1/n!) Σσ σ(T) for symmetric tensors, and (1/n!) Σσ sign(σ)·σ(T) for alternating tensors. The checked equivalences need only (n.factorial : k) ≠ 0. Thus characteristic zero suffices, and characteristic p also works in degrees n < p. Their inverses take an invariant or alternating tensor to its quotient class. The statements identify the quotient with a subspace; they do not conflate the two constructions or claim that averaging works when n! vanishes.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: The trace formulas do not require an eigenvector basis
explanation: The tensor-power map applies A to every factor and descends to the two quotients because it commutes with permutations. For the trace formulas, the hypotheses say that V has dimension N and charpoly A = ∏i (X-C(λᵢ)). This records every eigenvalue with its algebraic multiplicity and requires them to lie in k. A triangular basis is constructed from that factorization; A need not be diagonalizable.

The exterior trace is the sum of ∏i∈s λᵢ over n-element subsets s of the N indices. The symmetric trace is the sum of the products over multisets of n indices, with repetition allowed. They are the elementary and complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials, respectively. The proofs and formulas work in any characteristic.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.3.title: The one-dimensional top exterior power detects the determinant
explanation: With N = dim V, the induced exterior map is det(A) • LinearMap.id. The determinant-multiplication proof applies the exterior-power composition law to A and B, substitutes this scalar-action formula, and cancels the action on a nonzero vector in the one-dimensional top exterior power. It therefore follows the requested exterior-power argument, rather than simply invoking the existing determinant-multiplication theorem.

Chapter2/Problem2.11.6.title: The development supplies the balanced quotient, not the full bimodule calculus
explanation: The basic encoding uses Module A V for a left action, Module Bᵐᵒᵖ V for a right action, and SMulCommClass A Bᵐᵒᵖ V for their commutation. The available relative tensor-product construction is the abelian-group quotient from Remark 2.11.4. These definitions alone do not prove the scalar-compatible bimodule actions, associativity or Hom–tensor adjunction requested here.

explanation: The displayed reassociation formula is part of the original exercise, but no checked bimodule isomorphism proving it is supplied in this development. The later application, Frobenius reciprocity, is proved directly through Mathlib's representation induction–restriction adjunction; that does not constitute a proof of this standalone tensor-calculus exercise.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.12_heading.title: The tensor algebra is algebra-equivalent to the direct sum of its tensor powers
explanation: Mathlib's TensorAlgebra k V is constructed by its universal property. The algebra equivalence below identifies it with ⨁ n : ℕ, ⨂[k]^n V. Multiplication concatenates homogeneous tensors, adding their degrees; the compatibility theorem relates this graded multiplication to multiplication after embedding in the tensor algebra. The basis comparison identifies the tensor algebra with the free algebra on the basis index type, with no finite-dimensionality assumption.

Chapter2/Definition2.12.1.title: Commuting the generators produces the symmetric algebra
explanation: Mathlib's symmetric algebra is the tensor algebra modulo the ring congruence generated by commutation of its vector generators. Over a field this is the stated ideal quotient. A chosen basis b gives an algebra equivalence with MvPolynomial ι k, sending the image of b i to the polynomial variable indexed by i. The basis may be infinite; polynomials still have finite support.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.SymmetricAlgebra.auxiliaryModelEquivMvPolynomial
declarations.label: A basis identifies the symmetric algebra with a polynomial algebra
declarations.documentation: The symmetric algebra of V is algebra-equivalent to multivariable polynomials on the chosen basis indices.

Chapter2/Definition2.12.1.title: Square-zero generators impose the exterior relations in every characteristic
explanation: The exterior algebra is Mathlib's Clifford algebra for the zero quadratic form, so every vector generator has square zero. This condition is retained in characteristic two; it is not replaced by anticommutation alone. The basis-coordinate equivalence transports V through b.repr : V ≃ₗ[k] (ι →₀ k), giving the exterior algebra on finitely supported basis coordinates.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.ExteriorAlgebra.generator_sq_eq_zero
declarations.label: Every exterior generator squares to zero

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.ExteriorAlgebra.auxiliaryModelEquivFinsupp
declarations.label: The exterior algebra in basis coordinates
declarations.documentation: A chosen basis induces an algebra equivalence with the exterior algebra of the finitely supported coordinate module.

Chapter2/Definition2.12.1.title: The enveloping relation compares degree two with degree one
explanation: Lean writes the vector's image in its enveloping algebra as ι k v. The checked identity is ι(v)·ι(w)-ι(w)·ι(v) = ι([v,w]), with the Lie bracket embedded as a degree-one generator. Mathlib constructs the quotient by a ring congruence expressing this relation. The chosen-basis quotient from Section 2.9 is separately proved algebra-equivalent to this basis-free construction, with both inverse maps checked.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.generator_commutator
declarations.label: The canonical generator images satisfy the enveloping relation

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.auxiliaryBasisEquiv
declarations.label: The basis presentation is equivalent to the basis-free enveloping algebra
declarations.documentation: The generators-and-relations quotient defined using a basis is algebra-equivalent to UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra k L.

Chapter2/Definition2.12.1.title: The degree decompositions are checked linear equivalences
explanation: The two maps identify the symmetric and exterior algebras, as vector spaces, with direct sums of the symmetric and exterior powers defined above. The symmetric map is implemented using a chosen basis and regrouping monomials by total degree. The exterior map uses the graded exterior-algebra decomposition and the equivalence between the exterior-power implementations. The signatures are linear equivalences, not separately bundled graded-algebra isomorphisms.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.SymmetricAlgebra.auxiliaryModelDirectSumEquiv
declarations.label: The symmetric algebra decomposes into symmetric powers
declarations.documentation: A chosen basis gives a linear equivalence from the symmetric algebra to the direct sum of symmetric powers, regrouping basis monomials by total degree.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.ExteriorAlgebra.auxiliaryModelDirectSumEquiv
declarations.label: The exterior algebra decomposes into exterior powers
declarations.documentation: The graded decomposition gives a linear equivalence from the exterior algebra to the direct sum of the exterior-power quotient models.

Chapter2/Problem2.13.1.title: The geometric invariant and its cut-additivity are not formalized here
explanation: The definition of the Dehn invariant and part (a) are preserved as original book prose. The project intentionally omits the required polyhedron, dihedral-angle and dissection infrastructure, so it supplies no checked proof that the invariant is additive under straight cuts. Part (b), in contrast, has the complete irrationality proof below.

Chapter2/Problem2.13.1.title: An integer recurrence proves the tetrahedral angle is irrational in units of π
explanation: Writing θ = arccos(1/3), the proof defines integers b₀=b₁=1 and bₙ₊₂=2bₙ₊₁-9bₙ, and proves bₙ = 3ⁿ cos(nθ). It also proves that no bₙ is divisible by 3. If θ/π were a rational r, choose n=2·denominator(r)>0; then cos(nθ)=1, forcing bₙ=3ⁿ, a divisibility contradiction.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Geometry.TetrahedronAngle.irrational_arccos_one_third_div_pi
declarations.label: arccos(1/3) / π is irrational

Chapter2/Problem2.13.1.title: The cube–tetrahedron scissors-congruence obstruction is intentionally omitted
explanation: The checked angle result alone is not the full solution to Hilbert's third problem. This development does not compute the two polyhedra's Dehn invariants, prove their inequality in the rational tensor product, or derive the impossibility of the dissection. Those geometric steps, as well as part (a), are recorded as intentional omissions.

Chapter2/Definition2.14.1.title: The Lie action adds the actions on the two tensor factors
explanation: Lean writes the action on a vector as ⁅x,v⁆. On a pure tensor it is ⁅x,v⊗w⁆ = ⁅x,v⁆⊗w + v⊗⁅x,w⁆. Mathlib constructs this as the sum of the two induced endomorphisms and verifies the Lie-module identity and scalar compatibility. The alias retains this existing tensor-product action; it does not merely introduce a tensor space and assume it is a representation. The construction works over commutative base rings and does not require finite-dimensional modules.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.AuxiliaryTwoModuleType.AuxiliaryLieModuleType.lie_bracket_tmul
declarations.label: The checked Lie action on a pure tensor

Chapter2/Definition2.14.2.title: The minus sign makes the dual action a Lie representation
explanation: The dual is Module.Dual k V, and the checked evaluation formula is (⁅x,f⁆)(v) = -f(⁅x,v⁆). This is the negative transpose action in the book. Its Lie-ring-module and scalar-compatible Lie-module structures are already supplied by Mathlib, and the source checks that both are available on the alias. Neither finite-dimensionality nor characteristic zero is assumed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.AuxiliarySingleModuleType.auxiliary_lie_bracket_apply
declarations.label: The dual action evaluated on a vector
declarations.documentation: The contragredient action evaluates as (x·f)(v) = -f(x·v).

Chapter2/Problem2.14.3.title: Currying and the dual-tensor equivalence preserve the Lie action
explanation: An equivariant map V⊗W → U first curries to an equivariant map V → (W →ₗ[k] U). The checked Lie-module equivalence (W →ₗ[k] U) ≃ U⊗W* then transports the target. Its bracket-preservation proof uses the sum action on tensors and the negative dual action. The resulting Hom spaces are linearly equivalent over k, with inverse maps bundled in the equivalence. Only W, the space being dualized, needs to be finite-dimensional; the source also verifies the equivalence without finite-dimensionality assumptions on V or U.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LieModule.HomTensorAdjunction.lieModuleHomTensorDualEquiv
declarations.label: The equivariant Hom–tensor-dual linear equivalence

Chapter2/Definition2.11.1.title: The notation separates the tensor space from a pure tensor
explanation: Lean writes the space as V ⊗[k] W, or TensorProduct k V W, and an element supplied by two vectors as v ⊗ₜ[k] w. The alias below is that tensor space, not an additional construction. Mathlib's implementation uses a quotient of a free additive monoid by additive and balanced-scalar relations, rather than the book's initial free-vector-space quotient. Its resulting module has the displayed bilinearity identities; the next exercise gives a checked comparison with the free-abelian-group construction. The definitions apply to modules over commutative rings as well as vector spaces.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryTwoModuleType.AuxiliaryModuleType
declarations.label: The tensor-product type used by the formalization
declarations.documentation: The tensor product V ⊗[k] W of modules over a commutative ring.

Chapter2/Exercise2.11.2.title: The free-abelian-group quotient is linearly equivalent to the tensor product
explanation: The subgroup is the additive subgroup generated by the three families of relations in the exercise. The map sends the class of a generator (v,w) to v ⊗ₜ[k] w; the inverse sends a pure tensor back to that generating class. Both composites are proved to be identities by induction on tensors and on the free abelian group. A scalar action is then transported through the additive equivalence, yielding the module structure and linear equivalence below. This establishes the quotient construction, not merely its relations, and works over any commutative ring.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.TensorProduct.Quotient.quotientToTensorProductLinearEquiv

Chapter2/Discussion_pure_tensors.title: A concrete sum of pure tensors need not itself be pure
explanation: In ℚ² ⊗[ℚ] ℚ², take T = e₀ ⊗ e₀ + e₁ ⊗ e₁. The checked example proves that T differs from every v ⊗ w. Its proof applies the coordinate-product functionals: the diagonal coefficients of T are one and the off-diagonal coefficients are zero, which cannot all be products vᵢ·wⱼ. Associativity is supplied separately by Mathlib's linear equivalence TensorProduct.assoc; differently parenthesized tensor spaces are identified by a map, not assumed to be identical Lean types.

declarations.documentation: In the tensor square of Fin 2 → ℚ, e₀⊗e₀ + e₁⊗e₁ differs from v⊗w for every pair v,w.

Chapter2/Discussion_pure_tensors.title: Tensor type (m,n) keeps vector and dual factors separate
explanation: The tensor power is represented by PiTensorProduct on the finite index type Fin n. The mixed tensor space has n copies of V and m copies of Module.Dual k V, in the book's order. The space exists without finite-dimensionality; identifying every tensor of type (1,1) with an arbitrary linear endomorphism, however, uses finite-dimensionality, as the later dual-tensor equivalence states.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TensorProductAuxiliary.moduleAuxiliaryType
declarations.label: The mixed vector-and-dual tensor space
declarations.documentation: The tensor product of n copies of V with m copies of its k-linear dual.

Chapter2/Discussion_tensors_type.title: The basis indices are tuples, not an untyped table
explanation: Given a basis b : Module.Basis ι k V with a finite index type ι, the constructed tensor basis is indexed by (Fin n → ι) × (Fin m → ι). The first tuple selects vector-basis elements and the second selects dual-basis elements. The construction uses the tensor-product bases of b and b.dualBasis. Coefficients are supplied by the basis's repr map, and the reconstruction theorem expresses the tensor as the sum of its coefficients times these basis vectors. No special Einstein-summation parser is being used.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.TensorProductAuxiliary.moduleAuxiliaryType_basis

Chapter2/Discussion_tensors_type.title: An index-convention correction in the original prose
explanation: In the displayed expansion, the upper indices of the coefficients T label the V factors, and the lower indices label the V* factors. The sentence above assigning the lower indices of T to V and the upper ones to V* reverses that convention. The original wording is preserved here. The checked tensor-basis construction follows the displayed expansion; it does not supply the requested change-of-basis formula for component tables.

Chapter2/Discussion_tensor_product_maps.title: The universal property makes the formula well defined
explanation: Mathlib constructs TensorProduct.map A B by lifting the bilinear map (v,w) ↦ A(v) ⊗ B(w). This produces a bundled linear map on the quotient, so it respects all tensor relations. The theorem map_tmul gives its value on a pure tensor. Since pure tensors span the tensor space, these values determine the whole linear map, not just a restriction to selected elements.

links.label: The tensor product of two linear maps

Chapter2/Remark2.11.4.title: The opposite ring records the right action
explanation: A right A-module is expressed as Module Aᵐᵒᵖ V: the book's v·a becomes MulOpposite.op a • v. The balanced tensor product is the free abelian group on pairs modulo the additive subgroup generated by the two additivity relations and (op a • v,w) - (v,a • w). Its constructor is additive in both arguments and satisfies the balancing equation below. A need not be commutative. The construction here is an abelian group; no A-module structure is claimed without extra commuting scalar actions.

declarations.label: The right–left balanced tensor-product quotient
declarations.documentation: The quotient of the free abelian group on V × W by additivity in each factor and the balancing relation (v·a)⊗w = v⊗(a·w).

declarations.label: The checked balancing equation
declarations.documentation: Moving an A-element from the right action on V to the left action on W does not change the generating tensor class.

Chapter2/Exercise2.11.5.title: Scalar extension changes both the algebra and its module
explanation: The algebra A ⊗[K] L receives its L-algebra structure from the right tensor factor; the scalar l maps to 1 ⊗ l. Its action on V ⊗[K] L is (a ⊗ l) • (v ⊗ l′) = (a • v) ⊗ (l·l′). The checked existence statement bundles a module structure with that formula. The proof uses the tensor-factor commutation equivalence to obtain the L-action and verifies that it commutes with A's action. K and L may be commutative rings with an algebra map, rather than fields with an injective extension; A may be noncommutative. IsScalarTower K A V expresses compatibility of V's K- and A-actions.

declarations.label: The new scalars act through the right tensor factor

declarations.label: The extended module and its pure-tensor action

Chapter2/Exercise2.11.7.title: Commutativity lets the balancing relation support scalar multiplication
explanation: Mathlib's tensor product already carries a module structure over the commutative base ring. On pure tensors the scalar action is a • (m ⊗ n) = (a • m) ⊗ n = m ⊗ (a • n). The tensor relations ensure that this action descends to the quotient, and additivity extends it to sums. This applies to arbitrary modules, without freeness or finite-generation assumptions.

Chapter2/Discussion_concrete_Lie_example.title: The cross product is the Lie bracket on real three-space
explanation: Vectors are functions Fin 3 → ℝ. Mathlib supplies the Lie-ring structure for the cross product; the local LieAlgebra ℝ instance supplies scalar compatibility. The equation below identifies the bracket with u ⨯₃ v. The construction is explicitly real, not an assertion about an arbitrary base field.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.ThreeDimensional.bracket_eq_crossProduct

Chapter2/Discussion_concrete_Lie_example.title: Coordinates and matrices give the same sl(2) Lie algebra
explanation: The coordinate triple (a,b,d) represents a·e + b·f + d·h. The checked Lie equivalence sends it to the matrix with rows (d,a) and (b,-d); its inverse reads the upper-right, lower-left and upper-left entries. Thus it identifies the coordinate bracket with the matrix commutator, not just the underlying vector spaces. The generators basis0, basis1 and basis2 are e, f and h. The construction works over any commutative ring, including characteristic two where the coefficients 2 and -2 vanish.

declarations.documentation: The map (a,b,d) ↦ [[d,a],[b,-d]] is a Lie equivalence onto the trace-zero two-by-two matrices.

Chapter2/Discussion_concrete_Lie_example.title: The Heisenberg matrices realize a three-coordinate bracket
explanation: The coordinates (a,b,d) stand for a·x + b·y + d·c. Their bracket is (0,0,b·a′-a·b′). The matrix equivalence places b and d in the first row and a in the second row, at the positions shown in the book. In particular x is the matrix unit (1,2), y is (0,1), and c is (0,2), using Lean's zero-based indices. Both inverse maps and preservation of the bracket are checked over any commutative ring.

declarations.documentation: The bracket of the y generator with the x generator is the central generator c.

Chapter2/Discussion_concrete_Lie_example.title: The affine Lie algebra has the displayed two-element basis
explanation: The algebra is initially defined as the Lie subalgebra generated by the two matrix units X and Y. A second description imposes exactly the two zero entries in the bottom row, and the two subalgebras are proved equal. The checked basis and dimension calculation show that no additional matrices arise from closing under brackets. The field is arbitrary; there is no characteristic-zero assumption.

declarations.documentation: The bracket of the matrix units (0,0) and (0,1) is the latter matrix unit.

declarations.documentation: The Lie subalgebra generated by X and Y consists of all two-by-two matrices with zero bottom row.

Chapter2/Discussion_concrete_Lie_example.title: Skew-symmetry defines a bracket-closed matrix subspace
explanation: Mathlib's LieAlgebra.Orthogonal.so bundles the skew-adjoint matrices for the identity bilinear form as a Lie subalgebra. The membership theorem says Aᵀ = -A, and the bracket is the associative commutator. This definition works over commutative rings. In characteristic two, that equation does not force diagonal entries to vanish, so its meaning should not be silently replaced by the familiar real-matrix picture.

Chapter2/Exercise2.9.5.title: A vector acts by cross product through a skew-symmetric matrix
explanation: The checked equivalence sends (v₀,v₁,v₂) to the matrix with rows (0,-v₂,v₁), (v₂,0,-v₀) and (-v₁,v₀,0). The matrix of u × v is the commutator of the matrices of u and v. The inverse extracts entries (2,1), (0,2) and (1,0); skew-symmetry proves that these reconstruct the whole matrix. This is a real-linear Lie equivalence, which establishes the exercise in both directions.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.ThreeDimensional.crossProductLieEquivOrthogonal
declarations.label: The explicit equivalence ℝ³ ≃ so(3)

Chapter2/Example2.9.12.title: The three relations present the entire enveloping algebra
explanation: The presented algebra is the free algebra on three generators, indexed by Fin 3, modulo the listed commutator relations. Generator 0 is e, 1 is f and 2 is h. The algebra equivalence below identifies this quotient with the enveloping algebra of CoordinateTriple k, the coordinate model already proved Lie-equivalent to the trace-zero matrices. Its proof constructs homomorphisms in both directions and checks both composites, so the result is stronger than just verifying the three relations inside the enveloping algebra. It holds over any commutative ring.

Chapter2/Example2.9.13.title: The central generator appears in a checked presentation
explanation: The Heisenberg Lie algebra is implemented by coordinate triples on x, y and c, with [y,x] = c and c central. The quotient of the free algebra on these three generators is algebra-equivalent to its enveloping algebra. The equivalence sends each generator to the canonical image of the corresponding Lie-algebra element, and the inverse and both composite identities are checked. These constructions require a commutative base ring, not a field or a characteristic-zero hypothesis.

Chapter2/Example2.9.13.title: Setting c equal to one gives the Weyl relation
explanation: The quotient uses the two-sided ideal generated by ι(c)-1, where ι is the canonical map into the enveloping algebra. In it, yx-xy=c becomes yx=xy+1. The checked algebra equivalence sends x to the Weyl algebra's first operator and y to its second operator. It constructs the inverse from these generators and verifies both round trips. This is an isomorphism of abstract algebras in any characteristic; it does not assert that the action by multiplication and differentiation on polynomials is faithful in positive characteristic.

Chapter2/Remark2.9.14.title: The Lie-group correspondence is background, not a checked theorem here
explanation: This development formalizes algebraic Lie algebras and their representations, but it does not supply the manifold construction, the identification with the tangent space, or Lie's correspondence with simply connected real Lie groups. The differentiation and integration of group representations described here are also outside its checked coverage. The original discussion is retained as mathematical context; the earlier exponential result concerns derivations of an associative algebra and does not prove this correspondence.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.9_Lie_groups.title: The generated group and its universal cover are not constructed in Lean here
explanation: No checked result in this development constructs the Lie-group structure on the subgroup generated by these matrix exponentials, or identifies the Lie algebra of its universal cover. The appeal to Ado also uses a theorem intentionally left unproved in this development, as noted above. These claims belong to the book's background discussion, not to the checked matrix-Lie-algebra and enveloping-algebra constructions.

Chapter2/Definition2.9.6.title: A Lie homomorphism bundles linearity and bracket preservation
explanation: The notation L₁ →ₗ⁅k⁆ L₂ means LieHom k L₁ L₂. It extends a k-linear map with a proof that f ⁅a,b⁆ = ⁅f a,f b⁆. The alias below introduces no additional condition. These maps are defined over commutative base rings, so the book's field setting is a special case.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.PairedAuxiliaryTypes.LieAlgebra.AuxiliaryType
declarations.label: The bundled Lie-homomorphism type
declarations.documentation: Linear maps preserving the Lie bracket, expressed as Mathlib LieHom.

Chapter2/Definition2.9.7.title: Lie modules describe the action directly on vectors
explanation: Lean writes the action as ⁅a,v⁆, where a is a Lie-algebra element and v is a vector; here the notation is an action, not a bracket of two algebra elements. The Lie-ring-module axiom is ⁅a,⁅b,v⁆⁆ = ⁅⁅a,b⁆,v⁆ + ⁅b,⁅a,v⁆⁆, which says that the resulting operators preserve Lie brackets. The LieModule k L V structure adds compatibility with scalars in both arguments. The alias below refers to that structure, not to an extra auxiliary predicate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Module.Predicates.LieModule.AuxiliaryPredicate

declarations.documentation: Compatibility of a Lie-ring action on V with the k-module structures on L and V. This is Mathlib's LieModule structure.

Chapter2/Example2.9.8.title: The trivial representation has zero action, not necessarily zero space
explanation: The type copy TrivialLieModule k L V retains V's vector-space structure and defines ⁅a,v⁆ = 0 for every a and v. Taking V to be PUnit, with its one-element additive group, gives the zero representation in part (1). For a nonzero V this remains a trivial action on a nonzero space.

Chapter2/Example2.9.8.title: Jacobi makes the adjoint map preserve brackets
explanation: The adjoint map is LieAlgebra.ad k L. Its value is ad(a)(b) = ⁅a,b⁆, and its Lie-homomorphism property says ad(⁅a,b⁆) = ad(a) ∘ ad(b) - ad(b) ∘ ad(a). Evaluating that equation on a vector is the derivation form of Jacobi. The two formulas below are checked for an existing Lie-algebra structure; they do not assert faithfulness of the adjoint representation.

declarations.label: The adjoint map preserves brackets
