Chapter2/Example2.9.8.title: Extending the action to the enveloping algebra
explanation: For a fixed vector space V, the equivalence is between Lie homomorphisms L →ₗ⁅k⁆ Module.End k V and unital algebra homomorphisms U(L) →ₐ[k] Module.End k V. Restriction uses the canonical map from L to U(L); extension uses the universal property. This is an equivalence of action data on the same V, with no finite-dimensionality assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.UniversalEnveloping.representationAlgHomEquiv
declarations.label: The checked restriction–extension equivalence

Chapter2/Definition2.9.9.title: A basis presentation is compared with a basis-free construction
explanation: For a basis b : Module.Basis ι k L, the relation at (i,j) is the free-algebra element X_i*X_j - X_j*X_i - Σ_r c_r X_r, where the finitely supported coefficients c_r are b.repr ⁅b i,b j⁆. Thus even an infinite basis produces a finite sum for each relation. The quotient by these relations is algebra-isomorphic to Mathlib's basis-independent UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra k L. The equivalence sends each presented generator to the image of its basis vector.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.auxiliaryBasisPairElement
declarations.label: The relation associated with two basis vectors
declarations.documentation: The commutator of the two free generators minus the basis-coordinate expansion of their Lie bracket.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.auxiliaryBasisEquiv
declarations.label: The basis presentation is equivalent to the basis-free enveloping algebra
declarations.documentation: An algebra equivalence from the chosen-basis generators-and-relations quotient to UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra k L.

Chapter2/Remark2.9.10.title: The choice of basis changes the presentation, not the algebra up to isomorphism
explanation: The formalization supplies an algebra equivalence from each chosen-basis presentation to the same basis-independent enveloping algebra. Composing one such equivalence with the inverse of another compares two presentations. The proof constructs the maps in both directions and checks their composites on generators; it does not identify the two quotient types by equality.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryLieModuleConstructions.UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.auxiliaryBasisEquiv
declarations.label: The comparison equivalence for an arbitrary basis
declarations.documentation: Each chosen-basis presentation is algebra-isomorphic to the basis-independent universal enveloping algebra.

Chapter2/Exercise2.9.11.title: The universal property proves both directions
explanation: Given the Lie action ρ, the enveloping algebra's universal property supplies a unique unital algebra homomorphism extending ρ. Conversely, restricting an algebra homomorphism along UniversalEnvelopingAlgebra.ι gives a Lie action. Mathlib's lift packages the inverse laws, and the equivalence below specializes it to the endomorphism algebra of V. Neither L nor V is required to be finite-dimensional.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.UniversalEnveloping.representationAlgHomEquiv
declarations.label: The two action descriptions and their inverse correspondence

Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_notation.after: We denote the set of vertices
Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_notation.title: Bundling an arrow together with its endpoints
explanation: The book's set of all edges is represented by Arrow Q = Σ i j, i ⟶ j. Each bundled arrow therefore includes its source, target, and an inhabitant of the arrow type between them. The source and target projections recover h′ and h″; hom recovers the edge with its endpoints in its type.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Arrows.Arrow.source
declarations.label: The source projection

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Arrows.Arrow.target
declarations.label: The target projection

Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_irreducible_i.title: Nonzero is a condition on the whole representation
explanation: The representation is zero when every vector at every vertex is zero. Its negation means at least one vertex space has a nonzero vector; it does not require every vertex space to be nonzero. Irreducibility requires this nonzero condition and says that any subrepresentation is zero at all vertices or the whole space at all vertices. Indecomposability instead rules out an isomorphism to a binary direct sum with two nonzero summands. The checked definitions allow arbitrary quivers and commutative coefficient semirings.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverLinearDiagrams.AuxiliaryQuiverModuleData.IsIrreducible
declarations.label: The irreducibility condition

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverLinearDiagrams.AuxiliaryQuiverModuleData.IsIndecomposable
declarations.label: The indecomposability condition

Chapter2/Problem2.8.11.title: Hilbert series are formal series of integer dimensions
explanation: A LocallyFiniteGrading records homogeneous submodules, their internal direct-sum decomposition, multiplication respecting degree, and finite-dimensionality of each piece. Its hilbertSeries has type PowerSeries ℤ, with degree-n coefficient equal to the integer dimension of the n-th piece. The identities below are formal power-series identities: they make no assertion about analytic convergence. The example-specific results calculate dimensions and series separately; they do not themselves construct a complete grading record for each example.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.hilbertSeries_coeff
declarations.label: The coefficient formula for a locally finite grading

Chapter2/Problem2.8.11.title: Commuting monomials give 1/(1-t)^m
explanation: The degree-n monomials in m variables are counted by choose(n+m-1,n). Lean proves both the homogeneous-component dimension formula and that the series of these counts multiplied by (1-X)^m equals one. Writing the latter as an inverse avoids an analytic interpretation of the fraction. The statements include m = 0: the series is then one.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.finrank_mvPolynomialHomogeneousSubmodule
declarations.label: The dimension of a homogeneous polynomial piece

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.one_sub_X_pow_mul_powerSeries_multichoose
declarations.label: The formal inverse identity for the polynomial series

Chapter2/Problem2.8.11.title: Words give 1/(1-mt)
explanation: The free algebra is identified with the monoid algebra of the free monoid on Fin m. Words of length n correspond to functions Fin n → Fin m, so the degree-n dimension is m^n. The second theorem proves the geometric-series identity by comparing coefficients. The displayed series identity has coefficients in the chosen field; the dimension counts themselves are natural numbers.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.finrank_freeMonoidDegreeSubmodule
declarations.label: The word-length component has dimension m^n

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.one_sub_nat_smul_X_mul_powerSeries_pow
declarations.label: The formal geometric-series identity

Chapter2/Problem2.8.11.title: Exterior powers give (1+t)^m
explanation: The n-th exterior power of Fin m → k has dimension m.choose n. Its basis is indexed by n-element subsets of the m basis vectors. The binomial theorem identifies the series of these dimensions with (1+X)^m. No restriction on the field's characteristic is imposed: in characteristic two, the separate relation x_i^2 = 0 remains essential to the exterior-algebra interpretation.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.finrank_exteriorPower_finFunction
declarations.label: The dimension of the n-th exterior power

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.powerSeries_choose_eq_one_add_X_pow
declarations.label: The binomial formula for the exterior series

Chapter2/Problem2.8.11.title: Adjacency-matrix powers count paths
explanation: Here the vertices and the arrows between each pair of vertices must be finite, so each fixed-length path space is finite-dimensional. The adjacency entry M(i,j) counts arrows from i to j, and (M^n)(i,j) counts length-n paths with those endpoints. Summing over all endpoint pairs gives the degree-n dimension. The series is therefore 1ᵀ (I-tM)⁻¹ 1. The inverse is a matrix over formal power series; its constant matrix term is the identity.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.finrank_quiverDegreeSubmodule
declarations.label: The degree-n component counts all length-n paths

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.card_paths_length_eq_adjacencyMatrix_pow
declarations.label: The path-counting matrix-power formula

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.GradedAlgebra.HilbertSeries.pathCountSeries_eq_ones_mul_matrixInverse_mul_ones
declarations.label: The closed formal-series formula

Chapter2/Discussion_2.9_heading.title: Alternation is stronger than skew-symmetry in characteristic two
explanation: The LieRing structure requires ⁅x,x⁆ = 0. Skew-symmetry follows from this and additivity. In characteristic two, skew-symmetry alone would not force a self-bracket to vanish; Lean uses the alternating condition stated in the parenthesis. The notation ⁅x,y⁆ denotes the bracket, and the LieAlgebra k L structure supplies scalar compatibility.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LieAlgebra.BracketIdentities.bracket_self
declarations.label: Every self-bracket vanishes

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LieAlgebra.BracketIdentities.bracket_eq_neg_bracket_swap
declarations.label: Swapping the arguments negates the bracket

Chapter2/Definition2.9.1.title: The cyclic Jacobi formula follows from the Lie-ring axiom
explanation: Mathlib packages additivity, alternation, and the Jacobi identity in LieRing L, with scalar compatibility in LieAlgebra k L. Its Jacobi axiom is written in the derivation form ⁅a,⁅b,c⁆⁆ = ⁅⁅a,b⁆,c⁆ + ⁅b,⁅a,c⁆⁆. The theorem below rearranges this into the cyclic formula displayed in the book. It assumes an existing Lie algebra; it does not construct one from an arbitrary bracket satisfying only the displayed identity.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Basic.LieRing.cyclic_iterated_bracket_sum_eq_zero
declarations.label: The displayed cyclic Jacobi identity

Chapter2/Example2.9.2.title: The zero bracket is installed on a copy of the module
explanation: The type AbelianLieAlgebra k V keeps the underlying additive group and scalar action of V, but installs the zero bracket. The checked Lie-ring and Lie-algebra instances then prove the axioms. The type copy lets this bracket coexist with other possible brackets on the same underlying module.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Constructions.AbelianLieAlgebra.instLieRing
declarations.label: The Lie-ring axioms for the zero bracket

Chapter2/Example2.9.2.title: Composition gives the commutator bracket on endomorphisms
explanation: For an associative algebra, the bracket is a*b - b*a. On Module.End k V, multiplication means composition, so ⁅F,G⁆ v = F(G v) - G(F v). The algebraic constructions here work over a commutative base ring, not only a field, and do not require finite-dimensionality of V.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Constructions.endomorphismLieAlgebra

links.label: The commutator Lie-ring construction in Mathlib

Chapter2/Example2.9.2.title: The commutator of two derivations is again a derivation
explanation: The subalgebra contains the linear endomorphisms satisfying D(a*b) = D(a)*b + a*D(b). Expanding this rule for two derivations and subtracting proves closure under their commutator. The construction works even when A is noncommutative. The separate equivalence with Mathlib's Derivation k A A additionally assumes that A is commutative; that restriction is not needed for this subalgebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Constructions.mem_derivationLieSubalgebra_iff
declarations.label: Membership is exactly the Leibniz rule

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Constructions.derivationLieSubalgebra.bracket_apply
declarations.label: The bracket of two derivations is their commutator

Chapter2/Example2.9.2_continued.title: Bracket closure is the extra field of a Lie subalgebra
explanation: Mathlib's LieSubalgebra k L bundles a linear subspace and a proof that its bracket stays inside that subspace. Its carrier inherits the Lie-ring and Lie-algebra structures. The local helper below specializes this inheritance to a Lie subalgebra of an associative algebra with its commutator bracket; the general construction for any ambient Lie algebra is in Mathlib.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.Constructions.subalgebraLieAlgebra
declarations.label: The inherited structure in the associative-algebra case

links.name: LieSubalgebra
links.label: The general Lie-subalgebra structure

Chapter2/Remark2.9.3.title: Ado's theorem remains unproved in this formalization
explanation: The source marks the finite-dimensional faithful-representation theorem as proof_wanted ado; it is not a checked proof of Ado's theorem. This is an intentional scope omission. What is proved is a reduction: a faithful finite-dimensional representation exists if and only if the universal enveloping algebra has a map to a finite-dimensional associative algebra that is injective on the Lie algebra's image. Neither side of this equivalence is established for an arbitrary finite-dimensional Lie algebra. The checked reductions below must not be mistaken for the theorem itself.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Lie.InjectivityExistenceAuxiliary.auxiliary_exists_iff_exists_envelopingMap_injective
declarations.label: The checked equivalence used to reduce the remaining problem
declarations.documentation: Existence of a finite-dimensional faithful Lie representation is equivalent to a finite-dimensional enveloping-algebra image separating the Lie algebra elements.

Chapter2/Remark2.9.4.title: Differentiate the multiplication identity; exponentiate the derivation
explanation: The derivative theorem is over the reals and uses a curve of continuous real-linear endomorphisms. If it starts at the identity and preserves multiplication, differentiating that multiplication identity at zero gives the Leibniz rule. Invertibility of each map is not needed for this direction. The theorem as written assumes multiplication preservation for all real parameter values, rather than only on the book's interval.

For the converse, D is a continuous real-linear derivation of a finite-dimensional real normed algebra. The proof compares solutions of the linear differential equation to show that exp(t • D) preserves multiplication and one. The inverse is exp((-t) • D); the group law is checked separately. A complex algebra can be regarded as real, but the exported automorphism here is real-linear, not a separately bundled complex-algebra automorphism.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.Algebra.DerivationExponential.derivation_of_hasDerivAt_multiplicativeCurve
declarations.label: Differentiating a multiplicative curve gives a derivation

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.Algebra.DerivationExponential.derivationExponentialEquiv
declarations.label: The real-algebra automorphism obtained by exponentiating D

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Analysis.Algebra.DerivationExponential.exp_add_smul
declarations.label: The one-parameter group law

Chapter2/Discussion_path_algebra_intro.title: Here 'the same' is a bijection of isomorphism classes
explanation: The checked correspondence below assumes finitely many vertices, [Fintype Q], and a field k. It gives an equivalence between the quotient of path-algebra modules by module isomorphism and the quotient of quiver representations by vertexwise linear isomorphisms commuting with the arrows. It also identifies the two constructions used in the correspondence. This is not literal equality of the representation types, nor does this theorem state an equivalence of categories or an infinite-vertex version.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.existsModuleRepresentationQuotientEquiv
declarations.label: The finite-vertex correspondence and its construction formulas

Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_rep_bijection.title: Vertex idempotents recover the vertex spaces
explanation: For a path-algebra module V, vertexSubmodule i is the range of the projector v ↦ p_i • v. The arrow map is the action of its one-edge path restricted to the source and target ranges. The target-idempotent relation proves that it lands in the right submodule. Together these data construct representationOfModule.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.vertexSubmodule
declarations.label: The vertex space as a projector range

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.arrowMapOnVertexParts
declarations.label: The arrow action restricted to the vertex spaces

Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_rep_bijection.title: Paths act by composition on the direct sum
explanation: Starting from a quiver representation, Lean uses DirectSum Q R.obj. A path from i to j first projects to the i-component, applies the successive arrow maps, and includes the result in the j-component. This is zero on every other starting component. Finite linear combinations of paths extend this action to the path algebra.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.pathLinearMap
declarations.label: Compose the linear maps along a path

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.pathEndomorphism
declarations.label: The resulting endomorphism of the whole direct sum

Chapter2/Discussion_quiver_rep_bijection.title: The round trips return isomorphic representations
explanation: The proof reconstructs a path-algebra module from the direct sum of its vertex parts and recovers each quiver space from its corresponding projector range. These are algebra-linear and vertexwise linear equivalences, respectively, not definitional equalities. Passing to isomorphism classes gives the equivalence below. Its RealizesRepresentation condition records that the reconstructed module's path action agrees with the original composed-arrow action. All these statements assume finitely many vertices.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.existsModuleRepresentationQuotientEquiv
declarations.label: The checked bijection of isomorphism classes

Chapter2/Definition2.8.1.title: Vertices are a type; arrows are a family of types
explanation: Mathlib's Quiver Q assigns a type v ⟶ w to each pair of vertices. An empty arrow type means there is no edge, while several inhabitants give parallel edges. Taking v = w allows loops. There is no composition operation in this structure: paths are built separately. No finiteness assumption is imposed.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Foundations.TypeFamilies.AuxiliaryTypeFamily
declarations.label: The quiver structure used here
declarations.documentation: A quiver on the vertex type Q: for each ordered pair of vertices, a type of arrows between them. This is an alias for Mathlib's Quiver.

Chapter2/Example2.8.2.title: The four vertices and exactly three arrows
explanation: The formal example labels the vertices by Fin 4. Its arrow type is Unit for the pairs 0 → 1, 2 → 1, and 3 → 0, and Empty for every other pair. Thus each displayed edge is unique and there are no additional edges or loops.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Combinatorics.Quiver.FourVertices.fourVertexQuiver
declarations.label: The complete arrow-type definition for this example

Chapter2/Definition2.8.3.title: One module per vertex and one linear map per arrow
explanation: The obj field assigns the module at each vertex; map assigns a k-linear map to each arrow, with its source and target already fixed by the arrow's type. The additive and module structures on all vertex spaces are included in the record. Lean allows a commutative semiring as the coefficient ring; taking a field gives the book's vector spaces. The record imposes no extra relations on compositions of arrows.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverLinearDiagrams.AuxiliaryQuiverModuleData
declarations.label: The fields of a quiver representation
declarations.documentation: A quiver representation consists of a module at each vertex and a linear map along each arrow.

Chapter2/Definition2.8.4.title: The opposite algebra enforces 'first b, then a'
explanation: A basis index bundles a source vertex, a target vertex, and a path between them. Algebra elements are finitely supported coefficient functions on these indices. The underlying construction concatenates left to right; taking its multiplicative opposite makes multiplication follow the book's convention. If p : i → j and q : j → l, the element of q times the element of p is the element of the concatenated path from i to l.

Under 'first b, then a', the endpoint condition for ab is target(b) = source(a). The preserved footnote gives the reverse condition; the checked multiplication follows the main definition, not that sentence. Noncomposable basis paths multiply to zero. The nonunital ring exists for arbitrary vertex types; a unit is installed when the vertices are finite.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.auxiliaryElement_mul_auxiliaryElement
declarations.label: The checked composition order for basis paths
declarations.documentation: The element of q multiplied by the element of p traces p first and then q, when their intermediate vertices match.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.auxiliaryElement_mul_auxiliaryElement_eq_zero
declarations.label: Noncomposable paths have zero product

Chapter2/Remark2.8.5.title: Only the vertex set needs to be finite
explanation: The theorem assumes [Fintype Q], where Q is the vertex type. It sums the length-zero path elements over those vertices to obtain the identity. Neither the arrow set nor the set of paths needs to be finite: loops may give infinitely many paths. For an infinite vertex set the same construction remains nonunital, since algebra elements have finite support.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.AuxiliaryPathStructures.Quiver.AuxiliaryOppositeType.sum_auxiliaryVertexElement_eq_one
declarations.label: The sum of the vertex idempotents is the identity

Chapter2/Problem2.8.6.title: Generation and a universal property are separate checked results
explanation: The generation theorem says that the vertex and arrow elements generate the whole algebra as a k-subalgebra. Its proof builds every path from its starting vertex and successive arrows, then extends to finite linear combinations.

The universal-property theorem goes further: in any target k-algebra, chosen vertex and arrow values satisfying all four groups of relations determine a unique algebra homomorphism with those values. This is the assertion that these are defining relations, not merely identities true of the constructed generators. The hypotheses require finitely many vertices, but allow infinitely many arrows.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.UniversalProperties.oppositeVertexArrow_adjoin_eq_top
declarations.label: Vertex and arrow elements generate the algebra

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.UniversalProperties.existsUnique_oppositePathAlgebraHom
declarations.label: The complete generators-and-relations universal property

Chapter2/Problem2.8.6.title: Source idempotents are on the right; target idempotents are on the left
explanation: For an arrow e : i ⟶ j, the checked identities are a_e * p_i = a_e and p_j * a_e = a_e. Using any other source or target idempotent makes the product zero. These positions agree with the convention that the right-hand factor is traced first.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.UniversalProperties.oppositeArrow_mul_sourceVertex
declarations.label: The source idempotent acts on the right

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Quiver.PathAlgebra.UniversalProperties.targetVertex_mul_oppositeArrow
declarations.label: The target idempotent acts on the left

Chapter2/Definition2.8.8.title: Arrow-invariant submodules supply the restricted representation
explanation: The record's carrier v is a submodule of the space at vertex v. Its map_mem field certifies that every arrow sends its source submodule into its target submodule. The toDiagram construction then uses LinearMap.restrict to obtain the representation on those submodule types. The restricted arrow maps are constructed, not independently chosen.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverAuxiliary.AuxiliaryType
declarations.label: The submodules and arrow-invariance condition
declarations.documentation: A subrepresentation is a submodule at each vertex preserved by every arrow map.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverAuxiliary.AuxiliaryType.toDiagram
declarations.label: Constructing the representation on the submodules
declarations.documentation: Restrict each arrow map to the source and target submodules to form the subrepresentation.

Chapter2/Definition2.8.9.title: The binary direct sum is built vertex by vertex
explanation: At vertex v, the space is ρ₁.obj v × ρ₂.obj v; along an arrow e, the map is (ρ₁.map e).prodMap (ρ₂.map e). For two modules this product is the direct sum, and the arrow map acts componentwise. This construction is binary; it does not identify an infinite product with an infinite direct sum.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverLinearDiagrams.AuxiliaryQuiverModuleData.auxiliaryBinaryConstruction
declarations.label: The vertex spaces and arrow maps of the direct sum
declarations.documentation: The binary direct sum of quiver representations, with product vertex modules and componentwise arrow maps.

Chapter2/Definition2.8.10.title: Linear component maps make every arrow square commute
explanation: The component app v is bundled as a k-linear map. For e : v ⟶ w, the naturality field states app w (ρ₁.map e x) = ρ₂.map e (app v x) for every x. This is the displayed commutation condition, written pointwise. Linearity is required explicitly in the formalization; arbitrary functions commuting with the arrows are not homomorphisms here.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.CategoryTheory.QuiverLinearMaps.AuxiliaryQuiverLinearMapData
declarations.label: Linear components and the commutation condition
declarations.documentation: A homomorphism of quiver representations is a family of linear maps commuting with every arrow map.

Chapter2/Problem2.4.1.title: The ring must be nonzero
explanation: The three existence theorems assume [Nontrivial A]. This condition is necessary: the zero ring has no proper ideals. Maximality is expressed by IsCoatom I, meaning that I is proper and every strictly larger ideal is the whole ring.

Left ideals are submodules of the left regular module; right ideals are treated over the opposite ring. The two-sided proof applies Zorn's lemma to proper two-sided ideals. A chain's union remains proper because, if it contained 1, one member of the chain would already contain 1.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Ring.CoatomExistence.exists_maximal_leftIdeal
declarations.label: Existence of a maximal proper left ideal

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Ring.CoatomExistence.exists_maximal_rightIdeal
declarations.label: Existence of a maximal proper right ideal

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Ring.CoatomExistence.exists_maximal_twoSidedIdeal
declarations.label: Zorn's lemma proof for two-sided ideals

Chapter2/Discussion_2.7_intro.title: The Weyl relation is imposed in a quotient
explanation: Lean starts with FreeAlgebra k (Fin 2) and uses a ring quotient to identify y * x with x * y + 1. The first and second generator images are the book's x and y. The checked relation below holds over any commutative base ring, in every characteristic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FreeAlgebra.PolynomialOperators.AuxiliaryAlgebra
declarations.label: The quotient defining the Weyl algebra
declarations.documentation: The free algebra on two generators modulo the relation y*x = x*y + 1.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.FreeAlgebra.PolynomialOperators.AuxiliaryAlgebra.secondOperator_mul_firstOperator
declarations.label: The defining relation in the quotient

Chapter2/Discussion_2.7_intro.title: An invertible-parameter twisted-shift model
explanation: The q-Weyl calculations use endomorphisms of (ℤ × ℤ) →₀ k, the finitely supported coefficient functions on the integer lattice. The parameter is bundled as q : kˣ: it has an inverse. Over a field this is the book's assumption that q ≠ 0.

The shifts in the two coordinate directions are x and y; the negative shifts are their inverses. They satisfy y * x = q • (x * y). These declarations describe the generated operator subalgebra and check its relations; they are not a separate equivalence theorem identifying an abstract generators-and-relations quotient with that model.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.twistedLatticeShiftSubalgebra
declarations.label: The subalgebra generated by the four shifts

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.twistedLatticeShift_generators_commute_up_to_unit
declarations.label: The q-commutation relation

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.auxiliaryThree
links.label: Check that the positive and negative x-shifts are inverses

links.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.auxiliaryFour
links.label: Check that the positive and negative y-shifts are inverses

Chapter2/Proposition2.7.1.title: Spanning and independence are both checked
explanation: The theorem below combines LinearIndependent k for the family (i, j) ↦ x^i * y^j with the assertion that its span is the whole algebra. It allows any nonzero commutative base ring, so no characteristic-zero assumption is hidden in this basis result.

For independence, the proof formalizes the book's larger representation as ℤ →₀ Polynomial k. The integer index records the power of t, and the polynomial variable records the formal parameter a. Applying a monomial to the vector at index zero produces a falling-factorial polynomial of degree j, with leading coefficient one; this separates a finite relation even in positive characteristic.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.IntegerIndexedPolynomialOperators.operatorMonomials_linearIndependent_and_span
declarations.label: The characteristic-free Weyl monomial basis theorem

Chapter2/Proposition2.7.1.title: The integer-indexed basis in the twisted-shift model
explanation: Writing T(i,j) for the twisted shift, the multiplication formula is T(i,j) * T(i′,j′) = q^(j*i′) • T(i+i′,j+j′). It proves that products stay in the span of this family. Negative indices account for the inverse generators.

The second theorem proves linear independence and identifies the span with the generated subalgebra's underlying module. Independence follows by applying the shifts to the vector supported at (0,0): their images are the distinct standard basis vectors. The statement is about the concrete operator model used throughout the q-Weyl formalization.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.twistedLatticeShift_mul
declarations.label: The twisted monomial multiplication formula

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.Module.TwistedLatticeShifts.twistedLatticeShifts_linearIndependent_and_span
declarations.label: Independence and spanning for all integer pairs

Chapter2/Remark2.7.2.title: Ordinary polynomial differential operators require characteristic zero
explanation: The operator subalgebra is generated by multiplication by t and polynomial differentiation on k[t]. The Weyl algebra maps onto it in every characteristic. The algebra equivalence below additionally assumes [CharZero k] and [NoZeroDivisors k]; these hold for a characteristic-zero field.

In characteristic p, differentiation to the p-th power is zero on every polynomial, although y^p is a nonzero Weyl monomial. Thus this ordinary polynomial action does not identify the Weyl algebra with its image in positive characteristic. The larger representation in the preceding proof avoids this obstruction.

declarations.documentation: The Weyl action's image is the subalgebra generated by multiplication by t and polynomial differentiation.

declarations.documentation: Over a characteristic-zero commutative ring without zero divisors, the Weyl algebra is equivalent to its polynomial differential-operator image.

Chapter2/Definition2.7.3.title: Faithfulness means that vectors distinguish algebra elements
explanation: The predicate is Mathlib's FaithfulSMul A V: if a • v = b • v for every vector v, then a = b. Equality of linear endomorphisms is equality of their values on every vector, so this is the book's injectivity condition on the action homomorphism. Faithfulness does not say that each individual vector distinguishes all algebra elements.

Chapter2/Discussion_faithful_example.title: Two actions, with different characteristic restrictions
explanation: For the action on Polynomial k, injectivity is proved under [CharZero k] and [NoZeroDivisors k]. For a nonzero commutative ring of prime characteristic p, a separate theorem proves noninjectivity: y^p ≠ 0, but its image is the zero endomorphism because the p-th derivative vanishes.

For the action on ℤ →₀ Polynomial k, injectivity needs only a nonzero commutative base ring. Here lowering the index multiplies the coefficient by the formal parameter plus the index. Even in characteristic p, the p-fold product is a monic polynomial of degree p, not the zero polynomial. This is why the two actions have different behavior.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.4.title: In characteristic zero, only the zero finite-dimensional module survives
explanation: Taking traces of Y*X - X*Y = 1 gives the dimension as zero in the field. Characteristic zero then forces Module.finrank k V = 0, so the finite-dimensional representation is zero. A second theorem proves that the Weyl algebra is a simple ring: its only two-sided ideals are zero and the whole algebra. Neither theorem needs algebraic closedness.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.4.title: The whole center is generated by the p-th powers
explanation: For a field of prime characteristic p, Lean proves center = Algebra.adjoin k {x^p, y^p}, not merely that those two elements are central. The proof compares coefficients in the characteristic-free monomial basis: commuting with both generators eliminates every exponent not divisible by p. Algebraic closedness is not required for this center calculation.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.4.title: The irreducible models have dimension p and two scalar parameters
explanation: This classification assumes that k is algebraically closed, as needed to choose the eigenvector in the hint. Every finite-dimensional simple module has a basis indexed by Fin p. On that basis, x shifts forward with wraparound coefficient α; y is the lowering operator plus c times the identity. Thus x^p acts by α and y^p by c^p.

The constructed models are simple for every pair (α,c), and the classification theorem gives a unique such pair for any finite-dimensional simple module. The type named ModuleScalarParameterType in its statement is an algebra-linear equivalence to the corresponding model on Fin p → k, not an additional condition on representations.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.5.title: The multiplicative order of q determines the center
explanation: All statements here are for the twisted-shift model over ℂ, with q : ℂˣ. If q is not a root of unity, its center consists of the scalar operators, and the ring is simple. In the center theorem, ⊥ means the smallest complex subalgebra—the scalars—not the zero vector space.
If q has order N, the center is generated as a complex algebra by x^N, x^(-N), y^N, y^(-N). The inverse powers matter because both generators are invertible.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.5.title: Nonzero finite-dimensional representations exist exactly at roots of unity
explanation: The word 'nonzero' is necessary: the zero representation exists for every q. Since X and Y are invertible, taking determinants of YX = qXY and canceling gives q^(dim V) = 1. For a nonzero finite-dimensional module the dimension is positive, forcing finite order. Conversely, the formalization constructs a simple model of dimension orderOf q whenever that order is finite.

Chapter2/Problem2.7.5.title: Cyclic shifts and distinct weights give all irreducible models
explanation: Let N = orderOf q > 0. The models have underlying space Fin N → ℂ: x is a cyclic shift with wraparound coefficient α ≠ 0, and y is diagonal with weights β*q^i, where β ≠ 0. The distinct weights isolate a basis vector in any nonzero invariant subspace; the cyclic shift then generates all basis vectors.

Every finite-dimensional simple module is isomorphic to one of these models and has dimension N. Two parameter pairs give isomorphic models exactly when α = α′ and β^N = (β′)^N. The uniqueness theorem states this power relation, not literal uniqueness of β.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.5_heading.title: Quotient classes and their multiplication
explanation: Lean constructs A/I as the quotient of the ring congruence associated with I : TwoSidedIdeal A. The projection is an algebra homomorphism, so multiplication of classes is multiplication of representatives followed by projection.
The equality theorem below supplies the coset criterion: π a = π b ↔ a - b ∈ I. These constructions allow any commutative base ring k, not only a field.

explanation: The two checked congruence lemmas follow the displayed argument. Replacing the left factor uses closure of I under multiplication on the right; replacing the right factor uses closure under multiplication on the left. A one-sided ideal alone does not generally give a quotient algebra.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.5_well_defined.title: Quotient representations need only an invariant subspace
explanation: For W : Submodule A V, the quotient type is V ⧸ W. Its inherited action satisfies a • [v] = [a • v]. In particular, a left ideal gives a quotient of the left regular module even when it is not two-sided: the result is an A-module, not necessarily a ring.

Chapter2/Problem2.5.1.title: High-degree truncation prevents a direct-sum decomposition
explanation: The hypothesis is N ≤ d → p.IsHomogeneous d → p ∈ I, for a proper ideal I in MvPolynomial (Fin n) k. The conclusion is indecomposability of its regular quotient module. There is no algebraic-closedness assumption on the field.

The proof shows that every class with zero constant term is nilpotent. Consequently, for each quotient element a, either a or 1 - a is a unit. An idempotent is then zero or one, which rules out a complementary pair of nonzero submodules.

declarations.label: Checked indecomposability proof for the truncated polynomial quotient

Chapter2/Problem2.5.2.title: A cyclic vector generates the whole module
explanation: The predicate is Submodule.span A {v} = ⊤. For a nonzero module, the theorem says that simplicity is equivalent to every nonzero vector satisfying this predicate. It works over any ring A, with no finite-dimensionality assumption.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.DualModules.isSimpleModule_iff_forall_ne_zero_isCyclicVector
declarations.label: Proof of the cyclic-vector criterion for simplicity

Chapter2/Problem2.5.2.title: A cyclic module is a quotient of the regular module
explanation: For a cyclic vector v, the map a ↦ a • v is surjective. Its kernel is a left ideal, represented by Submodule A A; the quotient-kernel theorem gives an A-linear equivalence with V. Conversely, the class of 1 generates any such quotient. The result is an isomorphism of modules, not equality of their underlying types.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.DualModules.isCyclicModule_iff_nonempty_linearEquiv_quotient
declarations.label: Checked equivalence between cyclic modules and regular quotients

Chapter2/Problem2.5.2.title: The dual square-zero algebra gives the noncyclic example
explanation: The algebra is modeled as TrivSqZeroExt ℂ (Fin 2 → ℂ), with basis 1, x, y and all products of x and y zero. A checked algebra equivalence identifies this model with the polynomial quotient in the hint. Its dual action evaluates as (a • f)(b) = f(b * a).

Every nonzero submodule of this three-dimensional dual contains the functional extracting the constant term, so two nonzero submodules cannot be complementary. On the other hand, a single functional generates a space of dimension at most two. The final theorem proves both indecomposability and failure of cyclicity.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.6.title: Imposing relations means quotienting by a two-sided ideal
explanation: The formalization uses a generator type X and a family rel : R → FreeAlgebra k X. The presented algebra is the free algebra modulo the two-sided ideal generated by the range of rel. The two theorems below show that the specified relations vanish and that the generator images generate the whole quotient.

The construction also supplies a universal property: values assigned to the generators extend uniquely to an algebra homomorphism from the quotient whenever every relation evaluates to zero. The source proof linked below states and proves that property. Arbitrary generator and relation types, and a commutative base ring, are allowed; the book's finite presentation over a field is a special case.

explanation: The implication is checked over any ring: simplicity forces each submodule to be zero or the whole module, so a complementary pair must have a zero member. The converse fails for the size-two nilpotent Jordan block. Its proper invariant line does not have an invariant complement.

Chapter2/Discussion_proof_Corollary2.3.1.title: Where commutativity enters the dimension-one argument
explanation: Commutativity makes multiplication by each algebra element an intertwining operator. Scalarity then follows from Schur's lemma, using algebraic closedness and finite dimension. Chapter2/Discussion_2.4_heading.title: Left, right, and two-sided ideals are different objects
explanation: A left ideal is a submodule of the left regular module Submodule A A. A right ideal can be viewed, after applying op to its elements, as Submodule Aᵐᵒᵖ Aᵐᵒᵖ. A two-sided ideal is bundled as TwoSidedIdeal A, with maps to those two one-sided ideals. These constructions work for arbitrary rings; the compatible scalar action supplies the book's vector-space structure in the algebra case.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.4_heading.title: The generated ideal is the least ideal containing the set
explanation: The theorem below states that the two-sided ideal generated by S lies in I exactly when S ⊆ I. A second theorem describes its elements as the additive closure of the products a * s * b. This is the ring-level formulation of the book's span description; in a unital algebra, scalar multiples can be absorbed into the left coefficient. The simplicity predicate is Mathlib's IsSimpleRing A, which includes the nonzero condition.

explanation: Lean expresses a right A-module as a left module over Aᵐᵒᵖ. When A is commutative, the constructions below transport the action between these two rings without changing what it does to a vector. Commutativity is an explicit assumption: this identification is not available for arbitrary noncommutative algebras.

Chapter2/Example2.3.3.title: Zero, regular, and freely specified actions
explanation: The zero representation is modeled by PUnit, a type with one element, equipped with its additive and module structures. The regular left action is the usual Module A A; the right regular action is Module Aᵐᵒᵖ A, where op a • b = b * a.

For the free algebra, FreeAlgebra.lift is the equivalence between a family of chosen endomorphisms and an algebra homomorphism into Module.End k V. This supplies the reason requested in part 4: the generators may act by arbitrary operators, because the free algebra imposes no relations on them.

explanation: The hypothesis is Module.finrank k V = 1. Any A-submodule is also a k-subspace, so it must be zero or all of V. Unlike the converse in Corollary 2.3.12, this direction requires neither algebraic closedness of k nor commutativity of A.

Chapter2/Example2.3.14.title: Vector spaces: classification up to isomorphism
explanation: For A = k, the checked results say that any simple or indecomposable vector space is linearly equivalent to k. Thus 'the only representation' here means the only isomorphism class, not equality of the underlying types. These statements work over any field and do not assume finite dimension.

Chapter2/Example2.3.14.title: Jordan blocks as polynomial modules
explanation: The module JordanBlockModule λ n has underlying coordinates Fin n → k, with X acting by λ • id + jordanNilpotent n. The coordinates are indexed from zero; the shift gives the same Jordan block as the book's basis indexed from one.

Classification of an arbitrary finite-dimensional k[X]-module assumes IsAlgClosed k explicitly. It produces a finite product of positive-size blocks and a k[X]-linear equivalence. The proof uses the structure theorem for torsion modules over the polynomial PID rather than invoking a matrix Jordan-normal-form theorem. For finitely many blocks, the product also represents their direct sum.

explanation: The checked counterexample is the size-two block with eigenvalue zero. Its invariant line prevents simplicity, but it has no decomposition into two nonzero submodules. This distinction already holds over any field; algebraic closedness is unnecessary for this particular example.

explanation: Lean's Representation k G V is a homomorphism from G to the multiplicative monoid of linear endomorphisms. Because G is a group, the images are automatically invertible. The first equivalence below extends that action linearly to k[G]; the second packages each image as a linear automorphism V ≃ₗ[k] V, matching the book's map to GL(V).
These are equivalences of the action data on the same space V, not merely a correspondence between isomorphism classes. The base k may be any commutative ring here.

explanation: The existence statement assumes Nontrivial V and Module.Finite k V and produces S : Submodule A V with IsSimpleModule A S. The nonzero condition on S is part of simplicity, not a missing hypothesis. The proof finds an atom in the Artinian submodule lattice.

For the counterexample, take the regular k[X]-module k[X]. Every nonzero submodule contains a nonzero polynomial s; multiplying by X gives a smaller nonzero submodule. The checked contradiction uses the fact that X is not a unit.

explanation: The center is bundled as Subalgebra.center k A. For a finite-dimensional simple module over an algebraically closed field, centerCharacter is an algebra homomorphism from that center to k, and the action theorem states z • v = χ(z) • v. Algebraic closedness is essential here even though the problem's opening sentence only says 'a field'.

Chapter2/Problem2.3.16.title: One eigenvalue does not mean a scalar operator
explanation: For an indecomposable module, the formalization expresses the single-eigenvalue conclusion by nilpotence: the difference between the central action and χ(z) • id is nilpotent. It also constructs a simple submodule on which the same character gives the scalar action. This uses finite dimension and an algebraically closed base field.

Part (c) has a negative answer: in the regular module of the dual-number algebra, multiplication by ε is central and nilpotent, but is not scalar multiplication. The displayed counterexample proves the nonscalar action; it does not by itself bundle a separate proof of indecomposability of that module.

Chapter2/Problem2.3.17.title: Why the opposite multiplication appears
explanation: An A-linear endomorphism of the left regular module is determined by its value at 1: it acts by right multiplication by that value. Composing two right multiplications reverses the order of their factors. Lean therefore states the result as a ring equivalence Module.End A A ≃+* Aᵐᵒᵖ, not equality of the two types. The theorem works for any ring A; it does not separately state a base-field algebra equivalence.

Chapter2/Problem2.3.18.title: Dixmier's lemma: countable rank replaces finite dimension
explanation: The theorem uses Module.rank ℂ V ≤ Cardinal.aleph0, expressing the existence of an at-most-countable basis, and IsSimpleModule A V. It concludes that every A-linear endomorphism agrees pointwise with multiplication by a complex scalar. There is no finite-dimensionality hypothesis.

Following the hint, the proof injects the endomorphism algebra into V by evaluating at a nonzero vector. A nonscalar endomorphism would be transcendental; its shifted inverses indexed by ℂ would form a linearly independent family. The resulting continuum-sized rank contradicts the countable bound.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_overview.after: An associative algebra over a field
Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_overview.title: Algebras and their endomorphisms
explanation: The book assumes a unit here. In Lean, [Algebra k A], together with the ring and scalar structures, expresses a unital algebra over k. The endomorphism algebra is Module.End k V: its multiplication is composition of linear maps.
The separate multiplication structure used for Definition 2.2.1 records associativity and bilinearity, without a unit. These are different assumptions, not two names for the same definition.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_overview.title: A representation is an algebra action
explanation: Lean writes the book’s representation map as ρ : A →ₐ[k] Module.End k V. This is an algebra homomorphism from A to the linear endomorphisms of V: it preserves multiplication, the unit, and the k-linear structure.

Lean also expresses the same action as [Module A V]. The constructions below convert between these descriptions. Compatibility with the existing k-vector-space structure is recorded by IsScalarTower k A V; the round-trip theorems establish that these conversions recover the original map and action. The formal statements work over a commutative base ring, not just a field.

Chapter2/Discussion_2.1_overview.title: Invariant subspaces and direct sums
explanation: Once the representation is expressed as an A-module, its invariant subspaces are exactly Submodule A V. Such an object bundles a subspace with the proof that it is closed under the action of every algebra element.

For two representations, the binary direct sum is represented by the product V₁ × V₂, with componentwise scalar action. This is the binary case; it does not identify arbitrary infinite products with direct sums.

Chapter2/Definition2.2.1.title: Associative, bilinear multiplication — no unit yet
explanation: The formal structure records a multiplication op : A → A → A, an associativity proof, and distributivity and scalar-linearity in both arguments. Its assumptions are a field k, an additive commutative group A, and a k-module structure on A.

It does not require a multiplicative identity. That matches this definition; the unit is introduced separately. The source still gives this structure a generic identifier, so the exact statement below retains that identifier rather than pretending a differently named declaration exists.

declarations.label: Exact Lean structure and assumptions
declarations.documentation: An associative bilinear multiplication on a vector space over k, without a unit requirement.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.1.title: The homomorphism and the module describe the same action
explanation: Lean writes the representation map as ρ : A →ₐ[k] Module.End k V. The module notation for its action is a • v, with a • v = ρ a v.

The two constructions below pass from a compatible module action to the algebra homomorphism and back. Their proofs establish both round trips. The base ring k may be any commutative ring in these statements; the book’s field case is included.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.1.title: Right actions use the opposite algebra
explanation: A right A-module is expressed as a left module over Aᵐᵒᵖ, the opposite algebra. Its multiplication reverses the order, so an ordinary homomorphism out of Aᵐᵒᵖ expresses the book’s antihomomorphism out of A.

declarations.label: The homomorphism for the right action

Chapter2/Definition2.3.1.title: The associativity laws are checked
explanation: For left modules the equation is (a * b) • v = a • (b • v). For right modules, acting by the opposite of a product acts first by the opposite of a, then by the opposite of b. These are the two equations in the book’s final paragraph.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.4.title: A subrepresentation is an invariant submodule
explanation: With the action represented by [Module A V], a Submodule A V is an additive subgroup closed under the action of every element of A. Compatibility with the k-action makes it a k-subspace as well. The closure proof is W.smul_mem: if v ∈ W, then a • v ∈ W.

example (W : Submodule A V) (a : A) (v : V) (hv : v ∈ W) :
    a • v ∈ W := W.smul_mem a hv

Chapter2/Discussion_2.2_intro.title: The base field is an explicit hypothesis
explanation: Lean writes the field assumption as [Field k] and algebraic closedness as [IsAlgClosed k]. A result that needs algebraic closedness includes that second hypothesis; it is not silently inherited from the surrounding chapter.

The equivalence below characterizes algebraic closedness by the existence of roots for polynomials of nonzero degree. The separate instance for ℂ supplies the book’s main example. For prime p, AlgebraicClosure (ZMod p) is algebraically closed and has characteristic p.

declarations.label: The complex numbers are algebraically closed

Chapter2/Definition2.2.2.title: An identity element, not an invertible element
explanation: Here “unit” means a two-sided multiplicative identity. For the bilinear multiplication op of Definition 2.2.1, the condition on e is ∀ a, op e a = a ∧ op a e = a.

This is different from Mathlib’s predicate IsUnit e, which says that an element of an already unital monoid is invertible. The formal definition below tests the identity equations; it does not use that invertibility predicate.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryStructure.AuxiliaryStructure.auxiliaryPredicate
declarations.label: The two identity equations
declarations.documentation: The element e is a two-sided identity for the given associative bilinear multiplication.

Chapter2/Definition2.2.5.title: Commutativity belongs to the ring structure
explanation: A commutative unital algebra is expressed by [CommRing A] together with [Algebra k A]. The ring structure supplies mul_comm, the equality a * b = b * a.
The source alias below names the algebra structure on an already commutative ring. It does not prove that an arbitrary algebra is commutative; that is an assumption on A.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.AuxiliaryFieldCommRingType.AuxiliaryFieldCommRingType
declarations.label: Algebra structure on a commutative ring
declarations.documentation: A k-algebra structure on A, with commutativity already supplied by the CommRing A assumption.

Chapter2/Definition2.2.6.title: Algebra homomorphisms bundle the preservation laws
explanation: The type A →ₐ[k] B bundles a map with its additive, multiplicative, unit-preserving, and scalar-compatibility proofs. The equations in the definition are available as f.map_mul and f.map_one.
This construction works over a commutative base ring k. A field, as assumed in the book, is a special case.

declarations.label: The type of algebra homomorphisms
declarations.documentation: Algebra homomorphisms from A to B over their common commutative base ring k.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.5.title: Simplicity includes the nonzero condition
explanation: Lean expresses irreducibility of an algebra action as IsSimpleModule A V. This says that the submodule lattice has only its bottom and top elements, and that those elements are distinct. The distinction excludes the zero representation.
The source alias below is a name for this standard Mathlib condition, not an additional property of representations.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.ModuleConditions.AuxiliaryModuleCondition
declarations.label: The irreducibility condition
declarations.documentation: Simplicity of the A-module V, including that V is nonzero.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.6.title: Intertwiners are linear maps over the acting algebra
explanation: With the representations expressed as A-modules, the type V₁ →ₗ[A] V₂ bundles an additive map and the law f (a • v) = a • f v. This is the intertwining equation in the book. Compatibility with the base-field action also makes such a map k-linear.

An isomorphism is bundled as V₁ ≃ₗ[A] V₂, with its inverse and inverse laws. Saying that the representations are isomorphic means Nonempty (V₁ ≃ₗ[A] V₂): an isomorphism exists, but no particular one is selected.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.6.title: The inverse is also an intertwiner
explanation: For an A-linear equivalence e, the inverse e.symm is itself an A-linear equivalence. Its scalar-linearity law is already checked, so no separate invariance argument is needed to use the inverse as a representation isomorphism.

Chapter2/Definition2.3.7.title: The action on the binary direct sum is componentwise
explanation: For two summands, Lean uses the product type V₁ × V₂ with its componentwise module structure. The theorem below is the book’s formula: acting on a pair acts on each coordinate.

The statement works for modules over any ring A. For infinitely many summands, direct sums require a finite-support construction; this binary product presentation does not extend to an arbitrary infinite product.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.ProductModules.smul_prod_mk
declarations.label: The componentwise action formula

Chapter2/Definition2.3.8.title: External decompositions and complementary submodules
explanation: One formal condition says that V is nonzero and admits no linear equivalence with a product of two nonzero A-modules. Another says that, whenever two submodules of V are complementary, at least one is zero.

The equivalence theorem below connects these external and internal descriptions. IsCompl W₁ W₂ records both that the intersection is zero and that their sum is all of V. Neither description assumes finite dimension.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.ModuleDecompositions.auxiliaryDecompositionPredicate_iff_auxiliaryDecompositionPredicate'
declarations.label: Equivalence of the two indecomposability conditions
declarations.documentation: A nonzero module has no nontrivial external binary decomposition if and only if every pair of complementary submodules has a zero summand.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.LinearAlgebra.ModuleDecompositions.AuxiliaryDecompositionPredicate'
declarations.label: The external-decomposition condition
declarations.documentation: The module is nonzero and cannot be expressed as the product of two nonzero modules by an A-linear equivalence.

Chapter2/Proposition2.3.9.title: Schur’s lemma does not need an algebraically closed field
explanation: The three formal statements work for modules over any ring R. A nonzero R-linear map is injective when its source is simple, surjective when its target is simple, and bijective when both are simple. No finite-dimensionality or field hypothesis is needed for these conclusions.
The book proves the result using the invariant kernel and image. In the module presentation these are LinearMap.ker φ and LinearMap.range φ, both submodules by construction.

declarations.label: Part (i): a simple source gives injectivity

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.SimpleLinearMaps.linearMap_surjective_of_ne_zero_to_simple
declarations.label: Part (ii): a simple target gives surjectivity

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Module.SimpleLinearMaps.linearMap_bijective_of_ne_zero_between_simple
declarations.label: Both simple: the map is bijective

Chapter2/Corollary2.3.10.title: Scalar endomorphisms need the extra hypotheses
explanation: Here the formal statement explicitly assumes [IsAlgClosed k] and [FiniteDimensional k V], as well as simplicity. Its conclusion is pointwise: there is a scalar c : k such that φ v = c • v for every vector v.

This stronger conclusion is not the general-ring statement of Proposition 2.3.9. The proof uses Mathlib’s theorem that the scalar map onto the endomorphism algebra of a finite-dimensional simple module is bijective over an algebraically closed field.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.SimpleModule.Endomorphisms.endomorphism_eq_smul
declarations.label: Every intertwining endomorphism is scalar

Chapter2/Discussion_proof_Corollary2.3.1.title: The formal proof uses the endomorphism algebra
explanation: The book’s argument chooses an eigenvalue and applies Schur’s lemma to φ − λ Id. The source proof of the scalarity theorem takes a shorter route through Mathlib’s bijectivity result for the map k → End_A(V).
The hypotheses and scalarity conclusion agree, but the displayed source proof is not a line-by-line transcription of this eigenvalue argument.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.SimpleModule.Endomorphisms.endomorphism_eq_smul
declarations.label: Inspect the scalarity theorem and its proof

Chapter2/Corollary2.3.12.title: The algebraic-closedness assumption is still in force
explanation: The formal statement spells out the assumptions carried from the section: k is algebraically closed, A is a commutative k-algebra, and V is a finite-dimensional simple A-module. Its conclusion is Module.finrank k V = 1.

Commutativity alone is not enough over an arbitrary field. For example, ℂ acting on itself is a simple two-dimensional representation over ℝ. The explicit IsAlgClosed k hypothesis prevents that misreading of the abbreviated corollary.

declarations.name: RepresentationTheory.Algebra.SimpleModule.Dimension.finrank_eq_one
declarations.label: The one-dimensionality conclusion and all hypotheses
